Researchers at the LHCb, ATLAS, and CMS collaborations have collected large datasets at the LHC, allowing for precise measurements of B^0_s meson lifetimes with various final states. By analyzing these decays, which involve a flavor-changing process, researchers can gain insights into the underlying physics, potentially revealing the presence of new particles beyond the Standard Model. In this review, we examine the current status of LHCb's measurements of B^0_s meson lifetimes, focusing on data-driven methods used to determine the systematic uncertainty in lifetime estimates and the strategies employed to enhance sensitivity to new physics. As a result, we summarize the world's most precise lifetime measurements for individual B^0_s meson decay modes, as well as combined measurements for certain final states, and discuss the implications for new physics searches. With anticipated increases in dataset sizes in the coming years, a thorough review of strategies to optimize time-integrated and time-dependent flavor-violation processes in the LHCb experiment is timely, as it will be crucial in new physics searches in the future. As an example, new, more sensitive searches for beyond-Standard-Model physics through precision measurements of B^0_s meson lifetimes could be feasible with enhanced dataset sizes. As such, this review aims to contribute to ongoing discussions within the LHCb collaboration on optimizing time-dependent flavor-violating process searches in the experiment's future research framework. As a result, we recommend prioritizing research on the most sensitive new physics searches in B^0_s meson decays, as well as exploring new, untapped search avenues, to ensure the effectiveness of the LHCb experiment in this context throughout its duration. This research focuses on solving stochastic control problems with rough data by implementing a combination of the Euler method and a specific type of rough path technology. Key aspects of this work include: (1) establishing the convergence of approximations as the time step decreases, (2) demonstrating the existence of an optimal control strategy within a particular class of alternatives, and (3) identifying the value of the control problem through the solution of a related Hamiltonian system. These findings address several open questions posed in the literature. Moreover, this study reveals that the optimal control strategy can be realized through a progressive procedure, characterized by the iteration of Hamiltonian maps that capture the effects of control and diffusion on the underlying stochastic process. This advances our understanding of rough stochastic control problems and paves the way for exploring more general schemes in future studies. Although primarily developed for control problems, the methods employed here also provide a general framework for analyzing approximate solutions to certain Hamiltonian systems and can be applied to analyzing the convergence of certain algorithms in connection with the solution of Hamiltonian systems. Notably, this includes the case of Hamiltonian systems that are relevant to the study of the convergence of approximations in default theory and the study of the properties of the least squares estimator in the face of default. Lastly, this research lays the groundwork for investigating more general schemes, such as the construction of numerical approximations using Runge-Kutta methods. This hope is supported by preliminary analyses conducted as part of this research. Ultimately, this study is an initial step towards creating a broader numerical framework for solving a wide range of stochastic control problems and related systems of stochastic differential equations. This framework would provide a suitable alternative to traditional approaches, such as the scheme proposed by Buckdahn, Dear, and Jean, especially in scenarios where the driving raw data exhibits limited regularity. In such contexts, the Euler scheme, augmented by rough path technology, offers an appealing and more efficient numerical solution method. This research is an essential precursor to applying this numerical scheme in a broader context, such as when evaluating the performance of asset management styles or evaluating the performance of portfolios in the presence of defaults and liquidity risks. In these scenarios, the underlying raw data is typically characterized by rough paths, and the Euler scheme, augmented by rough path technology, is the only known numerical scheme that is capable of accurately capturing the effects of asset management and portfolio management strategies. In such scenarios, the Euler scheme is the only known numerical scheme that is capable of accurately capturing the effects of asset management and portfolio management strategies on the underlying stochastic processes.

Further analyzing nearby and distant sources, we found a significant correlation between cosmic ray anisotropies and nearby extreme active galactic nuclei, with a $p$-value of 0.02 excluding a potential influence of magnetic fields and deflected cosmic rays. Additionally, we found an energy dependence for dipole anisotropies at $\sim 2.4$ EeV energy scale, with an amplitude increasing from 1.2$\sigma$ to 6.2$\sigma$ as energy increases from 4 EeV to 40 EeV. On the other hand, quadrupole anisotropies exhibit no significant dependence on energy across the studied range. Our findings provide evidence supporting the extragalactic origin of ultra-high energy cosmic rays. The ATLAS detector at the LHC gathered p+Pb data with a centre-of-mass energy of 5.02 TeV and 25 nanobarns of integrated luminosity, enabling the measurement of differential quantities in forward rapidity. This study examines the $K^0_s$ meson production in minimum bias and zero-yet-central collisions, considering four rapidity ranges: 1.6, 2.4, 3.1 and 4.0. The results are expressed as transverse momentum spectra, mean $p_T$ values and mid-point $p_T$ values for various centrality categories and rapidity ranges. The nuclear modification factor is also calculated in relation to reference collisions, revealing an increase in $K^0_s$ production with more central collisions at higher rapidities. In low-centrality collisions, the $K^0_s$ production is similar to that in $pp$ collisions, while central collisions exhibit a higher $K^0_s$ yield than expected, with the ratio increasing by a factor of about two in the most central collisions at 4.0 rapidity. The additional $K^0_s$ production in central collisions increases with rapidity. This trend may be attributed to the introduction of strange quarks as massless degrees of freedom in the quark-gluon plasma, in line with perturbative quantum chromodynamics predictions. The study also examines the ratio of pion to $K^0_s$ production, revealing a rise in this ratio with increasing centrality and rapidity. This increase in the ratio's value may be linked to enhanced strangeness freeze-out temperatures relative to charge densities. The findings open up possibilities for further investigation into the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and the behavior of hadrons in this medium. The study's methods and data allow for comparisons with computational models, featuring direct comparisons with PYTHIA and AMPT and indirect comparisons with EPOS and EPOS3, EPOS-NCL, EPOS-HQ, EPOS EPOS-HQ variants, in an effort to gain a deeper understanding of hadron production in high-energy nuclear collisions. The research presents initial observations that could contribute to further research aimed at determining the quark mass's effect on the behavior of hadrons in the quark-gluon plasma. The study's findings can also inform the development of models aimed at describing hadron production in nuclear collisions and ultimately informing research aimed at determining the properties of the quark-gluon plasma.

The success of cancer immunotherapy depends on an intricate understanding
of the interplay between tumor cells and the lymphocytes that infiltrate them.
This understanding requires analyzing digitized tissue sections to extract
valuable information from histopathological images, which involves classifying
lymphocytes into specific subtypes and determining their functional status.
To address this challenge, we introduce a multi-classifier system consisting
of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that can accurately identify and
classify lymphocytes within images of the cell nucleus. We employ a unique
approach, using two separate CNNs to analyze morphological features and the
lymphocyte's cytoplasm and nucleus, respectively. To further enhance the
system's performance and efficiency, we apply a technique called efficient
network searching (ENS) to find the optimal combination of network components.
Relying on data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), our system demonstrates
outstanding results in both classification accuracy and processing speed when
comparing it to other state-of-the-art network architectures. By integrating
this system into a workflow, we are able to efficiently assess tumor lymphocyte
infiltration (TLI) by quantifying the total number of lymphocytes present. Our
method holds significant promise for contributing to the development of precise
and effective cancer immunotherapies. To facilitate replication and further
development of our approach, we have made the source code for our multi-classifier
system and TLI quantification available on GitHub at https://github.com/ku-nlp/lymphocyte-classifier.

In recent years, TCNs have gained popularity due to their ability to handle sequential data, however, they suffer from low efficiency caused by extensive parameter usage and high inference latency, ultimately hindering their deployment in real-time applications. To address this challenge, a novel deep learning approach known as the Squeeze-and-Average optimizer was proposed, enabling the creation of lightweight TCNs with reduced inference latency. This proposed method achieves a notable decrease of approximately 18.5% in model size and a decrease of approximately 21.3% in inference latency when compared to the standard optimizer. Moreover, the model size and inference latency are further minimized by approximately 11.5% and approximately 13.8% respectively when the default dilation rate is set to 1, without compromising the accuracy of the model. The experimental results demonstrate a high accuracy of 83.96% along with a low error rate of 16.04% achieved by the proposed method in the public SpikingBrain Organism dataset, thereby establishing a new benchmark for the field. The model size and inference latency are measured on a real hardware platform, and the experimental results show that the proposed method features a model size of 145KB and an inference latency of 45.45ms, both of which are significantly improved in real-time applications. Moreover, the proposed method is compared to other prominent deep learning models including Inception, ResNet, and MobileNet, among others, and is found to be highly competitive in terms of accuracy while being highly optimized in terms of model size and inference latency. The code for the proposed method is openly accessible on GitHub, and the experiment was conducted on a GPU platform utilizing the TensorFlow framework. The proposed method addresses the challenge of low-efficiency TCNs, and is highly suitable for real-time applications in the areas of sequence data analysis, video classification, and audio classification. This study proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a field is either nilpotent, soluble, or a Hamiltonian algebra. This finding specifically shows that a Zinbiel algebra with a nilpotent cokernel, relative to its adjoint representation, is an solvable algebra. Moreover, this situation occurs when the underlying field is algebraically closed or has a characteristic other than two. In addition, simple Zinbiel algebras are classified, and examples of nilpotent and solvable Zinbiel algebras are provided. Furthermore, the classification of finite-dimensional simple Zinbiel algebras over the field of real numbers is determined, and the classification of finite-dimensional simple Zinbiel algebras over the complex numbers is also established, with the identification of a non-degenerate simple Zinbiel algebra over the complex numbers. Some examples of nilpotent and solvable Zinbiel algebras are given, and the paper concludes with constructing new examples of Zinbiel algebras using a specific construction method.

In the realm of database research, our proposed four-valued logic approach addresses the issue of inconsistent databases by dividing answers into four value categories: truth, falsehood, unknown, and inconsistency. Databases are frequently updated by different users, leading to updates that may result in logical inconsistencies. To resolve this problem, our method prioritizes achieving consistent query results over ensuring updates are logically sound. Updates that introduce inconsistencies are handled by our system's inference capability, which identifies the problematic updates and proposes new, consistent updates to rectify the issue. The introduction of ALCHF description logics axioms within our framework enables us to tackle the problem of inconsistent databases in a more comprehensive manner, incorporating notions of hierarchy and Hierarchy with Cycles, in addition to reasoning about Kif and NDF. Furthermore, our method allows for querying databases utilizing SPARQL, coupled with the integration of external domain knowledge to resolve queries that yield inconsistent results. The amalgamation of these capabilities equips our approach with the ability to tackle a wide range of inconsistencies stemming from diverse updates, external queries, as well as external domain knowledge. The functional components of our system, along with a description of its key features and its application to real-world scenarios, are also detailed. Moreover, an evaluation of our approach, encompassing consistency preservation, query answering from external knowledge, and the system's scalability, has been conducted. Lastly, future directions for our four-valued logic approach, encompassing enhanced SPARQL queries and distributed reasoning, among other possibilities, have been outlined. In conclusion, our four-valued logic approach presents an original framework addressing the complex issue of inconsistent databases, coupled with a comprehensive method for achieving consistent query results, along with a novel description logics-based system capable of addressing a broad spectrum of inconsistencies, and has been successfully applied to a real-world scenario. Additionally, our approach has been successfully evaluated and is primed for further development. In light of the numerous, far-reaching applications of database research, particularly in the realm of description logics, we believe our four-valued logic approach has the potential to yield valuable contributions to other fields, such as the development of more robust and adaptable software frameworks, capable of managing diverse, evolving datasets with minimal user intervention. In this context, our approach may serve as a model for addressing the issue of dataset drift, a pervasive challenge in areas like data mining, machine learning, and statistical analysis. We introduce the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model as a novel adaptation of the Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates model. TV-PARX addresses issues of nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks in time series by allowing parameters to evolve over time. We develop an expectation-maximization algorithm for estimating TV-PARX model parameters. Additionally, we establish the convergence of these estimates in theoretical terms. For model selection, we propose the use of information criteria such as AIC and BIC for time-varying and time-invariant models, respectively. We further explore methods for conducting inference and predicting future counts, as well as providing confidence intervals for time-varying parameters. Our approach is demonstrated through simulated examples and an empirical analysis of infectious disease spreads. All necessary computational tools are available within our R package implementation, enabling users to easily employ our methods. In robotics, learning complex tasks from a small number of demonstrations is a significant challenge. This challenge becomes even more daunting for tasks that require grasping and manipulating objects, as the action space is highly dimensional. In our work, we introduce a novel framework called Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs) that allows us to learn these complex tasks in a data-efficient manner. By leveraging a neural descriptor network to identify key features of an object and a spatial network to predict the object's local structure from a first-person perspective, we can model the object's presence and movement in a bin. We can then optimize the action plan for bin-picking or assembly tasks by minimizing a cost function, taking into account potential collisions with other objects and the bin's walls. To demonstrate the capabilities of our framework, we successfully trained it on a variety of Bin-Picking and Assembly tasks using a limited number (5-10) of demonstrations, and it generalizes effectively to novel target objects. Moreover, our approach can be applied to multiple scenario types, including scenarios with partially visible objects and those requiring the manipulation of multiple objects. To facilitate research, we also introduce the Neural Descriptor Fields (NDF) Bin-Picking Dataset, which features a variety of bin-picking tasks and target objects. This dataset is accompanied by a user-friendly interface for easily creating new datasets and evaluating performance metrics. Our code, dataset, and accompanying tools are available at https://github.com/robotrajesh/ndf-bin-picking.

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, and it will be thoroughly tested through various simulated data analyses. The SiD's calorimeter system, consisting of a highly granular and fiber-reinforced prestack and tailstack with 36 layers, contributes significantly to its jet energy resolution across all energies. In this submission, we highlight the progress made on jet energy resolution research, correcting an earlier finding presented at the 2019 Large Hadron Collider Physics Conference. Additionally, we present the outcomes of two anti-kT R$\mitosis$=0.5 jet analysis configurations, one employing the full calorimeter dataset and the other using only the prestack component, up to 1 TeV. These results position the SiD Detector for meaningful comparisons with ATLAS and CMS data in future studies. Our analysis of seven metal-poor red clump giants in the high-metallicity globular cluster Tononzintla-2 yields insights into the cluster's early history. By comparing the abundance of multiple elements in these giants, we find a notable difference in the [α/Fe] ratios typical of traditional high-metallicity globular clusters. Tononzintla-2 exhibits higher [α/Fe] ratios for elements like magnesium, silicon, and oxygen but lower ratios for carbon, aluminum, and iron, with iron peak elements showing a range of +0.07 to +0.33 deviations. These patterns suggest a complex multiple-population scenario in Tononzintla-2, with possible interactions between first and second generations of stars. We also derive the cluster's metallicity distribution function, showing a narrow range from -0.44 to -0.23 in [Fe/H], with an estimated median of -0.26, and a metallicity spread of 0.21 units. Given its unique multiple-population features and narrow metallicity range, Tononzintla-2 may serve as a benchmark to study the development of multiple populations in globular clusters. Additionally, with an estimated age of 10.4 billion years, Tononzintla-2 represents one of the oldest clusters to exhibit multiple populations, offering a chance to examine how second-generation elements were incorporated into multiple populations of stars in this cluster. Our research on Tononzintla-2 contributes to a deeper understanding of multiple-population phenomena in globular clusters and sheds light on the complex early history of these ancient clusters in the Galactic halo. Furthermore, with future surveys expected to discover numerous multiple-population globular clusters in the Galactic halo, studying clusters like Tononzintla-2 will be essential in developing a comprehensive theoretical framework for the origins of multiple populations in these clusters.

The peridynamic model introduces a perceptive approach to describing the microstructure of materials with defects, specifically cracks, by defining a nonlocal bond-slip relationship between points within a material. Historically, researchers have developed various types of nonlocal kernels, including the micromechanics-based double-slope kernel and the damage-based trapezoidal kernel. In this study, we propose a new kernel, shaped like an isosceles triangle, which effectively models the distribution of damage within a material by efficiently capturing the maximum bond-slip value within a specified distance. In addition, we demonstrate that this kernel meets the essential criteria of peridynamic theory and can be derived from a nonlocal potential energy functional. We compare its performance to the double-slope and trapezoidal kernels through numerical simulations of a stationary crack problem and a dynamic crack propagation problem. The results show that the isosceles triangular kernel can accurately predict crack nucleation and propagation, even with a reduced number of degrees of freedom. We also investigate the relationship between the maximum bond-slip value and the width of the damage zone for different material stiffness, finding that the isosceles triangular kernel exhibits a similar behavior to the trapezoidal kernel, in contrast to the double-slope kernel. Overall, the isosceles triangular kernel provides a simple and efficient alternative to the trapezoidal kernel for modeling cracks within a material. Moreover, we propose that the width of the damage zone, rather than the kernel itself, should be the primary variable in peridynamic formulation. This study introduces a new method for calculating node importance in multilayer networks that takes into account the interconnections between network layers. Unlike previous methods, our approach considers the transitive projections of all network layers simultaneously, not separately. By leveraging the properties of the resulting generalized adjacency tensor, we can effectively determine the importance of nodes across all layers. In addition, our method facilitates the identification of the highest-ranking nodes within each specific network layer. A notable advantage of our approach is its flexibility in handling different types of network layers, including those with directed and weighted connections. Furthermore, we have developed an efficient algorithm for calculating node importance, and our method is particularly useful for examing the spread of information and the diffusion of opinions in multilayer social networks. A numerical example is provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

To address this, a camera with a modulated aperture is proposed, alongside an innovative blind deconvolution method, capable of recovering the PSF from images, even in the absence of control over the camera. By leveraging a specially designed aperture with varying opacity, this proposed method can accurately determine the PSF, bypassing the need for external light sources or controlled laboratory conditions. Based on a camera with a modulated aperture, a computational camera architecture is outlined, featuring a spatially variant deconvolution process to rectify the PSF impact, resulting in clearer images. A mathematical framework for the proposed method is formalized, with a corresponding optimization problem solved through a convex relaxation method. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in both simulated and real-world scenarios. In reinforcement learning, the presence of corrupted data episodes can hinder the efficiency of the least squares temporal difference (LSTD) learning method. To mitigate this issue, we introduce the filtered policy gradient (FPG) algorithm, which can provide a reliable learning guarantee even in the presence of corrupted data episodes. The FPG algorithm involves an initial phase of LSTD learning, followed by a filtering phase where the expected value is estimated using a robust LSTD estimator. We demonstrate the theoretical convergence properties of the FPG algorithm and show that it achieves the same optimal learning rate guarantee as the LSTD algorithm in scenarios with no corrupted data episodes. Additionally, the FPG algorithm is able to learn at a rate of $\Omega\left(\frac{1}{t+1}\right)$ in scenarios with a constant fraction of corrupted data episodes. We also provide an analysis of the computational complexity of the FPG algorithm and show that it can be implemented using a robust LSTD estimator with a computational complexity of $O(1)$ per sample, significantly outperforming the LSTD algorithm in scenarios with corrupted data episodes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the FPG algorithm through numerical experiments and showcase its ability to learn from a stream of corrupted data episodes in a variety of policy evaluation scenarios. However, our investigation also uncovers a fundamental aspect of the paradox - one aspect of the argument presented by the source is genuinely sound. In particular, we find that selecting a specific element from the set 'chooseness' is indeed the key to resolving the paradox. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of a minimal, computable extension of the theory of choice arithmetic, which we dub $C^{\omega}_0$. We then establish that $C^{\omega}_0$ is Turing complete and demonstrate the computable completeness of $C^{\omega}_0$ with respect to computable trees. Furthermore, we show that any computable complete extension of choice arithmetic is computationally equivalent to $C^{\omega}_0$. We employed the full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method to perform an in-depth investigation of the cubanite compound's structure and properties. Our study focused on the effects of temperature and lattice parameters on the electronic and magnetic properties of this compound, using three different unit cells obtained from experiments conducted at different temperatures. Initially, our calculations revealed that the highest energy state corresponds to a ferromagnetic metal state, with significant hybridization between O $2p$ and $3d$ shells and the presence of a relatively small energy gap in one of the $3d$ shells. Next, our analysis of the temperature effects using the GGA+U method showed that the increase in temperature results in a rise in the occupation of the highest energy state, accompanied by a rise in the Fermi energy and the magnitude of the spin splitting per atom. Furthermore, our investigations of the lattice parameter effects using the PBE+U method revealed that the spin splitting per atom and the Fermi energy exhibit a linear relationship with the lattice parameter, increasing in proportion to the distance between atoms. Notably, our results also indicate that the cubanite compound exhibits charge stability across a wide range of lattice parameters, with the electronic structure transforming from a metal to an insulator in response to changes in the lattice parameter. Lastly, our analysis of the phonon dispersion curves calculated using the linearized augmented plane wave method showed that the cubanite compound exhibits no signs of structural instability, with all calculated frequencies within expected ranges. Additionally, our comparison with experimental data revealed a satisfactory agreement, with a slight overestimation of lattice parameters due to the inherent limitations of DFT methods. Our study provides a comprehensive theoretical understanding of the cubanite compound's structure and properties, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying its remarkable charge stability and ferromagnetic ordering. Moreover, our results suggest that the substitution of heavier elements for lighter ones in the 3d shell of this compound may result in a significant energy gap formation. Lastly, our findings pave the way for further investigation of the superconducting properties of the A$_3$Cu$_5$O$_{10}$ (A=Hg, Tl, Pb) family of compounds, incorporating the heavier elements mentioned above.

We examine the impact of various environmental disturbances and control settings on a quantum dot-coupled acoustic cavity system, observing how Rabi oscillations behave under different conditions. When the driving laser is misaligned or operates at an incorrect frequency, even small perturbations can cause significant Rabi oscillation decay, but improving the laser's alignment and frequency accuracy can restore Rabi oscillations close to their ideal state. Additionally, we find that increasing the strength of the driving laser can eventually overcome the impact of these imperfect control settings, and that the coupled system's dynamics can be restored to its ideal form following a sudden perturbation, provided the duration of the disturbance is brief enough. However, we also note that in some situations, the system's hysteresis effect can lead to irregular behavior even after a disturbance has ceased, and that increasing the driving laser's power may not always prevent decay caused by other environmental factors. Several methods for mitigating these issues are also explored.

The global crisis due to COVID-19's rapid spread has caused a high demand for ventilators, surpassing the available supply. To address this shortage, we focus on using a single ventilator to ventilate multiple patients simultaneously, utilizing a manual resuscitator as an intermediate device. This approach requires developing an automated control system to ensure each patient receives their desired tidal volume, despite the phase delay caused by the resuscitator. We investigated two control methodologies - Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Proportional Integral Derivative (PID) - for this ventilator network. To model the ventilator network dynamically, we incorporated the effects of the resuscitator, ventilator, and patient's body into a system of ordinary differential equations. A key challenge arose from the delay in the system's dynamics, which compelled us to employ delay-aware controllers. In our experiments, we found the MPC controller yielded the most satisfactory results in terms of accuracy and robustness, successfully meeting the requirements for a high level of precision (5%) under normal conditions and more lenient precision (10%) in critical situations. Notably, the MPC controller performed effectively even with a significant delay (around 0.5 seconds) and a broad range of patient respiratory times (4-11 seconds), indicating its potential for safe application across different patients using the same ventilator. Moreover, we assessed the performance of the MPC controller with imperfect model data and found it capable of adapting to a 20% error in model parameters. To facilitate seamless integration with our control algorithm, we developed a user-friendly graphical user interface. The developed control system and GUI were successfully validated through clinical simulations and testing with a mannequin. In conclusion, our delay-aware MPC controller, supported by the GUI, has been effectively designed and successfully tested for use in ventilating multiple patients with a single automated ventilator. This innovative solution has the potential to address the current ventilator shortage caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Additionally, it may also provide a more adaptable and flexible approach to ventilator management in various clinical scenarios. To further enhance performance and adapt to various image bases, attention mechanisms are being combined with unet structures. In this work, we propose the Dilated Dense Attention Unet, an advanced network that incorporates a novel attention module, specifically designed to tackle whole-slide imaging. This module leverages a unique combination of dilated convolutional layers and spatial pyramid pooling for enhanced feature extraction, followed by a competitive activation function to select relevant contextual information. Additionally, boundary refinement is achieved through a localized attention mechanism. To evaluate our approach, we conducted experiments on the ESOP-18 dataset, yielding state-of-the-art results of 0.854 in dice similarity coefficient. Our method's efficacy is further validated through comparisons with prominent attention-unet variants and traditional methods. Moreover, quantitative assessments of models incorporating the proposed attention module show significant improvements in performance. Real-time formation evaluation in oil and gas exploration requires both speed and accuracy. To achieve this, a model is needed that can quickly and effectively use data from multiple wells to map subsurface formations. Given the complexity and variability of these formations, a simple linear model is insufficient, leading to the use of more advanced models such as Gaussian processes. However, these models fall short in real-time applications due to their computational demands. To address this challenge, we propose the use of an efficient Gaussian process model called LM-EnRML, which offers a balanced solution to accuracy and speed. By comparing it to other models including the traditional linear model and the fully Bayesian model, we demonstrate that LM-EnRML provides precise results while maintaining computational efficiency. Moreover, LM-EnRML proves to be an excellent choice for forming evaluations involving multiple data points, outperforming the other models in terms of speed and accuracy. To further enhance its performance, we also present an iterative version of the algorithm, which is then applied to a real-world scenario to showcase its effectiveness. Through our experiments, we highlight the key benefits of LM-EnRML, which include enhanced predictive accuracy, improved robustness, and significantly faster computation time. Overall, LM-EnRML represents a significant advancement in the efficient evaluation of formations in real-time, making it an invaluable tool for the oil and gas industry. To facilitate easy adoption, we have made the algorithm publicly accessible to support collaborative research. The creation of visual art through language has made significant progress in recent times, primarily through the use of generative models like sequence-to-sequence networks. While this technology holds immense potential to benefit visually impaired individuals by providing them with detailed image descriptions, its current implementation is limited to text-based inputs and outputs. To facilitate more practical applications, there is a pressing need for guidelines that can help generate accurate and comprehensive descriptions across various visual themes and settings. In an effort to address this issue, we propose a novel framework that leverages collaborative work between computer vision experts and language model engineers to establish a set of high-quality guidelines. To validate the effectiveness of these guidelines, we employ a cost-evaluation framework that involves both human assessments and automated metrics. Through experiments conducted on the MS COCO dataset, with evaluations using both automatic and human metrics, our findings demonstrate that guidelines generated through this framework can significantly improve image description quality when neural models are used. Notably, our results show a notable improvement of 10-15% in description accuracy as measured by human raters. Moreover, we observe that certain pre-trained language models, such as T5 and BART, exhibit a marked increase of 5-10% in accuracy when using these guidelines, as compared to models without guidance. Our work offers a pioneering attempt to explore the creation and utilization of guidelines for the generation of image descriptions, an area that is sure to spark further research in the future. All code, data, and additional results are made freely available at this link https://github.com/rahulrajesht/visuguidelines. With this work, we aim to facilitate dialogue among computer vision experts, language model engineers, and the broader research community on the design of high-quality guidelines for the generation of image descriptions. In doing so, we hope to establish a collaborative framework that drives collaborative work, fosters open discussion, and encourages the sharing of expertise and resources. In the long term, our ultimate goal is to create a centralized repository where guidelines for image descriptions can be collected, with accompanying datasets, models, and evaluation metrics. This initiative is sure to benefit not just the large language models employed in this work but also any future neural models used in this domain. In this inaugural study, we focus on one such theme, namely the creation of high-quality guidelines for the visual theme of furniture, with expert input from computer vision specialists. Calculating the energy loss functions for Tantalum oxide using a quantum language is complicated due to the high symmetry of these structures and the absence of a suitable reference material for comparison. Incorporating local field effects, spin-orbit coupling, and advanced scattering modes into the calculation can aid in obtaining more accurate results. By utilizing the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof exchange-correlation function and considering local field effects and spin-orbit coupling, we have conducted simulations of Tantalum oxide using the gamma-alkali metal oxide structure, with a specific investigation of $\alpha$-Tantalum oxide. The results show that including local field effects and spin-orbit coupling leads to a more distinct peak in the energy loss spectrum near 19 eV, consistent with observations from spectroscopic experiments. Furthermore, a comparison with experimental data from spectroscopic experiments reveals a good agreement between the calculated and measured results across a wide range of energy losses. A many-body effect, accounting for interactions between electrons in the conduction band, has a significant impact on the energy loss spectrum, with an indication that this effect is more pronounced at higher energy losses. A comparison between two different simulations, one using a first-principles method and the other using the tight-binding model, indicates that the latter yields a better agreement with experimental data from spectroscopic experiments, with a more accurate representation of the energy loss spectrum's features. A correlation between energy loss peaks and core-level binding energies in the conduction band is demonstrated, with an indication that this correlation holds across different structures of Tantalum oxide. An analysis of the electron states contributing to specific energy loss peaks has identified that these peaks are primarily associated with oxygen and Tantalum electrons in the $\alpha$-Tantalum oxide structure. An understanding of the electron scattering and the calculation of electron interaction with these structures is crucial for the development of devices that rely on electron scattering, such as field-emission devices. Additionally, the ability to model the interaction between electrons and these structures will facilitate the development of new materials with tailored electron scattering properties, leading to enhanced field-emission performance. The theory of the big sort suggests that in the US, voting districts have become increasingly homogeneous in their ideological leanings since the 1960s. This study explores a lesser-studied consequence of this homogenization: its impact on the online dissemination of false information among voters in these districts. As people's worldviews have likely shifted due to the big sort, they may be more likely to share misinformation that confirms their values, but only if their local community shares the same viewpoint. We use a sophisticated method to measure community values and analyze the sharing of false news on Facebook, revealing that big sort does indeed contribute to the spread of misinformation and that this effect is largely driven by homogeneous communities. Additionally, we find that users' willingness to share misinformation is influenced by both the false news's confirmation of their own values and the prevalence of those values within their community's social network. This effect holds true for both liberal and conservative users and is more pronounced for users with homogeneous community networks. It is also evident across various news articles and is linked to users' propensity to share content that is factually accurate as well as inaccurate. Finally, we propose a mathematical model that captures this phenomenon and provides policy recommendations to mitigate the effects of big sort on the online dissemination of false information, including targeting homogeneous communities in counter-spread campaigns and promoting diversity within online social networks. These strategies have the potential to reduce the online spread of misinformation, especially in areas with highly homogeneous communities. The methods employed in this research can be applied to the study of the spread of information and other phenomena on online platforms. The effects of big sort on the online dissemination of false information have implications for the role of geography in this context and suggest that counter-spread initiatives should be community-based. The research raises further questions about the interplay between community values and online information spread, including the potential for big sort to influence users' willingness to share accurate information and the potential for community values to shape users' perceptions of truth and falsehood. The study provides a framework for analyzing the effects of big sort on online information spread and could be applied to other research questions, such as the impact of big sort on voting behavior or the spread of information within organizations. The data and methods employed in this research could also be applied to the study of online information spread in other countries and cultures. The study provides a theoretical and practical framework for mitigating the effects of big sort on online information spread, including the targeting of homogeneous communities in counter-spread campaigns and the promotion of diversity within online social networks. The vast potential of machine learning in an organization is often hindered by two challenges: accessing sufficient computational power for complex models or affording the necessary annotation for pre-trained models. This problem stems from a narrow approach to machine learning, which views it solely as a tool for complex model computation or data labeling. In contrast, this paper argues that machine learning's true value lies in its ability to represent human reasoning and problem-solving skills. By leveraging this insight, we can employ simple machine learning methods to solve pressing issues, such as extracting relevant information from unstructured documents, combining external knowledge, and generating accurate inputs for downstream tasks. This paper presents a novel, versatile approach called the Knowledge Representations and Reasoning Framework, which utilizes minimal annotation and simple machine learning to address these challenges. This approach prioritizes representational reasoning over complex computation and has been effective in multiple applications, including document understanding, external knowledge graph integration, and data input generation. The results demonstrate that this approach surpasses alternative methods in accuracy and efficiency, with a particular notable improvement in extracting information from unstructured documents and generating accurate inputs for downstream tasks. The proposed framework has been successfully deployed in real-world settings at Yahoo and Verizon Media, yielding substantial gains in performance and efficiency. We investigate the complex interactions between speech, vision, and the varied conditions of teaching, which involves multiple factors including:  Following different demonstration types (e.g. action-only vs. action-with-object demonstrations)  Using audio instructions in place of visual ones  Altering the subtasks being demonstrated (e.g. from a single step to multiple steps)  Introducing errors in the demonstration  Our approach involves crowdsourced data used to study the effect of these conditions, along with their combinations, on the concepts expressed in speech. Our analysis reveals the following key points:  Even in the absence of action, observing demonstrations of action-only or action-with-object can convey distinct concepts (our findings disagree with a competing proposal).  Auditory instructions are shown to convey the same concepts as visual ones.  Error introduction affects the basic concepts being communicated, yet concepts about the goal and the object's appearance remain largely unchanged.  Changing the subtask also affects the concepts about the object's appearance.  Our analysis of the conditions' effects, along with their combinations, can be accessed at our project website. Building upon this understanding, we propose a model that leverages the proven capabilities of visual recognition models, while incorporating new multimodal attention mechanisms that handle demonstrations of action-only or action-with-object, along with concepts about the goal and the object's appearance. Our proposed model is shown to improve performance over a baseline model in a series of tasks.  In addition, our model is able to generalize to new demonstrations and object appearances, as shown through a series of generalization tests.  Ultimately, our approach achieves a new high water mark in performance over prior work.  We also explore the use of this model in planning the actions required to complete a goal, along with the challenges it faces in this domain.  In conclusion, our research offers a new model that is capable of successfully learning from demonstrations of various types, along with the conditions under which they are presented, and provides a foundation for future research in the domain of action understanding through speech and vision. Researchers in quantum field theory encounter the Euler-Arnold equations when attempting to minimize an energy functional with constraints imposed by linear parabolic equations. To circumvent these complex equations, we employ a stochastic integral approach, specifically utilizing the stochastic gradient flow to converge to the optimal solution. By analyzing the long-term behavior of the resulting stochastic system, we establish the connection between the equilibrium point of the system and the minimum energy level. Additionally, we investigate the uniqueness of the equilibrium point, providing conditions under which it is unique, and demonstrate the uniqueness of the solution to the original constrained optimization problem under those conditions. Furthermore, we examine the uniqueness of the equilibrium point in the context of two specific quantum field theory models. One of these models concerns the Kirkwood-Swendsen algorithm, and the other involves the Euler-Arnold equation for a monotone operator with a constant of regularity $\gamma$ between 0 and 1, with particular emphasis on the case where $\gamma$ equals 1/2. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our findings for quantum field theory when the target space has a high dimension. This research is an extension of our previous study (arXiv:2106.04818), and it provides an opportunity to showcase the quantum field theory applications. Conversational systems are increasingly integral to user interaction via interfaces, yet they present a complex challenge for developing automated testing frameworks. Current methods for evaluating conversational interfaces rely on user-reported feedback and manual testing procedures to identify defects, which can be time-consuming and unresponsive to the rapid evolution of these systems. To address this issue, we propose a novel automated testing approach, guided by formal specification methods, which can create and validate conversational experiences while simultaneously ensuring the integrity of underlying backend services. Our framework, driven by a unified data model, integrates a type-state exploration algorithm to detect potential errors and anomalies in the conversational flow and associated data modifications. Furthermore, we investigate ways to optimize the performance of this framework, experimenting with different data model designs and validation strategies to minimize testing time. Through empirical testing and analysis of a real-world application, we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach, yielding a testing tool called PyConverse-Tester. PyConverse-Tester outperforms manual testing procedures and existing testing frameworks in terms of discovery rate and testing time, ensuring the integrity of backend services and conversational experiences. To facilitate adoption, we provide PyConverse-Tester as an open-source testing framework for conversational systems, along with a data model library featuring several built-in validators to support quick integration with custom data models. In the broader context, our research addresses key challenges in automated testing for conversational systems and presents strategies for optimization, with implications for other complex, distributed systems. In addition, we introduce a new language, PyAnnotate, for expressing valid state and transition annotations within conversational applications, enabling more precise testing and analysis. Through PyAnnotate, we aim to spark interest in exploring other formal specification languages and related techniques for the automated testing of conversational systems. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the advancement of testing and validation methods for the ever-evolving ecosystem of conversational systems. In this work, we focus on dialog systems but acknowledge the potential applicability of our approach and language to other types of multimodal systems and interactive experiences. This approach allowed them to study a region of 10^-6 radian around the direction perpendicular to the Milky Way plane, with an accuracy of 0.2 angstrom per square degree, achieving a sensitivity to a mass of approximately 10^8 Earth masses within 10^13 solar masses at a 90% confidence level, or the ability to detect a 0.1 Earth-mass object at a 50% confidence level within 10^12 solar masses. This method also made it possible to place upper limits on the density of massive compact objects in the Galactic bulge and the halo, with density limits of 0.013, 0.007, and 0.005 objects per liter, respectively, without detecting anything within the 1.6 solar mass range, which would include the mass range of dark matter in the Milky Way's halo. Utilizing pre-trained models for multilingual language understanding has yielded significant advancements in various NLP applications. Our study leverages a cross-lingual memory retriever to develop a bilingual translation memory model, enabling the recall of relevant past translations to inform current translation decisions. By integrating a contrastive learning approach with a memory retriever, our bilingual memory retriever model can effectively retrieve similar sentence embeddings across languages, circumventing the need for explicit parallel data. The model excels in low-resource settings and handles out-of-domain translation scenarios. In evaluations on WMT 2012 EN-DE, WMT 2015 EN-RO, and WMT 2018 EN-DE tasks, our system demonstrates improved performance over a strong baseline, ultimately achieving a 1.1% improvement in BLEU score for the low-resource WMT 2015 EN-RO task. The model also achieves a 6.1% improvement in BLEU score for the more challenging out-of-domain settings of the WMT 2012 EN-DE validation set, facilitating more cost-effective data preparation for the model. Our code and data repositories are available at https://github.com/THU-CLSA/BilingualMemoryRetriever.

Recent studies suggest that certain topological features such as Hawking points and low-variance circles may be observable in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). However, these findings rely on unrealistic simulations of a multiverse, which do not accurately reflect the actual scenarios. Therefore, it is essential to investigate whether the presence of the CMB anomalies, which are deviations from normal behavior in the CMB, significantly impact the presence of these topological features. To achieve this, a comprehensive analysis across various scales was conducted. The research revealed that the absence of anomalies does not hinder the presence of Hawking points and low-variance circles. Conversely, the presence of these anomalies facilitates the detection of these features by an appreciable margin. Consequently, a more robust method for identifying topological features in the CMB has been developed, which is an integral component of the $A_{\rm lens}$ code. Moreover, the research discovered that the most pronounced low-variance circles are approximately $4.5\sigma$ deviations from the norm, occurring in approximately $30\%$ of the sky. The study also found that the most distinctive Hawking points are $2.5\sigma$ deviations from the norm, present in approximately $50\%$ of the sky. The relationship between the radius of low-variance circles and the corresponding $\sigma$ values was also defined through a power-law equation. In addition, it was found that the distribution of the total curvature within these low-variance circles is consistent with a Beta distribution with specific parameters. The research further revealed that the most distinctive Hawking points exhibit an almost uniform distribution in terms of their angular separation. The findings of this study provide a more accurate framework for interpreting topological features in the CMB and may have implications for understanding the multiverse. Moreover, this research offers a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between the CMB and the multiverse, the causes of CMB anomalies, and the significance of topological features in the CMB. The study also presents a robust method for identifying topological features in the CMB, which is an integral component of the $A_{\rm lens}$ code. The code is available for download at http://www.lsw.uni-heidelberg.de/dewincode. In the domain of few-shot learning, the common issue of outlier examples poses a significant challenge for the fundamental goal of the framework, which is to establish a general and efficient method for learning from minimal data. The present research endeavors to address this problem by developing a protocol to identify and filter outlier samples. The proposed technique builds upon the premise that learning from a few instances should be accomplished through the employment of a prototype-based method. Consequently, the generation of supports and queries within each novel class is achieved via the generation of conditional prototypes, which are produced by manipulating existing prototypes rather than generating entirely new patterns. The technique is further enhanced by the introduction of an outlier filter, which leverages prototype distances to discriminate between genuine and fictitious samples. The proposed protocol is applied to a range of datasets, including miniImage-omniglot, miniFormations, and miniBirds, to evaluate the technique's efficacy. The experimental outcomes obtained indicate that the introduction of outlier samples significantly complicates the learning process; by contrast, the removal of such samples yields compelling results, with an average accuracy rate of over 90%. The technique is also found to be robust in scenarios where additional classes are introduced and is capable of adapting to new classes with minimal additional learning. The results show that GAPE achieves a notable improvement in recommendation accuracy when utilizing off-policy transitions, in comparison to other alternatives that are more computationally demanding. The study of formulation size in integer programming has been recently revitalized, 
espousing the use of exotic cones to represent problems naturally, often with fewer 
variables than traditional extended formulations. This research explores the unique 
formulations using exotic cones and extended formulations, comparing their variable and 
constraint counts across different settings. The examination is conducted for several 
key applications, including systems of minimal covers, multi-knapsack problems, network flow and cut problems, and graph matching. The findings provide insight into the relationship between the size of exotic and extended formulations, revealing both instances where the exotic formulations are non-polynomial while the extended counterparts are polynomial, and scenarios where both formulations scale polynomially. Furthermore, the comparison highlights instances of equivalent or similar variable and constraint counts between exotic and extended formulations, and instances where the exotic formulations have non-polynomial counts while the extended counterparts do not. The comparison also raises questions about the relative merits of using exotic versus extended formulations. The research demonstrates the potential of using exotic formulations to model complex problems naturally, yielding models that are highly interpretable, in contrast to the often complex extended formulations. However, both the ease of constructing both types of formulations, as well as their future applications, remain areas of ongoing research and discussion. The research presented here contributes to the ongoing exploration of formulation size in integer programming by examining both exotic and extended formulations, comparing their variable and constraint counts across different settings, and raising both computational and theoretical questions for further investigation. The research is conducted with publicly available software, using specific instance counts, and is subject to verification by the research community. The research is further contributed to the integer programming community through the availability of all used instances, formulation counts, and software, facilitating the replication and extension of the research and providing a foundation for future research in this area. A centralized federated learning approach for MRI segmentation is proposed, 
utilizing a strong and efficient UNet architecture. The primary focus is on 
exploring the impact of dataset composition in a broad range of clinical settings. 
Data from seven publicly available sources is employed in the experiment. 
Following an initial two-rounds phase of centralised federated learning, 
the model is tested on an unprecedented collection of 200k MRI images. 
The results show substantial improvements in performance when using the federated learning approach, 
with a RoBUST-DA score of 6563.35 compared to the non-federated score of 4345.08. 
However, the model's performance is found to be prone to bias, 
with a median RoBUST-DA score of 4345.08 for the test dataset. 
The findings suggest that utilizing a diverse range of datasets in training 
can result in varying performance levels for different anatomical regions. 
For instance, the F1-score for the cerebral cortex ranged from 0.876 to 0.983, 
while that for the cerebellum ranged from 0.571 to 0.793. 
Enhancing the dataset, particularly for the cerebellum, is identified as a key area 
for future improvement to achieve more reliable and accurate MRI segmentation.

under the name 'zheng062/mri-segmentation-fl-unet'.

frequent writes, it doesn't have a notable impact on small, sporadic writes.

high latency and slow database query execution. In contrast, our experiments
show that using NOVA-relaxed results in a significant reduction in write transactions

and an improvement in database query execution speed. Our research also shows

In 2019, the Motivation Dynamics (MD) theory was enhanced with a new model, considering agents influenced by multiple internal and external forces, addressing concerns about consistency, smoothness, and their interplay. This expanded framework now rigorously captures a variety of complex behavior, including agents transitioning between equilibrium points - a phenomenon known as rendezvous. By incorporating a general preference function, the Multi-Agent MD (MAMD) model provides a computationally efficient way to determine preferred equilibrium points, thus enabling the computation of solutions to the rendezvous problem. Furthermore, the MAMD framework facilitates valuable insights into the impact of external forces, force fields, and stationary targets on rendezvous solutions. By establishing a connection to the gradient flow, the invariance property of reachable sets is also analytically defined. The theoretical advancements in the Multi-Agent MD model are supported by computational tools, including a numerical method for computing preferred equilibrium points and rendezvous solutions through the utilization of a gradient descent algorithm. The effectiveness of these solutions is demonstrated via simulation examples and experimental validation on a quadrotor testbed. This shift indicates a rise in the hybridized density of 4f states with Sn character and a decline in the hybridized density with Cu character as Cm is replaced by Gd. The large-scale halo structures of galaxies are critical to understanding various cosmic phenomena, including dark energy's impact on the universe. By analyzing spatial correlations in quasars at high redshift, this study finds constraints on a key fundamental theory of these structures. Specifically, it places limits on a parameter related to the size of these structures and another related to their density. These constraints become more precise as the field is observed at lower redshifts. When combined with data from a specific redshift, these results place the most stringent limits to date on those fundamental parameters. Those limits are placed in a theoretical framework that assumes a halo distribution similar to that found in the Milky Way. When combined with other data sets, including those from a related study and a cosmic web construction, these constraints provide a coherent picture of the size and density of these structures across a range of redshifts. Those findings support a theoretical framework that suggests these structures grow through a refining process that involves the merger of smaller, similar structures. Those mergers occur at a rate that is placed within observed limits and is placed within a range of 10-30% of those limits. This study proposes an automated method for detecting brain tumors by combining morphological analysis and region growth. The plan is to utilize a pair of morphological tools, specifically Euler-Lagrange and Gray-Scale Skewness, along with region growth, to identify and outline tumors within MRI images. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, it will be tested on a dataset provided by the ISBI 2012 challenge, along with creating and assessing a database of 120 MRI images that feature tumors, with the goal of determining how reliable this method is when identifying tumors and outlining their borders, as well as comparing it to a widely-used industry standard. The method's accuracy will be assessed in two scenarios: once with a database of healthy brain images, and again without, to determine the impact of this factor. The study aims to explore a low-cost alternative to using deep learning techniques for tumor detection. The results show a high degree of correlation with the industry standard, and the method is particularly effective when the background brain images are similar to those containing tumors. However, the method may produce inaccurate results when there are significant differences, as seen with the ISBI 2012 challenge images, but it demonstrates a level of robustness when tested with the custom database of 120 images, without using background brain images, and shows potential for further development with additional features. The code and dataset used in this study are available for public access.  Our method yields a high degree of accuracy when compared to industry standards, our findings suggest, using a technique known as Dice Index.  We believe this approach could be applied to detecting tumors in other parts of the body by modifying the feature extraction tools. This study introduces the concept of degenerate Bernoulli numbers, a theoretical model that shares properties with traditional Bernoulli numbers, specifically in relation to quadratic residues in finite fields. We demonstrate the connection between these new numbers and other mathematical constructs, including circulant matrices, linear operators, and Gauss sums. Furthermore, we show that the degenerate Bernoulli numbers can be used to define a recurring sequence in the field, analogous to the behavior of prime numbers. Additionally, we derive an estimated frequency with which these new numbers exhibit specific properties, similar to the distribution of prime numbers classified as twin primes. Building upon this understanding, we can apply this framework to various types of sequences and functions to analyze their behavior within finite fields. As an example, we investigate the properties of an related sequence that exhibits fractal-like characteristics. This research is an extension of previous work on the subject and provides a more comprehensive framework for studying the properties of constructs within finite fields through their relationship with Bernoulli numbers. This framework has implications for broadening our understanding of number theory and could potentially inform new approaches to analyzing number-theoretic constructs. This research is an extension of our joint work with Professor Richard J. Mawhinney. This work is part of my Ph.D. dissertation, which was defended on August 12, 2021, at the University of Tennessee.

Researchers estimate that nearly 70% of main-sequence stars in the Galactic disk require exoplanet detection through radial velocity techniques. However, the high sensitivity of RV measurements is hindered by stellar noise, specifically RV jitter. This study examines a data-driven approach to minimize the impact of jitter by selecting a limited line list from a large pool of spectral lines. Utilizing a set of 63 red giant stars from the PASTIS survey, we show that a random selection method from line lists trained on spectral energies yields a 30% improvement in model fit and a 25% decrease in residual scatter compared to a parametric approach. Interestingly, the random selection method performs equally well to a more computationally intensive method using atmospheric conditions and stellar parameters. This simple line-list selection method may help mitigate RV jitter and facilitate the detection of exoplanets. Further research is necessary to apply this method to main-sequence stars. Nonetheless, this study offers an accessible technique for improving the precision of RV measurements, which can be incorporated into existing exoplanet detection pipelines. Additionally, this method may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of stellar spectra structures. By reducing the dimensionality of spectral data, this method raises interesting possibilities for other astrophysical applications, such as identifying small-scale features in stellar spectra and constructing more precise line lists for chemical abundance analysis. This study may also facilitate the development of more accurate models of stellar spectra and ultimately, exoplanet host star characterization. This method can be incorporated into existing exoplanet detection pipelines and may contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of stellar spectra structures. Conditioned on the sum of independent Bernoulli random variables, we derive both brief-term and long-term concentration inequalities for convex functions and polynomial functions of these variables. Our results remain robust even in scenarios where the independence of the Bernoulli variables is slightly compromised, as long as the graph representing their interconnections has a sufficient number of edges. Our concentration inequality for convex functions is an extension of a recent proposal by Alevras, Kontis, and Vaggennos, and our concentration inequality for polynomial functions is an adaptation of a suggestion made by Boppana. Moreover, our findings include an unconditional result and a conditioned result on the sum of these variables, and they are equally applicable to both down-set polynomials and general polynomials. Our main technique involves the application of a powerful graph theoretical inequality, as well as innovative uses of the Farkas' Lemma, and these tools allow us to provide an intuitive understanding of our results through graph representations. Lastly, our results have implications in the study of tail-spaces and their connection to the Boppana's epsilon-nu conjecture. 

This research is part of the writer's PhD thesis, which was completed under the supervision of N. S. Trivedi at the University of Oxford. 

Keywords: Concentration inequality, Bernoulli variables, convex function, polynomial function, graph theory, Boppana's epsilon-nu conjecture.

This understanding is critical in establishing the connection between the system of invariants and the classification of conjugacy classes within the symplectic group. By exploring this method, we are able to provide a detailed classification of conjugacy classes based on their system of invariants, a fundamental framework that lays the groundwork for examining the Chevalley group G$_2(q)$ through its natural action on the set of conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp$_2(q)$. For example, on an e-commerce platform like Amazon, a product recommendation might be influenced by the category of products displayed, with suggested items appearing alongside a primary product of interest. In such scenarios, entity representations are ideally both aesthetically pleasing and logically organized, with recommendations reflecting both aesthetic and structural aspects. However, creating effective recommendations that balance look and feel with underlying organization is a complex task. In this research, we focus on developing a novel recommendation framework that leverages both visual layout and hierarchical structure in entity representations to enhance recommendations. By applying this framework to various datasets, our findings show that our approach outperforms traditional methods, with improved recommendation accuracy. The benefits of this framework are demonstrated through a case study on the recommendation of Wikipedia entries, with recommended entities positioned within a hierarchical structure of subcategories. The recommended entities are placed at multiple levels of this hierarchy, with the look-and-feel of recommendations influenced by both the structure and layout of entities. By integrating incompatibility as a state variable in an MDP, our new model, called Incompatible MDP (IMDP), addresses the complex decision-making process in kidney transplantation by considering both patient Incompatibility and utility maximization. In this transplantation context, when an offer is made, a patient must either accept the donated kidney or reject it. Rejection doesn't alter the transition probabilities, but acceptance does, as it removes the offered kidney from the available pool. Building on the IMDP framework, our algorithm derives optimal strategies by applying value iteration, with a notable increase in computational complexity due to the vast number of states resulting from repeated transitions. To manage this, our approach employs a state-lifetime concept to limit the lookup table required for computation. Empirical analysis on real-world data demonstrates that our algorithm achieves near-optimal results with a significantly reduced number of computations, at approximately one-thousandth the original size, indicating a significant computational efficiency gain. Additionally, our model and derived algorithm can be employed to analyze the impact of transition rules and utility functions on decision-making processes. As the underlying framework is highly versatile, we suggest the use of IMDP as a general model for similar problems involving repeated transitions and irreversible actions. This study presents a novel Bayesian method for estimating parameters in multivariate copula models, specifically a dynamic copula model. The approach leverages historical average parameters as a prior distribution to improve estimation accuracy. The analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of this method in a simulated scenario, using the Clausis-Haenkin copula, with time-varying copula parameters. The results show that the proposed Bayesian method outperforms alternative methods such as the maximum likelihood estimator, with the smallest Mean Squared Error. The study also finds that the Bayesian approach produces the most accurate estimates, with a MSE of 0.0231, surpassing the 0.0275 MSE of the MLE and the 0.0261 MSE of the historical average method. The analysis further examines the performance of the proposed method under different sample sizes, finding that the Bayesian method yields the lowest MSE in all scenarios, with a notable improvement in smaller sample sizes. The study concludes by applying the dynamic copula model to real-world data from the S\&P 500 stock market index, revealing significant changes in the copula parameters and a corresponding increase in the GARCH effect. The findings suggest that the time-varying copula model provides a more accurate representation of the data, with a higher R-squared value of 0.928 compared to 0.854 for the constant copula model. The results further indicate that the proposed Bayesian method outperforms the alternative methods, with an estimated value of 0.0833 for the GARCH effect. The study concludes by highlighting the potential of the time-varying copula model for analyzing multivariate financial time series data. The R code for the novel Bayesian method has been made available online.
