When machine learning models, such as word2vec and BERT, are used to analyze financial text and apply semantic reasoning, they incorrectly treat opposites like "buy" and "sell" as similar or the same, not as distinct. This incorrect interpretation leads to inaccurate decisions when trading and other financial actions are predicted. To address this limitation, we propose a new method called FINBERT-OP, which extends the BERT model by incorporating a novel mathematical structure that accurately captures the opposition between words. By leveraging this structure, FINBERT-OP successfully recovers the correct relationships between words, including both frequentist (similar or same) and oppositional (different) relationships. We demonstrate that FINBERT-OP outperforms other machine learning models, including BERT, when predicting trading signals and other actions in the stock market. Additionally, we show that FINBERT-OP effectively incorporates oppositional relationships into its representations of words and phrases, leading to more accurate performance. Notably, we find that FINBERT-OP excels when opposites are involved, achieving a 9.5% higher precision rate than BERT in one dataset and a 14.1% higher precision rate in another. We also successfully apply FINBERT-OP to other machine learning tasks, including natural language inference and question answering. Our code, models, and data, are available for download at https://github.com/ali476/finbert-op. We plan to release the code for the baseline models used in our experiments as well as the financial action dataset at a later stage. The abstract structure we propose can be generalized to capture oppositional relationships in other domains and languages, and we anticipate that our research will stimulate further investigation into the application of mathematical structures to machine learning models, particularly in domains with complex semantic relationships. Lastly, we hope that our research will contribute to the development of more accurate and reliable machine learning models in finance and other fields.

This paper explores the optimization of fair-throughput and sum-throughput in
wideband waveforming by employing an optimization problem that considers the
fairness and sum-throughput objectives. To tackle this high-dimensional problem,
we develop a hybrid optimization approach that combines an initial search via
the differential evolution method with a local refinement using the trust-region
method. The success of our approach is validated through Monte Carlo simulations,
and the results show that it achieves near-optimal performance with a high degree
of certainty. The proposed method is further evaluated in terms of computational
complexity, fairness, and sum-throughput, and the findings indicate that our
hybrid approach provides excellent solutions with relatively low average computational
cost. The study also investigates the impact of the number of antennas, Monte
Carlo trials, and initialization strategies on the proposed method's effectiveness.

A recent deep learning approach introducing a convolutional neural network-based model for an infinite number of heated plates in a viscous fluid under the influence of gravity was presented. The deep learning model was initially trained on numerically generated data to counter the Rayleigh-Bénard instability challenge. However, the analysis revealed that the model's success depends heavily on the choice of the x-domain, with optimal results achieved in the intermediate x-domain and decreased accuracy observed at the boundaries. A possible explanation for this phenomenon is the model's failure to represent the stable solid boundary conditions accurately. A novel framework, incorporating a external Lagrange multiplier layer within the CNN architecture, was subsequently proposed to address this issue. The addition of the multiplier layer enables the capture of the boundary conditions within the model, allowing for a significant improvement in predicting the model's behavior at the x-domain boundaries with minimal error. The enhanced model demonstrates reduced residual norms of $\mathcal{O}(10^{-4})$ compared to the original model, with an improvement of approximately two orders of magnitude. The modified model also demonstrates the capacity to accurately determine the wavelength of the instability in real-world scenarios, an aspect where the original model consistently underestimates this parameter by roughly 30%. The enhanced model's performance is coupled with the original Hamiltonian operator, ensuring the conservation of key quantities across time. The model's precision was validated across diverse training scenarios, including the analysis of melting patterns in the x-domain, the development of instabilities within the model, and its integration with the original Hamiltonian operator. The implementation of the novel framework through the introduction of an external multiplier layer layer provides a viable solution for addressing the boundary challenge associated with the Rayleigh-Bénard instability. The enhanced model is accompanied by the open-source code repository DeepBénard. The code is publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/CheneyHuang/DeepBénard, with the numerical data employed in the study available upon request. Many NLP applications, including neural theories of the mind and neural language models, often struggle with distinguishing between multiple possible interpretations of a single linguistic input. This problem is particularly pronounced when NLP systems are asked to explain the underlying reasoning behind their outputs or predictions. In this work, we present a novel framework for resolving ambiguous interpretations in language. This framework is founded on the principles of Type Theory and incorporates the concepts of dependent function extension and elimination. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to the task of natural language inference. Our method first employs a neural network to generate a set of possible interpretations, which are subsequently ranked in order of relevance through the application of a theoretical inference algorithm. The utility of our approach is validated through both theoretical and practical assessments, as well as a comparison with more straightforward models. Our technique achieves state-of-the-art accuracy in the SNLI benchmark, outperforming the current leaders in the field by a significant margin. Moreover, our method exhibits an intriguing property known as neural mixtup, where the model's neural representations of individual premises can become'mixed up' when presented with sufficient amounts of unlabeled data, resulting in a neural state that is now capable of supporting all possible interpretations. This framework is made available to the broader research community through a publicly accessible repository.

In complex cooperative games, some actions are consistently outperformed by others, which can complicate the learning process for agents. We observe that in the multiagent learning environment of Hanabi, many actions are inferior and the standard approach of exploiting known patterns is insufficient. To overcome this challenge, we propose a method for players to learn which actions to avoid, by applying a strategy that reduces the occurrence of less desirable actions. This approach involves creating a simplified model of the game's value function and using counterfactual policy evaluation to determine the effect of alternative actions. By implementing this approach, players can significantly reduce the occurrence of weak actions and achieve better outcomes in Hanabi, even without relying on an accurate understanding of the game's patterns. In the worst case, this approach limits the occurrence of weak actions and prevents them from becoming the dominant choice. In the best case, it allows players to discover new patterns of cooperation. We show that this approach is efficient, robust, and compatible with other learning strategies. By avoiding weak actions, we can also combine our approach with external knowledge, leading to further improvements and outcomes close to optimal. We validate our method through extensive simulations and compare its performance to alternative approaches. Additionally, we examine the behavior of our method in Hanabi with an increasing number of players and provide insights into its actions and outcomes. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of our research for multiagent learning and suggest areas for further exploration. We make our code publicly available to facilitate replication and further development of this research.

Building upon previous research, we develop a stochastic model to study the spread of infectious diseases within changing social networks. Unlike models that rely on deterministic equations, our model utilizes a time-discrete approach to examine the effects of temporary network modifications on epidemic dynamics. We analyze the impact of adapting the network's structure after each time step on a Monte Carlo simulation, where the network is redrawn at random after every individuals' infections, and compare it to a more realistic model where the network's layout evolves naturally. Notably, we find that even with the network changing rapidly, a persistent epidemic can still occur if the average time it takes for an infected individual to recover is greater than twice the network's basic reproduction number. Additionally, we investigate how the size of the epidemic is influenced by the network's structure and size, and how it relates to the model's equilibrium points. Our study demonstrates that introducing temporary changes to a network can significantly impact the epidemic's spread, and may help clarify the outcomes observed in Monte Carlo simulations. Furthermore, we propose that future research in epidemic dynamics within changing social networks be guided by a general framework, and suggest suitable models can be derived through adaptation of this framework to fit specific contexts. We also examine the model's limitations and suggest alternative methods to address these limitations. Finally, we discuss potential applications and areas for further research, including the potential for field trials and extensions to multi-group and spatially-organized networks.

A detailed explanation of the DGLAP evolution equation is crucial for understanding how parton distribution functions (PDFs) evolve from one energy scale to another. As a key component of the theory, PDFs need to evolve from a low scale, used in fits, to a higher scale, relevant to the data it needs to match. In our research, we have been fitting the MRSSR2019 neural network to data at different scales, and as a result, it showed significant discrepancies. To resolve this issue, we re-examined the DGLAP evolution equation and proposed modifying the evolution to account for scale-dependent mixing coefficients. By doing so, our findings indicate that the neural network can be made scale-independent with minimal adjustments, and more importantly, this change allows for a better fit to data at different scales. Furthermore, we observed that the primary PDFs exhibit kink behavior at an invariant scale of approximately 1.7 GeV, and our proposed model successfully smooths out these kinks. To support our analysis, we have included a set of parton distributions at a low scale, along with the modified evolution equation, in the NNPDF framework via an open-source code, and this code is freely accessible online. Our research highlights the importance of carefully examining the evolution of PDFs, especially when using artificial neural networks, and emphasizes the need to control the evolution equation to prevent unphysical kinks in the parton distributions. Additionally, we suggest that future PDF initiatives prioritize controlling the scale evolution of PDFs, and we look forward to exploring our findings further in future studies. Our research is currently available on arXiv, and we intend to submit it for review in an academic journal. Nonetheless, our findings have significant implications for the development of artificial neural network parton distribution functions and suggest that researchers control the evolution equation to prevent unphysical kinks in the parton distributions. Moreover, this development could lead to improved theoretical understanding of deep artificial neural networks. In conclusion, this research letter presents an issue we encountered with an artificial neural network parton distribution function fit to data at different scales, and it highlights the importance of carefully examining the evolution of parton distributions, especially when using machine learning models. Additionally, it emphasizes the need to control the evolution equation to prevent unphysical kinks in the parton distributions and sets the stage for future studies to explore our proposed model and related code. We introduce a variance reduction based experience replay (VRER) framework for policy evaluation in reinforcement learning, which is highly versatile and adaptable to multiple algorithms, including policy gradient methods and value-based algorithms. By formulating experience replay as an optimization problem, we derive a general framework that is theoretically sound and effectively enhances policy gradient estimation by leveraging a broad range of value estimates. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework by implementing VRER on top of the well-known TRPO algorithm and achieving significant improvements in performance across four challenging benchmark problems. The challenging MultiMassTask domain also showcases the benefit of using a broad range of value estimates, which results in an average return more than double that of the baseline TRPO algorithm. Our work provides a meaningful contribution to the study of experience replay frameworks and sheds light on the benefits of using variance reduction techniques in reinforcement learning. The libcommute library has been revised to utilize Python 3 APIs, which provides enhanced functionality and is accompanied by a revised command-line interface. Additionally, a graphical user interface has been created for libcommute using the PyQT5 framework to simplify interaction with the library's features. Furthermore, a set of example scripts has been included to illustrate successful implementations of the libcommute Python 3 API, encompassing both standalone scripts and a Jupyter Notebook containing multiple demonstrations. These examples highlight the libcommute library's capabilities in computing spectral properties, constructing many-body states, and performing operations on second quantization representations. All libcommute Python 3 API and associated example projects are available on open-source platforms, along with the libcommute repository on GitHub. Due to the extensive utility of the libcommute Python 3 API, it is being utilized as a primary tool for teaching the theoretical aspects of second quantization and many-body physics at the University of Bristol. The libcommute Python 3 API, along with the associated projects, can be accessed through the University of Bristol's research cloud, making the library's capabilities openly accessible to the scientific community worldwide.

Using ARPES, we studied the superconducting state of GdFeAsO ($\bf k}$-space around the zone corner, an area previously inaccessible due to crystal orientation constraints. Our findings reveal a significant superconducting gap of 13 meV, present in multiple samples, with an anisotropic shape mirroring the tetragonal symmetry breaking observed in the normal state. Near the zone center, in contrast, the superconducting gap vanished in our study, consistent with earlier reports, and may be related to the emergence of an isotropic Fermi surface there. The discovery of a substantial gap at the zone corner provides crucial evidence for the theory of unconventional superconductivity originating from a mixture of antidimer and nested dirac bands, and suggests that the superconducting state is stabilized by a combination of all these factors across the entire $\bf k$-space. The variation of superconducting gap sizes across different locations within the $\bf k$-space may be addressed by a suitable BCS-BEC crossover criterion, and offers an insightful perspective on the complex interplay between electron interactions, crystal structure, and superconductivity in iron-based materials.

We establish the equivalence between the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the superbosonization formula using the Hamiltonian formulation of the Weyl-Wigner transform. This equivalence is demonstrated for both even and odd fermion numbers. Furthermore, we apply a modified version of the superbosonization transformation to show that the one-dimensional Hubbard model can be represented using a pair of decoupled massless dipolar boson models. This involves using the Weyl-Wigner transform in conjunction with the Hamiltonian formulation. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the ground states of the original and bosonized models as the interaction strength varies. Our study employs the Weyl-Wigner representation to analyze the one-dimensional Hubbard model at half-filling. We examine the interplay between electron-electron interactions, electron condensates, and dual fermion dynamics within the ground state. This enables the identification of distinct superfluid and insulating phases based on the zero-temperature dynamical correlation functions of the electrons. Our findings provide a new perspective on the phase structure of the one-dimensional Hubbard model. This research is significant as it paves the way for applying bosonization to more complex models and facilitates the study of interacting boson systems using the Weyl-Wigner representation. Our study is relevant to ongoing experimental research on ultra-thin electron intercalation materials that can be well-approximated by the one-dimensional Hubbard model. These materials, such as O$_3$-TiSe$_2$ and Ta$_2$Te$_3$, exhibit strong interactions, strong correlations, and strong dipolar interactions that can give rise to unique ground states and the possibility of emergent mass and other exotic phenomena. The standard model predicts that the top quark will exhibit a zero spin asymmetry when produced with a single polarized $W$ boson. By analyzing top quark decays to leptons and jets, both experiments found results that deviated from the standard model's expectation. The ATLAS collaboration found a spin asymmetry value of $0.25\pm0.09$ in $8$ TeV data and $0.08\pm0.09$ in $13$ TeV data. We investigate how the thickness of LaNiO$_3$ layers in superlattices made from LaNiO$_3$/LaMnO$_3$ influences their transport properties.  By examining a variety of different thicknesses of LaNiO$_3$, ranging from 1.5 to 10.5 atomic layers, we discover both LaNiO$_3$ layers with a small number of layers that behave like liquids and show a significant change in resistance with temperature change, as well as an unexpected increase in resistance with decreasing temperature when the thickness of LaNiO$_3$ is between 4-6 layers.  We suggest that this unexpected increase in resistance with decreasing temperature is due to an imbalance in the competing interlayer tunneling and intergranular transport in this specific thickness range.  We also discover that thicker LaNiO$_3$ layers with a resistance that is less dependent on temperature behave more like solids. In this work, we examine the relationship between ToM and the ability to generate conversation, with a focus on the capacity to respond to statements that are either true or false about the interlocutor. This outcome highlights the significance of integrating ToM into the generation process, as it enables the creation of more coherent and plausible conversations. We have created MG-GLAM, a new code that uses the tree multi-grid method to tackle N-body problems in computational physics. This code takes a given set of positions and corresponding gravitational potentials as input, allowing it to compute new positions and potentials through N-body N-time N-step interactions for a specified time period. MG-GLAM builds upon the structure of an earlier code called Entgarn, with significant enhancements that utilize multiple CPU cores and integrate a sophisticated algorithm from the Gadget-2 code to reduce computational costs by approximately a factor of ten, when solving the same set of the same N-body problems, for moderate to large N. Additionally, MG-GLAM includes a range of innovative features that enhance the performance and flexibility of the code, such as an adjustable time-step algorithm and the ability to handle diverse types of particles with distinct masses and interaction properties. Although initially designed for multi-Messenger Astronomy-related N-body simulations, MG-GLAM can address a broader range of computational challenges in astrophysics and other fields. As this code is an open-source project, it is available for free download at the appropriate website. Furthermore, MG-GLAM comes with an open-source license that permits users to modify and distribute the code freely, with the condition that they contribute any significant improvements back to the community. As an added benefit, the code includes a comprehensive set of test cases and benchmark problems that can be used to evaluate its performance and validate new developments against established benchmarks. We develop the chordal Schramm--Loewener evolution (CSLE) in the context of a randomly evolving curve in the Riemann sphere, under a localization that ensures the existence of an analytic surface associated with the curve for a limited time. This surface, described as an "imaginary" object in the complex analysis book of Chen, Geng, and Wang, divides the Riemann sphere into two regions, with one region containing a growing disk-shaped area. We demonstrate that any stationary, unit-density CSLE surface in the Riemann sphere is equivalent to a combination of a time-dependent conformal mapping and a standard L\'{e}vy process, specifically the radial part of a chordal Brownian motion, for a finite time duration. This surface evolution model encompasses various types of growth on the Riemann sphere, including the Schramm--Loewener evolution and the chordal L\'{e}vy process, for which we derive local and stationary surface parametrizations. We also establish the existence, uniqueness, and stationarity of CSLE surfaces in the Riemann sphere, as well as the existence and uniqueness of a CSLE surface parametrization for a given stationary unit-density CSLE process. Finally, we establish a representation for a unit-density CSLE surface through a combination of a time-dependent conformal mapping and a standard chordal Brownian motion process. The surface evolution model provides a new perspective on the types of growth on the Riemann sphere, including the Schramm--Loewener evolution and the chordal L\'{e}vy process. The linearized approach to analyzing turbulent reactive mixtures relies on a single equilibrium solution from a set of adiabatic combustion models, with the eddy-permeable model recently being found to provide the best fit. This model can be expressed through a system of algebraic equations, with solutions determined by an appropriate selection of degrees of freedom, or parameters, that describe the reaction front's properties. By leveraging the concept of mass action, the model can be represented as a polynomial system with respect to chemical species concentrations, enabling the examination of the model's thermodynamic consistency. A numerical method, based on the interlacing theorem, can efficiently identify the real solutions to this system of equations by organizing the model's parameters into a hierarchy. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to one kinetic energy release parameter model, resulting in the organization of model solutions in a hierarchical order. This hierarchical structure is then analyzed in relation to the mixing intensity and fuel concentration variables. By exploring the models' parameter hierarchies, valuable insights can be gained that are essential for developing and testing numerical methods for simulating turbulent reactive mixtures. These methods typically utilize the linearized approach as a building block and rely on the representation of equilibrium reactive front solutions. Consequently, this understanding can inform the development of simulation tools that accurately predict the behavior of turbulent reactive mixtures. Furthermore, this method can also provide a framework for evaluating the performance of numerical solvers in simulating reactive mixture simulations. By leveraging this method, a potential limitation of the concept of mass action has been identified, which may have implications for the development and assessment of numerical solvers, particularly those that employ the eddy-permeable model. Additionally, this method can facilitate the comparison of different combustion models by organizing the model solutions in a hierarchy based on their thermodynamic properties, which can provide a foundation for evaluating the models' performance in various scenarios. Recent advancements in Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) have been fueled by various research approaches, but a unifying design framework for them is lacking so far. As a result, existing CRDT theories often focus on specific designs, resulting in a dispersed knowledge base. This study aims to provide a comprehensive design framework that encompasses various Conflict-free Replicated Data Types, facilitating a unified theoretical understanding of them. By leveraging this framework, we are able to establish precise definitions and categorizations of these types, as well as identify key properties that drive their behavior. Furthermore, this design framework enables us to categorize multiple established CRDTs, including Counter, Map, Set, Multi-Counter, Multi-Map, and Multi-Sets, as specific instances. With this framework in place, we are also able to define a general approach to designing new Conflict-free Replicated Data Types. To illustrate this, we present an innovative new data type called MultiCounterMap, a counter-based data type with multiple counters stored within a map, and show how it behaves correctly even across different network protocols. This design framework and the newly introduced MultiCounterMap example provide a foundation for designing new Conflict-free Replicated Data Types and encourage the exploration of additional novel data types. This study is available online at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03056. It has been presented at PODC 2022.

The distinction between weak and strong shocks lies in their ability to propagate at sub- and supersonic speeds, respectively. In one-dimensional flows, the classification of shocks as weak or strong is determined by the initial conditions. This classification can change over time as the shocks move and the flow evolves, influenced by the transport equation governing shock strength and a first-integral of the Euler equations in the absence of heat conduction or diffusion. We examine the dynamics of weak-strong shock transitions in one-dimensional flows, identifying conditions under which such transitions occur and analyzing the role of initial conditions, location, and velocity of the shock in determining the outcome. Our analysis shows that when the shock is located near a critical point, where the flow velocity changes abruptly, and has a moderate strength, it may transition from being weak to strong. This transition can happen either gradually, as the shock is strengthened by the downstream flow, or suddenly, as the shock is weakened by the upstream flow. We also find that when the shock is located far from a critical point and has a strong initial velocity, it remains strong; in contrast, when the shock is located near a critical point and has a low initial velocity, it remains weak. We analyze the role of the shock's velocity in determining the outcome and find that it can be understood by considering the velocity of the shock as a control parameter of the Euler equations' flow map. We validate our theoretical analysis with numerical simulations of the Euler equations using a strong shock as an initial condition, showing that the outcome depends on the shock's velocity at the time of formation. We also discuss implications of our findings for the transition of weak shocks to strong shocks in multi-dimensional flows. Ultimately, we find that while the dynamics of weak-strong shock transitions are complex and influenced by various factors, they can be understood through a simple analysis of the shock's dynamics in one-dimensional flows. This understanding provides new insights into the nature of shocks and may inform research on the transition of weak shocks to strong shocks in multi-dimensional flows. Despite significant advancements in natural language generation, much of the research has focused on measures such as accuracy and consistency, while the diversity of generated text has often been sacrificed for the sake of these goals. In our work, we aim to enhance the semantic diversity of pre-trained text models through a technique called "diversified sampling," which involves creating a pool of models to sample from based on their mutual information. By applying this diversified sampling method to a neural dialogue system, we successfully increased the semantic diversity of generated responses without compromising consistency and accuracy. Our results show a notable increase in the diversity of generated text, as measured by the minimum difference required to distinguish two sentences, with only a minor decrease in consistency and essentially no change in accuracy. Furthermore, we found that the model's diversity can be fine-tuned to suit various applications by adjusting the threshold for mutual information. To facilitate further research, we made the code and data for our diversified dialogue system publicly available. By addressing the semantic diversity shortcoming of language models, we hope to provide a useful tool for researchers seeking to evaluate the true semantic variety of generated text. Additionally, our diversified sampling technique can be applied to any text generation task that employs a generation-to-one setting. Hydrogen burning in low-mass stars and brown dwarfs is influenced by several factors including rotation, magnetic fields, and external stimuli. The behavior of this process is highly dependent on the object's angular momentum, which affects convection and thermal regulation through the Schwarzschild criterion. The objects' angular momentum is represented by $\tau_{\rm rot}$, which is compared to $\tau_{\rm conv}$ and $\tau_{\rm mag}$. The limits of these parameters are used to create a ternary diagram to map possible outcomes. The objects' thermal states are classified along the $\tau_{\rm conv}$-$\tau_{\rm mag}$ plane based on convective stability and thermal penetration depth. The $\tau_{\rm rot}$-$\tau_{\rm conv}$-$\tau_{\rm mag}$ diagram helps illustrate how the weak internal heat source in ultracool objects may lead to freeze-out of hydrogen burning, and how this process is affected by the angular momentum threshold, beyond which magnetic breaking dominates. Objects with magnetic fields that manage to maintain convective envelopes can host stable or unstable convection, while those with lost magnetic fields may have stable convection if the magnetic field decay is rapid enough. The diagram also shows how external stimuli, such as tidal interactions, can influence the weak internal heat source in ultracool objects. This is particularly relevant given the increasing number of discovered tidally synchronized brown dwarfs and low-mass stars. Finally, the diagram may provide insights into future radial velocity surveys and the detection of exoplanets in low-mass stars and brown dwarfs. It is also a useful tool for modeling hydrogen burning in low-mass stars and brown dwarfs, and can help identify potential targets for biosignature searches in ultracool objects in the near future. The implications of this study are particularly relevant given the upcoming launch of the James Webb Space Telescope and the Euclid and PLATO missions in 2023-2025. The model predictions are compared to data for the Hubble Radial Velocity Survey and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey, as well as the most massive exoplanets and the coolest T dwarfs. It is found that the objects with the highest surface gravities, such as the hottest M dwarfs and the reddest M dwarfs with esoteric chemistry, tend to have the highest masses, and are therefore likely to be the strongest radial velocity variables. This paper introduces a novel approach to estimating hadron decay density distributions using artificial neural networks, and applies this method to calculate decay densities for specific $B$ meson decays. By training the network on a large dataset of $B$ meson decays with known density distributions, we can make accurate predictions for new, unseen data. We report on the development of a dataset containing $B^0\rightarrow K^0_\mu \mu^-$ decays with precise measurement of decay density distributions, and demonstrate that neural network predictions excel in this context. Furthermore, we compare these results to alternative methods employing Mitchell's algorithm and decision trees, and find that neural network performances consistently outmatch these methods. In particular, we find that neural network predictions of density distributions display a high level of accuracy, with an RMSD of $\approx 0.0033$ for quark density and $\approx 0.0023$ for antiquark density. Additionally, we successfully extend this approach to $B^0\rightarrow K^0_\mu \mu^-\mu^+$ decays with complementary kinematic cuts, and showcase the network's sensitivity to scalar resonances in this decay channel. With this method showing great promise, we anticipate it to become a valuable tool for analyzing this and other related decay channels at future $B$-factory experiments.

We present a comprehensive jet model that addresses the limitations of traditional approaches, which typically require separate models for ultra-relativistic and non-relativistic afterglows. Our new framework seamlessly connects the two regimes, providing a consistent description from highly relativistic to non-relativistic velocities through a gradual transition. This model successfully bridges the gap between afterglows in both limits, making it suitable for interpreting observational data across various velocity ranges. We calculate the synchrotron radiation spectrum and associated energy flux for each specific relativistic and non-relativistic scenario, covering from highly relativistic to moderately non-relativistic afterglows. Our new model also takes into account the effects of magnetic fields on the relativistic pair populations, enabling a more accurate assessment of electromagnetic emissions. Furthermore, our model incorporates the influence of external photon fields on the synchrotron process. Additionally, we provide a publicly accessible code that utilizes our model, allowing for quick comparison with observational data through light curves, spectra, and distributions of brightness temperatures. With our new model, we re-analyze the sample of gamma-ray burst afterglows and the data on GRB-SWIFT-EROES correlations. Our model's code is available at https://github.com/zhmyk/3D-Jet-Model, along with the data necessary for the analysis presented in this study. In the context of graph drawing, identifying a minimal set of split vertices in a bipartite graph can be beneficial in creating planar representations. This research introduces an iterative algorithm for determining a minimal set of split vertices in bipartite graphs, which allows for planar representations through vertex splitting. The algorithm's application in finding a maximum weighted matching is also explored, and it demonstrates promising, albeit less competitive, results against established methods. The algorithm's source code is made available for review and use. Future directions for improvement and investigation are also discussed. Deep learning models in the classification domain have achieved remarkable success, yet they often suffer from a fundamental flaw: being poorly calibrated. This issue is particularly pronounced when dealing with imbalanced datasets, as the models' lack of calibration can significantly hinder their performance in critical applications, such as ranking and decision-making. Consequently, various post-training calibration techniques have been devised to refine the models, enhancing their reliability. Nevertheless, the impact of these methods has not been thoroughly assessed, particularly in scenarios with significant class imbalance. In this research, we thoroughly investigate the effect of different calibration methods, including temperature scaling, vanilla Wasserstein calibration, entropic regularization, and Hoffman bound calibration, among others, on deep learning models dealing with class imbalance. Our experimental findings, encompassing a range of datasets and scenarios, reveal that while the calibration methods generally improve the models' performance, they can sometimes exacerbate the impact of imbalance, depending on the specific conditions. Moreover, we introduce a novel metric, the normalized expected calibration error, which provides a unified framework for comparing the calibration effectiveness of different models confronted with imbalance. Our research offers valuable insights into the design of deep learning models and calibration algorithms for imbalanced datasets, along with concrete recommendations to balance the trade-off between calibration and prediction accuracy. Furthermore, we make the code, models, and datasets employed in this research openly available, along with the calibrated models, to facilitate further exploration and advancement of this critical issue. In the process, we also introduce a comprehensive, easy-to-use PyTorch toolkit, known as PyTorch Calib, designed to facilitate seamless access to a broad spectrum of calibration methods and efficient comparison of their performance. This comprehensive toolkit, encompassing 24 distinct calibration techniques, is fully integratable with popular deep learning libraries like PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Keras, making it an indispensable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to refine and compare the calibration of deep learning models. In our research, we also introduce a novel Hoffman bound calibration method, characterized by an efficient implementation, a user-friendly API, and exceptional flexibility, along with an innovative way to estimate the calibration error. Ultimately, our research is aimed at catalyzing a collaborative effort to address the crucial issue of calibration in deep learning models, especially when dealing with imbalanced datasets, to ultimately ensure the safety and reliability of these models in real-world applications. Closed-loop feedback control systems in bipedal robots are comparable to optimal, gravity-resistant walking trajectories when gait cycles are 1 second long, according to a study. This research analyzes the resilience of these walking paths in relation to gait cycle duration. The findings show that these robust walking paths can withstand variations in gait cycle length up to 30% without losing stability. The study also demonstrates that using a limited number of state measurements for feedback control can produce stable walking patterns, even with longer gait cycles. In addition, the research compares the performance of feedback control using optimal walking trajectories and that of a simpler, non-optimal approach. The results indicate that feedback control can produce stable walking patterns using both methods, but the optimal approach yields more stable and durable walking patterns. The study further explores the potential for these robust walking patterns to be applied across various robot sizes, demonstrating that smaller robots can walk stably using larger robot trajectories and vice versa. However, there are limitations to this size transfers, especially for longer gait cycles. The research also examines the impact of changing step length and leg mass on walking stability, revealing that these factors can compromise the stability of robust walking patterns, especially with longer gait cycles. We analyze the decidability of tuned Hensel lifting algorithms for power series fields over fields of characteristic zero, taking into consideration an infinite field condition. When the field is not infinite, we prove the effectiveness of combining an infinite field condition with an additional condition on the residue map's injectivity, resulting in the decidability of the power series field's geometry via its parametric representation. However, we demonstrate that over infinite fields, the power series field's geometry cannot be deterministically determined from its parameters. Additionally, we establish the undecidability of the power series field's algebraic structure when the base field is infinite. Furthermore, we find instances of fields and series fields over those fields that cannot be deterministically determined from their parameters. Lastly, we explore the decidability implications for the power series field's algebraic structure when the base field's algebraic structure is decidable, resulting in the requirement for the base field's ability to determine its own additive and multiplicative groups implicitly. Finally, we identify specific requirements for the power series field's algebraic structure to be implicitly determinable, involving the ability to determine implicit values of series and their derivatives at zero, given their values and derivatives at any point, a fundamental ability referred to as the strong implicit determinability property. We demonstrate that this strong implicit determinability property holds for fields, complex numbers, and Laurent series over non-zero elements, as well as series fields over non-zero elements and fields of characteristic zero. However, we show that this property fails for Laurent series over zero, series fields over zero, and fields of positive characteristic two. Moreover, we explore the relationship between the strong implicit determinability property and the ability to determine implicit values of polynomials, resulting in the requirement for the base field's ability to determine implicit values of polynomials with coefficients from the base field. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of Flush+Reload attacks in detecting memory disclosures, but these techniques are impractical due to their high computational cost in each attack, making them expensive to implement in a low-entropy context. To address this limitation, we present HyperDegrade, a technique that enhances the efficiency of Flush+Reload attacks by (1) reducing the required time granularity from milliseconds to microseconds and (2) decreasing the number of necessary traces from thousands to just over a hundred. By leveraging a custom high-precision timer and attack optimization strategies, HyperDegrade significantly improves the technique's effectiveness while minimizing the computational burden. Our results show that HyperDegrade can achieve accurate detection rates in various applications, including the detection of sensitive memory disclosures in popular desktop and web applications, the detection of SgxOcall access control in Intel SGX, and the detection of out-of-order combi-Flushes in combination with other techniques. We also demonstrate the feasibility of HyperDegrade on an embedded platform, showcasing its potential for Flush+Reload attacks on resource-constrained devices. In conclusion, HyperDegrade represents a groundbreaking enhancement for Flush+Reload attacks, making them more efficient while maintaining the same level of effectiveness, and paves the way for the development of more sophisticated attack techniques. Moreover, we introduce a new benchmark, HyperBench, designed to evaluate the efficiency and efficacy of various Flush+Reload attack techniques. This benchmark is available for download at: https://github.com/hyperdegrade/hyperbench. We have released HyperDegrade as an open-source project, and it can be accessed via the following repository: https://github.com/hyperdegrade/hyperdegrade. We have also published a paper detailing our research, which has been accepted for presentation at USENIX Security 2022.

The discrepancy in the muon's magnetic moment, specifically the anomaly in $g-2$, could be explained by the presence of a scalar or fermionic new physics at a scale of around 500-1000 GeV, a finding that contradicts the notion of New Physics lying beyond the reach of the LHC. In this study, we examine the possibility of interpreting these particles as dark matter constituents within the framework of an $SU(3)_C \otimes SU(3)_L \otimes U(1)_X$ gauge model. By adjusting the quantum numbers of the new physics particles, we can make them stable or almost stable, capable of making up the remaining 4-dimensional dark matter, thus providing a direct connection between the $g-2$ anomaly and dark matter. Additionally, we analyze the circumstances under which these new physics particles can become multi-TeV in mass, even with the constraint imposed by the non-observation of them at the LHC. We also investigate the prospects for detecting these new physics particles at the LHC in its upgraded form, as well as in future leptonic colliders, such as the ILC or CLIC, with the latter potentially providing access to dark matter itself via direct detection or via the reconstruction of missing energy in combination with electro-weak precision data. The findings indicate that while the multi-TeV reach of the LHC or a future 100 TeV hadron collider may be necessary for a comprehensive understanding, the ILC at 1 TeV to 3 TeV has a strong potential to uncover these new physics particles and make significant inroads into solving the $g-2$ anomaly and the dark matter problem. The implications of this research extend beyond the $g-2$ anomaly to other anomalies, such as those in $B$-physics or the $(g-2)_u$. The constraints and new physics solutions to these anomalies could be the subject of a separate study. By examining the highest kachey (knees) of the image and how they relate to the pull-back of valuations from the image, we are able to show that the kachey of the image correspond exactly to the kachey of the domain in a harmonic map. This understanding allows us to visualize the structure of the image by analyzing the kachey of the domain and how they map under a harmonic map. This visualization capability is particularly useful when dealing with highly degenerate harmonic maps. By analyzing the structure of the image and how it is composed of the pull-back of rational function semifields from the image, we are able to derive a complete description of the structure of the image for a harmonic map from a tropical curve. This description enables us to visualize the structure of the image by examining the composition of the map and the structure of the domain. This understanding of the structure of the image is an essential component of our investigation into the connectedness of the space of harmonic maps between tropical curves. By examining the connectedness of the space of harmonic maps from a tropical curve to another, we are able to show that this space is disconnected if and only if there exists a harmonic map from the domain to a tropical curve that has a non-trivial kachey in the image. This study introduces a pairing of cocycles integrated from a combination of the Seifert form and a variation of the Casson invariant, resulting in an expanded set of invariants for knots within an integral lattice. This development arises from the recognition that certain combinations of the Seifert form and the extended Casson invariant, typically related by cocycles, yield distinct and independent knot invariants, providing a comprehensive understanding of the extended Casson invariant in relation to the Seifert form. These integrated cocycles demonstrate closure under the knot sum operation, representing a fundamental aspect of the Casson invariant's properties. As such, they constitute fundamental building blocks for the casson invariant in its integral form. Furthermore, this framework facilitates the creation of new, universally normalized knot invariants by integrating a wide range of cocycles with respect to the extended Casson invariant, offering numerous outcomes, including several explicitly computed examples. Notably, some of these integrated cocycles exhibit direct connections to various volume and hyperbole mutations of knots. Additionally, this development enables the definition of a 2-cocycle, denoted as Z(L), by integrating a specific combination of the Seifert form and the extended Casson invariant, resulting in a universally normalized knot invariant. Z(L) demonstrates closure under the knot sum operation and multiplicativity at the level of natural maps, indicating it forms part of the ring structure for the extended Casson invariant in its integral form. Several volumes and hyperbole mutations of knots have directly computable values for Z(L), while others have an unknown value. Notably, Z(L) exhibits a significant connection to the Kontsevich's integral, facilitating the direct computation of (Z(L) * K(L^(bar)))(t), yielding a combinatorial expression that matches the expected outcome, indicating that Z(L) aligns with the properties defined by the Kontsevich's conjecture. Consequently, this implies that Z(L) can be interpreted as a refinement of the LMO invariant. Moreover, this relationship enables the definition of a 2-cocycle, denoted as Z(W), for knots within an integral lattice, derived from combining the Seifert form and the extended LMO invariant, resulting in a universally normalized knot invariant. Z(W) demonstrates closure under the knot sum operation and multiplicativity at the level of natural maps, indicating it forms part of the ring structure for the extended LMO invariant in its integral form. Researchers explored the link between massive compact stars and the smallest neutrino mass state, assuming a normal neutrino mass ordering, in their latest findings. Using a range of microscopic interactions that connect neutrinos to stars and relying on relativistic mean-field theory for the stellar properties, they limited the magnitude of these interactions based on the stability of white dwarfs and neutron stars. The restrictions on anti-neutrino nucleon interactions were established by setting an upper bound on the maximum neutron star mass at $2M_{\odot}$. The data allowed for the determination of a minimum value for the smallest neutrino mass, found to be around 5-10 times more substantial than the current experimental limit, set by the half-life of Co-57. The matrix operation'matmul' is the most frequently called Python function in popular machine learning frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, representing the core building block of linear transformations and neural network connections. Despite its simplicity,'matmul' can lead to substantial computational costs when dealing with large input matrices. To address this, leveraging parallel computing through multiprocessing can provide a viable solution. However, implementing parallel'matmul' efficiently is not as straightforward due to issues like data parallelism, model parallelism, and communication overhead. In this research, we present novel strategies for parallel'matmul' that cater to both data and model parallelism, along with corresponding system design recommendations. Our proposed methods are then integrated into Python-based deep learning frameworks and extensively evaluated across various computational platforms, showcasing exceptional performance gains with minimal additional overhead. Our parallel'matmul' implementations, along with relevant framework modifications, are made publicly accessible to inspire further research and enable direct reproducibility of our findings. Furthermore, we outline computational cost reductions achievable through parallelization, accompanied by detailed analysis of performance, memory, and throughput metrics. To facilitate seamless adoption in machine learning system builders, we provide actionable guidance, encompassing adjustable parameter settings and corresponding performance outcomes, to aid in balancing performance against memory consumption and additional overhead. Our research and findings are supplemented by the open-source Python code, allowing for direct replication and usage within Python-based deep learning contexts. The code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/hpc-etras/parmatmul-4hpc. Our study aims to contribute to the acceleration of machine learning system building through high-performance computing, facilitating faster training and inference while reducing memory consumption, with potential applications in various computational domains. To further the discussion on matrix operation acceleration and machine learning system building through high-performance computing, we invite readers to explore our research and share their perspectives, suggestions, and related research, accessible at https://hpc-etras.github.io/parmatmul-4hpc/. In multi-agent systems, tasks often vary in difficulty, with some demanding high levels of capability and others requiring little. The task selection problem arises when an agent must decide which task to undertake, considering factors like reward potential and required capability. This problem becomes particularly challenging in dynamic environments, where task availability and difficulty change rapidly. Our research investigates how the distribution of task difficulties influences the effectiveness of a simple learning algorithm in a complex environment. We demonstrate that an intelligent adversary design, aimed at exploiting the challenges faced by an unsophisticated agent in discovering optimal solutions, can indeed succeed. Additionally, we show that in static environments, our agent employs a strategy of risk-aversion, favoring easier tasks over more lucrative but more difficult ones. In contrast, in dynamic environments, our agent adopts a strategy of risk-seeking, preferring tasks that balance difficulty and reward potential. Our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of how agents make decisions in the presence of capability-based challenges and may inform the design of more sophisticated algorithms capable of handling dynamic, capability-dependent tasks. We introduce an innovative approach to modeling task selection problems, drawing parallels with load balancing and queueing theory. Our method involves an analytical approach to modeling agent decision-making, leveraging large deviations theory to analyze the behavior of our algorithm in static environments. In dynamic settings, we employ a sampling approach to determine the effectiveness of our algorithm. Our research is complemented by the development of an open-source simulator, allowing for the efficient evaluation of algorithms in dynamic environments. This simulator facilitates the rapid testing of new algorithms and includes a simple learning algorithm as a baseline, with source code available at the specified link. Our research is an initial step towards addressing the task selection problem in dynamic environments and invites further exploration and the development of more advanced algorithms. The designed simulator is versatile and can be applied to various multi-agent system problems, involving capability-based decision-making. The underlying theory provides a general framework for evaluating the behavior of our algorithm and can be applied to distinct problem domains, provided the underlying dynamics are sufficiently similar. The simplicity of our learning algorithm invites replacement with more complex algorithms, with potential enhancements including the incorporation of value-based methods, such as Q-learning, and more sophisticated sampling approaches, such as Monte-Carlo methods. As the underlying theory is domain-agnostic, we anticipate the general applicability of our approach to capability-based decision-making problems, with potential relevance to the study of agent decision-making in scientific domains, such as economics and political science. To achieve a deeper understanding of the Higgs boson and develop more comprehensive theories in particle physics, the next generation of precision research will rely heavily on cutting-edge experiments at the LHC, the ILC, the Future e+e- Colliders, the CLIC, and the LHeC. In this research, we explore the potential for using data from these experiments to study the rare decay of the Higgs boson, specifically Higgs boson physics, and also investigate the rare magnetic dipole moments of the top and bottom quarks, closely linked to this decay. Given the theoretical limitations of current time-sensitive constraints, we employ multi-dimensional global fits to evaluate the impact of these experiments on the evolution of these physics phenomena, taking into consideration various new physics scenarios at the scale of the LHC or slightly above. Our research indicates that, even with the LHC at its maximum capacity, its rare Higgs boson decay data will be highly sensitive to a wide range of new physics theories, with an expected precision of better than $10^{-4}$ when combined with top quark data. Furthermore, this research shows that the LHeC and future e+e- Colliders will significantly enhance this sensitivity by a factor of five to ten, respectively. In addition, this study highlights the importance of combining all relevant data from these experiments, as this will significantly enhance the sensitivity to a wide range of new physics theories at the LHC or slightly above, or even new physics scenarios at the scale of the ILC or slightly above, as an essential step in achieving this level of sensitivity. In the context of several new physics scenarios, this research provides a detailed assessment of how the rare Higgs boson decay and the rare magnetic dipole moments of the top and bottom quarks are affected by new physics, as well as an expected level of precision that can be achieved by the LHC, the LHeC, and future e+e- Colliders, and suggests that these research areas have the potential to provide highly sensitive constraints on a wide range of new physics theories, making them crucial components of a comprehensive research agenda in particle physics beyond the LHC era. In addition, this research offers a detailed assessment of how the rare Higgs boson decay and the rare magnetic dipole moments of the top and bottom quarks are linked, as well as theoretical limitations and potential experimental approaches to study these phenomena at future colliders. Approximating kernel methods like Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Gaussian Process (GP) typically employs Random Fourier Features (RFF), which generates pseudo-random Fourier features to reduce the feature dimension. However, the RFF method's randomness leads to inconsistent performance and decreased accuracy in prediction. In contrast, Pseudo-Random Fourier Features (PRFF) generate deterministic equivalent Fourier features using a known distribution, effectively reducing features dimensions while maintaining consistent prediction accuracy across multiple iterations. This paper demonstrates the theoretical increase in feature dimensions offered by PRFF, comparing it to RFF's pseudo-feature counterparts. Furthermore, our results show that PRFF's deterministic features yield better and more stable logistic regression predictions when compared to RFF. Lastly, we show that PRFF can provide an alternative to the expensive GP hyperparameter optimization process by achieving comparable validation sets accuracy with significantly reduced training time. Our method demonstrates particular success in time-sensitive applications, such as online settings where models need to be rapidly trained and deployed. We provide a practical example of this efficiency gain in the context of GP hyperparameter optimization. A companion implementation is available at the address indicated in the reference section.

This study introduces Cartesian Decomposition as a multifaceted mathematical framework, encompassing regular group actions, diagonal groups, and solvable groups operating through direct products of involutions. The underlying theory is illustrated using the configuration of reflection groups over finite fields, and the concept of Cartesian Vectors is explored to facilitate group classification. The proposed framework offers a novel, unified approach to examining group properties and dynamics. By leveraging this framework, a distinctive group, found within the parameterized reflection group family, is identified and its dynamical properties are analyzed using Cartesian Decomposition, revealing a resilient rotation in a higher-dimensional space. The research also provides the rotating group's expression and accompanying diagrams, offering a comprehensive understanding of the phenomenon. The study also explores the relationship between this high-dimensional rotation and the quadratic field's infinite nature. The research is relevant to ongoing work on the classification of dynamical components arising from infinite group actions over the rational numbers. The studied reflection group's dynamical component is shown to persist across infinite extensions of the rational numbers and global fields' infinite extensions, as demonstrated using the field of finite fields' infinite extensions. The research also establishes a connection between the superhyperbolicity of this dynamical component and the rational field's infinite extensions' infinite nature. The research is further validated by the emergence of this group in contexts involving the infinite proliferation of roots of polynomials over the rational field. Kirchler's Ph.D. thesis, supervised by the author, where a fundamental group is developed to analyze the dynamics of a continuously expanding arc pattern, based on a geometrically defined monodromy group. A multitude of deep learning methods for cardiac image analysis has flourished in recent years, with several prominent approaches including U-Net, U-Net variants, attention UNet, and Lie groups-based models. While research on cardiac multi-organ segmentation has made significant progress, a comprehensive evaluation of these models across various datasets and pathological conditions remains limited. To address this, we present a comprehensive assessment of 12 deep learning models, comparing their performance in segmenting four cardiac structures from four datasets containing diverse ranges of pathologies. Our findings indicate that model complexity is matched by complexity in pathology, with simpler models exceling in scenarios with fewer lesions. Conversely, more complex models thrive in scenarios with extensive lesions. Our research offers a thorough evaluation of cardiac multi-organ segmentation models and their adaptability across different datasets and pathological conditions, providing valuable insights for selecting appropriate models for specific clinical applications and potentially informing the development of more robust and transferable models. The code and datasets are available at: https://github.com/gh0stfk/Cardiac-MOS-Eval. The study has been accepted for presentation at MICCAI 2022.

This research focuses on developing a robust framework for modeling the degradation of materials with spatially varying properties, particularly in the presence of brittle damage. We draw from the theory of homogenization to create a suitable three-dimensional model, incorporating the effects of small-scale waves on material degradation. The proposed model consists of a nonlinear equation describing damage propagation, along with a heterogeneous material property tensor that varies in an oscillatory manner. The associated boundary value problems are formulated and analyzed to establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions, as well as the homogenization of the material tensor. The convergence of the homogenized tensor is demonstrated under minimal assumptions about the material properties, leading to a simplified two-dimensional model. The proposed framework effectively mitigates the development of singularities and bounds on the material tensor are derived, providing valuable insight into the homogenized tensor's behavior. The proposed model is further validated through numerical computations, showcasing its ability to capture the evolution of damage within materials exhibiting complex, heterogeneous behavior. The proposed model is also compared to a related recent study. The implications of wave propagation on material degradation are explored through an analytical investigation, as are the effects of material heterogeneity on wave behavior. The relative measures of stress and damage are examined to distinguish between material failure precipitated by waves and localized damage accumulation. The influence of material heterogeneity on wave behavior is explored through an analytical investigation of the homogenized model, revealing the emergence of second-order oscillations in the material tensor and implying the failure of the strong ellipticity condition. The proposed framework provides a suitable foundation for wave-damage interaction models and can inform the development of more advanced computational damage simulations. The proposed model's capabilities and limitations are discussed, as are potential avenues for further research and improvement. The associated computational toolkit is freely available online. The proposed framework is an essential precursor to computational damage simulations, as it addresses critical theoretical and computational challenges. The developed toolkit is an effective computational tool for modeling wave-induced damage propagation in heterogeneous materials, encompassing a broad range of applications, including the study of material degradation in construction, geophysics, and biomedical engineering, as well as research into the mechanics of materials and structures in civil engineering. The proposed framework is already being utilized in ongoing research projects by several international teams of scientists and engineers. The potential of the developed toolkit to address complex computational problems is evident in various fields beyond material science and structures, such as the analysis of cancer progression, research into earthquake dynamics, and the study of blood vessel physiology. The proposed framework is already being utilized in ongoing research projects

Furthermore, we introduce an innovative harvesting strategy that divides time into two parts: information transmission and energy transmission. Through mathematical optimization, we develop a generalized antenna-switching technique and examine its energy-proximity properties. Numerical analysis and simulations demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in achieving optimal energy efficiency and throughput performance. As the number of antennas increases, the Generalized AS's performance exhibits increasing proximity to optimal energy-proximity values. Moreover, the Generalized AS's performance is sensitive to changes in asymptotic parameters and network temperature, and it is less sensitive to heat generation. We also investigate the Generalized AS's performance in scenarios with and without heat generation, as well as in scenarios with and without information transmission costs. Furthermore, we examine the Generalized AS's performance in scenarios with increasing energy-proximity values, demonstrating its optimal energy-proximity performance. Lastly, we highlight the Generalized AS's potential for practical implementation in SWIPT-enabled networks.

This study undertakes a comprehensive analysis of the Base-Anchor Feature Pyramid Network (BA-FPN), a prominent building block of modern object detection algorithms. We first present an in-depth examination of the motivations underlying BA-FPN and subsequent object detection methods, followed by a clear segmentation of the component architecture of BA-FPN. To enhance the base network within this framework, we propose an iterative strategy known as the Progressive Base-Anchor strategy (PBA). In this approach, the base network is upgraded through successive substitutions of the feature extraction module, accompanied by a corresponding update of the anchor strategy. We demonstrate the efficacy of PBA by adapting BA-FPN to process images and employing it in two scenarios: single-image object detection and video object detection. Our experiments indicate that the PBA method successfully yields a 1.3% gain in mAP for the COCO dataset without employing additional resources like automatic annotation and temporal supervision. Furthermore, our findings show that the PBA method is highly effective in addressing scale issues in object detection. The code for our research has been made publicly accessible.

Recent studies utilizing the conditional distribution for tail analysis are limited to a single variable, whereas our research extends this framework to two interconnected variables. We have developed a bivariate conditional model that can accurately capture the tail characteristics of a specified quantity, taking into consideration the complex relationships between the two interconnected variables. The model incorporates the Bradley-Westfall rank correlation test as a method for identifying significant correlations, and it effectively estimates the tail index and shape parameters through a simulation-based approach. The proposed method is applied to a real-world example involving the analysis of tail characteristics of a portfolio consisting of two interconnected assets. Notably, our results indicate that when the assets in question are highly correlated, such as the combination of oil and a company operating within the oil industry, the model may struggle to provide a reliable estimation of the tail index and shape parameters. In contrast, less correlated assets, such as oil and the S\&P 500 index, yield more accurate parameter estimations. The model is openly available on an online repository. The implementation details of the proposed model are outlined in the supplementary materials provided along with relevant software codes. 

Keywords: Bivariate conditional tail distribution, Bradley-Westfall rank correlation test, tail index and shape parameters estimation.

Understanding language solely through text classification overlooks the nuances of language influence on machine learning models. To address this limitation, we are proposing a novel evaluation framework that assesses the capacity of models to grasp language context and predict word meanings. This framework involves a unique setup in which models are forced to anticipate words in a sequence of sentences, evaluating their ability to learn words' meanings from context and phonetic information. We demonstrate the challenges and advantages of this framework using 50 basic terms from the Dolch vocabulary, and it offers a valuable tool for analyzing the semantic capabilities of NLP models. Our experiments with this framework reveal that both transformer-based and linear models struggle to learn words' meanings in isolation, yet they exhibit better performance when given a list of words to choose from, implying a degree of semantic capacity. Nonetheless, our research indicates that these NLP models are largely insensitive to context and word forms when trained on text classification tasks. Consequently, we recommend developing more rigorous evaluation methods to ensure a deeper understanding of NLP models' semantic capabilities. The proposed framework is available online for public access.

The intricate dynamics of network disruption were recently quantified by assigning a precise measure to the size of an avalanche in response to the removal of a single node. This metric indicates the total number of nodes affected by the initial disruption, regardless of the distance from the starting point. It's observed that this avalanche size varies significantly among different network types, including both regular and random structures. Interestingly, when comparing these networks to their fragmented counterparts, the difference in avalanche size becomes minimal, implying a limited increase in the disorder. Notably, this minimal increase in disorder is sufficient to trigger a percolation transition within the network. Furthermore, the maximum size of an avalanche is found to correlate with the scaling of the network's largest component, which is driven by the number of nodes available for participation in the avalanche. It's also discovered that the optimal strategy for minimizing the impact of an avalanche involves targeting the smallest number of nodes possible to initiate a localized effect, rather than aiming for a more widespread effect. The diversity of network responses to single-node removals provides a unique framework for exploring complex network phenomena and may be applied to better understand other global effects resulting from local changes. In addition, the introduced measures can be utilized to assess the vulnerability of specific networks to the dissemination of hazards or the spread of information. Lastly, the universal characteristics of the avalanche size, evident across various network architectures, suggest that there are fundamental principles governing network reconfiguration in response to local disturbances. In the context of directed networks, the distribution of the avalanche size exhibits a universal relationship with the in-degree of the network's nodes, mirroring the structure of the network. This finding is coupled with the discovery that the disorder induced by a single removal remains minimal and that targeted attacks aim the same nodes over and over, which is intuitive, yet also implies that there are high-degree nodes waiting to be targeted in these networks. Lastly, the proposed framework can be applied to study the spread of information or hazards in complex networks, especially when the network architecture changes over time. In such dynamic scenarios, traditional targeted attack simulations are no longer valid, and a re-evaluation of the network's response is necessary to accurately assess the spread or decline of the disseminated information or hazard. As an example, this is explored in the context of social networks, where the network's architecture is modified to simulate the spread of information or a hazard, and the average avalanche size provides valuable insights into the effectiveness of targeted attacks or spreading mechanisms. Recurrence relations for Freud weights are significant in mathematics, particularly in the study of orthogonal polynomials. To date, comprehensive results have been limited to quartic weights or their specialized forms. This study introduces a novel, generalised sextic Freud weight based on an analytical expression that diverges from the standard Airy weight. By manipulating the generalized sextic Freud weight, we derive closed-form formulas for bounded and unbounded recurrence relations, providing a deeper understanding of the relationship between Freud and super-Airy weights. Additionally, the derived formulas demonstrate equivalent closed-form expressions for bounded and unbounded recurrence relations, establishing a connection between these weights and their quartic weight counterparts. Furthermore, this connection yields closed-form formulas for bounded and unbounded recurrence relations for the super-Airy weights, addressing a previously unexplored mathematical area. To validate the correctness of our closed-form formulas, numerical computations are performed, yielding exact results for key indices. This study is a comprehensive expansion of my previous paper, introducing new results and incorporating additional derivations and calculations. A novel design for an gravitational wave detector, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer, is presented, offering enhanced sensitivity through a innovative new approach. This proposed system takes advantage of a specially modified Sagnac interferometer, where changes in the configuration of the detector's test masses allow for a significant improvement in signal amplification, achieving up to two times greater sensitivity at 100 Hz compared to the upgraded AdVirN and LIGOPlus-1000 designs, without increasing detector strain, and with potential for further gains through backscattering reduction techniques. This design is relatively low-cost and technologically straightforward, making it an attractive consideration for next-generation gravitational wave detectors. In simulation tests, the sloshing-Sagnac's performance is evaluated against current and future detector designs, with promising indications of its effectiveness. In addition, this design facilitates a reduction in thermal noise through the repositioning of suspended test masses, allowing for a potential 2.5 times improvement in signal-to-noise ratio at 100 Hz, with implications for advanced future detectors. In this work, we tackle the high traffic volume caused by massive access transmissions in XL-MIMO systems and propose a novel nonorthogonal variable gain rapid access protocol called NOVR-XL-RAP. Our NOVR-XL-RAP design divides access users into two groups, prioritizing fast-access enabled for higher-gain signals in the nonorthogonal section and optimizing user gains for improved detection accuracy in the orthogonal section. By simulating a practical XL-MIMO scenario, we show that our proposed NOVR-XL-RAP leads to a significant increase in system capacity, a substantial improvement in throughput, and a notable reduction in latency compared to existing protocols. We also observe that NOVR-XL-RAP supports a notably higher traffic volume in XL-MIMO systems and provide insights into the protocol's performance under varying antenna configurations and user densities. Additionally, we highlight the practical implications of our findings and identify potential research areas within this domain.
