Accurate real-time organ tracking during minimally invasive surgery is crucial for enhancing intraoperative visualization and the detection of internal pathologies. Registering preoperative 3D models with actual intraoperative sensor data is the primary challenge. However, the accuracy of this registration is severely impacted by noisy sensor data, which can result in model drift. This study focuses on developing a robust real-time tracking framework for the kidney during surgery, leveraging a novel optimization technique called iterated L1 optimization. This approach is utilized for both initial alignment and continuous updating of the model position. We evaluate and compare our method with a conventional RANSAC-based framework and a state-of-the-art deep learning approach, through experiments conducted on 12 kidney cancer surgeries. Our results show that our technique achieves the highest accuracy, with a model position error of 4.4 mm, outperforming the L1 method (4.9 mm) and the deep learning approach (5.1 mm) with model drift addressed, demonstrating our method's capacity to maintain precision even with prolonged exposure to noisy sensor data. Our technique offers enhanced robustness and precision, making it suitable for real-time kidney tracking during surgery. Additionally, our method's efficiency enables registration updates at a rate of 1.44 Hz, supporting high-speed, low-latency display. This study presents a robust real-time tracking framework with implications for the enhanced visualization and detection of internal pathologies. It is available as a module for the 3Dslicer software platform.

While self-supervised learning has significantly progressed in recent times, estimating optical flow from a single image remains a challenging task in the field. Many studies have attempted to apply bidirectional matching to circumvent issues with occlusions, but these attempts have been limited due to the increased computational complexity involved. In contrast, our proposed method, SBFNet, leverages unidirectional matching while utilizing a learned cost volume module that can determine the direction of optical flow without resorting to additional supervision. To achieve this, SBFNet utilizes two key components: a learned cost module and a bidirectional matching module. The former enables the estimation of occlusions by utilizing a unidirectional approach and minimizing unnecessary computations, while the latter enables the refinement of estimates by modeling and reversing the bidirectional optical flow. By combining these two components, we were able to develop a method that learns self-supervised optical flow estimation without the need for additional supervision. Compared to the currently leading self-supervised method, SFNet, our proposed method demonstrates improved results on the MVSO dataset while matching the performance on the wild dataset, with both being datasets composed of easy cases. Moreover, our method demonstrates competitive results to the currently leading supervised method, OFNet, on the KITTI dataset, with only self-supervised learning. The code and model have been made available at the following link: https://github.com/zh1168/SBFNet.

A 2-factor in a graph G is considered even-2-factorable (E2F) if there exists a pair of edge-disjoint 2-factors in G, one even and the other odd, for the case of non-trivial graphs. An important question in this context is whether the combined parity of these two factors is significant in determining a graph's even-2-factorability. To address this, we focus on a subclass of cubic graphs, namely those derived from the Kautz construction. A key finding shows that these graphs have an E2F property linked to the presence of a particular odd 2-factor, known as a Kirkman triple system. Another crucial result reveals that this odd 2-factor can be freely 'rotated' with an E2-factorable graph. Building upon these insights, we establish a rotation system for odd 2-factors in these cubic graphs, thereby developing a method for determining an E2F factor in them. Finally, we explore the connections between the E2F property and the Kirkman triple system's components, and present open questions for further research. These achievements contribute to a deeper understanding of even-2-factorability in these cubic graphs, and provide a foundation for analogous studies in other graph types. As such, our results may also facilitate the examination of 2-factorability in certain group constructions, as well as related questions concerning the enumeration of graphs equipped with 2-factors. Additionally, our findings introduce novel terminology and definitions to accurately capture the concepts of even-2-factorability, 2-factor rotatability, and their related components. Lastly, a selection of the newly defined graphs, featuring their even-2-factorability, will be contributed to the library of E2F graphs, providing a valuable resource for future research in this area. In this paper, new results are achieved by strengthening and refining the modified Bateman-Horn Conjecture of Li, which deals with the frequency of prime values taken by a specific quadratic polynomial expression as inputs grow larger. Given an algebraic integer $\alpha$, a real number $b$, and a non-zero integer $q$, the paper considers the quantity $A(N, \alpha, b, q)$ which counts the instances of $x^2+bx+\alpha$ equaling a prime in the ring of integers of a totally real number field with Galois group $D_4$ or $A_4$, up to a Galois automorphism $\sigma$. For large enough values of $N$, the paper attempts to estimate the ratio of $A(N, \alpha, b, q)$ to $(N+1)/\phi(q)$, where $\phi$ represents the Euler totient function. By making Li's conjecture's additional assumptions, the paper is able to set an upper limit for this ratio, while dropping that assumption, the paper is able to set a lower limit. Given that Li's conjecture holds for a majority of cases with sufficiently large coefficients, the paper is able to set an estimate for the highest frequency of prime values for the quadratic polynomial expression, showing this frequency is less than any given small enough number. The paper also explores additional related conjectures, providing upper and lower limits for the frequency of prime values for certain cubic and quartic polynomial expressions. The paper's results for these expressions, however, are less definitive due to a lack of control over the coefficients. The paper's results for the quadratic polynomial expression are particularly notable, as they address a long-standing open question first identified as an unsolved problem by Hoheisel in 1930. The paper's results for the frequency of prime values for the quadratic polynomial expression, however, do not provide a direct solution to this problem. The paper's results for the frequency of prime values for the quadratic polynomial expression are achieved with a new approach, different from earlier attempts by Bombieri, Pomerance, and Schoof. The paper's results for the frequency of prime values for the quadratic polynomial expression are also limited to a specific type of polynomial, as opposed to more general types considered by Li in his modified Bateman-Horn Conjecture. System calls in a web language like PHP or Python are typically managed by the language's built-in functions, which serve as wrappers for core system functions. However, these wrappers are often poorly optimized for security and performance because they are written with a high-level programming style. Our research, called Timeloops, takes a novel approach by creating two sets of system call wrappers - a fast, low-level set for critical system calls and a secure, high-level set for the rest. To achieve this, we employ a technique called plasmid system call switching, which allows for seamless system call switching between the two sets depending on the system call being made. This method takes only a nanosecond to switch, which is virtually instantaneous. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that this system call switching can occur during system call execution, without the need to restart the system call or lose system consistency. We also present a performance comparison between the two sets of system call wrappers, which shows that the fast set outperforms the secure set by a significant margin, while the secure set outperforms the fast set by a much smaller margin. Overall, our research indicates that this system call switching technique can yield a substantial performance improvement, along with improved security, which can lead to better system call optimization. To further improve system call optimization, we also propose a technique called "system call speculation", which enables system calls to be speculated about during application execution, which can result in improved application performance. To achieve this, we employ a technique called "path prediction", which enables the prediction of system call paths during application execution, which can result in improved application security. We also present a performance comparison between the predicted system call paths and the actual system call paths, which shows that the predicted system call paths outperform the actual system call paths by a significant margin, which can lead to better system optimization. For example, our research demonstrates that the MySQL database engine can achieve a 30% improvement in performance using the Timeloops technique, which is a substantial improvement. We believe that our research can lead to better system optimization and may have implications for other high-level programming languages like Java and C#.

To tackle the high computational complexity of multiple target tracking (MTT) in scenarios with limited sensor fields of view or undetected targets, a new approach has been developed, reducing calculation demands dynamically. This dynamic method, known as the variable complexity multiple target tracking (VCMTT), utilizes a Bayesian estimation technique to evaluate all possible target states and their probabilities. VCMTT then selects the most critical states to update and predict, minimizing unnecessary calculations and effectively reducing complexity. As a result, VCMTT demonstrates a significant computational efficiency improvement, achieving a high performance comparable to that of complex methods, in simulations conducted for radar tracking in an airborne environment. Comparative analysis with a conventional integrated probability mass (IPM) method reveals VCMTT's superiority in terms of average gate count, miss distance, and log likelihood ratio (LLR). Furthermore, VCMTT's performance is consistently high across multiple radar configurations, also showing an improved robustness against varying radar parameters. In addition to its application to radar tracking, the variable complexity approach can be adapted for utilization in other imaging and sensor-based target tracking scenarios. 

This research is an extension of a previous study presented at the 2019 International Radar Conference. It includes an updated VCMTT algorithm, along with a new probability density function (PDF) implementation, along with four distinct radar configurations, in addition to an exploration of the algorithm's adaptability across different tracking scenarios. The algorithm has been refined with a reduced false neighbor count and improved robustness, achieved through the minimization of calculations for unnecessary target states. A comparative analysis with the IPM method is also conducted, utilizing five evaluation metrics, and demonstrates VCMTT's superior performance in terms of average gate count, miss distance, and log likelihood ratio (LLR), with computational efficiency as the primary driver.

The refined algorithm exhibits improved robustness, achieved through the minimization of calculations for unnecessary target states, and is capable of effectively reducing complexity in scenarios with limited sensor fields of view or undetected targets.

A new approach is introduced to develop an observability inequality for a population model, described by a Schr\"{o}dinger equation, based on the internal observation of a specific integral quantity. This method bypasses the standard strategy of identifying and controlling the observability multiplier in a bounded domain. Instead, the innovative technique directly establishes a non-negativity condition for the solution's square within a subdomain, thereby indirectly proving the observability inequality. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, it is applied to a population model involving a competitive Lotka-Volterra system and a weakly damped Schr\"{o}dinger equation. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to validate the theoretical findings. Notably, the proposed technique appears to yield comparable or better results than the classical approach when evaluated through the total energy's decay rate for the weakly damped Schr\"{o}dinger equation. Moreover, this approach reveals that the observability inequality for the population model can be achieved with a significantly smaller observation time. Ultimately, this method demonstrates potential in exploring control and stabilization problems for other PDE systems.

Research on soccer has been focused on action recognition and prediction, yet little is known about the value of different actions in isolation. To address this, we propose using transfer learning to utilize pre-trained policy-value networks for action-value network training. By leveraging the knowledge from trained action-value networks, we can effectively estimate the expected outcome of individual actions. Our method allows for the comparison of actions like committing a foul or causing the ball to go out, which have similar reward potential to shooting on goal in certain situations. Our analysis reveals that our pre-trained network already grasps basic action values and demonstrates how it can be fine-tuned for more accurate outcomes. Moreover, we showcase the challenging nature of supervised action value learning by evaluating our method on a dataset constructed from real soccer matches. Our technique can also be employed to analyze the behavior of soccer players, particularly their tendency to commit fouls, as exhibited in our experiments. Ultimately, our study highlights the capability to compare actions of varying degrees of difficulty and provides tools for analyzing soccer player behavior from visual observations. We are investigating the potential of a novel time-domain Full Waveform Inversion (FWI) framework, one that utilizes time-domain wavefields while addressing issues like non-convergence and regional flattening in the recovered model. By reformulating the time-domain wave equation as an Euler-Lagrange operator, we derive an explicit formula for the adjoint operator, making it feasible to compute the adjoint time-domain wavefield even after time-domain discretization. However, this approach introduces challenging non-linear boundary conditions that can be managed by employing a flexible artificial boundary formulation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this time-domain FWI method through synthetic test cases, showing promising results compared to conventional time-domain FWI methods. Furthermore, we analyze the impact of different time sampling rates and sampling schemes on the inversion results. Our findings indicate that the new time-domain FWI method yields more accurate results than conventional time-domain FWI, especially when using the new method's optimized time sampling scheme. Additionally, we observe that the conventional time FWI method is sensitive to time sampling rate and sampling scheme, while the new method is relatively insensitive. This suggests that the new time-domain FWI method can handle challenging data scenarios with missing data more effectively. We also explore the application of this time-domain FWI method to seismic imaging problems with complex models and discuss potential future directions and improvements for the method. Moreover, we discuss the mathematical connections between the time-domain FWI method and other optimization methods, such as Bregman iterative methods and the Chambolle-Pock algorithm. Finally, we provide the Python implementation of the time-domain FWI method as an open-source code. 

Keywords: Full Waveform Inversion, Time-domain, Wavefield, Euler-Lagrange operator, Adjoint operator, Artificial boundary formulation, Optimization methods, Bregman iterative methods, Chambolle-Pock algorithm.

This research examines the behavior of an asymmetric noisy voter model, which involves two species competing for resources in a spatial environment. The model incorporates random disturbances, and our analysis explores the long-term consequences of these factors on the competition between the species. Depending on specific parameter values, particularly the probability of switching from one species to the other, the model exhibits diverse outcomes, including the extinction of one species, coexistence of both species, or the dominance of one species over the other. Our study aims to identify the conditions that lead to these outcomes and examine the size of the species population as it adapts to changing environmental conditions. Furthermore, we investigate how the model responds to changes in the probability of switching and the size of the population, and our results are supported by numerical simulations and visualizations. Additionally, we provide analytical evidence to validate our findings, utilizing the technique of subcritical and superscritical analysis to gain insights into the model's behavior. This research provides a comprehensive analysis of an asymmetric noisy voter model, and our results can inform policy decisions in applications related to forest ecology and species competition. The performance of scanning transmission electron microscopes relies heavily on the function of electrostatic phase plates, and optimizing the design of these plates is, therefore, crucial. We examine various designs, ranging from basic octagonal shapes to complex patterns, and assess how parameters like fill-factor and pixel pattern affect performance. Our findings indicate that the optimal design balances probe size and current density, and suggest that highly efficient designs can be achieved through geometric optimizations, yielding probes with diameters as low as 0.4 angstroms and current densities exceeding 10^8 A/angstrom^2. Notably, we found that performance can be improved through multiplexing schemes, incorporating multiple probes within a single plate, and demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through geometric optimizations. Our analysis highlights the importance of accounting for electron beam diffusion and the effects of mini-probes on image formation when evaluating the performance of phase plates. Finally, we showcase the capability of these designs to enhance the spatial resolution of images in realistic scenarios, and examine the potential for further improvement through the use of optimized mini-probes and beam multiplexing. This paper introduces a cutting-edge Convolutional Neural Network, aptly named MFC-Net, which tackles the challenge of loop closure detection in images. Loop closure detection is a critical function in mobile robot navigation, where it identifies and verifies previously visited locations. To enhance accuracy, the system utilizes a bidirectional design, processing input in both forward and reverse directions. Furthermore, the incorporation of an attention mechanism within specific network components, namely the Feature Extraction Unit and Context Unit, is presented to concentrate on relevant contextual information. By systematically evaluating MFC-Net against six prominent loop closure detection datasets, our research indicates that our proposed model achieves remarkable precision and efficiency while requiring minimal training data. Comparative analysis with renowned baseline models reveals that MFC-Net excels in terms of performance and processing speed, outperforming the competition by at least 1.5% in terms of precision and achieving comparable results with the models in terms of mean average precision (MAP). Moreover, a thorough investigation of attentional fusion units' behavior is conducted to provide insight into the effects of attention on loop closure detection. Our research demonstrates that attention significantly enhances performance, especially in scenarios with high occlusion rates. To facilitate replication and advancement of our work, the MFC-Net model along with accompanying code has been made publicly accessible.

We calculate the renormalized quasiparticle velocity in doped graphene layers using the memory function approach and relate it to the thermal diffusivity measured experimentally. Subsequently, we determine the renormalized quasiparticle velocity and thermal diffusivity in doped graphene, considering the effects of electron-electron interactions and temperature. Furthermore, we assess the renormalized specific heat of doped graphene, examining how it is influenced by the thermal mass of Dirac electrons and temperature, in addition to the interplay between thermal and quantum factors. We establish a connection between the renormalized specific heat and thermal capacity through the electron heat capacity and examine the implications of using different models of the Fermi distribution function. We also investigate the impact of temperature on the renormalized specific heat and compare it with the thermal capacity of a free electron model. Moreover, we investigate the effect of doping concentration on the renormalized specific heat and thermal capacity, taking into consideration the interplay between quantum and thermal effects. Notably, we find that the renormalized specific heat exhibits a linear relationship with the thermal capacity at high temperatures but deviates from this linear relationship at lower temperatures due to the electron-electron interaction, thereby demonstrating the significance of incorporating interaction effects when interpreting specific heat measurements in doped graphene layers. We also propose that the renormalized quasiparticle velocity and thermal diffusivity could serve as directly measurable indicators of the quasiparticle velocity and thermal mass in doped graphene layers. Lastly, we suggest that the renormalized specific heat provides a meaningful framework for comparing experimental specific heat measurements with theoretical predictions derived from strong coupling models. Ultimately, our theoretical framework offers a feasible pathway for interpreting experimental specific heat measurements in doped graphene layers and paves the way for exploring the renormalized specific heat in graphene-based heterostructures and multilayers. Despite significant advancements in neural speech synthesis, generated speech still lacks the natural, nuanced tone of human conversation.  This limitation is particularly pronounced in settings like voice assistants, where the primary goal is not mere intelligibility, but rather engaging and effective communication with users.  To tackle this challenge, we introduce the MaskedSpeech framework, a novel approach that incorporates an innovative masking technique in a data augmentation strategy.  This method involves randomly obscuring certain aspects of acoustic features during synthesis, either globally across the entire sequence or locally within specific segments.  By training the model to recover the masked information, we observed a notable enhancement in the quality and expressiveness of synthesized speech, with particular improvements in tone and prosody.  Our experiments demonstrate that the MaskedSpeech approach yields superior performance compared to conventional methods, with notable enhancements in both automatic and human evaluations.  Notably, the model's ability to manage acoustic prosody and tone is significantly improved, with a marked decrease in over-regularization.  We also found that the MaskedSpeech framework is highly versatile and can be seamlessly integrated with other techniques such as style editing and diffusion models, with minimal modifications required.  To facilitate further research, we have made the MaskedSpeech codebase and associated data available publicly.  With the MaskedSpeech framework, we are confident that we have taken a crucial step towards creating more natural and engaging speech synthesis, with vast potential for applications in voice assistants and human-computer interaction. We examine the presence of harmonic and anharmonic oscillator interactions in a one-dimensional discrete nonlinear Schr\"{o}dinger model to determine the effect on the stability of solitary waves. Our analysis focuses on a system featuring nearest-neighbor interactions in a continuous limit, with the potential modified by adding a term describing an anharmonic oscillator. Through a mathematical approach, we find that this modification can lead to a decrease in the stability of a specific type of solitary wave when the anharmonic oscillator is present, and instead results in the emergence of an unstable wave solution in another case. Our research employs a numerical method to plot spectra and determine the stability of both discrete and continuous models. The results demonstrate that the anharmonic oscillator can induce orbital instability in a stable continuous model, and the breakdown of discrete orbital stability is accelerated by increasing anharmonic oscillator strength. Our study provides a theoretical framework for understanding the effect of anharmonic oscillator interactions on the stability of solitary waves in one-dimensional systems. Moreover, it paves the way for exploring other nonlinear phenomena and higher-dimensional systems.

By drawing on theories of context and reference from Ryan (1999) and J. S. Mill (1843), we suggest that context-driven semantic shifts in language are best captured through a combination of central tendency and variance metrics. Utilizing a dataset of embedded sentences with varying context means and precisions, we demonstrate the significance of considering the second moment of context distributions to accurately model semantic shift. Our findings indicate that high-precision contexts tend to pull the inferred meaning towards the expected meaning, whereas high-variance contexts allow more deviation from the expected meaning, often resulting in the inferred meaning shifting further than predicted. Notably, using a context distribution's second moment to model semantic shift in inference reveals a relationship with the first moment that is nonlinear. By examining the interplay between context means and precisions, we show that some contexts drive the inferred meaning further from the expected meaning than the actual meaning, implying a distinction between local and global semantic shifts. The methods proposed here can be applied to any analysis of the distribution of meanings in language, enabling a more nuanced understanding of how context affects meaning and necessitating a revision of classic theories of reference and context. Ultimately, our research highlights the significance of accounting for the variance of contextual meanings in language, which has implications for research in language understanding, machine learning, and the philosophy of language. Understanding the complex processes of retinal development in the zebrafish requires analyzing the dynamic movement of retinal nuclei. By creating detailed maps of the retinal microtubule network and tracking the positions and movements of retinal nuclei across various stages of development, researchers have gathered substantial amounts of data. However, analyzing these large datasets poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we have developed a computational tool specifically designed to compare large datasets obtained from multiple sources. This tool allows for assessment of data consistency, comparison of data distributions across different conditions, as well as the identification of significant differences. Furthermore, it facilitates visualization techniques to present the findings in an engaging graphical format. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this computational tool, we have conducted a series of experiments using previously obtained data on the movement of retinal nuclei in zebrafish. Our results show that our tool can accurately pinpoint the initial and final positions of the retinal nuclei, as well as the intermediate points along their migration path. Additionally, we have observed that the retinal nuclei exhibit a non-uniform distribution across the retina, with a preference for certain areas over others. Our tool has also revealed that the retinal nuclei display a diverse range of movement speeds, with some nuclei migrating quickly while others migrate slowly. Moreover, we have found that the retinal nuclei exhibit a complex migration pattern, with some migrating directly to their final position and others taking a more circuitous route. We believe that our computational tool will be a valuable asset in analyzing the complex processes of retinal development in the zebrafish. However, it is essential to acknowledge that this tool has its limitations, primarily due to the challenges associated with tracking the movement of retinal nuclei through time-lapse imaging. Despite these challenges, we are confident that our tool will be a useful resource for researchers in this field. Additionally, we are exploring ways to adapt this tool for analyzing the development of other cellular systems. We invite other researchers to contribute their data and share their expertise with us, as we continue to refine and expand the capabilities of this tool. We have made the computational tool we have developed publicly available, along with a sample dataset and a user-friendly interface, which can be accessed through our website. We are eager to collaborate with other researchers and receive their feedback on this tool, which we are continually updating to better address the complex challenges associated with analyzing the development of cellular systems. We are confident that by working together, we can create a comprehensive resource that will provide valuable insights into the intricate processes of cellular development

Compressive sensing (CS) has revolutionized signal processing by enabling the reconstruction of high-quality images from limited data. However, the effectiveness of CS depends heavily on the quality of the sensing matrix used. A poorly designed sensing matrix can significantly impede the performance of reconstruction algorithms, leading to subpar results. In our research, we employ machine learning-based optimization techniques to develop custom-made sensing matrices tailored to specific image processing tasks. By fine-tuning the sensing matrix in an end-to-end manner, we've seen substantial improvements in reconstruction quality. Our approach involves creating a generative adversarial network (GAN) that generates highly optimized sensing matrices, ultimately leading to better performance than traditional random matrix methods. In our experiments, we demonstrate the benefits of our custom-designed sensing matrices for compressive sensing applications, leveraging the capabilities of graphics processing units (GPUs) to generate highly effective sensing matrices. Our results showcase notable gains in reconstruction quality, with minimal alterations required to the baseline algorithm. To further illustrate the prowess of our approach, we present a case study involving magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), one of the most prominent applications of CS. Our experiments highlight the design challenges and innovative solutions involved in creating custom sensing matrices, with potential to revolutionize how we collect and process complex data. By openly sharing our sensing matrix generator and associated projects, we aim to spark a broader exploration of optimized sensing matrices across various image processing scenarios. The code and datasets are publicly accessible on our GitHub repository.

We investigate the long-term behavior of actively moving step-like particles in dimensions 2 to 5, discovering that the linearized hydrodynamic model falls short of capturing the full-scale dynamics when 2 < d < 5. In these dimensions, the hydrodynamic model exhibits a non-trivial, fractal-like scaling, whereas it accurately predicts the motion in dimensions 5 and above. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations of interacting active particles and demonstrate the limitations of linearized hydrodynamics in three-dimensional space, suggesting that higher-dimensional active systems may rely on alternative mechanisms to achieve persistent motion. Furthermore, we develop an analytical approach to determining the scaling properties of the hydrodynamic model's susceptibility in dimensions 3 to 5. Our study offers a comprehensive understanding of the hydrodynamic model's validity across various dimensions.

However, the main challenge lies in accurately measuring the neutron energy spectrum due to the complex nature of scintillation signals resulting from superimposed elastic and inelastic scattering events. By combining advanced machine learning algorithms with detailed simulations of the scintillation process, we successfully develop a reliable neural network capable of predicting the underlying true neutron energy distribution from observed and simulated training data, by accounting for various physical interactions including multiple scattering and inelastic events. The evolution of a driven quantum system can be intricately understood through the use of coherent states, which serve as a basis for an expanded Hilbert space. This expansion allows the precise simulation of driven dynamics within a simplified and computationally efficient manner. However, maintaining the fidelity of these states requires constant adjustment as the system and laser parameters evolve. In this research, we introduce an innovative approach that leverages machine learning to an unprecedented degree. By establishing a functional relationship between the Hamiltonian and propagator functions, we successfully devise a method to maintain the fidelity of coherent states through an unprecedented degree of machine learning. This innovative approach achieves remarkable results, exceeding the capabilities of even the most sophisticated numerical methods. Notably, it demonstrates the ability to replicate intricate behaviors observed in quantum systems, including the emergence of synchronized states and robust oscillations, using a simple Hamiltonian model. The online discussion community around elections has drawn increasing attention in recent years, with many studying these communities to better understand online political discussions and their potential impact on voting behavior. However, communities are not static entities; users can engage with multiple groups by providing content and receiving messages. Therefore, existing methods, which solely focus on measuring a user's influence within a single community, are no longer sufficient. This study aims to develop a comprehensive approach to assessing a user's influence across multiple communities by considering various roles. Initially, community classification is used to determine the communities a user is part of and then community membership prediction is employed to identify the communities users are likely to contribute to and engage with. Following this, a community-based approach is introduced to assign users to roles and a score is calculated to measure a user's performance in each role. Finally, a community-based approach to calculating influence scores is proposed, and the results show that this method outperforms existing methods that focus on individual communities. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments using data from the Chinese election discussion community (CEDC) during the 2012-2015 presidential elections, and the results show that our approach effectively captures a user's influence across multiple communities by considering their roles within those communities. Notably, our method reveals interesting insights, such as users tend to maintain long-term connections with the same communities and tend to occupy different roles in different communities. Additionally, our method discovered correlations between roles and community characteristics, such as users who contribute to smaller communities tend to occupy the authority role, while users who contribute to larger communities tend to occupy the whale role. Furthermore, our method found that users who interact with the media or receive messages from other users are more likely to occupy the whale role. Lastly, our method found that users who contribute to communities with higher authority scores tend to occupy the authority role. Overall, our approach provides a community-based influence assessment method that effectively captures a user's influence across multiple communities by considering their roles within those communities, and our experiments using data from the Chinese election discussion community during the 2012-2015 presidential elections validated our approach. In our research, we tackle the complex issue of evaluating queries that involve self-joins in SQL databases. Our key finding reveals that the categorization of these queries into manageable and uncomplicable forms relies solely on the interconnections of specific matrix components, known as the Cline decomposition, which can be determined through a straightforward set of rules. Consequently, this insight allows us to assess the feasibility of any query with self-joins swiftly. Moreover, we propose an innovative algorithm that utilizes this feasibility assessment to identify efficient evaluation plans for self-join queries. By leveraging our feasibility tool within this algorithm, we demonstrate significant performance enhancements, with some queries being processed at least five times faster. Our innovative approach and innovative use of the Cline decomposition also facilitate clear communication among database administrators, even in complex database scenarios, by providing a visual representation of query feasibility and suggesting optimal data sampling strategies. These contributions address fundamental challenges in database query processing and query understanding, addressing critical issues in database research and management. Our research and technology are now available as part of the iSQL-Star system.

Complex systems, characterized by multiple time scales and competing dynamics, present a significant challenge for prediction methods. Despite being highly effective for simple systems, traditional forecasting techniques often struggle with this level of complexity. In our research, we examine the ability of reservoir computing to tackle this challenge. By utilizing a single-neuron reservoir model and the extreme complexity of the Lorenz '96 system as a test case, we demonstrate that high-precision predictions can be achieved for short time scales and moderate accuracy for longer time scales, even in the presence of a relatively small reservoir. Furthermore, we show that by incorporating an external input and optimizing the reservoir parameters, the quality of the predictions can be substantially improved, with minimal loss of accuracy over time. Our findings indicate that reservoir computing has great potential as a powerful tool for predicting small-scale atmospheric systems, with further advancements likely to be even more effective. Additionally, we highlight the limitations of our single-neuron approach and suggest that multi-neuron reservoirs may be necessary for predicting larger-scale systems. In conclusion, our research lays the groundwork for exploring the application of reservoir computing in predicting time series data in other complex domains.

To mitigate this problem, a revised, bias-reduced estimator has been proposed, adapting a well-known correction method that assumes a specific form of the process's intensity. However, this assumption is not necessarily valid in practice, leading to a proposed alternative that utilizes a kernel smoothing approach to counter the bias. We examine the state reachability analysis of automated transportation systems with controller zones as barriers, focusing on computing states that can become hazardous within a certain time frame. We establish a mathematical framework using control Lyapun UNiform (CLUNIF) barriers and prove the equivalence to a set of continuous, piecewise differentiable functions meeting specific conditions. We leverage this equivalence to approximate the reachability set by solving a series of ordinary differential equation problems, with each problem representing a narrow time segment. Our method involves iteratively applying a state prediction algorithm, with each iteration using the previous result as an initial condition to prevent infinite loops. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method with an example of an automated lane-changing maneuver. Finally, we outline the advantages of using controller zones as feedback control to prevent states from becoming hazardous, and highlight the computational efficiency of our method in comparing to a more comprehensive reachability analysis. No prior knowledge of transportation systems is required to understand the main findings, as the discussion is generalized through the use of symbolic mathematics and algebraic manipulation. However, the implementation details for large-scale systems require additional consideration and may result in computational infeasibility for very complex systems due to the limitations of our current algorithm. Nonetheless, our method offers an innovative approach to approximating reachability analysis, especially when compared to more complex numerical integration methods. We present an innovative strategy for enhancing the performance of neural networks when dealing with low-dimensional signals. By leveraging a detailed mathematical analysis of functionals and their connections to signal characteristics, we develop a precise and efficient method for generalizing networks to handle higher-dimensional inputs while maintaining accuracy. This approach, which we call the generalized Frobenius norm, serves as a versatile tool, applicable to a broad range of scenarios, including the construction of neural operators and the improvement of generalization across different dimensionality. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that our method achieves superior results, outperforming alternative strategies, and facilitating the creation of highly precise neural networks with improved generalization capabilities. The benefits of this approach are particularly evident when working with low-dimensional signals, and it finds valuable application in various domains, such as the analysis of material properties and image processing. To further advance understanding, we open-source our method and related tools on public repositories.

Research on the animacy continuum has focused primarily on auditory cues, neglecting the significance of visual appearance in categorizing living beings. Through a series of experiments combining machine learning and human evaluations, this study reveals that visual features play a crucial role in categorizing living beings and explores the animacy continuum from a dual perspective: one end (visual categorizability) represents the ease of identifying a being's appearance within a specific category, while the other end (agency) represents the impression of independent movement and decision-making. The findings show that visual categorizability and agency independently contribute to the animacy continuum, with the former primarily influenced by visual face and body features and the latter by movement and interaction, suggesting that the animacy continuum spans from easily recognizable living beings to elusive and self-motivated entities. This research provides new insights into the animacy continuum and suggests that visual features hold significant potential for creating engaging characters in interactive technologies and animating virtual entities with perceived life in artistic applications. By exploring the interplay between visual appearance, movement, and interaction, this study offers a framework for designing characters and virtual entities that evoke a sense of life and can be used to guide human attention and facilitate human-computer interaction. The research includes the development of an open-source dataset (TACO-VIS) containing 3D animated characters and a machine learning-based attention model (TACO-ATT) for reducing the computational complexity of model training. This research introduces QrelHl, a quantum relational Hoare logic for programs in a monadic quantum imperative language.  The preconditions and postconditions in QrelHl are described using a quantitative relational specification, which measures the likelihood of program input-output correlations. The quantification of the relation's strength is reflected in the logic's type theory as a density value. The quantification rules in QrelHl ensure the validity of both classical and quantum hoare theory principles, as well as the conservation of closed terms' denominators. By verifying a simple quantum teleportation program using QrelHl, we demonstrate its effectiveness. The implementation of QrelHl is supported by a proof assistant tool, providing a functional programming environment that can be used to develop quantum programs with relational specifications. The implementation is accompanied by an exploration of the trade-offs between different quantum relational logic approaches. The most notable comparison is made with the quantum extension of the Hoare logic for superdense programs, particularly in terms of program expressibility and efficiency. The research and development of the QrelHl proof assistant and the underlying quantum relational Hoare logic are ongoing, with opportunities for further contributions. The source code for the QrelHl proof assistant is openly accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. A $C_0$-semigroup of operators $\mathfrak{T}$ on a Banach space $\mathfrak{X}$ is codiskcyclic if there exists a vector $\mathfrak{x}\in\mathfrak{X}$ such that the set $\{\mathfrak{T}(t)\mathfrak{x}:t\geq 0\}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{X}$. In this study, we explore conditions under which codiskcyclicity is achieved through the application of an operator that is integral with respect to a semigroup. Specifically, we investigate conditions on the operator $A$ and the Banach space $\mathfrak{X}$ that ensure a codiskcyclic vector exists for the semigroup $\mathfrak{T}(\cdot)A$. We also examine circumstances under which the codiskcyclicity of $\mathfrak{T}(\cdot)A$ is equivalent to the cyclicity of a related operator. Furthermore, we establish criteria for codiskcyclicity that are applicable to specific types of Banach spaces and operators, including those defined on $L^p(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $C_0(\mathbb{R}^d)$. Finally, we provide examples and counterexamples to demonstrate the implications of these conditions. Additionally, we discuss potential connections to disk-cyclic operators and the related concept of the minimal regularity space.

The success of space weather forecasting relies heavily on accurate modeling of solar wind and geomagnetic field interactions, achieved through precise measurements of the solar surface magnetic field. To accomplish this, global vector magnetic field maps are created at solar synodic 27-day intervals using high-resolution magnetograms from the Solar Orbiter and a single vector magnetic field from a solar disk region of interest observed by a ground-based telescope network. These observations from multiple sources must have the same magnetic field orientation, known as fill factor, to produce accurate forecasts. However, current methods only use a simple ratio to align these observations, which is not always sufficient. To address this limitation, a more complex relationship between the fill factor and the observed and actual magnetic field properties is proposed and tested. Results show that using the new approach, there is a significant reduction in the difference between observed and predicted magnetic field properties and the associated errors are minimized. The new method also demonstrates the ability to identify potential sunspots with strong magnetic fields. Furthermore, using the new approach to create global vector magnetic field maps results in an improvement in magnetospheric energy available and the Kp index index, with a reduction in associated errors. The proposed method is set to enhance the accuracy of space weather forecasting tools and is available for use within the WFS4.0 framework. Using data from the Hubble Legacy Archive, we analyzed 4,000 star clusters in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) to investigate the distribution of star clusters as a function of mass, age, and spatial location. For young star clusters (under 100 million years), we discovered a significant decrease in density with age and a distinct density peak at 50-60 million years. In contrast, more ancient star clusters showed a reduced density peak at 10-20 billion years and a less pronounced age curve. The shape of these curves varied across the LMC, with younger star clusters displaying similarities to the Small Magellanic Cloud and the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, while older star clusters exhibited greater density in the central regions of the LMC. The density of star clusters also declined with increasing distance from the LMC's center. We also examined the mass distribution of star clusters in the LMC, finding a power-law index of 1.64 +/- 0.01 for young clusters and a steeper index of 2.14 +/- 0.01 for older clusters, with a possible break point at 1 billion years. The mass density of star clusters in the LMC peaked at 10^5 M_⊙, with a standard deviation of less than 0.5 dex. We believe these findings provide valuable insights into the formation and evolution of the LMC, given the limited current observational data on cluster formation. Additionally, they may serve as a basis for comparisons with other galaxies, given the extensive, uniformly collected data set used in this analysis. This study offers a comprehensive examination of star cluster populations in the LMC, with implications for our understanding of cluster formation and galaxy evolution. Further research is proposed to analyze specific populations of star clusters within the LMC, such as young clusters, old clusters, and globular clusters, as well as to study the interactions between the LMC and its satellite galaxies through the analysis of star clusters in these systems. This research is expected to contribute to ongoing and future research on the LMC, such as the APOGEE-2 and RAVE+ surveys, as well as the upcoming Euclid and LSST missions. Given the limitations of current observational data on cluster formation, this analysis may serve as a basis for comparisons with other galaxies, such as the Small Magellanic Cloud and the Sagittarius Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy, as well as future simulations of the LMC's cluster population. This research introduces a novel approach to calculating decay widths in quantum field theories, addressing finite-volume effects in a meaningful way. By connecting two observables in a way that eliminates volume dependence, a stable decay width estimate can be obtained through lattice simulations. We apply this method to the specific case of a complex scalar field, determining the decay width of a scalar meson at various masses within a lattice framework. Additionally, we investigate how this decay width is affected by the lattice volume and temperature. We utilize this approach to study the scalar meson decay width as a function of temperature, observing how it changes with volume and temperature due to the shift in the meson spectrum caused by these parameters. We perform these calculations using one HMC ensemble from a $(0.9~$GeV$\())$-flavor lattice QCD simulation, with a particular focus on the scalar meson. We find the decay width to increase with temperature, albeit slightly, and is moderately affected by the lattice volume. Notably, when considering the real part of the complex energy, we find that the real part of the eigenvalue of the lattice thermal bulk susceptibility matches the volume-dependent part of the decay width, with the same order of magnitude. However, this connection is seen only after accounting for the shift in the real part of the complex energy due to temperature, and does not hold for the imaginary part of the eigenvalue. We explore the connection between the thermal bulk susceptibility and the volume-dependent part of the decay width, finding it follows an $O(2)$ symmetry pattern in the temperature-volume plane. We also examine how the finite-volume effects influence the decay width, and suggest using the second-order polynomial fit as an alternative to account for this phenomenon. Lastly, we discuss the applicability of this approach to other theories, such as the $\lambda\phi^4$ field theory in $(2+1)~$d$ and lattice QCD with multiple flavor fields. No finite-size effects were observed in the calculations of the complex scalar mass in $(1+1)~d$ $\lambda\phi^4$ field theory for lattices of $16\cdot 32$ spatial sites, due to the large minimum extent of $4.24$ times the correlation length. By contrast, a notable difference in the spectrum of the Dirac operator in $(0.3~$GeV$\())$-flavor lattice QCD is observed at lattices of $24\cdot 48$ spatial sites, with significant finite-size effects on the spectrum

We introduce a novel, high-performance Monte Carlo method that utilizes complex-valued affine coupling layers in combination with the Le Mans formula. This method accelerates the computation of cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) by bypassing the inversion of a precise algorithm, such as the Krylov subspace method, and instead leverages the structural properties of affine coupling layers to achieve significant speed gains. The proposed algorithm is an efficient, general-purpose way to compute CDFs for any probability distribution that can be represented using a differentiable probability density function (PDF), with the potential to greatly expedite various Monte Carlo simulations. We showcase the algorithm's efficacy by applying it to an intricate scenario from the field of stochastic processes, namely the pricing of Russian options. The results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm yields highly accurate solutions with a remarkable level of speed and scalability, surpassing even the efficiency of highly optimized C++ implementations. We also derive related estimates for the counts of integers that are the product of two prime numbers, also under the same assumption. These results lead to estimates for the distribution of numbers that are of the form $ab^h$ with $h$ being the highest power of $b$ in the factorization of $ab^h$, and can be viewed as a variant of the original problem proposed by Chowla, Erdős, and Straus in 1957. Contrastive learning in language models has proven effective in reducing overfitting, but this method's effectiveness is contingent on accurately pairing similar and dissimilar samples. We introduce the ReCross method, which utilizes mismatched pairs to train a more robust and generalizable language model using an unsupervised contrastive approach. By leveraging the inherent contrast between pairs, ReCross enhances the model's performance without requiring labeled data. Our experiments demonstrate notable improvements in performance on various unsupervised language modeling tasks, surpassing the benchmarks set by supervised contrastive learning methods. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at the specified link. 

https://github.com/whunlp/ReCross

We have also observed that the generalization capabilities of ReCross are unique in certain cases. For instance, fine-tuning a model trained with the ReCross method on unlabeled text achieves comparable performance to that of a model trained from scratch on labeled data for the GLUE dataset. Moreover, the method demonstrates adaptability across diverse language models, with the swap-to-frozen strategy yielding consistent improvements across T5 and BART. We have found that the ReCross method is particularly effective at reducing the gap between unsupervised and supervised models, with the gap reduced by half when evaluated on the PPL metric. The enhanced performance of the ReCross model is attributed to the increased robustness and capability to capture general language patterns rather than memorizing specific labeled examples. We have also validated our findings through both theoretical and empirical analysis. 

With the exceptional performance of the ReCross method and its unique generalization capabilities, we have explored various extensions to the method, including the application to few-shot learning and the use of external unlabeled data. Our results indicate that the method yields high performance in these settings as well. 

To summarize, the primary contributions of this study are as follows: 

*   This research introduces an unsupervised contrastive learning method called the ReCross method, which effectively trains a language model using mismatched pairs and has achieved notable performance improvements in various unsupervised language modeling tasks.
*   We have observed unique generalization capabilities of the ReCross method, with the model performing comparably to a supervised contrastive learning model, demonstrating adaptability across different language models, and exhibiting a significant reduction in the gap between unsupervised and supervised models.
*   This research provides theoretical and empirical justification for the performance of the ReCross method and has explored several method extensions, with the results indicating high performance in few-shot learning and the use of external unlabeled data

This research introduces the m-ar-X function, a variant of the minimum-arithmetic mean-distance-to-kth-neighbor function, used for high-dimensional data representation. The m-ar-X method offers an alternative to popular dimensionality reduction techniques, such as Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) and Principal Component Analysis (PCA), by determining a set of optimal features that capture the average distance from the kth nearest neighbor in the original dimension space. The proposed approach is demonstrated through a case study involving the classification of Emotionally Intelligent Personality traits with micro-expression data, where feature extraction is applied to decrease the input dimensionality of image features from 4800 to 112. The evaluation compares the classification performance of several machine learning algorithms employing the m-ar-X function, MDS, PCA, and a combination of PCA and MDS to that of a baseline model using a linear discriminant analysis classifier, revealing that the best result is achieved with the m-ar-X function variant when k=3 and a specific value of the parameter m. The exceptional performance of the m-ar-X function in this scenario is found to correlate with the dataset's characteristics, specifically its relatively low dimensionality and the presence of distinct classes, suggesting that the m-ar-X function has significant potential as a dimensionality reduction method. However, it is also noted that the method's efficiency and practical application may be limited by its computationally expensive nature and the absence of a established optimization technique for the m-ar-X function parameter. As such, the development of more effective and adaptable methods for optimizing the m-ar-X function, particularly with large datasets, is considered a priority for future research. The proposed approach and associated findings are subject to validation and potential improvement through further experimentation and analysis. The accompanying code and dataset are made available for replication purposes. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/zhengyuanwu2021/marX, and the dataset used is the MSRE collection accessible at https://umich.cc/kezheng/research/adicw.html. Hyperparameter optimization is a critical challenge in machine learning, especially when working with large, private datasets, for which external access is restricted. As a result, direct evaluation of models becomes impossible, necessitating a framework for hyperparameter tuning without accessing the data itself. Our proposed framework, HPRun, utilizes theory-driven optimization methods and a resource allocation strategy to efficiently tune hyperparameters on multiple processes simultaneously, even in a distributed environment. By leveraging a cost model tailored to each optimization algorithm, HPRun ensures minimal unnecessary computations and effectively handles processes with varying performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework by conducting hyperparameter searches for three different models – linear regression, decision trees, and support vector machines – using a large, private dataset, and also examine its scalability and privacy preservation capabilities. Our findings show that HPRun yields comparable performance to exhaustive grid search methods while substantially reducing computational costs. Additionally, our framework exhibits strong concurrency support, as evidenced by its ability to achieve similar performance with a small number of processes despite significant performance differences between individual computations. Furthermore, we highlight the privacy benefits of our hyperparameter tuning approach, which ensures no sensitive data is shared with the tuning framework. Our project is openly available at https://github.com/chen0045/HPRun. It has been successfully deployed in real-world applications at several large-scale enterprises. In particular, a leading e-commerce company utilized our framework to optimize the recommendation system, resulting in a significant increase in sales. Moreover, a prominent airline company employed our framework for optimal pricing, resulting in enhanced revenue. We invite researchers and practitioners to contribute to our framework and explore its applications in machine learning hyperparameter optimization.

In 1968, Bernd and von Driggs characterized all Coxeter groups of type A_n by identifying a specific arrangement of n mutually tangent spheres in a wedge-shaped configuration. We expand upon their work by determining the number of spheres needed for any given generating set within a Coxeter group of type A_n, demonstrating that it correlates directly with the number of generators employed. Furthermore, we analytically visualize 3D arrangements of hyperplanes for Coxeter groups A_1, A_2, and A_3 through projection onto a suitable 2D hyperplane, and graphically depict the corresponding arrangements of spheres within the wedge for Coxeter groups A_2 and A_3. Lastly, we define and illustrate the 3D projections of the arrangements of hyperplanes and spheres for Coxeter groups F_4 and H_4. Lastly, we define and illustrate the 3D projections of the arrangements of hyperplanes and spheres for Coxeter groups F_4 and H_4. However, due to technical constraints, the accompanying graphic for the Coxeter group F_4 cannot be displayed. The animation for Coxeter group H_4 is available at https://www.math.unc.edu/~czemeryn/animations/H4.html. The number of spheres used for Coxeter group A_n corresponds directly to the number of generators employed from the standard presentation of the group. The number of spheres used for Coxeter group A_4 is 13, yet it's noteworthy that Bernd and von Driggs initially claimed the number was 12 in their publication from 1968. We correct this earlier finding in our research. We also establish that the number of spheres used for Coxeter groups A_n, for n>=3, is greater than n. Additionally, we establish a lower bound for the number of spheres used in arrangements for Coxeter groups D_n and E_n. Due to the complex nature of these systems in 3D space, we find it challenging to provide a general formula for the number of spheres required in Coxeter groups A_n, as this is not a straightforward, analytically resolvable problem. However, we are able to provide the number of spheres required for a range of values of n from 1 to 10. In contrast, the number of spheres required for n=4 is greater than the number of generators required in the fundamental representation of the group, as opposed to lower ranks of Coxeter groups A_n. To determine the optimal strategy for selecting final candidates in a search for weakly-interacting massive particles (WIMPs) using the ATIC detector, we simulate various approaches under assumptions of ideal and real-world measurement conditions. When WIMP detection is considered, the ATIC collaboration employed an efficiency-based method for selecting candidates, which, however, fails to account for the interdependence of its energy measurements. Instead, using a mathematical model of the detector's response to radiation and genuine energy values, we propose using a likelihood ratio test to select final candidates and assess their reliability. Furthermore, by incorporating a factor for correlated statistical fluctuations in the energy measurements, we successfully mitigate noise interdependence issues. The implementation of this strategy proves particularly effective in mitigating over-trending issues and pinpointing optimal threshold settings. As a result, the likelihood ratio test yields significantly improved predictions of final candidate flux and count rates, both with and without the presence of WIMPs, when compared to the earlier method. This methodology is equally applicable to other particle detectors subject to correlated noise issues. To facilitate adoption, we provide a simple computational tool for comoving WIMP density and mass predictions, along with count rate predictions, based on the ATIC full-year WIMP scan data, incorporating the new threshold settings. Using this, we re-evaluate the three sigma exclusion limits for spin-1/2 WIMPs, with and without the presence of gauge boson mediators, and find that the new limits are more stringent than their previous counterparts. Interestingly, the new limits are only marginally more stringent than the earlier ones based on raw energy measurements, indicating that the impact of correlated noise is relatively limited. The APOGEE-2 dataset allows us to examine chemically normal stars for the first time in the Milky Way's bulge, using a machine learning tool to identify and analyze subpopulations within this region. Residual abundances, generated by removing the effects of gravity, metal content, and location within the galaxy on chemical composition, reveal patterns of abundance that provide insight into the most chemically distinctive stars and greatest uncertainties in the data. By applying this approach, we identified seven stars with unique chemical signatures in the bulge and pinpointed regions of the abundance spectrum with the highest uncertainty, suggesting potential tidal streams or globular clusters. Using a simple tidal stream model, we mapped potential paths of these objects and found that three of the chemically distinctive stars may be connected to previously identified streams, specifically the Mainen and Bosque streams and the one associated with the globular cluster NGC 6528, and that two potential globular cluster candidates, one with low metal content and another with solar metal content, were found. We also found a group of stars with overabundances of $\alpha$-elements and [Fe/B] ratios, indicating that they originated from a globular cluster with a population like that of $\omega$ Centauri. Furthermore, we found a group of stars with low metal content and [Fe/B] ratios, indicating that they originated from a stellar stream with a connection to the Sagittarius dwarf spheroidal galaxy, specifically the Reticulum II stream. We also found a group of high-metal content stars that may be associated with the globular cluster M2, and finally, we found a group of high-metal content stars that may be a previously unreported stellar stream connected to the globular cluster F. This study demonstrates the capability of using a machine learning tool to analyze chemical abundances in large datasets and paves the way for more in-depth analysis of these subpopulations using additional observational and theoretical chemical properties. Through further research, we aim to compare the subpopulations found in the bulge to those in the galaxy's disk. Ultimately, this research will contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the galaxy's chemical evolution and the development of its stellar populations. In the context of online rumors, the model used to forecast peak adoption and attenuation over time is the PEAK model. The model's key components, precursor features and location and time-based factors, affect adoption and attenuation. Previous studies have analyzed the impact of precursor features and location on model predictions but have not examined the effect of time-based factors. This paper's contributors collected a large dataset of Chinese microblog posts in order to analyze the model's precursor feature and location components. The results show that certain precursor features have a significant effect on peak adoption and attenuation, while location has a less substantial impact, and that the model can forecast these effects with reasonable accuracy. Notably, the data reveal that the model's precursor feature effects are largely driven by both positive (e.g., sensational content) and negative (e.g., false information) effects that quickly diffuse and are difficult to eliminate. The findings also indicate that location can influence adoption and attenuation, albeit to a lesser degree, with locations that diffuse rumors quickly but struggle to slow their spread. The research includes an examination of external factors, such as offline events, that can impact online rumors and provides data in the form of charts illustrating the model's predictions and actual outcomes, as well as examples of the precursor features that contribute to the spread of rumors. The research contributes to the study of online rumors by analyzing the model's components and examining the relationship between precursor features, location, time, and external factors, among others. In the process, the research uncovers new factors that accelerate the spread of rumors, provides data that illustrates the model's predictive accuracy, and offers a method for identifying the precursor features responsible for the diffusion of rumors. The research may be used to develop more effective online rumor-debunking strategies and could be applied to the study of the diffusion of innovations and other contagious phenomena. Using observations from the VLT for 4610 faint nebulae across five fields within the Fornax cluster, a new study has determined the distance to the cluster through the nebulae's absolute magnitudes and a standard formula. This method yields a mean distance of approximately 19.86 megaparsecs (±0.34 megaparsecs) for the cluster's central regions. A more in-depth analysis of the surface brightness and density of the nebulae within this area also indicates the presence of a core radius of 1.17 megaparsecs (±0.08 megaparsecs) and a spherical tidal radius of 6.8 megaparsecs (±1.1 megaparsecs). Past research on the cluster's velocity dispersion is confirmed at a value of 45.4 kilometers per second (±4.9 kilometers per second), with no notable variations across different distance ranges. Alongside multiple planetary nebulae with known velocities, the study finds evidence of mass loss along the major axis of the cluster and a velocity dispersion of 24.6 kilometers per second (±4.9 kilometers per second) when considering only objects within one degree of the cluster's core. Deep neural network models primarily utilize mean squared error as their loss function, which is not the only possible metric for assessing their performance. To examine the limitations of this standard approach, we manipulate the loss function while keeping the network architecture and training methodology consistent. By applying a variety of loss functions with different properties, we find that some lesser-used metrics such as KL Divergence can result in better performance compared to more commonly employed options like cross-entropy and binary cross-entropy. However, our method to apply these metrics involves a significant issue - an unbalanced class distribution in the dataset. Resolving this imbalance proves crucial, and we investigate the fundamental connections between data imbalance and temperature scaling in order to successfully deploy more complex loss functions even in the presence of significant class imbalance. Our proposed technique, which involves adjusting the temperature parameter in accordance with the degree of class imbalance, enables us to utilize loss functions like KL Divergence and negative log likelihood, which would otherwise be impractical due to the extensive class dimension. By demonstrating the applicability of our approach to a range of challenging classification problems, including the classification of distant satellites and the identification of malicious mobile applications, we showcase the efficacy of our proposed technique. Our code is openly accessible at: https://github.com/0jza/temperature-scaling-for-ibn-neural-networks. Our research indicates that a well-balanced and well-designed technique like our temperature scaling approach can effectively deploy a wide range of under-represented loss functions, even in scenarios characterized by significant class imbalance. By integrating Fermi surface segmentation, we developed a comprehensive and consistent theory of magnetic susceptibility in superconducting materials. Our approach accurately accounts for topological features of the Fermi surface, including circular, hole-like and elliptical, electron-like areas, and the connections between them. We applied this framework to a variety of materials, including copper oxides, pnictides, and chalcogenides, and found that the vortex lattice exhibits an unusual arrangement of hexagonal and square patterns. Our model predicts that the magnetic susceptibility of these materials exhibits distinct anomalies corresponding to the locations of nodal points on the Fermi surface. Near a nodal point, the magnetic susceptibility exhibits a singular $T^{2n-1}$ dependence for any nodal point, with a specific heat capacity $\gamma \propto T^2n-2$. For an isolated nodal line, this yields $\gamma \propto T^3$, while for a nodal ring, this yields $\gamma \propto T^5$. We further investigated the impact of interband interactions on the magnetic susceptibility and found that it can be significantly modified by the folding of Brillouin zones in layered materials, with possible outcomes including nodal lines becoming rings, nodal rings becoming multiple nodal lines, and nodal points becoming nodal lines or vice versa. We applied our framework to specific materials, including Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_7$ and LaOFeP, to gain a deeper understanding of their vortex states and the topological features of their Fermi surfaces. Our research provides a foundation for further investigation of the complex interplay between the vortex state and electronic structure in superconducting materials with highly complex Fermi surfaces. It also offers a promising framework for identifying and categorizing nodal lines, a topic of ongoing research in the broader materials science community. In advanced recommendation systems, several diverse situations often arise, 
especially in online learning platforms, where the goal is to provide learners 
with accurate corrective feedback to aid their progress. Given the numerous 
possible outcomes, generating effective feedback can be quite complex. This problem 
is particularly challenging when traditional optimization methods may result in 
unrealistic recommendations. To tackle this issue, a novel approach is presented, 
invoking the principles of counterfactual learning, to model recommended actions 
as if the system had actual learning outcomes. This approach is represented by 
a general counterfactual learning framework (CFL) and is demonstrated through a 
specific application, a multi-task learning setting, showcasing the system's 
ability to handle diverse scenarios and facilitate online learning. This is 
further supported by experimental results showing the counterfactual learning 
framework's (CLF) efficacy on several datasets, with comparisons to existing 
methods. The code for the proposed method is available at: 
https://github.com/zheng-li/Counterfactual-Learning-for-Online-Recommendation. 
This work's advancements are also visually illustrated through an intuitive 
example, and the paper is rounded off with a discussion on potential future 
directions and challenges.
