When using human feedback to speed up reinforcement learning, a common strategy is to group similar actions together and receive feedback on the entire batch, rather than individual actions. However, this method's effectiveness depends on accurately assessing the quality of the batch's best and worst performances. We argue that making comparisons across batches is even more efficient when human feedback is limited. To tackle this challenge, we develop a method to compare multiple action batches based on their expected reward distributions. By leveraging a novel, efficient distance measure and a robust ranking approach, we can recover a reliable ordering of the batches' best and worst cases. This comparison tool can be applied to any reinforcement learning setup, and we showcase its performance on both a simple grid world game and the more complex Vizdoom game. Our results demonstrate that using our method to compare batches yields a significantly faster and more efficient learning curve than traditional approaches. Furthermore, we find that comparing comparisons -- in turn comparing more diverse sets of actions -- speeds up the learning process even further. Overall, our findings suggest that comparing multiple action batches efficiently is a crucial component of a reward learning system. We also explore alternative methods for refining our comparisons and discuss potential avenues for further research. By leveraging human feedback to compare multiple action batches efficiently, we can accelerate the reinforcement learning process by a factor of up to five in our experiments. Additionally, our approach enables us to learn from human demonstrations that are significantly noisier than the values we are trying to achieve. We believe that our results have important implications for the broader goal of creating a more efficient reinforcement learning pipeline. Moreover, our work demonstrates the feasibility of our approach when combined with a simple neural network policy learning method, and we see numerous opportunities to enhance our comparisons further. Ultimately, we view our research as a crucial initial step towards developing a robust and efficient reward learning system that can compare multiple action batches based on their expected reward distributions. By doing so, it can accelerate the reinforcement learning process by a factor of up to five when combined with a simple neural network policy learning method, and we are eager to explore alternative policy learning methods that can take advantage of our comparison tool. As a result, we plan to continue investigating alternative value function estimation methods that can refine our comparisons even further, as well as exploring other avenues for further research. Depending on the signature chosen, set theory can have multiple model companions or none at all. Our findings indicate that the existence of a single model companion for set theory greatly depends on the signature used. Furthermore, when the signature includes only the basic relational symbols, set theory does not have a model companion. However, when the signature is expanded to include unary function symbols, a model companion does exist. This study explores the existence of non-trivial solutions to a Branson-Paneitz type equation of fourth order, under specific boundary constraints in n-dimensional space, characterized by the use of fractional boundary values for the unknown function u. Additionally, when n is greater than two, the problem admits a non-trivial solution, provided certain parameters meet certain criteria. A new ground state is also identified for the related Branson-Paneitz type equation of fourth order, defined within the entire n-dimensional space. A rigorous proof is provided for both of these theoretical findings, with the aid of a mountain pass theorem and a compactness argument, modified to accommodate space-time fractional boundary conditions. A Dela-Humbert type estimate and a Moser-Trudinger type inequality, with Sobolev embedding, serve as critical components in this proof. A ground state solution is demonstrated through an explicit expression, derived through an approach that combines separation of variables and a determination of the constant multiplier, necessary for the equation's validity. A detailed analysis of the solution's properties, including monotonicity and zero-set characterization, is also provided. Furthermore, when n is equal to two, the problem does not admit a non-trivial solution, due to the presence of a trivial ground state. An example illustrating the problem's solution, along with graphical representations of the solution and its derivative, is also included. A discussion on the problem's fractional boundary condition, its relation to the Hardy inequality, and the implications of this condition on the problem's solution are also explored. A comparison of this problem's solution to that of the standard Branson-Paneitz equation, along with a discussion on the effects of the fractional boundary condition, are also presented. An open question, regarding the existence of a least energy solution, is also posed. An appendix, providing a Dela-Humbert type estimate and a Moser-Trudinger type inequality, with Sobolev embedding, completes this study. By analyzing data from 35 European countries for the years 1990 to 2012, we analyzed consumption trends of four psychoactive substances: cannabis, cocaine, heroin, and amphetamines. We discovered that the consumption patterns of these substances were closely linked, with some trends appearing across all four, and weaker correlations found between specific pairs of substances. For example, cannabis and hashish consumption exhibited the strongest correlation, followed by cocaine and amphetamines. We also found that Western European countries tend to follow the trends set by the United States, and that the influence of the United States on cannabis and hashish consumption is particularly notable. Additionally, we identified a significant increase in the consumption of all four substances during the 1990s, often referred to as the 'epidemic decade'. This trend was found to be linked to an increase in available heroin, and a peak in amphetamine consumption occurred in 2002. We used dynamic proximity to analyze these trends and the spatial diffusion of substances across different regions within Europe. We identified a west-to-east diffusion of heroin consumption, with consumption rising earliest in the United States and Western Europe, followed by Eastern Europe. We also found evidence of a north-to-south diffusion of cocaine consumption, with consumption rising earliest in Spain and Portugal, followed by Eastern Europe. Amphetamine and cannabis consumption, on the other hand, exhibited multiple peaks and no clear diffusion pattern. We believe that the findings from our analysis can contribute to the development of more effective strategies for combating substance abuse. We recommend that policymakers consider implementing targeted and adaptable measures, such as increasing funding for prevention and treatment programs during periods of rising consumption, and providing support to countries experiencing increased consumption rates. Quantum algorithms like HHL's for matrix inversion have the potential to significantly reduce computational costs in certain applications, however, implementing them on near-term quantum hardware poses a challenge due to the large number of gates required. To overcome this limitation, we present NISQ-HHL, an optimized version of the HHL algorithm that utilizes the circuit QED architecture to perform matrix operations using the square of the quantum state as a variable. This implementation leverages the properties of the annealing phase to achieve matrix applications with only a linear increase in the number of gate operations, making it more suitable for execution on near-term quantum devices. Using the example of a linear system with a sparse matrix, we compare NISQ-HHL to the classical multi-problem approach and find that even with the limited number of qubits available on these devices, the matrix application in NISQ-HHL offers a higher simulation advantage than the classical method. Furthermore, we examine the impact of qubit loss during matrix application and investigate potential solutions to mitigate this issue. As a result, NISQ-HHL makes it feasible to execute the HHL algorithm on quantum devices in the NISQ era. In addition, we present an open-source simulator and a Python-based tool for calculating and comparing the simulation benefits of matrix application, along with a proposal for enhancing the HHL algorithm through the integration of quantum discarding techniques. We examine the behavior of superconducting nanowires under the influence of an external magnetic field from mesoscopic to macroscopic scales. Our theoretical analysis uses a multibridge model to account for different critical voltages in the nanowire's junctions. When the applied voltage exceeds the highest critical voltage, a point of charge decay forms, allowing for dynamic control of the nanowire's critical voltage via an applied voltage. This control mechanism is achievable due to the large difference in capacitances between the nanowire's junctions. We demonstrate that an approximate solution can be obtained by balancing the potential differences across the Josephson junctions, and that this model yields results comparable to those from a full numerical simulation. Our analysis further reveals that an applied magnetic field can shift the point of charge decay significantly. Notably, in large-scale nanowires, the influence of an applied magnetic field can be countered by an applied voltage, enabling the precise adjustment of the point of charge decay and thus the nanowire's critical voltage. This finding has important implications for improving the efficiency of phase-voltage rectification in superconducting nanowires. Our theoretical framework can be experimentally verified and utilized to optimize the performance of large-scale superconducting nanowire sensors in sensing applications. Moreover, this research paves the way for exploring novel quantum phenomena in large-scale nanowires and could facilitate the development of sensitive magnetic field sensors and efficient phase-voltage rectifiers. Finally, we suggest that this model may be extended to study SIS nanowire resonators and that research on large-scale nanowires has the potential to contribute to quantum metrology and interferometry.

This study develops an algorithm that takes a given D-dimensional transitive polyhedron and produces all N-dimensional totally transitive polyhedra, making it suitable for D+1 dimensions and above. We demonstrate the algorithm's capability by generating the $d$-dimensional Coxeter polytopes of type A, D, and E using the Fano polyhedron as input, a 3-dimensional transitive polyhedron. For types A and D, the resulting polytopes are well-known, but those of type E, specifically in 4-dimensional space and above, have not been previously described in the literature. Our algorithm identifies 83 distinct 4-dimensional totally transitive polytopes of type E, extrapolating to over 2.5 million in 5-dimensional space, and an astonishing 10^11 in 6-dimensional space. Some of these polytopes are remarkably symmetrical, with others displaying lesser symmetry. None of the type E polytopes match the Coxeter polytopes found in lower dimensions. This research expands our understanding of totally transitive polytopes and suggests that many more such polytopes exist in higher dimensions. The algorithm and resulting polytopes are now available online for further exploration and visualization.

This research introduces a novel public-key encryption method called "unclonable encryption," along with a new framework for understanding "copy-protection" in unlearnable functions. By leveraging the principles of unclonable encryption, this method ensures the creation of digital assets that cannot be accurately replicated. These assets serve as a concrete example of "unlearnable functions," which, when given input, yield outputs that cannot be forecasted using any logical approach, even with unlimited computational power. In essence, unclonable encryption provides a solution to a long-standing problem of creating "copy-protection" mechanisms for software and other digital content. This work also paves the way for exploring other applications of unclonable encryption, such as securing communication channels and developing new forms of cryptographic primitives. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the feasibility of unclonable encryption using a specific construction based on indistinguishable obfuscation, in conjunction with a particular type of one-way permutation, which can be securely instantiated using various techniques known today. By showing that both essential components can be securely created independently, it follows logically that the entire unclonable encryption system can be securely built as well. This work thus presents the first public-key unclonable encryption scheme based on a specific set of fundamental computational assumptions, which, interestingly, does not rely on any form of RSA-based construction. In addition, this research also explores various other properties and variations of unclonable encryption, including its behavior when multiple parties attempt to replicate the same asset, as well as considering scenarios where the asset's original creator has limited access to its own copy. Lastly, this research proposes several potential applications and related research directions, which may spark further innovation in the field of unclonable encryption and related areas of cryptography and computer science. By laying the groundwork for a broader understanding of copy-protection through the concept of unlearnable functions, this work also aims to facilitate more in-depth exploration of these topics in the future. Ultimately, this research has the potential to open new avenues for the secure creation and management of digital assets in various computational contexts.

In this research, we address the fundamental challenge of creating channel codes that can be used for both information transmission and authentication. We demonstrate that any code capable of accurately transmitting and verifying information must tolerate high levels of error, effectively rendering its coding rate negligible. To overcome this limitation, we focus on generating lists of encoded messages, with the understanding that some lists may contain contradictory information. We show that such a code can be designed with a coding rate that approaches one unit, enabling its utilization for both data transmission and authentication, while maintaining scalability across various scaling factors for error tolerance. We also establish an upper limit for the size of generated lists in relation to the error tolerance and block length, with specific examples illustrating this upper limit's applicability. Our findings build upon prior work by Haghi et al. and incorporate new concepts, with implications for the development of codes that balance error tolerance, size, and computational complexity. We explore potential applications and examine potential research directions in this field.

Using density functional theory and time-dependent density functional theory, we examine how lattice structure and doping influence plasmon behavior in twisted bilayer MoS$_2$. Our analysis considers multiple MoS$_2$ twist angles, ranging from $\Gamma$-M to K-K' (10.5$^{\circ}$ to 26.7$^{\circ}$), three distinct doping levels, and two lattice relaxations - one with an ideal lattice and the other with an experimentally observed lattice rotation. We investigate the impact of these factors on plasmon energy, dispersion, and spatial distribution across different moir\'e layers. Our findings show significant variations in plasmon behavior due to the twist angle, with more indirect twist angles exhibiting lower plasmon energies and reduced interlayer coupling. In contrast, more direct twist angles lead to higher plasmon energies and increased interlayer coupling. Doping, whether ideal or nonideal, also significantly affects plasmon behavior, with electron doping causing a decrease in plasmon energy across all twist angles, in contrast to hole doping which exhibits varying effects. Furthermore, we identify specific twist angles with plasmon energies comparable to graphene at 2.7 eV, and demonstrate that the plasmon quantum size effect can be utilized to enhance plasmon energy through miniaturization. Our research provides a theoretical framework for understanding the intricate relationships between lattice structure, doping, and plasmon behavior in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides. This knowledge can guide experimental research and facilitate the design of devices that leverage controlled plasmon behavior for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings suggest that MoS$_2$ may serve as a suitable platform for plasmon-based applications, and that further investigation is warranted to explore its potential in fields like plasmonics and optoelectronics.

This research paper examines the theoretical underpinnings of almost conformal Ricci solitons, with a specific focus on their connection to almost conformal gradient Ricci solitons. We analyze the soliton equations in the context of almost conformal geometry and identify particular solutions that can be classified as almost conformal gradient Ricci solitons, provided certain compatibility conditions are met. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between these solitons and Einstein metrics, with discussions on the implications of conformal changes to Einstein metrics. We also derive conditions under which an almost conformal Ricci soliton can be classified as an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton. Additionally, we establish the compatibility of a specific class of solitons with parallel vector fields, and demonstrate the distinctness of this class from Einstein metrics. Lastly, we provide examples of almost conformal Ricci solitons constructed from the rotation of the Einstein metric on the Euclidean space $R^3$, along with solutions to the soliton equations on the Euclidean space $R^3$ and the sphere $S^3$. These solutions, however, are found to be incompatible with the condition of being almost conformal gradient Ricci solitons. We also discuss the relationship between these results and prior research on the topic.

The intricate relationships between the magnetospheres of stars and planets are being increasingly studied, revealing the significant influence these magnetospheres have on planetary environments. As we explore the comparative dynamics of stellar and planetary magnetospheres, it's essential to consider the distinct factors that shape each system. In the case of stars, their massive size and extensive plasma fields make them susceptible to weak stellar winds, whereas planetary magnetospheres are substantially affected by their planets' internal dynamos and nearby solar wind interactions. Furthermore, the variety of planetary types and possible biosignatures they may offer make it essential to develop observational and theoretical research methods, such as global modeling, that can help us better understand the magnetospheric processes and possible implications for exoplanet habitability. In this review, we examine current modeling approaches and available data sources, while also highlighting promising areas for further research and the necessary advancements to effectively tackle these complex problems. In the process, we'll clarify the terminology and underlying physics of magnetospheric processes, setting the stage for more in-depth discussions on the implications of stellar magnetospheres for exoplanet research and the potential for future research directions. Ultimately, this review aims to provide an authoritative overview on the magnetospheric processes of stars and planets, while also highlighting the necessary areas for further research and development in this exciting and interdisciplinary field. 

This review is accompanied by a graphical encyclopedia illustrating the various magnetospheric processes discussed, as well as a comprehensive glossary that defines key terminology and underlying physics for both stellar and planetary magnetospheres. The appendix also includes a list of relevant research papers and a roadmap for further research, along with recommendations for necessary computational tool upgrades to effectively address these complex problems.

The effect of Bismuth layers is not uniformly the same in all materials.  Depending on the material's structure, Bismuth layers either significantly impact the Hall effect in a non-integral manner or have a minimal effect on it.  This study investigates the impact of Bismuth layers on the Hall effect in a series of Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers using X-ray diffraction, Transmission Electron Microscopy, and electrical transport measurements.  Due to the presence of Bismuth anti-domains at the Cobalt/Bismuth interfaces, these layers have a major impact on the Hall effect in a non-integral manner.  However, Bismuth layers without anti-domains have a minimal effect on the Hall effect.  The results of this study indicate that the Bismuth anti-domains act as scattering barriers that increase the lateral resistance of the multilayers, thereby enhancing the anomalous Hall effect in a proportional manner.  This finding is corroborated by the results of a lateral resistance model, which indicates a direct correlation between the lateral resistance and the anomalous Hall effect.  This study provides a theoretical framework that explains the origin of the anomalous Hall effect in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers and offers a viable method for controlling this effect through the manipulation of Bismuth layers. In this research, we examine the possibility of solutions to N-dimensional Schrödinger equations within an exponential potential that varies according to the fractional parameter α in N-dimensional space. We demonstrate the feasibility of converging the bound state solutions for specific values of the parameter α, particularly when it assumes positive values in 1D and negative values in 2D and 3D dimensions. Our primary objective is to investigate the potential's behavior in relation to the fractional parameter α. To accomplish this, we derive an analytical expression for the mass spectrum, which explicitly reveals how the energy levels E_n in N-dimensional space are influenced by the fractional parameter α, the number of dimensions N, and the dimensionless quantity n. Our secondary aim is to present the wave function ψ_n(x, \alpha, N), which we have obtained through the variational method, as an entity dependent on x, the fractional parameter α, and the number of dimensions N. Our study offers a comprehensive examination of two-dimensional and one-dimensional bound state solutions in the exponential potential's framework, which may have implications for Quark-Confinement and Cosmological models. Furthermore, our investigation paves the way for exploring other potential applications of this model, such as the hydrogen atom and Harmonic Oscillator, and could potentially inspire new research in Mathematics and Physics. To facilitate replication of our results, we have made available the source code for the numerical solution of the Schrödinger equation. In recent years, research on the performance of neural networks with $p$-norm constraints has gained significant attention. Our study investigates how different $p$-norms influence the training of a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant, and we find that the choice of $p$ impacts both the training speed and accuracy. Specifically, we found that training a neural network with a $p$-norm constraint results in an increasing error rate as $p$ exceeds $2$. To address this issue, we propose a novel method for adaptively adjusting the $p$-norm constraint during training. Our proposed technique not only considers factors such as model complexity and training data, but also takes into account the current Lipschitz value to prevent overfitting. We demonstrated the effectiveness of our method on two complex image classification tasks – CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 – achieving enhanced accuracy and stability compared to the baseline model. Moreover, we found that our adaptive technique successfully identifies the optimal $p$-norm value for each task, and we found $p=4.5$ to be the optimal value for both CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. We believe our findings contribute positively to the ongoing discussion on the choice of $p$-norms in neural network research. To facilitate further research, we have made our code and data available publicly.

Sequential models are highly effective at grasping sentence hierarchies, with trees serving as a fundamental framework for syntactic analysis. Although some sequential models can leverage local heuristics to inform their understanding of sentence structure, it's unclear how these models use them to build a hierarchical representation. To gain insight into this process, we investigate the relationship between sequential models' understanding of sentence structure and their performance on certain local heuristics tests. We find that while these tests do provide some information about a model's ability to recognize hierarchical relationships, they do not paint a complete picture. We also identify specific challenges that arise when evaluating sequential models using these tests and propose a new evaluation framework that takes into account the relationships between different parts of speech. This framework enables us to conduct a comprehensive analysis of how sequential models use local heuristics to build a hierarchical representation of sentences. Our results show that both BERT and RoBERTa rely heavily on the most likely parse tree when making predictions, with BERT exhibiting a preference for shorter tree paths and RoBERTa exhibiting a preference for longer tree paths. When evaluating the ability of these models to recognize hierarchical relationships using the tests, we find that they are able to recognize local heuristics up to three words in depth. However, when evaluating the same models using our proposed framework, we find that they are only able to recognize hierarchical relationships up to two words in depth. This suggests that sequential models are able to recognize hierarchical relationships of greater depth when given more context. To demonstrate this, we create a task that requires recognizing hierarchical relationships of greater depth and demonstrate that pre-trained sequential models are able to perform this task with high accuracy. We also investigate the role of attention in this task and find that models pay attention to the beginning of the tree path when predicting the end of the tree path. To further investigate this phenomenon, we conduct a series of additional experiments that provide insight into the relationship between sequential models' understanding of sentence structure and their performance on local heuristics tests. The ultra-hot Jupiter planet HD80606b is notable for its significant orbital eccentricity, resulting in its surface temperature rising dramatically as it approaches its star during periastron. Researchers used the CHARA array to obtain high-resolution spectrophometric data through three-dimensional imaging of the planet as it transits its star, and a new technique called exo-ASTRA. This data showed the planet's intense heat and light distribution, providing insights into its atmospheric structure and storm patterns. By analyzing the spectral and light curves, scientists discovered powerful stellar winds, massive atmospheric heating, a highly irradiated surface, and a massive equatorial bulge due to the star-planet tidal interaction. This study has revealed the most detailed visual representation of an exoplanet's appearance, offering a wealth of new information about this extreme planetary system and highlighting the capabilities of the exo-ASTRA framework. Through this analysis, researchers were also able to test the limitations of this new technique, with results indicating that it can effectively derive key atmospheric parameters for a variety of exoplanet systems, even when data is limited to a single transit observation. This research demonstrated the utility of the exo-ASTRA framework by applying it to spectroscopic transit observations, and it paves the way for utilizing this technique with even more powerful observational tools in the future. By leveraging the capabilities of multi-object spectrographs and a new generation of high-cadence light curves, exo-ASTRA can provide in-depth analysis of exoplanet systems, enabling a deeper understanding of how these systems are formed and how they evolve. With this new framework, a comprehensive set of exoplanet atmosphere models is available, incorporating a wide range of planetary temperatures, stellar irradiation levels, wind losses, and atmospheric compositions, as well as various atmospheric structures, storm patterns, and tidal bulges. By uniting these models with a parameterization of the star-planet interaction, exo-ASTRA can derive a comprehensive set of observables for a given exoplanet system, as well as predict the spectral and light curves at various wavelengths, and even short-term stellar variations, and it can handle data analysis and visualization of this data. By applying this technique to HD80606b, researchers were able to demonstrate its effectiveness, with results showing the planet's intense heat and light distribution, providing new insights into its atmospheric structure and storm patterns. This study has the potential to reveal the most detailed visual representation of an exoplanet's appearance, offering a wealth of new information about extreme planetary systems

Achieving a perfect balance between motivating patients to engage in rehabilitation gamified exercises and ensuring they follow through with the prescribed tasks is crucial. The value of player experience and real-world adherence can be leveraged to facilitate this balance. However, the challenge lies in pinpointing the ideal combination of interaction parameters within the game that promotes both desired outcomes. To address this issue, we first conducted a survey among healthcare professionals and gamification experts to identify key factors affecting player experience and adherence in rehabilitation contexts. Subsequently, we prioritized these factors and grouped them into functional and aesthetic categories. Next, we consulted the existing literature to determine the degree of association between each factor and the outcomes of interest. Based on expert feedback, we developed a theoretical model illustrating the relationship between player experience and adherence in rehabilitation settings. However, this model is not practical for empirical testing. Therefore, we propose an alternative approach, proposing a set of general guidelines for balancing player experience and adherence in rehabilitation gamified exercises. These guidelines suggest considering the inherent benefits of positive player experience on adherence, while also emphasizing the importance of adherence-focused design to enhance player experience. Finally, we provide directions for future research, suggesting that testing and validation of the proposed model could be accomplished via empirical studies involving actual users playing rehabilitation gamified exercises. Additionally, exploring the impact of distinct antecedents, such as exercise difficulty and motivation, on the relationship between player experience and adherence is an area worthy of investigation. Furthermore, comparing the effectiveness of our guidelines with established gamification frameworks through thorough testing is also a promising area for future research. By pursuing these directions, we can refine our understanding of balancing player experience and adherence in rehabilitation gamified exercises, ultimately contributing to the development of more effective and engaging rehabilitation games that prioritize both player experience and adherence. By incorporating a linearised elasticity operator, often in the form of a $p$-energystable formulation, we aim to capture the effects of linearised elasticity on the geometrically nonlinear fracture energy framework, commonly referred to as the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model. Our research focuses on analysing the existence and uniqueness of solutions to an associated boundary value problem, as well as examining the regularity properties of these solutions. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between linearised elasticity and fracture energies through numerical computations, which provide insight into how different linearised elasticity parameters influence fracture energy measurements. All of our results are derived within the context of an $L^2$-formulation and are substantiated by concrete numerical data. Notably, our findings indicate that the impact of linearised elasticity can be regarded as an additional boundary fraction term affecting the fracture energy measurements, with its magnitude dependent on the specific parameter values and geometric measurements of the boundary. This research hopes to contribute to a better comprehension of how linearised elasticity influences geometrically nonlinear materials with fractures, laying the groundwork for more advanced linearised elasticity frameworks that consider both geometric nonlinearity and fracture. For vector leptoquarks, our research suggests using the NLO plus distribution (NLO+PS) method to enhance signal simulations in LHC searches. To apply this method, we need to obtain NLO cross-section predictions and corresponding PS inputs. We have derived the analytical formulae for NLO cross-section predictions and PS inputs in the context of the Standard Model, involving the combination of an electron, a missing energy direction, and two jets. Furthermore, we have calculated the cross-section predictions for the vector leptoquark $R_{2(3)}^{e\bar e j j}$ at the 8 TeV and 13 TeV LHC, and the corresponding searches for the NLO QCD effects, pure electroweak effects, and total cross-sections. Our research also compares the NLO+PS signal simulations to leading-order parton-level simulations, revealing significant discrepancies of up to a 50% difference in cross-sections for the 13 TeV LHC. To facilitate the effective incorporation of NLO+PS signal simulations into LHC search analyses, we have developed public code based on the MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO framework. By integrating the MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO code into the Delphes fast simulation program, we have created a Delphes extension called Delphes\_aMCNLO, enabling the efficient evaluation of LHC cross-section predictions and event weights for NLO+PS signal simulations and other complex signal simulations. This development allows for the fast assessment of signal robustness in LHC searches, thereby streamlining the search strategy development process. To illustrate this, we have incorporated our findings into the stop naturalness simplified model discipline, demonstrating the benefits of employing NLO+PS signal simulations. Additionally, we have contributed the Delphes\_aMCNLO code to the standard LHC analysis toolkit, along with an example use case featuring the vector leptoquark $R_{2(3)}^{e\bar e j j}$. This research is part of an ongoing effort to elevate the theoretical precision of LHC interpretations of simplified model searches. The associated input files for obtaining the NLO cross-section predictions and PS inputs are available online. Through this work, we aim to promote the adoption of NLO+PS signal simulations in LHC search analyses, and encourage researchers to explore this methodology with other new physics models. In doing so, we have made the Delphes\_aMCNLO code publicly accessible on GitHub

A recent deep-neural-network (DNN) model, combining with MRI information, has shown significant potential in enhancing low-dose PET images. However, developing such a DNN framework for clinical use requires extensive testing on actual PET/MRI data cases, with varying low-dose PET images compared to reconstructed images, providing the ground truth. Here, we first validate the capability of a complex DNN framework, consisting of three components, to produce high-quality low-dose PET images from actual PET/MRI data, with the following conditions: (1) using simulated data with varying levels of TPC noise, (2) using actual PET data with different doses, and (3) using clinical use cases with MRI information. The proposed DNN framework de-Noise-Deblur-Resample (DNDR) consists of three modules: a noise-reduction module (NR), a motion-blur-reduction module (MB), and a resolution-enhancement module (RE). The NR module uses a U-Net structure with an attention mechanism, the MB module uses a UNet with a spatial-attention mechanism and adaptive convolution, and the RE module uses a Coarse-to-fine UNet. To train the model, simulated PET images with TPC noise were used for the NR module, and realistic PET images with motion blur were used for the MB and RE modules. The DNDR framework significantly improved the low-dose PET images compared to the TOF-OSEM reconstruction, with an average increase of 12.5% in the LVI and 1.9 in the SUV-NR. Moreover, the DNDR framework produced high-quality images from MRI-only scans, with an average increase of 24.4% in the LVI and 2.3 in the SUV-NR, outperforming the TOF-OSEM reconstruction and the deep-neural-network-based MRI-only reconstruction model DeepTOF. The results demonstrated the capability of the DNDR framework to produce high-quality low-dose PET images from actual PET/MRI data, with various TPC noise levels, different doses, and clinical use cases with MRI information. The code and data used in this research are available at: https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/DNDR-PET. The trade-off between personalization in news consumption and individual privacy concerns has gained significant attention in recent years due to increased online news access and social media usage. To explore this balance, we investigated the preferences of four age groups (18-24, 25-34, 35-44 and 45-54) regarding the collection and use of personal data for personalized news recommendations. A qualitative survey revealed both positive and negative reactions among the participants, with younger individuals showing a greater willingness to compromise privacy for a more personalized news feed, while older individuals were more concerned about privacy and desired a balance between personalization and data protection. To validate these findings, we conducted a series of experiments using the recommender system dataset, with results indicating a notable gap in privacy awareness among the younger age groups. Ultimately, our research identified key factors influencing the balance between personalization and privacy, including risk tolerance, information sensitivity and concern for privacy, with significant differences observed across the age groups examined. To address these disparities, we propose an adaptive framework for personalization, which adjusts the level of personalization based on the user's age group and associated risk tolerance. The performance of this adaptive framework was evaluated and showed potential in addressing the privacy concerns of younger age groups, with room for improvement in tackling the privacy awareness deficits among these groups. The proposed approach has the potential to serve as a foundation for developing effective solutions to the complex problem of balancing personalization and privacy in recommendation systems, with a particular focus on the unique needs of younger users. Previous studies in neural coreference resolution used general-purpose embeddings, which are now outdated. Utilizing contextualized embeddings, particularly those from the BERT model, within neural coreference resolution while exploring their connection to centering theory was the aim of this study. Initially, the addition of contextualized embeddings in a high-dimensional setting revealed a significant improvement in coreference resolution performance; however, this gain was short-lived when the dimensions were reduced to the number of elements in the centering theory matrix. Upon further analysis using a Fisher discriminant analysis, the benefits of using contextualized embeddings became apparent when the dimensions were increased to 7, aligning with the structural patterns identified in the theory. Moreover, certain coreference relations exhibited a preference for specific dimensional configurations. By incorporating contextualized embeddings and adjusting to the new 7D distribution, the models were able to replicate the coreference resolution patterns observed in the original BERT model. Ultimately, using the reduced 7D representation yielded an increase in coreference resolution accuracy across four evaluation metrics. In this study, two parameterized algorithms for detecting three-cycles in directed graphs are presented, with one approach utilizing treewidth and the other using two width parameters from two different chordal graph classes. A fixed-parameter algorithm is provided, with an underlying treewidth parameter 'k', with an overall time complexity of O(2^2k n^2). Additionally, two fixed-parameter algorithms are given for detecting three-cycles within chordal graphs, one utilizing the treedepth parameter 'k' with a time complexity of O(k n^2) and the other utilizing two width parameters from two different chordal graph classes, with a combined time complexity of O(2^kk * 2^p_k n), where 'k' represents the treedepth of the subgraph and 'p' represents the branchwidth of the original graph. These algorithms contribute to a deeper understanding of parameterized algorithms for identifying fundamental patterns in directed graphs.

We investigate the long-term behavior of certain operators in the SU(1|1) holographic duality using symmetry to facilitate our calculations. By applying a coordinate transformation and identifying key operators, we simplify our analysis and determine the rates at which these operators grow or decay over time. Additionally, we observe the emergence of a preferred time direction and classify the operators based on their response to this time reversal. Furthermore, we suggest that some of these operators may exhibit exponential growth or decay, and we estimate the associated coefficients. Our findings also indicate that the structure of the spectrum of these operators corresponds to that of a two-dimensional scattering system, and we aim to further explore this connection in future studies. Our research methods involve expressing the metric and bulk geometry in terms of interning coordinates, analyzing the symmetries of the system to identify effective Hamiltonians, and classifying the operator scaling dimensions under these transformations. We investigate specific examples of operators in this framework and present our conclusions on the operator growth problem. Our work builds upon prior research and demonstrates the utility of symmetry-based approaches in complex quantum systems, pinpointing key challenges that remain to be overcome in solving the long-term operator problem.

Studies utilizing WiFi fingerprints for geographical localization have largely relied on traditional methods such as multivariate analysis, and have largely neglected the use of machine learning tools that facilitate easy data processing and effective feature extraction. Our research proposes an innovative approach that leverages a simple deep learning model, specifically the Graph Neural Network, to enhance the accuracy of geospatial distance estimation between WiFi fingerprints. The concept of advanced civilizations being defined by their primary energy source serves as a useful framework for the SETI Paramount Theory. This theory categorizes civilizations into four types based on how they generate energy: Type I (stellar), Type II (white dwarf), Type III (neutron star), and Type IV (black hole). We examine the energy production capabilities of white dwarf bodies, specifically focusing on the M5 type, and compare them to those of lower and more massive helium and carbon white dwarfs. Using the mass-radius relationship and the formula for bolometric luminosity, we find that an M5 type white dwarf offers the highest luminosity among the three and pose questions about the long-term stability of such bodies as potential Type II civilizations. Additionally, we investigate the likelihood of finding suitable M5 type white dwarfs as partners for the creation of an M5 type white dwarf civilization through the merger of two suitable M5 type white dwarfs within a close approach of less than 1000 AU over a useful period for observational surveys. We estimate the number of potential M5 type white dwarf civilizations eligible for observation and consider various factors including the availability of suitable white dwarf pairs and the time required for a pair to converge, also taking into account the limitations imposed by the semi-major axis and the necessity for further research on white dwarf mergers to better understand the characteristics of detectable gravitational waves. We also consider alternative scenarios in which an M5 type white dwarf civilization may arise, such as a single M5 type white dwarf that converges with a suitable companion, such as a red dwarf, in order to facilitate its merger into a new M5 type white dwarf, potentially leading to a Type II civilization in the future. We estimate the number of potential M5 type white dwarf pairs that could be detectable with the help of gravitational wave observatories such as LISA and the anticipated next-generation DECIGO in the near future, also comparing this to the expected number of new Type II civilization signals that could be identified through optical verification of potential candidates, which could be in the range of only a few per year, and discuss the potential for a signal that could be a candidate for an M5 type white dwarf civilization to converge with a suitable red dwarf companion, such as one that could lead to a merger into a new M5 type white dwarf, such as the one represented by K2-25d that is on the edge of being able to generate sufficient energy through its own means to become an M5 type white dwarf, but could still become one through merger

Large-scale network service deployments often rely on sophisticated Service Level Agreements (SLAs) to ensure high network standards and efficient resource allocation. However, monitoring network performance to detect SLA violations becomes increasingly complex as the network size grows. A promising approach to address this challenge involves utilizing Peer-to-Peer (P2P) technology to create a decentralized system for network performance monitoring. In this context, a novel architecture is proposed, leveraging a P2P network to detect SLA violations proactively. The proposed architecture comprises four key components: (1) a definition of the expected network standard, derived from relevant SLA parameters; (2) a monitoring system to assess actual network performance; (3) a detection mechanism to identify deviations from the standard; and (4) a corrective action to prevent further violations. Furthermore, the architecture is enhanced by an advanced detection mechanism, inspired by the ring structure of Distributed Hash Tables (DHTs), to efficiently detect SLA violations in large-scale networks. The effectiveness of this architecture is demonstrated through simulations, showing a significant improvement in violation detection time, with an optimal performance achieved in networks of up to 512 nodes. The proposed architecture can serve as a reference for the development of existing monitoring systems, facilitating proactive detection of SLA violations. Additionally, this architecture lays the groundwork for extensibility in various network settings and can accommodate multiple monitoring systems and SLA definitions. Ultimately, this research provides a solid foundation for addressing the challenges of large-scale network SLA monitoring and can contribute to the creation of autonomous network management systems. As part of this research, an open-source framework is available for download, along with an example implementation of a monitoring system for an IP network. In this implementation, an artificial intelligence-based detection mechanism is used to detect violations, with the source code featuring approximately 3,500 lines of Java code. As network services continue to evolve with the growing demand for cloud computing and multimedia applications, the need for effective SLA monitoring and violation detection will escalate, underscoring the significance of this research. This study reports the measurement of total neutron cross sections using a combination of neutron time-of-flight and neutron-neutron scattering probability in a highly pure scintillator target at the MESA storage ring. The data were collected with a proton beam of up to 3.2 GeV and were analyzed for neutron energies between 98 and 688 MeV. The results show a level of accuracy that ranges from 0.5 to 5.5 percent, allowing for a precise determination of the real part of the neutron form factor to a level of accuracy that ranges from 0.5 to 2.1 percent. The real part of the neutron form factor was found to be in agreement with theoretical predictions from dispersive analysis but the results also indicate a slightly higher value than expected from solutions of the Schrödinger equation. The analysis of the imaginary part of the neutron form factor was performed for the first time at high energies and the results show that it increases more rapidly than expected from low-energy measurements. The accuracy of the total cross section measurement was verified through independent checks that included the comparison with previous measurements and the consistency of measurements that were collected with different proton beam settings. The results are relevant for ongoing and future experiments at storage rings that involve the measurement of electromagnetic form factors of light atoms and nuclei. The methodology presented in this study can serve as a model for similar measurements that will be necessary to understand the interplay between strong and electromagnetic interactions in complex systems of quarks and gluons. Our computer simulations suggest that a specific temperature range, between 10-20 times the temperature of absolute zero, may be the most suitable for the formation of planetesimals. This finding is supported by increased sticking forces observed in our simulations, which occurred when the solar wind was removed or reduced in intensity. Planetesimals are thought to be the first building blocks of large celestial bodies such as planets and dwarf planets, formed when grains of similar size stuck together in a primitive solar system. However, given the weak sticking forces typically observed in simulations of this process, it has been difficult to replicate this process realistically. Using a sophisticated simulation method that accounts for the complex behavior of atoms and molecules at very low temperatures, we explored how sticking forces change in response to changes in temperature. We discovered a significant discrepancy in sticking forces that arose when we included the effects of collisions with other atoms and molecules, known as the solar wind. When we removed the solar wind, we found that sticking forces increased more rapidly with lower temperatures when the solar wind was present, but only in extremely dry conditions. In more typical environments, the solar wind has a much more significant impact on sticking forces than the presence or absence of water ice. Our research also revealed distinct differences in how sticking forces change with temperature in different environments, which could provide valuable insights into a solar system's history if observed in its small celestial bodies. In particular, extremely dry conditions may be indicative of formation in a stable, long-standing planetary system, while more typical environments may indicate a system that has been exposed to a wide range of conditions. Our computer simulations also explored the impact of collisions between grains of different sizes on sticking forces, finding that the solar wind has a much more significant impact on sticking forces than the presence or absence of water ice. However, we discovered that even when the solar wind is present, sticking forces increase more rapidly with lower temperatures in super-dry samples, suggesting that water ice may still play a key role in planetesimal formation even when it does not lower the freezing point of a mixture. This finding is significant because it implies that water ice may still contribute to the formation of planetesimals in a warm solar system, a perspective that challenges existing thought. In addition, our research suggests that water ice may have a greater impact on the formation of small grains than larger ones, potentially paving the way for the formation of differentiated bodies with a distinction in the composition of their small and larger components. The R package LFD R is an updated version of the LFD package in R, which provides functions for performing and graphing Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and its extensions, including the collective and constrained variants. The new version offers more features and improves previous functionality to support the implementation of semi-supervised LFD, low-rank LFD, and block-diagonal LFD. Additionally, LFD R includes a random walk approach and manifold learning through locally linear correspondence and spectral correspondence. It facilitates the analysis of high-dimensional data, particularly in cases with limited labeled samples, by identifying non-linear boundaries and promoting data separation. The package also includes a plotting feature using 3D graphics to visualize the analyzed data and its associated boundaries. The LFD R package can be accessed on CRAN via the "LFD" package. Imitation learning has emerged as a key method for robot skill learning due to its ability to efficiently transfer human skills to robot tasks. However, imitating a single demonstration is often insufficient, as it's prone to being distorted by the presence of noise or an unlimited number of examples is required. In contrast to traditional imitation learning, Constrained Imitation Learning (CIL) tackles a more comprehensive problem by addressing nonlinear hard constraints in robot skill learning. This work provides a comprehensive overview of CIL, covering both its theoretical foundations and various computational methods. We delve into specific problems and associated loss functions, as well as techniques for constrained optimization, and examine the different strategies employed to circumvent the label-free issue. Furthermore, we examine the design of constraint-guided neural networks and discuss issues related to data conformance. Additionally, we conduct a thorough review of prominent CIL research, along with associated datasets, and provide guidance on conducting CIL experiments. With the CIL field still in its nascent stages, there are numerous open research questions, and we address some of the key challenges and potential solutions. As the field of CIL is highly interdisciplinary, with roots in both machine learning and robotics, we also discuss the relevant background and outline potential future directions and research questions. Using unitarity and the Mellin transform, we derive a comprehensive equation for a specific two-glue correlation function within conformal Yang-Mills theory. By comparing this equation to super Yang-Mills amplitude calculations for six gluons, we find a connection between the two-glue correlation function and the gluon amplitude. Furthermore, we establish a related dispersion relation linking the two-glue correlation function to a Mellin transformed amplitude for four negative helicity gluons. This connection facilitates the reconstruction of the conformal Yang-Mills four-gluon amplitude from the two-glue correlation function. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in determining the conformal Yang-Mills amplitude for six gluons, and analyze the convergence properties of the dispersion relation. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the two-glue correlation function and the conformal Yang-Mills amplitude for positive helicity gluons. No additional assumptions about the analytic properties of the amplitude are required in our analysis. For the six-gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory, we find the two-glue correlation function for all helicity configurations, allowing for the direct determination of the conformal Yang-Mills amplitude through the dispersion relation we have derived. This provides a new method for studying the six-gluon amplitude, eliminating the need for on-shell reconstruction. We anticipate that this new method will be particularly useful for the ongoing and planned precision studies of the six-gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. In particular, it will enable the direct determination of the conformal Yang-Mills amplitude for positive helicity gluons, facilitating improved precision in the comparison with $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory at next-to-next-to-leading order. This new method is timely, given the significant progress made recently in the precision study of the six-gluon amplitude in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. In addition to its application to the six-gluon amplitude, our analysis establishes a connection between the two-glue correlation function and any conformal Yang-Mills amplitude for multiple gluons, allowing for the reconstruction of such amplitudes from the two-glue correlation function. This new method for studying the six-gluon amplitude offers a fresh perspective on the field and is expected to be a valuable tool for ongoing and planned precision studies. In conclusion, our analysis provides an innovative method for studying the six-gluon amplitude in conformal Yang-Mills theory

We examine the topological characteristics of a spin-orbit coupled superconducting state in a three-dimensional graphene structure with a honeycomb lattice, interacting with a normal metal, in the presence of an external magnetic field. Utilizing a proximity effect with a strong spin-orbit coupling and considering only odd-parity superconducting states, we find one potential state with a non-trivial topological characteristic protected by a magnetic field, as well as another protected by a magnetic field and time-reversal symmetry. However, these protected states are destroyed by the presence of the normal metal. Between these two cases, we find that the superconducting state can be stable across a broad range of proximities to the normal metal, while the critical proximity effect shows a more complex dependence on the magnetic field due to the interaction with the normal metal, particularly when this state is not protected by time-reversal symmetry. This study is also applicable to ongoing experimental research on the interplay between superconductivity and magnetism in these honeycomb structures, as it investigates how a magnetic field interacts with the topological characteristics of these materials. Our research reveals a complex vortex lattice behavior in the doped topological insulator Bi$_{2}$Se$_{3}$, a $d$-wave superconductor, as investigated through London sum rule decomposition and Hall oscillation measurements. The study shows that the vortex lattice undergoes multiple transitions as the applied magnetic field increases, which is consistent with theoretical predictions of van Hove singularities and the associated Lifshitz transitions. We further identify the location of these transitions by analyzing the Hall oscillation amplitude and phase, and compare them with simulations based on effective mass variations. Notably, we find that while some of these transitions are well-explained by the interaction between the superconductivity and Dirac cones, others require an additional mechanism to account for them, suggesting a potential origin tied to the electron filling in the superconductivity gap. Our findings provide new insights into the unique properties of topological superconductors and suggest that the vortex lattice in Bi$_{2}$Se$_{3}$ could serve as a testing ground for theories of superconductivity in other materials with strong electron correlations, such as cuprates and pnictides. This research paves the way for a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between topological electron filling, van Hove singularities, and electron correlations in the vortex states of these materials. As a result, this study may inspire the development of materials with highly robust superconductivity, as well as the manipulation of vortex states through the adjustment of electron filling. This could potentially enable the control of superconducting currents and, ultimately, the efficient transport of magnetic flux by an external magnetic field. This groundbreaking research has the potential to open up new avenues for the scientific community in the fields of condensed matter physics and materials science. Despite the complexity of the vortex state, our research demonstrates the feasibility of extracting crucial information about the electronic structure of a material by analyzing Hall oscillation measurements in a magnetic field. This knowledge can be used to refine and improve theoretical models of the vortex state, particularly those that incorporate the electron correlation and Van Hove singularities. Ultimately, a deeper comprehension of the vortex state will enable researchers to design materials with robust superconductivity and manipulate vortex states for efficient superconducting current transmission. Moreover, this research may also inspire the development of novel control methods for magnetic flux by adjusting the electron filling, ultimately contributing to breakthroughs in both fundamental scientific knowledge and groundbreaking technological applications.

The extent to which a surface is covered by stretched polymers influences the effectiveness of brush coatings in various applications, from microbial resistance to drug delivery. Statistical mechanics principles can be applied to determine the free energy associated with stretching polymers on curved surfaces. By using a diagonalized harmonic approximation and taking into account the curvature effects on pair interactions between adjacent chain segments, we calculate the free energy of stretching brushes in a range of curvatures, from planar to spherical. Our method also allows for the inclusion of constraints that limit the extent of stretching and provide a comprehensive view of brush coverage. Our approach is validated through comparison with molecular dynamics simulations and offers a more detailed understanding of brush structure and stretching behavior. Our theory is utilized to analyze the impact of stretching on the distribution of forces between the brush and adjacent surface layers and to examine how the brush responds to changes in stretching constraints, surface curvature, and temperature. Our findings also reveal how the brush resists compression and how it behaves under flow conditions, with possible applications in the design of brush-based systems that interact with living cells and materials in flow-based technologies. 

By possible technologies we mean those that involve the movement of materials or cells over surfaces coated with brush structures, where the brush's ability to resist flow and stick to surfaces is crucial. Our research provides a framework for analyzing how different surfaces are covered by stretched polymers, an essential aspect of these technologies, and can be expanded to account for additional interactions between the surface, polymers, and other substances, as seen in multi-component brush structures. 

Our study specifically examines brush coatings under stretching and considers possible applications in flow-based technologies, but our general approach can be applied to other types of forces that influence the brush's structure and coverage, such as compression, covalent binding, and chemical reactivity.

The concept of truncated graphs and the metric dimension of these graphs has been recently explored, where a subgraph is obtained by removing edges with a distance greater than a certain value from the original graph. In this work, we investigate the metric dimension of truncated graphs, specifically for the case where the subgraph is obtained by keeping only the edges with a distance less than or equal to k from the original graph. We focus on the scenario where the original graph is an infinite, connected and undirected graph that does not contain cycles. We show that the metric dimension of a truncated graph, denoted as G_k, is equal to the minimum number of nodes required to identify all nodes in G_k, where this minimum is achieved when k is greater than or equal to the graph's branchwidth. We also established that the metric dimension of a truncated graph, denoted as G_k, is equal to the minimum number of nodes required to identify all nodes in G_k, where this minimum is achieved when k is greater than or equal to the graph's branchwidth. We further demonstrate that for the case of cycle graphs, the minimum number of nodes required to identify all nodes in G_k is equal to 2, where this minimum is achieved when k is greater than or equal to 3. We also established that for the case of tree graphs, the minimum number of nodes required to identify all nodes in G_k is equal to 1, where this minimum is achieved when k is greater than or equal to the tree's pathwidth. We further investigate the complexity of calculating the metric dimension of truncated graphs, where this complexity is classified as NP-complete for general graphs and this classification holds even in the scenario where the original graph does not contain cycles and all its nodes have a degree of either 1 or 2. We also established that the metric dimension of a truncated graph can be calculated in linear time when the original graph is a tree, where this calculation is based on the computation of the highest k value where the graph's k-truncation is a connected component. We also investigate the relationship between the branchwidth and the minimum number of nodes required to identify all nodes in a truncated graph, where this relationship is explored through an NP-complete problem that involves determining whether a given graph's k-truncation has a branchwidth of less than or equal to a specified value. Although the Gravitational Wave Interferometer (GWI) is highly sensitive, analyzing GW data in the context of GW signals is a complex task that demands a deep understanding of GW signals in the presence of real-world variability. Since GWI is expected to observe signals from hundreds of millions of stars, including those with AGN variability, it's crucial to investigate whether there's a connection between these variables. By utilizing the VLITE telescope and GW data, researchers can distinguish between transient and quasi-periodic variability. However, modeling this variability to predict potential signals in GW data is a challenging task. To address this issue, researchers have developed the Active Galactic Nuclei Variability Engine (AGE), a comprehensive model that accounts for all types of variability, including oscillations, by integrating the disk's thermal energy into its structure. However, simulating this process is computationally intensive and may not be compatible with GW simulation constraints. To overcome this limitation, researchers have developed a simplified model, the Lruk model, which focuses solely on the disk's thermal fluctuations. Despite its computational efficiency, the Lruk model fails to replicate the quasi-periodic variability observed in UV spectra. In contrast, the AGE model excels in capturing the phenomena of the Lruk model while also incorporating the effects of the jet and the influence of the central black hole's spin. Ultimately, the AGE model is the most suitable model to predict the occurrence of these variables in GW data, thereby enabling more accurate signal-to-noise ratio calculations. As a result, researchers can better assess the detectability of signals in GW data and refine its parameters more accurately. To further test the AGE model's performance, researchers modified the Lruk model to produce the same energy flux and variability characteristics, before inputting this modified output into the AGE model to assess its ability to replicate the original Lruk model's variability. Approximating social welfare in scenarios involving multiple agents is a fundamental challenge in decision-making processes. Recent research has shown that using valuations from bipartite matchings and directed graphs can result in substantially improved approximation quality. However, the computational complexity of these valuations often hinders their practical application. In this paper, we investigate the interplay between computational complexity and approximation quality in two settings: one involving bipartite matchings and the other directed graphs. Our contributions in each context represent an advancement over current state-of-the-art results. Specifically, in the context of bipartite matchings, we develop an approximation algorithm with a higher quality approximation ratio than existing methods, and in the context of directed graphs, we demonstrate that approximating social welfare computationally becomes NP-hard, in contrast to the much simpler computational complexity of the underlying valuations themselves. These research directions and the associated methods we propose may find usefulness in applications involving network flows, matching problems, and graph matching. These settings could be relevant to various economic scenarios such as market clearing, auction design, and the allocation of resources. As asteroids approach Earth, their composition, structure, and other key properties can be accurately determined through the analysis of their light curves and the point spread function of the imaging system. This method is particularly effective for detecting binary asteroid candidates from wide field surveys, especially when the asteroids' orbits make them suitable for in-depth study. Researchers frequently examine network effects by comparing differences within and across networks.  While many studies mention the possibility of peer effects at an intuitive level, their measurement is often overlooked due to data limitations.  A more systematic analysis aims to provide a framework for quantifying network effects, either through model specification or empirical analysis.  This framework involves assessing multiple factors including, but not limited to, the measurement of effects, variety of network structures, and potential for endogeneity.  In this paper, we introduce novel methods for estimating peer effects within networks, leveraging both structural and probabilistic approaches.  A key contribution involves demonstrating the applicability of these methods to a previous finding that employers' racial bias leads to higher unemployment rates for minorities.  In order to achieve this goal, we explore peer effects on the probability of being employed as well as the magnitude of racial bias.  Our analysis indicates that peer effects reduce the probability of being employed and the magnitude of racial bias, further highlighting their significance in the labor market network.  Specifically, a 10% increase in the number of employed members of one's own racial group increases the probability of being employed by 0.5-1.4%, whereas a 10% increase in the number of employed members of another racial group has a marginal effect of -0.5% to -1.1% on the probability of being employed.  Additionally, a 10% increase in the number of employed members of one's own racial group reduces the magnitude of racial bias by 0.5-1.5%, whereas a 10% increase in the number of employed members of another racial group has a marginal effect of -0.5% to -1.5% on the magnitude of racial bias.  We also explore how these peer effects operate across racial lines by estimating a model that accounts for the composition of networks in a flexible manner.  A key finding from this analysis reveals that minority peers have a negative effect on the probability of being employed and the magnitude of racial bias, whereas peers of European descent have no significant effect.  Notably, the magnitude of these effects is comparable to those estimated in the primary analysis.  This suggests that the observed peer effects are not merely a consequence of network composition, but rather an intrinsic phenomenon.  We further investigate the mechanism underlying these peer effects by estimating a model that accounts for the impact of network effects on the composition of networks in a flexible manner. This paper presents a machine learning-based, automated tool for analyzing galaxy spectra, specifically utilizing BPT (Baldwin, Phillips, \& Terlevich) diagrams to classify the source of ionization. The model is trained on a large dataset of 1,000,000 spectra extracted from the Vickers et al. (2017) database, which is derived from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The dataset is a representative sample of local galaxies and is used to develop a simple, automated, and fast code that can easily integrate with existing spectral analysis software. The code first removes noisy data and selects relevant sections of the spectrum before applying BPT diagrams to determine the source of ionization. It can determine six different ionization modes and calculate key line ratios used in BPT diagrams. The code also provides a classification based on the Baldwin-Phillips-Sargent diagram, which takes into account the stellar velocity dispersion. The model's performance is evaluated using various metrics, including scatter and bi-weight scale for its accuracy, and is compatible with the iJaffeW tool for visualizing results. The Gondwana supercontinent's breakdown is well documented, with links made between rifting marginal structures and the tectonic activities of adjacent passive margins. Yet, a comprehensive analysis of these structures' evolution across Africa is lacking. By integrating remote sensing, geological field data, and numerical modeling, we examine the East African rift system's extension history and its associated passive margin evolution. We find that changes in extension direction and velocity significantly impacted the development of these structures. Initially, extensions in a north-easterly direction and at moderate velocities led to the formation of numerous, narrow, and linear fault blocks. These eventually gave rise to the East African rift system's prominent western branch. However, a later shift towards a more easterly direction, coupled with increased extension velocities, resulted in wider, more irregular fault blocks characterizing the eastern branch. This shift towards irregular fault blocks in the eastern branch is attributed to a velocity increase that induced thermal weakening and strain localization in areas of thick crust. This research offers a detailed, regionally applicable model for predicting the evolution of rifting margins and contributes to a broader understanding of how passive margins evolve at the junction of active continental rift systems. It also highlights the significance of regional-scale extension direction and velocity in controlling the development of margin-parallel fault blocks and suggests that these factors play a critical role in determining the geometry and style of continental rifts. Finally, this study implies that the East African rift system's extension history may have been influenced by a combination of thermal and tectonic weakening, along with changes in extension direction and velocity driven by the movement of Gondwana and the African supercontinent within the surrounding oceanic plates. This research has significant implications for modeling and predicting the evolution of continental rifts and passive margins in the search for hydrocarbon resources. It also offers a framework for analyzing the extension history of other continental rift systems and provides a new perspective on the complex processes governing continental break-up and passive margin evolution. This perspective can be applied to a broader range of tectonic settings, including areas of reactivation and rejuvenation of pre-existing rifts and continental margins. Finally, this research paves the way for interdisciplinary collaborations that integrate remote sensing, geological field observations, and numerical modeling to tackle the most pressing questions in continental geology and geophysics. It is our hope that this study will spark a series of regional and global analyses of the extension history and passive margin evolution across Africa, contributing to a deeper understanding of the complex processes governing continental break-up and passive margin evolution.
