Approximations to evaluate the impact of future decisions are commonly computed using backward evaluation to reverse the effects of given functions in optimization and control problems. However, this process typically involves inverting functions that don't have known inverses, which can include non-invertible functions like integrals. To overcome this limitation, researchers have been using innovative techniques to represent the impact of future decisions using Monte Carlo evaluations, sparse approximations, or deep neural networks. In our work, we present a new approach that leverages problem structure to solve a broad class of optimal control problems by modeling the state and cost evaluations as operator equations. We then employ neural networks with sparse activation functions to approximate the cost evaluations and develop a sparse approximation method for the backward evaluation. By harnessing the structure of problems, our approach can significantly improve computational efficiency, with our results demonstrating that our neural network solutions can be up to 10 times more computationally efficient than traditional Monte Carlo methods. Moreover, our method allows us to solve high-dimensional optimal control problems efficiently, with a particular application in modeling the optimal deployment of renewable energy resources in high-voltage power grids. To facilitate further research, we are releasing an open-source Python package called Pymac that implements our sparse approximation method for backward evaluations and can be used in conjunction with popular solver libraries for optimization and control problems. As our approach leverages problem structure to enhance computational efficiency, we are open to exploring new techniques that can improve our results through innovative modeling of operator equations using neural networks with diverse activation functions. To this end, we are releasing a community roadmap that outlines key research questions and suggestions for further improvement, with a focus on enhancing computational efficiency, developing new approximation methods, and applying our results to real-world problems. In conclusion, our work presents a groundbreaking approach that combines problem structure and neural networks to solve high-dimensional optimal control problems more efficiently, and we invite the community to collaborate with us in achieving even greater computational efficiency and broader real-world applications. Through joint efforts, we can unlock the full potential of our approach to solve even more complex and high-dimensional problems. To facilitate collaboration, we are open to discussing research ideas, sharing results, and contributing to the ongoing development of the Pymac package. The mechanics of cells are primarily governed by stress fibers, which consist of bundles of actin filaments and myosin motors that generate force through contraction. The mechanical properties of single stress fibers have been the subject of several studies, and it has been found that they act as nonlinear viscous elements with a high level of contractility. The contractility of stress fibers plays a crucial role in their mechanical behavior and can be accurately quantified using the Kelvin-Voicebody model, which has been validated through experiments. The purpose of this study is to analyze how the contractility of stress fibers contributes to the mechanical properties of cells with multiple stress fibers. To achieve this, a simplified model consisting of two stress fibers was developed to investigate how the contractility of cells changes in response to changes in fiber contractility. It was found that the contractility of cells with multiple stress fibers can be accurately quantified using the Kelvin-Voicebody model, and that the total contractility is directly proportional to the average contractility of individual stress fibers. Notably, the ratio of total contractility to average contractility is independent of the number of stress fibers and is determined solely by the cross-correlation of their mechanical properties. This finding provides valuable insight into the contractility of cells with complex architectures and suggests that the contractility of cells can be effectively measured using a minimal model consisting of a single stress fiber. The mechanical properties of cells with complex architectures can be challenging to measure due to their intricate structure, and our study offers a novel approach to addressing this issue. The developed model can be applied to study the contractility of cells with complex architectures consisting of multiple stress fibers, and it can be particularly useful for investigating how stress fibers reorganize themselves in response to changes in cell contraction. Additionally, it can be employed to analyze the contractility of cells with diverse architectures, such as cells with polarized stress fibers or cells with stress fibers that are resistant to reorganization. The model can also be used in conjunction with flow and force-assisted reorganization of stress fibers, and it has the potential to be adapted to include stress fibers with complex architectures consisting of bundled filaments. Overall, our study provides a fundamental understanding of how the contractility of cells with complex architectures is governed by the contractility of individual stress fibers, and it offers a degree-of-freedom reduction approach that can be applied to study the contractility of cells with diverse architectures consisting of multiple stress fibers. Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum facilitate anonymous transactions, 
which can be comfortably masked by malicious actors to conceal their traces. 
To combat this, it's essential to analyze the temporal transaction graphs (TTGs) 
constructed from cryptocurrency transactions, which can reveal patterns of cyclic 
behavior indicative of suspicious activity. However, existing methods for detecting 
cycles in graphs are plagued by high computational costs and lack effectiveness 
against large-scale TTGs. To address this limitation, we propose a novel, 
efficient method called CMH-Cycle, which can accurately detect 3-node cycles in 
TTGs by utilizing a custom-made hash table to minimize computational overhead. 
Furthermore, CMH-Cycle is capable of identifying cycles of longer length by 
fragmenting them into 3-node cycles. We demonstrate the superiority of CMH-Cycle 
through comparative experiments, showing it achieves superior performance (in terms 
of cycle detection time and precision) compared to other leading cycle detection 
algorithms, including a custom-made deep learning-based alternative. Specifically, 
CMH-Cycle can detect 3-node cycles at a rate of 5.33 million per second, an 
increment of 1040% over the best performing alternative, while its precision 
stands at 99.97%. We also showcase the efficacy of CMH-Cycle in identifying 
cyclic behavior within large-scale cryptocurrency transaction graphs, which is a key 
focus area for cryptocurrency security. The proposed CMH-Cycle cycle detection 
method is now available online at https://github.com/zhengda924/CMH-Cycle.

The results show that the precision of fault-tolerant quantum computing can be enhanced by a factor of up to five using a hybrid decoder trained both classically and on a quantum simulator. Furthermore, the development of a hybrid decoder that leverages a neural network trained via reinforcement learning and mounted on top of a high-performance classical decoder resulted in a significant improvement of the threshold tolerance from 0.15 to 0.32, indicating a substantial increase in the stability of quantum computing precision. However, the incorporation of quantum neural network simulators did not yield notable improvements. The precise learning scenarios that are best suited for this approach are examined, and the potential for future advancements in quantum machine learning is also discussed. The open-source framework used in this research is an extension of the Quantum Simulator Framework and comprises approximately 1,500 lines of Python code, along with approximately 350 lines of Python code for the reinforcement learning decoder, and is compatible with the Cirq and Branca quantum programming frameworks. Quantum metrology investigates how using quantum systems can enhance precision in measurements. A new approach, known as quantum jump metrology, leverages the unique characteristics of quantum systems that exhibit spontaneous transitions between states to achieve better accuracy. This method involves using the quantum system as a probe to monitor a target variable affected by a coherent process, and includes conditions under which it offers a significant precision improvement. Compared to other methods, quantum jump metrology has the advantage of measuring variables that are not directly accessible, and requires relatively simple and robust quantum systems. We examine the limitations of this approach and and find that it can provide a precision improvement scaling with $N^2$ in applications such as the estimation of a phase shift caused by a coherent process involving multiple levels, and $N$ for the estimation of a decay rate in systems with spontaneous transitions between two levels. Quantum jump metrology can be performed using a sequence of measurements on a single application of the system, and offers a precision improvement over traditional methods under certain conditions, specifically when the number of spontaneous transitions is large, the number of coherent steps is limited, and the system has a low spontaneous transition probability in comparison to a situation where the system undergoes many spontaneous transitions in each measurement sequence. We propose the use of a laser with a long pulse duration and a low average power to meet these conditions, and discuss the potential for this approach to be applied to a wide range of systems, including ion traps and optical lattices. In recent years, researchers in the field of upper bounds for mathematical sequences has seen significant advancement, with various approaches being explored, including computational methods, pattern recognition, and algebraic techniques. This paper highlights novel strategies employed to investigate upper bounds for recursive sequences defined by non-linear equations and demonstrates their effectiveness. Specifically, sequences defined by polynomials and rational functions are examined, and the upper bound estimation method is applied to key number theoretic sequences, including the prime numbers sequence, obtaining more precise bounds than previously reported and showcasing the utility of this approach in upper bound estimation. Furthermore, this work also introduces an online database where upper bound estimates for sequences can be accessed and new lower bound estimates for the Riemann Hypothesis are proposed based on the sequence $\pi(x)-\li(x)$, with associated computational data being contributed to the database. The developed framework and computational tool have the potential to enhance research in the field of upper bounds in mathematics. These concepts are further illustrated through the analysis of upper bound estimates for sequences related to exponential sums and the distribution of primes in residue classes. The presented techniques and findings contribute to a deeper understanding of upper bound estimates and their intricate connections to fundamental problems in number theory. Cloud-based HPC systems face significant hurdles in achieving low latency and high bandwidth due to the inherent limitations of shared network resources, particularly when combined with memory-intensive workloads that heavily utilize last-level caches. As a result, there is a growing need to optimize cache efficiency in computational models, particularly in matrix-based operations commonly found in scientific simulations. In order to address this issue, we propose a novel architecture called the 'Cache-Aware Matrix Closer' (C2), which leverages a unique combination of cache hierarchy awareness and inexact design techniques to minimize data misalignment and associated performance penalties. By utilizing a hierarchical placement strategy, C2 effectively reduces data relocation across different levels of cache by approximately 30-50% and bands the memory access patterns, leading to a significant decrease in memory traffic by up to 25%. As a result, the 'Cache-Aware Matrix Closer' showcases a notable 10-25% improvement in FLOPS efficiency and a considerable decrease in average memory access time by up to 12.5 cycles, achieving a 10-40% increase in overall system throughput. Moreover, C2 demonstrates the ability to increase energy efficiency by up to 11% while maintaining comparable energy consumption per operation. To validate the effectiveness of C2, we applied it to two matrix-based applications from the HPC class and observed a notable 5-10% increase in performance on actual HPC hardware. By addressing the challenges posed by modern HPC cache hierarchies, C2 provides a general framework for optimizing cache efficiency in computational models and can be adapted to various matrix-based applications. As such, it offers a valuable resource for researchers and architects seeking to enhance the performance of matrix-intensive workloads. Furthermore, the techniques employed by C2 can be integrated into design automation tools, enabling the exploration of novel applications and architectures that prioritize cache efficiency. As cloud-based HPC systems continue to evolve, the issues addressed by C2 will persist, and the proposed architecture will remain a relevant and valuable contribution to the field. In order to facilitate further exploration of C2, we have made the underlying hardware model and the matrix-based workloads used in this research open to the public, along with the C2 architecture itself. By sharing these resources, we aim to stimulate collaboration and drive the development of innovative solutions for optimizing cache efficiency in modern HPC cache hierarchies. As such, the C2 architecture is now available on an accompanying webpage, along with all associated files and data, which can be accessed via the linked repository.

While Scrum methodology is widely adopted to manage projects, especially in software development, its effectiveness varies based on team and project characteristics. The COVID-19 pandemic's shift to remote work presents an opportunity to examine the suitability of Scrum in virtual settings. Through an online survey targeting software development professionals with experience working remotely using Scrum, this study aims to investigate the following research questions from a technical effectiveness and managerial usability perspective. A multiple factor analysis was conducted to evaluate the relationships between variables, revealing significant connections between self-reported technical effectiveness and usability of Scrum practices, as well as the intersection of these factors and remote work factors. Notably, remote work teams reported lower technical effectiveness and usability of Scrum, while teams that successfully integrated Scrum's planned aspects, such as sprint planning and backlog management, reported higher technical effectiveness and usability. In terms of anti-patterns, teams that experienced conflict over Scrum implementation, reliance on individual heroism, and deviation from best practices showed lower technical effectiveness and usability. Furthermore, there was a clear distinction between variables associated with technical effectiveness and usability from those related to remote work, suggesting that Scrum can be effective in remote settings when properly implemented. However, teams failing to adhere to Scrum's planned aspects experienced lower technical effectiveness and usability, indicating a need for caution when adopting Scrum in virtual environments without adequate support. In such cases, full-scrum may not be the best approach, and a hybrid method might be more suitable. To facilitate this understanding, this study introduces the Scrum Hybrid Maturity Model, providing a framework for assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of Scrum adoption in remote work settings. This model encompasses four levels: hybrid-form, hybrid-style, hybrid-team, and hybrid-full Scrum, offering a foundation for researchers and practitioners to explore and define the characteristics of these levels. By recognizing the challenges and anti-patterns associated with remote Scrum, as well as identifying variables related to technical effectiveness, usability, and remote work, this study contributes to a deeper comprehension of Scrum's technical effectiveness and usability in virtual environments. It also highlights the significance of distinguishing between hybrid Scrum forms and identifying the variables associated with anti-patterns in this context. Ultimately, this research sets the stage for further investigation into the Scrum Hybrid Maturity Model, providing a framework for exploring and defining the characteristics of the four levels and addressing the anti-patterns identified. In policy learning, using efficient value function estimates obtained from rollouts or simulated data can accelerate and optimize the learning process. However, the number of testing samples affects the variance of these estimates, with smaller batches leading to noisier predictions. This research explores the connection between sample size and the performance of value function estimates, demonstrating that even with smaller samples, a well-designed policy optimization method can still benefit from efficient estimates. By balancing the trade-off between estimation noise and computational cost, the method can be refined to achieve even better results. We analyze the impact of testing sample size on the variance of efficient value function estimates and establish an upper limit based on the model's complexity. This research sets the groundwork for developing policy optimization methods that adapt to varying sample sizes, providing a framework for addressing the challenges posed by noisy estimates. The described approach is applied to a concrete algorithm, the efficient policy optimization (EPO) method, and is evaluated in a simulated setting for both single and multi-step models. The results show that EPO can effectively mitigate the impact of estimation noise, leading to superior performance compared to baseline methods. The influence of sample size on EPO's performance is also examined, demonstrating that even with smaller samples, EPO can still achieve significant improvements over baseline methods. However, the method's performance does degrade with excessively small sample sizes. Furthermore, an analysis of the sample size's impact on the variance of value function estimates, as well as the associated bias, is examined through a series of sample size experiments. The findings indicate that the optimal sample size for efficient value function estimates is inversely proportional to the model's complexity. The research also explores the connection between the sample size and the variance of the value function estimates' bias, providing a quantitative assessment of the trade-off between variance and bias at different sample sizes. The ATLAS collaboration at the LHC has conducted a comprehensive comparison of charged hadron, pion, kaon, and proton transverse momentum distributions in minimum bias events across various collision energies, including the LHC at 2.76, 5.02, and 13 TeV, as well as the SPS at 17.3 TeV, the RHIC at 200 GeV and 62.4 GeV, and the LHC at 7 TeV. This comparison takes into account initial state dependencies represented by ECAL and ALICE's AMPT calculations, and for the first time, it examines how the distributions of second-order elliptic flow $v_2$ and mean $p_T$ correlate across different energies and species. It finds that the $v_2(p_T)$ distributions maintain a similar shape to previous findings at lower energies, while at 13 TeV, they exhibit a more pronounced curvature. Furthermore, the study reveals that the $v_2/p_T$ ratio exhibits little dependence on $p_T$ across various centrality intervals and collision energies, except for the 13 TeV case which shows a higher $v_2/p_T$ at lower $p_T$. Additionally, it finds that the $v_2(p_T)$ distributions become broader with increasing energy from 2.76 to 13 TeV, and that the initial state dependencies represented by ECAL and ALICE's AMPT calculations hold significant influence over the $v_2(p_T)$ distributions. It also finds that the $v_2/p_T$ ratio at mid-rapidity remains relatively constant across different centrality intervals and collision energies, except for the 13 TeV case which shows a higher $v_2/p_T$ at lower $p_T$. It also finds that the $v_2/p_T$ ratio at forward rapidity exhibits similar behavior to mid-rapidity, and that the $v_2$ and $p_T$ mean show a linear correlation across various centrality intervals and collision energies, except for the 7 TeV case which shows a higher $p_T$ mean than expected. It also finds that the $p_T$ mean exhibits a mass hierarchy across different collision energies, except for the 7 TeV case which shows a similar $p_T$ mean to pions and protons but an elevated $p_T$ mean for kaons compared to lower energies. It attributes the observed behavior at 13 TeV to increased gluon radial flow

These inequalities provide bounds for expressions involving the stockwell transform in terms of the Hardy-Littlewood inequality, the power means inequality, the weighted power means inequality, the Hardy inequality, and the Fejer inequality. Additionally, this research establishes the sharpness of these inequalities. Furthermore, we demonstrate the application of these inequalities to obtain integral inequalities for the real part of the stockwell transform by employing specific examples. These examples also illustrate the superiority of these inequalities over others. Furthermore, we define the stockwell operator and investigate its adjoint, identifying it as the Quaternion Linear Canonical Inverse Stockwell Transform. We establish new integral inequalities for the stockwell operator, including those related to the Hardy-Littlewood, power means, weighted power means, Hardy, and Fejer inequalities. These inequalities provide bound expressions involving the stockwell operator or its inverse, demonstrating their superiority over alternative inequalities through specific examples. These results expand our understanding of the stockwell operator and its inverse, introducing new integral inequalities that could be applied across various mathematical contexts. Lastly, this research is connected to the broader field of stockwell operators, offering novel contributions within the realm of the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform and its inverse. In 1963, Erdos and Straus posed the question of finding expressions equal to $7^n$ for any positive integer $n$, in the form of $a^2 + b^2 = 7^{n}$, with $a$ and $b$ being positive integers. This question remains unanswered to this day. However, in a related problem, we explore expressions of the form $a^2 + b^2 = 7^n$, where $a$ and $b$ are not necessarily distinct. We provide a mathematical proof that if $7^k$ can be represented as the sum of two squares in a base of $n$, then it can also be represented as such in a higher base of $m$, where $k$ is a positive integer, and $m$ and $n$ are integers with $m \geq 2$ and $n \geq 1$. We demonstrate this concept by showing that any number $7^k$ can be represented as the sum of two squares for any positive integer $k$. Additionally, we provide a mathematical expression $a^2 + b^2 = 7^{n}$ for any positive integer $n$, with $a$ and $b$ being positive integers. This leads us to the conclusion that the minimum number $7^k$ such that the expression $a^2 + b^2 = 7^k$ holds true for exactly two pairs of positive integers $(a, b)$, is $7^8$. Furthermore, we offer an unlimited number of instances $7^k$ for any $k \geq 8$. This implies that Erdos and Straus' question has an affirmative answer. This question has an affirmative answer when $7^k$ can equal 7 raised to the power of n, involving two distinct positive integers a and b, for any positive integer n. This is demonstrated through an infinite number of cases $7^k$ for any positive integer $k \geq 1$. This achievement provides a mathematical expression $a^2 + b^2 = 7^n$ for any positive integer $n$, with $a$ and $b$ being positive integers. This leads to solving another problem posed by Erdos and Straus in 1963, regarding expressions of the form $a^3 + b^3 = 7^n$. This achievement opens the door for exploring other similar problems in mathematics. This research has been conducted without any financial assistance.

A robotic hopping model is proposed, utilizing an inverted pendulum actuated by an electric motor on soft ground, and the development of a high-gain feedback controller is presented to successfully achieve precise tracking of pre-designed trajectories. The robotic hopping model is analyzed to identify its stable limit cycle behavior, and the effectiveness of the feedback controller is demonstrated through both numerical simulations and experimental implementations, showing accurate replication of desired trajectory patterns. Additionally, the proposed controller maintains the stability of the limit cycle, and a saturation margin analysis ensures that the controller does not cause Hopf bifurcations. We analyze the relationships between these radii and the corresponding meson masses, examining factors such as the hypercentral force and gluon orbital angular momentum that influence the radii. Additionally, we compare our calculations to empirical data and theoretical predictions from the relativistic potential model and the MIT bag model. Our hypercentral model exhibits the highest level of accuracy in matching calculated and observed mass splittings among the various meson groups. Furthermore, our model accurately predicts the mass splitting patterns for heavier mesons, positioned above the charm threshold, in agreement with $SU(3)$ flavor symmetry breaking. We also successfully reproduce the observed mass splitting patterns for the $D$-mesons and the $\Lambda_c$ baryon. We also calculate the charge radii for these mesons, which can provide further insights into the internal structure of these particles. The task of identifying negations in text has been a long-standing challenge in natural language understanding, with numerous existing approaches showing limited success when confronted with complex biomedical phrases. Notably, there is a significant gap between the performance of even the most sophisticated current models on this task and the accuracy achieved by humans. Our research aims to bridge this disparity through an innovative multi-task learning framework, which incorporates a novel data augmentation technique called WordMask Corpus Augmentation. This method leverages a vast corpus of masked words, with the goal of enhancing a model's ability to recognize negations by supplementing it with pseudo-samples containing artificially inserted negations. Our study compares the proposed method to alternative approaches, with evaluations conducted on both the 2012 i2b2 Negation Detection Shared Task and the recently introduced BioNLP-ClinicalTestSuite. Our results show that our multi-task learning framework utilizing WordMask Corpus Augmentation achieves state-of-the-art performance on i2b2 and surpasses human performance on BNC-TEST. Moreover, our research examines the interpersonal agreement among human annotators on negations within BNC-TEST, with findings indicating a high degree of consistency. We introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), a novel Bayesian model based on the Document Topic Model (DTM), which organizes topics into a hierarchical structure and assigns a document to a specific branch within this hierarchy. This model offers a sophisticated way to analyze complex information networks by identifying latent topics at multiple levels and linking documents to their appropriate hierarchical positions. Unlike conventional methods, our approach provides topic interpretations not just as lists of word probabilities, but as distilled summary phrases that capture their meaning. We evaluate the performance of HDTM in comparison to the widely used Correlated Topic Model (CTM) and a Gibbs sampling implementation of DTM, using two networks: one focused on scientific collaboration and another on co-authorships within economics disciplines. The results reveal that HDTM exhibits equal or better performance than CTM and comparable performance to the Gibbs sampling DTM. Furthermore, our model allows for a more intuitive understanding of topics through the distilled summary phrases, facilitating easier interpretation than the probability distributions returned by conventional models. To complement our analysis, we feature an interactive topic exploration dashboard for the co-authorship network within economics disciplines, available at an online companion site. This model is implemented in the Rtm package, accessible on CRAN. The Python implementation is available through the hdtm_py package on GitHub. Quantum annealing, a method for solving combinatorial optimization problems, has sparked significant interest in the field of quantum computing. Despite this, the process of quantum annealing itself remains not fully understood, particularly the transition from classical to quantum behavior as the system is progressively isolated. To enhance the performance of quantum annealing protocols, it is essential to investigate this transition phenomenon in depth. In this research, a widely used Hamiltonian model was employed to study this transition with the aid of a simulated quantum annealing process. A thorough analysis of the results revealed the presence of an annealing gap, which was found to be influenced by the strength of the Ising interaction and the number of qubits used. Furthermore, a detailed examination of the spectral flow of the Hamiltonian's eigenvalues during quantum annealing was conducted, which provided valuable insights into the creation of multiple degenerate minima and the associated barriers to quantum tunneling. The findings of this research have significant implications for the development of optimized quantum annealing protocols, which could be critical in addressing complex computational problems. In this context, the investigation of the annealing gap and the interplay between coherent and incoherent phases can inform the design of new quantum annealing protocols, which could be tailored to account for the unique characteristics of physical quantum annealing devices. Additionally, the development of simulation techniques capable of accurately modeling the spectral flow of the Hamiltonian's eigenvalues during quantum annealing could be instrumental in assessing the performance of such protocols. The results of this research, which involved the simulation of up to 1000 qubits using a combination of numerical and analytical techniques, demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach in achieving precise results. The research presented a case study involving the solution of an instance of the graph connectivity problem, which is a well-known NP-complete problem. The findings showed that the success probability achieved through the simulation of quantum annealing, which was approximately 0.999, was significantly higher than the probability obtained through classical annealing. The research also demonstrated the feasibility of applying this approach to larger-scale quantum systems with the aid of quantum hybrid simulations. The study concluded with an examination of the potential applications of this research to the development of quantum algorithms for hybrid quantum systems and the investigation of the annealing gap in physical quantum systems using simulated quantum annealing. As an illustration, we apply our model to analyze Twitter data related to COVID-19 cases and the adoption of preventive measures in India, using a dataset of Hindi language tweets. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity in cuprates remain unclear. Recent studies suggest the interlayer coupling may hold the key, as it appears more crucial for superconducting transitions than intralayer coupling. To further understand this, researchers compared the interlayer coupling energy of various cuprates to the band gap in silicon, as both depend on the square of the electron charge. The results showed a direct correlation between interlayer coupling energy and superconducting critical temperature, while intralayer coupling showed a less significant but still important influence. To take the band structure into account, researchers divided the data into two groups, as the direction of electron movement affects the interlayer coupling energy. Finally, the findings indicated that the highest critical temperature among the divided data sets occurs in the Hg/Bi-based family, suggesting these materials may be the most suitable candidates for achieving permanent superconductivity within these compounds. The research provides new insights into the relationships between interlayer coupling, band structure, and superconducting critical temperature in cuprates. The study's methodology is robust and could be applied to other materials and systems. Three different equation-of-state models are considered, and it is found that only the model developed by Rischke is capable of withstanding a phase transition without becoming overly dense, while the other two models become overdense. Furthermore, it is determined that a phase transition can occur within the mass range that is in line with the maximum mass constraint, and this implies that quark stars can exhibit a phase transition from the quark-gluon plasma phase to the meson phase, resulting in meson crust similar to that found in neutron stars. Lastly, it is noted that the detection of quark or antiquark stars would require a significant deviation in the $\gamma$-ray flux from pulsars or millisecond pulsars. We investigate a spatial compass state made up of three continuous-mode parametric amplifiers that share a pump mode and estimate the damping coefficients of their reservoirs using the metrological tool of total variance. Our analysis reveals that increasing variance in the compass state complicates the estimation process, wasting its potential for precise information gain. When the variance in the shared pump mode is low, our proposed scheme performs well and can accurately determine the damping coefficients. Researchers suggest that mid-infrared emission from these disks can reveal significant variations, possibly linked to the presence of small dust particles, and propose a method to quantify their effect on cooling rates. By examining the interplay between dust, radiation, and electron interactions in the context of X-rays and the specific temperatures and locations within the disks, a simple model identifies the cooling efficiency that can be achieved and assesses the significance of dust in influencing this process. Results show that while dust has a limited impact on the inner regions of the disks due to high energy X-ray absorption, its impact is more pronounced in the middle sections and negligible in the outer sections, where electron scattering from X-rays becomes the dominant cooling mechanism. A simple formula is also introduced to estimate the cooling power influenced by dust and X-ray energy across different locations within the disks. The model demonstrates that X-ray-driven electron scattering can contribute substantially to the total power emitted in the middle sections of the disks, and this effect should be considered when interpreting mid-infrared observations in the context of X-ray emissions from protoplanetary disks. By applying this model to ALMA observations of the HH 444 jet, which may be associated with the L1527 protostar, a possible connection to the protostar is identified and a finding that could be used to test the model. The model's predictions can be experimentally verified through radiative shock experiments that simulate the conditions in the disks and could provide insights into the role of X-rays in the evolution of protoplanetary disks. Ultimately, understanding the interaction between X-rays, dust, and gas in the disks is essential for accurately interpreting mid-infrared and submillimeter observations and gaining a deeper understanding of the development of protoplanetary disks. Deep neural networks have recently been vulnerable to backdoor attacks, which involve inserting hidden triggers into models to manipulate their behavior. However, creating dynamic backdoors that affect multiple models and avoid being detected by robust defenses has proven difficult. In response, we propose a novel attack approach utilizing a trigger-activated dimensionality reduction mechanism, which exploits the inherent dimensionality issues in deep neural networks. By manipulating input features through a triggered dimensionality reduction, this approach causes the model to misclassify certain classes as the target class. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach against a range of classification tasks and models, including both single-target and multi-target attacks, and show that it remains effective even against robust defenses, despite initially appearing to the model as normal input. Notably, we highlight the challenge of detecting this type of backdoor through input reconstruction, given its innocuous appearance. Our proposed solution involves creating a proxy model with an opposite trigger-activated dimensionality expansion mechanism to identify and remove the hidden dimension triggered by the attack. We provide a practical implementation of this approach using a trigger-activated PCA module and demonstrate its feasibility in both theoretical and practical contexts. Our code is available at: \url{https://github.com/chen308/trig-pca}. Our findings indicate that this approach can create highly effective and hard-to-detect backdoors in deep neural networks, and we believe it poses a significant challenge to current robustness defenses. Moreover, we propose a novel attack-agnostic input reconstruction method, involving a proxy model with an opposite trigger-activated dimensionality expansion mechanism, capable of detecting and removing the hidden dimension triggered by this attack. Although this specific attack is targeted at deep neural networks, we anticipate that our method for analyzing the activated dimensions may be applicable to other machine learning models and datasets. Overall, our research highlights an important vulnerability in machine learning models and proposes a pioneering attack-agnostic method for detecting hidden triggers. This research introduces two novel algorithms for nonlinear model reduction, 
building on the concept of a quasi-linear operator and approximating nonlinear 
behaviors through linear combinations of basis functions. The first algorithm, 
'Optimal Summation,' quickly identifies a limited subset of basis functions by 
minimizing the error in the operator norm. The second algorithm, 'Iterative 
Refining,' systematically builds on an initial guess by sequentially adding 
basis functions, leveraging the adjoint operator to guide the process. We 
demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods with a range extension example 
featuring a nonlinear wave equation, showcasing the ability to achieve accurate 
approximations with substantially reduced numbers of basis functions, often 
achieving sufficient precision with as few as 1-5 functions. The algorithms 
presented offer simple, efficient solutions for tackling complex nonlinear dynamics 
problems, making it possible to obtain reliable low-dimensional models that can 
captivate the high-dimensional dynamics with a high degree of accuracy. By doing 
so, these methods provide a valuable means to perform model reduction across a 
broad spectrum of applications and can serve as a key step in the design of 
reduced-order controllers. The algorithms are implemented in a user-friendly 
MATLAB package, accompanied by an example demonstrating its ease of use. 
The code can be accessed through the following link: 
https://github.com/CaltechDynamics/ReducedOrderModels/tree/main/QuasiLinearBases.

In a binary Bose-Einstein condensate composed of two interacting components, we investigate how interactions between these solitons behave when the interaction force changes sign, depending on the component, in a one-dimensional ring geometry. By analyzing this situation both mathematically and numerically, we find that the interaction force has an unusual effect - it causes solitons with effectively positive mass to be pushed towards each other, yet pulls solitons with effectively negative mass apart. Due to this distinct behavior, these solitons become unstable, merging into one large soliton while expelling a smaller one. Additionally, we observe that the size of the larger soliton increases as the interaction force's negative component strengthens, up to a point where it reaches an equilibrium where both solitons have the same effective mass. Interestingly, we find that the size of the smaller soliton diminishes in this equilibrium, indicating that the larger soliton exerts a force on the smaller one. We also examine the impact of varying the mass difference between the two components on these interacting solitons, discovering that large mass disparities can result in the collapse of one of the solitons, while also finding that the size of the larger soliton can become a significant portion of the ring's circumference. Finally, we demonstrate that these unusual interactions may be observable in experiments using a wide range of atomic species. Due to the unique properties of these interacting solitons, where the interaction force's sign and effective mass can be manipulated through optical lattices or external magnetic fields, they offer a unique opportunity to study the interaction between matter and opposite force dynamics. Our research introduces a homomorphic parallel computing technique called AMPS, which utilizes a unique encoding method called the binary sum encoding and employs a multitude of processor units called GAUs. By leveraging GAUs, AMPS achieves up to a 256-fold increase in secure machine learning inference speed, with minimal reductions in precision. In addition, our findings demonstrate that AMPS can support various secure multi-party computations, including secure ML training, through the incorporation of additional gadgets. By comparing our approach with other homomorphic encryption methods, we show that AMPS offers the highest level of efficiency among them. Our proposed system has already been implemented and is capable of performing secure inference for a range of Convolutional Neural Network architectures with high accuracy, with only a 3% reduction in precision following the encoding process. Furthermore, our study AMPS-GAUs incorporates a detailed design of the GAUs, providing a functional GAU that can perform up to 16 base operations per gate unit with a single 128-bit integer, along with a comprehensive analysis of the computational overhead of GAUs. By integrating multiple GAUs with approximately 2.6 GB of on-chip memory and a microcontroller, we are able to achieve a significant increase in secure inference speed for various MNIST-based CNN architectures while maintaining high accuracy. Our research also explores the feasibility of AMPS through secure multi-party computation, demonstrating its potential to support secure machine learning training. However, we also acknowledge the limitations of our research, including the requirement for large amounts of on-chip memory and data transfer latency associated with GAUs. In our research, we are able to mitigate these challenges by incorporating approximate encoding and combining computations within GAUs. Our research is accompanied by open-source code and tangible prototypes of our proposed systems, along with comparative analyses of our approach with other homomorphic encryption methods. Our research is also supported by Microsoft Research, with the associated technology being made available to the public through an open-source code. In addition, we are collaborating with cloud service providers and data center operators to explore the feasibility of AMPS in conjunction with existing infrastructure. As they slowly move in a circular pattern, these HI clouds provide valuable insights into the past collision between the LMC and the SMC, specifically the encounter that occurred about 200 million years ago. This study employs an advanced algorithm for optimizing wave functions and potentials in the context of molecular cations. By using a full spectral approach, researchers aim to create highly accurate potential energy surfaces for these molecules, but a significant challenge arises when the molecules contain oxygen due to its high ionization energy and the complex nature of its spectrum. On the other hand, optimizing wave functions and potentials through a one-electron approach can provide a high degree of precision, but it is limited by the absence of exchange interactions, which is particularly concerning for molecules containing oxygen. To overcome this limitation, we developed an algorithm that iteratively combines one-electron and full configuration interaction wave functions to create highly reliable and flexible wave functions for minimum energy paths, barrier heights, and other energetic transitions in molecular cations, particularly those containing oxygen. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm, we applied it to studies of the water molecular cation and the methanol and formic acid molecular cations, all of which are crucial for understanding astrophysical processes. For example, the water molecular cation can contribute to the formation of water molecules in water-rich environments, while the methanol and formic acid molecular cations can lead to the formation of these molecules in molecular clouds. By utilizing this algorithm, we created new potential energy surfaces for the water molecular cation and improved existing surfaces for the methanol and formic acid molecular cations, which will significantly enhance our comprehension of these molecules' energetic transitions and make it possible to perform more precise calculations for larger systems. These new surfaces will allow researchers to analyze the formation of water, methanol, and formic acid molecules in molecular clouds and, ultimately, contribute to a greater understanding of the chemistry behind the formation of molecular clouds. Furthermore, this algorithm can be applied to other complex molecular systems, particularly those containing oxygen, and will be an invaluable asset for researchers utilizing multi-configurational methods. By combining optimized one-electron and full configuration interaction wave functions, we can now tackle some of the most intricate challenges in molecular physics and chemistry. To facilitate further research, we have made the algorithm publicly available so that it can be utilized by the scientific community to tackle other complex molecular systems containing oxygen. Evaluating the performance of relational machine learning models in pharmacology, particularly target prediction, requires a comprehensive approach that goes beyond standard evaluation metrics. Since predicted targets often share close relationships with the actual targets, a well-designed evaluation framework should reflect the targets' connectivity structure to provide a more accurate and reliable assessment. In this paper, we present a key issue with the current gold standard evaluation approach, specifically concerns with overestimation of model performance. We then introduce an alternative approach that utilizes a graph-based filtering method to counter this problem. This new approach involves ranking predicted targets based on their connectivity to the actual targets and applying a threshold to filter out the most closely connected ones. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to three different datasets and show that it yields a more stable and reliable performance evaluation. Additionally, we investigate the impact of different evaluation strategies on the ranking of models and reveal that our proposed graph-based filtering approach consistently achieves better results. To facilitate reproducibility and model evaluation, we have made our code and the relevant dataset available for public access. 

Keywords: Relational machine learning; Target prediction; Graph-based evaluation; Pharmacology; Molecular recognition.

Distributed learning models require significant communication to aggregate data, leading to an inefficient process. A popular method for reducing this inefficiency utilizes a random walk-like approach, where a single node learns from multiple nodes in a hierarchical structure. However, this method's performance is suboptimal due to its sensitivity to the underlying data structure. To address this issue, we investigate a new approach based on a recent, efficient communication protocol called SPDC. SPDC reduces communication complexity from O(n) to O(log n) by utilizing a hierarchical structure of nodes with unique paths for communication. We examine the practical implications of this protocol on the new approach and analyze its performance under various conditions. Our results show that the new approach achieves optimal performance both theoretically and in real-world scenarios. To handle the increased data rates from the Large Hadron Collider's LHC-Phase II, a new series of highly advanced detectors called ATLAS and CMS will rely on upgraded data processing systems. A key component of these systems, the jet FemtoBose-Einstein condensate (FEX) system, is an innovative data processing technology based on atomic physics principles. With a data processing speed of 100 terabits per second and the ability to handle up to 10,000 simultaneous signal paths, the jet FEX system offers an impressive data processing capability. We present the design and development of a full-scale prototype of the jet FEX system, with a data processing unit featuring 24 individual FemtoBose-Einstein condensate modules. Each module is a self-contained unit with a 4 GB memory capacity and can process data at 50 gigabits per second. The system's performance is evaluated using both simulated data and real-world data from the Large Hadron Collider, with results showing that it can achieve an average data processing latency of less than 10 microseconds and a maximum latency of less than 30 microseconds. The development of the jet FEX system represents a groundbreaking application of atomic physics in high-energy physics, with the potential to inspire new approaches to data processing in other fields. Dynamic objects are challenging to model due to their intricate geometry and varied appearances, especially in scenarios with multiple objects. Traditional approaches to this problem have been confined to basic transformations and limited details. This research introduces Articulated Neural Rendering (ANR), a novel framework that enables the creation of realistic 3D models of dynamic objects by learning their geometric structure, positional relationships, and detailed appearances from video footage. ANR utilizes a hierarchical pose estimation module and stereoscopic stereo module to determine objects' local and global positions, building a 3D model through a reconstruction module. This model is refined through a collaborative process between a rendering module and optimization module, with the incorporation of physical constraints, to produce a photorealistic image. By integrating ANR with a reinforcement learning system, agents can be trained to control the movement of objects and manipulate their poses to achieve specific visual goals. This framework allows for dynamic object modeling and scene understanding from video data alone. It has been successfully applied to several complex scenarios, including multiple moving objects and interacting objects in a static environment. The method was found to surpass traditional approaches in multiple benchmark tests. The code for this project is available at: https://github.com/ChunEui-Zang/Articulated_Neural_Rendering. Understanding a material's local atomic structure is crucial for both fundamental research and industrial applications. By leveraging graph neural networks to analyze local atomic arrangements, the concept of message-passing nets can be applied to complex materials such as solids, ultimately facilitating the development of materials property prediction models and related design tools. Despite the success of graph neural networks in simple materials, their utilization in complex materials has been limited by the lack of quantifiable local atomic configurations. To tackle this challenge, we introduce a novel method called local atomic configuration generator (LACGen) that uses graph neural networks to generate distinct local atomic configurations for given elements and conditions, allowing the creation of highly detailed and realistic datasets. By employing a generator network within a discriminator-graph neural network framework, LACGen effectively produces authentic and varied local atomic structures, which are validated through multiple experiments. It demonstrates the ability to create realistic and representative datasets, even for elements with limited data, such as technetium and promethium. Furthermore, LACGen facilitates the development of tailored datasets, the generation of multi-element local atomic structures, and the creation of local atomic descriptors, which can be employed in materials property prediction models. To facilitate further research, we introduce LACGen-DB, a dataset generator database containing over 10 million realistic local atomic structures for 118 elements, in the form of binary and multi-element graphs, along with their corresponding spectral features. By providing an open-source code and an initial dataset with limitless customization potential, LACGen has the capability to revolutionize the generation of datasets for materials with complex local atomic structures. The code and dataset are available online at: https://github.com/zhengyuanfeng/LACGen.

This paper examines the utility of weak convergence methods in estimating functions of model parameters through the use of estimated smoothing equations. By leveraging the central limit theorem for estimators, we develop a straightforward approach to achieve the desired convergence rate of $n^{-1/2}$, and this method is applicable even when the true parameter values are unknown. Our results can produce the desired convergence rate of $n^{-1/2}$ without requiring specific conditions on the rates of convergence of the estimated equations or additional assumptions on the properties of the score equations. This method is particularly versatile and can be used in settings where nonparametric estimators are employed, such as in the context of partially linear models, where spline-based estimators are used to estimate the nonparametric component. We also establish the asymptotic normality of our estimator, and this is accompanied by a wider discussion of the methods and results in relation to alternative approaches. Through simulated data and real-world examples, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method in comparing the performance of different estimators, such as those based on spline and kernel methods. Notably, we apply our method to compare the performance of QMLE and ALE in a financial ARCH model context, and our findings show that the true log-spline density lies within the range that favors the QMLE estimator. All necessary code is available online for replication of the results presented in the paper. 

Keywords: Asymptotic theory, Estimated equations, Model selection, Smoothing equations, Weak convergence.

We examine the relationship between the surjectivity of second-order elliptic differential operators and approximate zeros of smooth functions, and this investigation yields new insights into the fundamental question of whether such operators are surjective on $H^2(\Omega).$ To address this, we consider a modified differential operator $P_\epsilon$ and investigate its properties, particularly its behavior with respect to approximate zeros and the relationship between its kernel and the kernel of the original operator $P.$ These investigations lead to an improvement of the recent results of Ammann-Gazzola-Hsu-Wang, providing a more general extension as well as a more precise description of the associated kernel space equivalence. Furthermore, this achievement is complemented by an investigation of the operator $P_\epsilon$-spectrum and a demonstration of the continuous dependence of its properties on $\epsilon.$ Lastly, this research is further substantiated by concrete numerical computations, and it is demonstrated that the kernel-based definition of approximate zeros is essentially unique. Ultimately, this work paves the way for formulating a precise and unique definition of approximate zeros based on the operator $P.$

The veriT proof format was initially presented five years ago at the PxTP workshop, and since then it has undergone significant evolution to meet the needs of various verification tools and theorem provers in the community. In this presentation, we provide an overview of the latest version of the veriT format, detailing the new features and improvements made to the format to address practical challenges and theoretical concerns. Specifically, we highlight advancements in proof step representation, proof structure, and support for multiple theories within a single proof document. In addition, we showcase the format's effectiveness through its application to at least three distinct use cases and highlight its growing adoption among multiple SMT solvers and theorems provers. The latest version of the veriT format is now officially endorsed by the PxTP community as the standard proof format for its workshop series. Moreover, this endorsement is complemented by a set of verification tools that can generate and check proofs in this format, as well as a suite of solvers and theorems provers which have committed to use and provide proofs in this format. In this presentation, we also outline our strategy and roadmap for maintaining and extending the veriT format in alignment with the community's requirements and standards. This strategy involves an open approach to updates, which will be managed through a set of defined principles and procedures, as well as a roadmap that focuses on further developing the format's capabilities to support multiple theories and a first-order logic paradigm. In this context, we present a set of key features and concerns that need to be considered in this development process, including the integration of partial functions, support for acyclic and cyclic proofs, and the development of a meta-theory for first-order logic. Ultimately, our objectives are to ensure the continued evolution and success of the veriT format as the standard proof format for the PxTP community, and to contribute to the advancement of proof verification and theorem proving in this community through the adoption of state-of-the-art techniques and research in this field. FedBuff is the first federated learning algorithm to balance user confidentiality with increased cluster efficiency, providing a significant boost to performance. Unlike other private FL algorithms that sacrifice scalability for enhanced privacy, our proposed method achieves optimal data compression while maintaining the same privacy level, achieving the best possible trade-off between privacy and efficiency. Based on the secure multiplication protocol from Scalable Yao's Immortal Table, FedBuff utilizes an average of two communication rounds and sublinear communication complexity for each data point, leading to substantial improvements in training time and cluster efficiency. Moreover, our proposed FedBuff (I) and FedBuff (II) architectures ensure secure computation on encrypted data, ensuring data protection and improving privacy protection for sensitive information. Through comprehensive experiments, FedBuff demonstrates superior performance and cluster efficiency on various datasets, supported by leading industry platforms. The source code of FedBuff is available at https://github.com/chenyusmith/FedBuff.

This study undertakes a comparative analysis of transfer learning techniques in cross-lingual automatic speech recognition systems. We assess the effectiveness of multi-lingual pre-training for speech recognition models using a large-scale dataset with significant language differences, namely English and Japanese. Unlike previous studies which primarily focused on European languages, our research reveals that simply applying multi-lingual pre-training is an efficient way to enhance performance, although it falls short of optimal results compared to solely training each language in isolation. Furthermore, we find that the utilization of a shared RNN layer instead of a transformer-based architecture facilitates successful transfer learning, thereby suggesting that the employment of attention mechanisms may be responsible for decreased performance in cross-lingual scenarios. Ultimately, our findings indicate that multi-lingual pre-training can be a valuable tool for speech recognition systems, with potential applications in low-resource language scenarios. Additionally, we observe that a carefully designed system leveraging both domestic and foreign data, i.e. Japanese and English, yields a 9.3% reduction in WER, thereby laying the groundwork for future research and analysis. The proposed technique has been made publicly available to facilitate replication and comparison of results.

Discovering node embeddings for a graph is crucial in various applications, particularly in those lacking explicit representations, such as proteins without defined primary structures. Although several node embedding algorithms are already available and effectively utilize side information, there is a growing need for methods that can efficiently handle small amounts of annotated data. In response, we propose two novel, unsupervised deep node embedding frameworks, one based on graph convolutional networks (GCNs) and the other on graph attention networks (GATs), designed to leverage limited annotated nodes to generate meaningful embeddings for all graph nodes. To assess their performance and reliability, we develop a rigorous testing approach, utilizing fixed-size subsets of annotated nodes for both training and validation purposes. The fixed-size setting is a critical aspect of our contribution, as it is absent in existing benchmark tests. When combined with a robust optimization technique and data augmentation, our proposed frameworks achieve exceptional results on various benchmark datasets and a diverse range of datasets featuring proteins without defined primary structures. Specifically, our results show significant improvements over existing unsupervised node embedding methods, with particular notable gains in the prediction accuracy of protein function in the AFP dataset and the classification of cancer subtypes in the TCGA dataset. To facilitate further advancements, we openly share our proposed frameworks, testing approach, and additional code via an accompanying repository. In conclusion, our work provides innovative solutions, a reliable evaluation framework, and freely accessible code to drive the development and assessment of unsupervised deep node embedding algorithms.

Anomalously enhancing the $K^+ K^+ K^-$ final state at 1.37 GeV, a mass previously reported by LHCb, remains a topic of interest in the study of $B^+ \to K^+ K^+ K^- \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays. To gain a deeper understanding, LHCb has performed an in-depth detailed analysis of $B^+ \to K^+ K_S K_S \pi^+ \pi^- \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays, incorporating full control of hadronic final state interactions through data from $B^+ \to K^+ K_S K_S$ decays and additional information from $B^+ \to K^+ K^+ K^- \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays. By accounting for systematic uncertainties in the measurement of $B^+ \to K^+ K_S K_S \pi^+ \pi^- \mu^+ \mu^-$ rates, a significant enhancement in the $S$-wave component within the $K^+ K^+ K-$ system at 1.37 GeV is confirmed. Furthermore, by examining several possible explanations, including a scalar meson or a charm partner, for this enhancement, no substantial evidence is found in excess of the known physics theories. An upper limit is set for the production of $s$-charmed scalar resonances in the $0^{-+}$ and $2^{++}$ spin-parity configurations below 1.4 GeV by at least a factor of fifteen more stringent than previous limits. Similarly, production limits are set for $d$-charmed scalar resonances in the $0^{+-}$ and $2^{-+}$ spin-parity configurations below 1.4 GeV, the most stringent to date. All results are based on an analysis of 24.5 $fb^{-1}$ of 7 and 8 TeV $pp$ collision data recorded by the LHCb detector. For example, in the mass range of 1.0 to 1.8 GeV, upper limits for the production of $s$-charmed scalar resonances in the $0^{-+}$ and $2^{++}$ spin-parity configurations are below 0.3 times the proton-proton total cross-section for processes of the type $pp \to pX\bar{p}$, a benchmark commonly employed in theoretical calculations

A notable phenomenon observed in raft systems composed of viscoelastic shells is the formation of cracks at the surface. These cracks stem from particles breaking due to external stress, and the resulting break-up influences how the surrounding fluid moves, causing a ripple effect that may lead to further shell failures. Research has shown that by controlling the rate at which the raft expands and the strength of the surrounding fluid, it's possible to modulate the spacing between adjacent cracks formed on the surface. This spacing is influenced by a competition between two processes: the reassembly of broken particles and the expansion of the surrounding fluid. As the fluid's stress is transferred to the surface, it can either cause additional shell failures or result in the reassembly of broken particles. The space between cracks can also be modified through the supply of broken shells, with an infinite supply leading to a different spatial distribution. A notable finding is that the distance between cracks follows a power-law distribution. Additionally, the space between cracks increases over time as broken shells are reassembled, and this process is accelerated in the presence of a strong stress from the surrounding fluid. However, when the rate of shell failures exceeds the rate of reassembly, the space between cracks decreases, and if the supply of broken shells is infinite, the distance between cracks is determined by the average size of broken shells. The analysis focused on three specific cases: the Z$_2$ symmetric massless case, the massless case without any symmetry, and a charged scalar field in a single component scalar theory with a Z$_2$ symmetric potential. The results showed that certain phase transition temperatures in the lattice models corresponded to the renormalization group flow in the continuum theories. In the absence of Z$_2$ symmetry, the renormalization group flow was found to be consistent with an S-shaped line describing tricritical behavior. The study also found that in a charged scalar field theory with a Z$_2$ symmetric potential, the tricritical behavior line was shifted due to charge effects. This approach can be applied to both uniformly rotating compact stars and slowly rotating compact stars. The two-fluid models are linked to their single-fluid counterparts through specific transformations, which guarantee the correspondence of their fundamental properties, including mass, charge, and surface redshift. By using this framework, we can examine the impact of interacting fluids on stellar structures and, conversely, use non-interacting models to gain insight into the properties of interacting stars. To illustrate this, we utilize general first-order perturbation theory to compare the effects of interactions on small oscillations in stars. This might be particularly relevant to future multiband X-ray telescopes like the Enhanced X-ray Imaging Moduöl (EIXM), which could study surfaces in compact stars. Additionally, we demonstrate the feasibility of our method by applying it to the specific two-fluid models proposed by Iozbenko and Strotman (2020) and Sedrakian (2020). We performed a comprehensive analysis using four distinct N-body simulations of spiral galaxies undergoing bar formation, focusing on evaluating the impact of scale length of the central bulge on bar formation through a series of NGSW models, as well as the effect of a massive bar on the development of HII region distributions within the bar and outer disk regions, including considering the influence of collisional gas on bar formation for one scenario. Our findings reveal that a bar can significantly influence the development of far-out HII region distributions for the first time, with patterns resembling great rivers. We also found that the density of HII regions generally decreases within the bar region due to bar destruction of molecular clouds, but may increase if the bar aids in the formation of dense gas discs in the outer regions. Additionally, for one simulation, where the effect of gas collisions was accounted for, we observed that bar formation led to gas shocks resulting in the Cores of bar rotation curves exhibiting high mass densities of gas, as well as the formation of star clusters at the ends of the great river patterns. We also developed a simple bar-based model to explain the increase in the rate of close encounters and mergers with bars, particularly for massive bars, as well as the increase in the rate of bar encounters with massive bars, particularly for galaxies similar in mass to the Milky Way. We also anticipate that the prevalence of bars will increase from 15% to 40% for galaxies similar in mass to the Milky Way, based on observations of the effects of bars in our own and nearby galaxies. The impact of magnetic fields and tidal interactions on the formation of galaxy mergers is being investigated through high-resolution simulations. By combining a set of simulations of gas-rich major mergers with both magnetic fields included and excluded, researchers compared the outcomes. The findings show that removing magnetic fields alters the behavior of magnetic-field-controlled outflows during these mergers, causing a significant increase in outflow mass, with rates exceeding five times the outflow rates observed in normal star-forming galaxies. The effect of magnetic fields also leads to smaller, more compact merger remnants, with greater mass concentrations at the center and a more distinct central black hole growth. The absence of magnetic fields results in increased black hole growth through gas accretion, with a more rapid increase in black hole mass. The simulations demonstrate that magnetic fields play a significant role in limiting the growth of black holes and the central mass concentration during these mergers, with the outcome being a more extended, less massive merger remnant. This research suggests that magnetic fields play a key part in shaping the features of low-redshift galaxy mergers and could have a notable impact on the formation of supermassive black holes in the early universe. The influence of magnetic fields on outflows and galaxy mergers has implications for observations of ultra/low-ionization broad H-alpha profiles, as well as the formation of quasars and the growth of supermassive black holes. The simulations will be compared to actual observations through high-resolution spectroscopy and UV-IR imaging. Recently, deep learning methods have significantly succeeded in medical image analysis, particularly in the field of severity measurement from X-ray images. Nonetheless, creating large, high-quality and diverse datasets remains a significant challenge for these methods. Moreover, real-world datasets often imbalance in data distribution, meaning certain categories have more images than others. In this research, we propose a novel 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network, which incorporates data augmentation and the concept of contrastive learning to enhance the representation of images, thereby improving classification performance despite data imbalance. The suggested method involves two primary components: (1) a Contrastive Mixup Classification network, which employs forward and reverse operations during training to enhance the representation of images and calculate augmented and original images as positive samples, thus facilitating the learning of a balanced representation; (2) a 3D projection layer to project images onto specific categories, accounting for the inherent two-dimensional nature of chest X-ray images while maintaining computational efficiency. To validate our method's efficacy, we employed the COVID-19 chest X-ray dataset from Guangdong Provincial People's Hospital, containing 14,074 images spanning five categories. Compared to existing methods, our proposed network achieved superior performance on the dataset. Furthermore, experiments on publicly available datasets, namely MIMIC-COVID19 and COVID-19 dataset containing radiology reports and images, demonstrated our network's capacity to measure severity accurately. Moreover, an intuitive visual representation of the learned balanced representation was demonstrated through a technique called neural vector visualization. Ultimately, our research indicates that the proposed 3D Contrastive Mixup Classification network is a cutting-edge method for severity measurement from X-ray images. Nonetheless, there is still room for improvement as the network requires a substantial dataset to operate effectively. In the future, we intend to explore methods that can efficiently learn a balanced representation from smaller datasets. Additionally, we aim to apply this method to a broader range of medical image analysis tasks. Moreover, we plan to make the dataset used in this research publicly available to facilitate comparison with alternative methods. Moreover, we aim to integrate our method with a reporting system that converts the learned severity scores into clinical reports. Ultimately, we aspire to collaborate with medical institutions and policymakers to bring our method to a broader range of medical applications, ultimately contributing to improved patient outcomes. Nonetheless, making this method accessible to a broader range of medical applications necessitates a thorough examination of the method's computational efficiency to ensure seamless integration into resource-constrained environments. Consequently, we intend to explore methods for enhancing the method's computational efficiency while maintaining its efficacy

This study presents a GEC adaptation technique using a form of multi-task learning that leverages the similarities between GEC and GPG. Unlike traditional multi-task transfer learning methods, our approach employs a shared knowledge-based model that integrates ETL (encoding, transformation, and learning) components to capture the commonalities between these tasks. We levarage a type of multi-task learning called progressive multi-task learning (PML) to model the tasks, allowing for the efficient adaptation of GEC models to multiple domains. Our experiments demonstrate that PML-based adaptation outperforms baseline multi-task transfer learning methods and even the original E2E model. Furthermore, we examine the effective adaptation of GPG to GEC through the addition of artificial data generated from GEC transformations, and find that PML can be applied to this reversed scenario with successful GEC to GPG adaptation. Our findings indicate that PML effectively captures the similarities between E2E tasks and can be employed for the efficient adaptation of GEC models to multiple domains, and also provide initial insights into the effective adaptation of GPG to GEC. Structurally, the Gd^3+ ions in GdInO3 form a hexagonal lattice, while in Gd3+0.02InO9/8, a random distribution of Gd^3+ and In^3+ ions within a delafossite structure is observed. Our study reveals a trend of increasing lattice parameter with temperature for both compounds, accompanied by the displacement of oxygen ions from their ideal positions due to the onset of magnetic ordering in GdInO3, as inferred from neutron scattering measurements. Additionally, we find that the thermal expansion in Gd3+0.02InO9/8 exhibits enhanced complexity, including a positive coefficient below 10 K and a negative coefficient between 10 K and 30 K, with further analysis suggesting these behaviors may be linked to the presence of a helical magnetic structure and a point defect disorder, respectively. Our findings also indicate a significant increase in spin-lattice coupling in GdInO3, as well as the presence of a large and negative thermal expansion coefficient in Gd3+0.02InO9/8, both of which are closely related to the thermal expansion of the lattice parameter. Our study suggests that these complex thermal expansion phenomena may be controllable through chemical doping in the GdInO3 system. Furthermore, we propose that the presence of a helical magnetic structure gives rise to a large and negative thermal expansion coefficient below the magnetic transition temperature in Gd3+0.02InO9/8. Our research provides a foundation for exploring the unique thermal expansion properties of the GdInO3 system through chemical and physical modifications, as well as the potential application of these materials in advanced technologies utilizing large and negative thermal expansion coefficients. Our findings also underscore the significance of a thorough structural characterization, as exemplified by our high-resolution PXRD and neutron scattering measurements, in gaining a deeper understanding of the complex thermal expansion phenomena observed in these materials. The method is essentially a variant of the cyclic allocation rule, where each agent in a predetermined order receives the allocated item. This paper explores an alternative cyclic allocation order, obtained by alternating between the two most profitable valuation profiles in an order specified by the agents, and demonstrates that this allocation satisfies a fairness guarantee related to the Shapley value, providing an alternative to the cut-and-choose algorithm.
