When attempting to reduce the gap between source and target domains through pseudo-labeling, utilizing additional translations of the same target image can be beneficial. By leveraging these extra translations, a single target image can be represented as an averaged collection of multiple translated versions. This averaging process effectively expands the set of target images available for training, thereby enhancing the ability to generalize across the target domain. In our research, we explore various strategies for implementing this idea. We first investigate a straightforward yet effective approach that employs a straightforward average of pseudo-labels generated for a single target image from multiple translated versions. This approach can be seen as a form of non-parametric low-dimensional interpolation. We also examine more advanced methods that incorporate techniques such as weighted averages, principal component analysis, and nonlinear dimensionality reduction. Our experiments demonstrate that these methods lead to significant improvements in the accuracy of target domain prediction and the reduction of the target-source domain gap. Notably, our findings indicate that even the most basic average approach can result in a 1% gain in target domain accuracy, while our proposed methods can yield even greater advantages. Our research also showcases the effectiveness of these techniques across various datasets and demonstrates their applicability to a range of pseudo-labeling scenarios. In particular, we find that they effectively utilize the target domain dataset by increasing the diversity of pseudo-targets generated for each target image, reducing the degree of over-smoothing, and producing more accurate target domain predictions. In order to facilitate further research, we introduce a new benchmark evaluation metric known as the diversity threshold, in addition to releasing our code, models, and generated pseudo-targets for public access. With these contributions, we are confident that our research will contribute meaningfully to the advancement of pseudo-labeling techniques within the domain adaptation community. Our findings and associated resources are currently available at https://yongicheng.github.io/DomainAdaptation_PseudoTarget/.

We present high-resolution radio observations of the HII region population in UGC 8839, a interacting galaxy similar to M51. Using these data and optical observations from the Hubble Space Telescope, we create a comprehensive 3D map of HII regions within UGC 8839. This map reveals a vast spiral structure almost 100 kpc in diameter, featuring numerous HII regions located in a ring-shaped pattern. Analyzing the distribution of these regions, we discovered a 4-fold increase in density towards the spiral arms. A total of 5480 HII regions were identified and categorized by distance from the galactic center. Those within the outer radii of 8-10 kpc occupy the spiral arms, while those closer to the center or further from the galaxy are less prevalent. Comparing UGC 8839 to M51, we found that HII regions in the latter are situated 2 kpc further from the galactic center on average. Both galaxies exhibit similar radial density profiles, yet UGC 8839's spiral arm density is twice as high as M51's. This could indicate that UGC 8839 is viewed edge-on, whereas M51 is seen at an angle. Analyzing the velocities of HII regions across UGC 8839, we measured a rotational curve that rises linearly with radius, similar to M51's, but at a slower rate. This slower rate could be attributed to UGC 8839's lower stellar mass. Both galaxies exhibit similar velocity dispersions of 20 km/s, indicating similar molecular gas turbulence. UGC 8839's star formation rate is 4.5/sr, similar to M51's 4.3/sr, yet UGC 8839's far-infrared brightness is twice as high as M51's. This could indicate a higher gas reservoir or more efficient starburst activity in UGC 8839. Analyzing far-infrared and radio continuum data, we measured a radio-far-infrared ratio of 1.04, within the range of local galaxies but higher than M51's 0.85 ratio. This could indicate a more efficient conversion of molecular gas to radio continuum emission in UGC 8839. Due to its interaction with M51, UGC 8839 offers a prime opportunity to study the effects of minor mergers on spiral galaxies. Observations of this galaxy will continue with ATLAS A+ radio observations and NOEMA molecular gas measurements, providing even more detailed data for comparison

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an innovative device that leverages ancient minerals, to investigate dark matter interactions with nucleons at low energy scales. These detectors draw from the rich history of geophysical research using ancient minerals, which have been subjected to intense pressure and temperatures over millions of years. Due to their sensitivity to rare events induced by dark matter, paleo-detectors could significantly contribute to the understanding of dark matter properties, particularly its interaction with nucleons at low energy scales. Furthermore, they offer a unique opportunity to investigate the dark matter self-scattering cross-section and whether dark matter constitutes a primordial halo surrounding galaxies. Additionally, paleo-detectors can provide insights into whether dark matter interacts with electrons and whether dark matter exists in excess abundance in planets and galaxies. To effectively utilize these detectors, a dedicated experimental approach is required, involving large-scale detectors and a sophisticated signal processing technique using machine learning algorithms. With an anticipated detection sensitivity to O(10^-47) erg cm^2 per day per kg, a 1-ton scale paleo-detector prototype could significantly contribute to ongoing multi-ton scale dark matter direct detection experiments. Ultimately, combining the capabilities of multiple paleo-detector arrays, with an anticipated total mass of hundreds to thousands of tons, could lead to a breakthrough in directly detecting dark matter, potentially occurring as early as the mid-21st century. The conceptual framework of paleo-detectors has been outlined, and researchers suggest collaborating with geophysicists and ancient mineral experts to advance this innovative approach to direct dark matter detection methods. Researchers have assessed the potential of several types of ancient minerals, including superheavy element nucleides and minerals with covalently bound dark matter, although it is clear that the most promising ancient detectors are those subjected to deep seismic damage, particularly gold and tungsten based ones, due to their sensitivity to rare events induced by dark matter, and the potential of multi-nucleon and electron dark matter interactions with these ancient detectors. The rapid evolution of databases in the cloud and IoT has created sophisticated data storage systems that continuously update sensitive information while maintaining a detailed history of changes. However, ensuring the privacy of these constantly evolving datasets poses a significant challenge, as even minor alterations can compromise sensitive information and make existing privacy protections ineffective. To address this issue, researchers introduce a novel framework that provides enhanced data privacy by leveraging differential privacy to safeguard data update histories in modern databases. This framework issues precise and adaptable privacy guarantees known as 'quantitative certificates,' which can be used to automatically generate private summaries of data updates via a newly developed algorithm called the'synonymizer.' These private summaries can be reused to create accurate and confidential databases, as demonstrated by concrete examples and experimental results. Additionally, the framework provides robust privacy protection against various attacks, as shown by attack and defense benchmarks on synthetic and real-world datasets. This work was formally presented at the 2021 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data. The research is ongoing with the development of new algorithms and applications in sight. Understanding the basis for a machine learning model's predictions is crucial in developing and refining trusted models. While the intricacies of modern scoring functions are often difficult to grasp, our research focuses on the important task of identifying key features responsible for a predictive model's unsatisfactory outcomes. We examine the concept of Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores (MUCs) within the constraints of Boolean satisfiability problems and demonstrate its practical application to unsatisfactory core determination. By leveraging MUCs, we demonstrate the effectiveness of a simple yet powerful approach for determining key features influencing a model's incorrect predictions. This approach, based on MUCs, can be executed in conjunction with existing sampling methods to provide precise and accurate feature importance assessments. Our research utilizes the Cardano ML model as an example, combining MUCs with core determination and sampling techniques to analyze the importance of features affecting incorrect predictions. The developed framework effectively pinpoints the crucial features leading to incorrect outcomes and provides a meaningful reduction of the large feature space. Furthermore, we investigate the core sizes and unsatisfiable core distributions for both correct and incorrect predictions, revealing interesting patterns and highlighting potential directions for future research in this area. Additionally, we explore the integration of this approach with incremental learning to refine models based on feature importance and provide a roadmap for integrating this research with existing hyperparameter optimization strategies. Along with the implementation details and experimental settings, we also make our code publicly accessible to facilitate replication and further exploration of this research. In conclusion, we believe the proposed approach offers an efficient and accurate method for assessing feature importance and addressing this research problem will have significant implications for the development and refinement of machine learning models. In the future, we intend to explore the application of this research to other scoring functions and models, as well as investigate new strategies for refining models based on the identified key features. With the rising demand for transparent and trusted machine learning models, we anticipate this research to play a crucial role in addressing this critical issue. In the future, we plan to explore additional applications of this research, including the use of MUCs in deep learning models, the integration with incremental learning, and the application to hyperparameter optimization. In the process, we will investigate new strategies for refining models based on key features and assess the scalability of this approach to complex machine learning models and deep learning models. Recently, deep learning techniques have achieved success in the automated detection and segmentation of surgical instruments within endoscopic images. However, most existing approaches focus solely on 2D image processing, neglecting the complex and dynamic nature of 3D endoscopic data. In contrast, we introduce the Dual Decoder Attention Network (DDANet), a cutting-edge 3D deep learning network capable of real-time instrument segmentation across multiple Endoscopic Viewpoints (EVS). DDANet leverages a Dual-Decoder Structure with two distinct attention modules, where a Coarse-Decoder generates an initial prediction, followed by a refined prediction from the Fine-Decoder, guided by an attention map derived from the input image. This Dual-Decoder framework ensures accurate segmentation by combining these predictions. Moreover, a rotation-invariant module is incorporated to mitigate pose-related variations. Comprehensive experiments and comparative analyses across four diverse datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed DDANet, with a notable improvement in mean Dice scores (+14.1%) over the current state-of-the-art model, T-CNN. Moreover, our network excels in real-time processing capabilities, with a throughput of 30.43 FPS on an GPU-1080Ti. The code and dataset used in this research are available online at https://github.com/zhengzhengfu/DDANet. Visualizations and additional results can be found at https://ddanet.github.io/.

Deep learning techniques in the field of Re-identification (ReID) have experienced significant advancements in recent years, but a major limitation in the development process remains - the scarcity of labeled data. To break through this bottleneck, deep learning researchers have turned their focus to unsupervised ReID methods, and contrastive learning has emerged as a prominent strategy due to its ability to learn distinct representations naturally. Although initial unsupervised ReID methods leveraging contrastive learning yielded promising results, they still fell short of their supervised counterparts in ReID. To address this disparity, our proposed framework, CLG-Net, introduces a novel dual global contrastive learning approach, combining a global contrast and a local contrast module to enhance the learned representations. By modeling the global contrast, CLG-Net captures the inter-domain information, while local contrast focuses on extracting unique features from multiple sources within a single domain. To address issues of negative sample selection and imbalance in unsupervised contrastive learning, we employed an over-sampling strategy to achieve more balanced contrastive learning. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, CLG-Net was tested on the MSMTL and UMist datasets, and results showed a significant improvement in ReID performance, with an average accuracy increase of 11.14% and 5.14% respectively, outperforming the current state-of-the-art unsupervised ReID methods. The code of our proposed framework is available online at: https://github.com/zhengyunui/CLG-Net.

This study presents a new, efficient methodology for Value-at-Risk (VaR) forecasting, bypassing the necessity to estimate complex GARCH models. The proposed framework leverages historical quantile regression specifications to provide accurate VaR predictions, outperforming the results obtained from a range of popular GARCH models via in-sample forecasting. A demonstration of the method's effectiveness is achieved through analysis of daily returns data from the DAX, S&P 500, and Euro Stoxx 50 indices. The method is further validated by assessing the reliability of its tail observations, comparing the results to those obtained from GARCH models. The findings indicate that the proposed framework yields the most trustworthy results, exhibiting superior performance in terms of backtesting VaR confidence levels and achieving a notable reduction in tail errors when compared to GARCH models. The method's ability to model quantile dependence is highlighted through a demonstration of the phenomenon of extreme events clustering. The results show that the proposed framework provides the most compelling evidence of this phenomenon, with the strongest indications of a positive quantile effect. The method's code is made available for public use.

An extensive analysis of the quark mass dependencies of the pion's spectral function and its correlation length within the temperature range of $0.6T_c \leq T \leq 1.5T_c$ has been undertaken using lattice QCD data. The study incorporates a broad range of quark mass variations to account for the effects of chiral symmetry breaking and the influence of temperature on the pion's properties. The results indicate significant variations in the pion's spectral shape and its correlation length across the temperature range studied, with the maximum change reaching up to $20\%$. The findings also reveal a marked disparity in the low-temperature and high-temperature behaviors of the pion, with the former exhibiting a more pronounced dependence on quark mass than the latter. The results have been further examined through the lens of the chiral condensate and effective quark mass within the chiral perturbation theory framework, allowing for a clearer understanding of the thermal and quark mass-driven variations in the pion's properties. Notably, while the quark mass-driven variations in the pion's properties are significantly tempered at high temperatures, with the interaction with the thermal environment continuing to hold sway across the entire temperature range studied. The detailed study of the quark mass dependencies of the pion's properties has been undertaken in order to provide a foundation for the development of effective theories capable of accurately capturing the interplay between quark mass and temperature within lattice QCD. The comprehensive analysis of the quark mass dependencies of the pion's properties will also enable a more precise determination of the QCD critical end point through lattice calculations. The study's results may also contribute to a deeper comprehension of the complex interplay between the chiral condensate, quark mass, and temperature within QCD. The findings presented have been generated utilizing an ensemble of $N_t=32$ lattices with $N_t$ denoting the inverse temperature, with further studies requiring a higher resolution of $N_t$ to be undertaken in order to verify the results obtained. The study's results provide a foundation for exploring the quark mass dependencies of the kaon's properties, with such investigations set to be undertaken in a subsequent study. The research has been conducted utilizing an in-house lattice QCD simulation program developed in-house, with the findings corresponding to the ensemble of $N_t=32$ lattices. Classical T Tauri stars (CTTSs), the youngest stage in the solar lifecycle, exhibit strong magnetic fields which influence their surrounding disk, causing significant and rapid changes in brightness and potentially hindering our understanding of how they evolve. Despite the importance of magnetized disk interactions, there is limited knowledge on the long-term impacts of these CTTSs due to their extreme variability. This study utilizes 5000 Angstroms spectroscopic data across 23.6 days for 16 CTTSs, obtained from the INT and TNG, in addition to light curve analysis from the TESS satellite, to investigate the behavior of ions with short and long lifetimes in these systems. By examining the Balmer line profiles and analyzing line width and shifts, this research identifies the prevalence of high-velocity jets or winds in these stars, with further analysis showing that mass loss rates are relatively stable over the observation period, with some objects displaying significant changes in wind acceleration and geometry. However, the findings suggest that mass loss rates are largely unaffected by the accretion process, with some exceptions. This discovery challenges the traditional notion of the wind-accretion relationship, with implications for our understanding of how these stars evolve. Moreover, this research introduces a new method for inferring mass loss rates from spectroscopic observations, offering a more precise approach than existing techniques. With this study, a sample of four targets is further analyzed over a longer period of 43.5 days, revealing short-term variations in mass loss rates that modulate the spectral line profiles. This research provides new insights into the dynamic behavior of magnetized disk environments and highlights the need for a fully numerical approach to modeling these systems. This study examines the interconnection between the Euler characteristics of specific geometric objects, particularly those related to maps from varieties to a target space defined by quantum parameters, and a set of invariants derived from algebraic geometry and representation theory, known as quantum K-invariants. By applying methods from Brion's and Littelmann's studies, we calculate these interconnections for stable maps from surfaces to spaces represented by Schubert varieties in Grassmannians, and for maps from surfaces to flag manifolds. These calculations showcase the relationship between these interconnections and quantum K-invariants in a comprehensive manner. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate connections between field theories, quantum geometry, representation theory, and the geometry of Schubert varieties and flag manifolds. By analyzing the underlying mathematical theories, we can derive non-trivial conclusions about the interconnections themselves. For instance, consistent quantum K-invariants can be inferred from the properties of these interconnections alone. Additionally, our results imply that interconnections for stable maps are equivalent to those for maps in a broader category, given certain conditions. This research is an extension of the authors' previous work, providing a fundamental framework that can be applied to various mathematical contexts. It is also the first step in formulating field theory as an algebraic geometric representation. The study considers specific surfaces, although the methods can be applied to other types of surfaces as well. The research also explores the relationships between the interconnections and other mathematical concepts, such as consistent quantum K-invariants, consistent quantum Schubert varieties, and Witten's invariants. The document includes an appendix containing additional calculations and proofs. The authors' previous studies have already been cited in the relevant sections. The research is part of the authors' ongoing investigation into the relationships between the Euler characteristics of stable maps, the interconnections, and the underlying geometric and algebraic structures. The study has implications for our understanding of the geometric and algebraic properties of the target spaces, the maps to these spaces, and the underlying representation theory. The research is also expected to contribute to the broader field of algebraic geometry and representation theory, promoting further exploration of the interconnections and the underlying geometric and algebraic structures. The authors are exploring the possibility of extending the research to other mathematical contexts and surfaces, as well as the potential applications to the broader field of algebraic geometry and representation theory. The study is an initial step in a more comprehensive investigation, and the authors are continuing to analyze the interconnections, the underlying geometric and algebraic structures, and the broader mathematical context

The effectiveness of a machine learning model heavily relies on the accuracy of its training data. As modern pipelines employ a data-intensive, distributed training process, pinpointing and correcting errors in the training data becomes increasingly time-consuming using traditional methods. To address this challenge, we present DataScope, an innovative approach that employs a cost-reduced sampling technique along with a data quality assessment metric to prioritize data rectification. By focusing DataScope on a small subset of poorly labeled data at each iteration, it enhances the model's training efficiency while maintaining comparable performance. Comparative evaluations conducted across three datasets demonstrate DataScope's sampling strategy yields substantial reductions in additional training time and improved metrics, with a mere 5% increase in misclassification rates in the few-shot setting. Furthermore, DataScope showcases appealing scalability, with a linear training time reduction in tandem with the reduction in samples. To facilitate reproducibility, the source code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/IBM/DataScope.

The ATCA Pulsar Survey and the FWHH GBS have significantly contributed to identifying radio sources within the cores of globular clusters. From these observations, we have discovered 22 new radio sources associated with the GCs, bringing the total to 24 sources across 14 clusters as of 2019. Thirteen of these sources are linked to known MSPs, three to NS XRBs, and eight remain unclassified, with four of the latter located near the cluster centers. Analyzing variability and spectral data has provided Lorentz factor information for seven sources and constraints on beaming patterns for four sources. We also present variability and spectral data for the newly discovered radio sources and update existing measurements for the unclassified sources within the GBS. Combining these results with future very large array (VLA) observations aimed at determining the positions and spectral indices of these sources will be crucial in distinguishing the nature of the few remaining unknown pulsars within the GCs and potentially facilitating targeted searches for pulsations. However, only a deep pulsar search has yielded a detection within the 5σ threshold for variability of the radio source G1-WGA 35-7, which is associated with the white dwarf XRB V407 Cygni, located in the WC. 

Keywords: radio sources, globular clusters, millisecond pulsars, neutron star X-ray binaries, variable sources, VLA, ATCA, FWHH GBS, ATCA Pulsar Survey.

When analyzing graph data, researchers often study hypergraphs, which are inferred from projected images of a higher-dimensional structure. However, the process of inferring hypergraphs from their projections is mathematically challenging due to the large number of possible structures. In a recent study, it was discovered that certain types of high-dimensional structures can be accurately identified using minimal information from their projected images. This finding extends the current understanding of these structures, now known as clutters with the SHL property, to include minimal structures of four elements. Further, researchers have introduced a new algorithm to reconstruct hypergraphs of any size from their projections, building on a more efficient method for smaller sized hypergraphs. This research also explores the potential applications of these developments to the study of families of sets. Additionally, open questions have been identified in the realm of clutters with the SHL property, specifically regarding the reconstruction of hypergraphs of three elements and the minimum number of four-element hypergraphs that cannot be reconstructed unambiguously. These questions raise the possibility of discovering new structures with the SHL property in a class of small size, as indicated by the Warrington density theorem. As a companion paper, recent discoveries in the field of clutters with the SHL property are presented, including the reconstruction of hypergraphs of four elements and the non-reconstructability of certain three-element hypergraphs. This research is accompanied by a downloadable dataset containing clutters with the SHL property of five elements or more. This dataset comprises all large-sized structures with the SHL property, as well as all hypergraphs of four elements with the SHL property, for general research purposes. This study is part of a larger research project aimed at understanding high-dimensional structures through graph analysis. As such, it contributes a collection of computational tools, available for download, that can infer and analyze clutters with the SHL property, as well as other multi-set systems, from their projected images. These tools are designed to rebuild clutters with the SHL property, determine the non-reconstructability of hypergraphs, and discover new structures within these classes of high-dimensional structures. Furthermore, an online service is provided for uploading clutters with the SHL property for analysis and possible publication in future research studies. As this research is part of a larger project, it raises further questions about the properties of clutters with the SHL property and the structures that can be reconstructed from their projections. The directionality of a laser's emission has been measured as $\theta_c$, or divergence angle, which typically ranges from 10 to 30 degrees, depending on the type of laser. However, research indicates that the emission directionality of a larger group of lasers, including semiconductors, gas, and fiber lasers, can be as high as 90 degrees. It is proposed to present the directionality of these lasers using two values: the divergence angle in the plane of lowest uncertainty and the emission broadening in that plane. Using this expanded definition, the directionality of a wide range of lasers can be better understood, and it is shown that even a 90-degree divergence in one plane does not necessarily indicate low directionality. The mean directionality of a laser can also be determined through the calculation of a new parameter, the emission area divided by the square of the wavelength of the laser, divided by $\pi$. It is proposed that this new parameter be referred to as the effective beam quality (BQ) and denoted as $BQ_{eff} = \pi \frac{A_s}{\lambda^2}$. The $BQ_{eff}$ of a linearly polarized laser can be further broken down into two components, one for each axis of polarization, and can be expressed as $BQ_{x/eff} = \frac{A_s}{\lambda^2/\pi}$ and $BQ_{y/eff} = \frac{A_s}{\pi \lambda^2}$. It is demonstrated that the $BQ_{x/eff}$ of a linearly polarized laser corresponds to the beam quality number (BQN) of the same polarization direction and is therefore denoted as $BQN_x$. We investigate the behavior of two-time second-order correlation functions for electric field measurements in atomic ensembles under the influence of a laser pulse. By applying a random phase screen to a monochromatic beam, we numerically simulate the effects of partial coherence on photonic correlations. Initially, we observe a connection between first-order field correlations and scattered light intensity, noting that coherent contributions directly translate to intensity patterns. In contrast, incoherent effects, stemming from the atomic ground state, re-couple to the measurement through two-photon processes, influencing the two-time second-order correlation function in a more intricate manner. The interplay between these coherent and incoherent components results in diverse patterns of correlation arris in frequency domain spectra, reflecting the fundamental two-photon transitions of the atomic system. Notably, the formation of sidebands in the frequency domain is modified by the presence of a control laser, with an atomic medium producing an asymmetrical spectrum, while a vacuum environment yields a symmetric spectrum. Furthermore, the duration of the laser pulse and its phase relationship with atomic transitions govern the sideband amplitude and shape, respectively. These findings provide a theoretical basis for controlling the correlation properties of photons scattered from atomic media, with implications for the development of atomic-based quantum light-matter interfaces. Additionally, this research paves the way for exploring the interplay between light-matter interactions and the effects of partial coherence on quantum correlations in atomic systems. This knowledge is expected to contribute to the advancement of photonic quantum technology, enabling the creation of atomic-based interfaces for quantum light-matter interactions and the manipulation of quantum correlations in the presence of partial coherence. When training models from past experiences in offline settings, multiple agents can make independent decisions, resulting in a vast, underexploited dataset. To address this, we introduce the Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) framework, allowing us to derive a collective trajectory from multiple individual trajectories across different agent identities. By leveraging this shared structure within trajectories, SIT facilitates several advantages, including enhanced learning through an expanded effective dataset and a more robust signal for inference. We demonstrate the benefits of SIT by developing fixed-fixture policy evaluation and offline online reinforcement learning methods that target collective trajectories. Experimenting with these methods yields superior performance compared to baseline methods that disregard shared structure. The code for our methods is openly accessible at: https://github.com/kuhr1329/sit_framework.

Deep learning techniques, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), have successfully integrated feature learning with a similarity metric, such as cross-correlation or mutual information, to accomplish medical image registration. By bypassing traditional deformation models, CNN-based methods directly produce a mapping function between images. However, most of these approaches rely on intensity information and often overlook the hierarchical nature of imaging modalities. For instance, MRI images contain spatially correlated tissue types and physiological parameters, which provide valuable contextual information essential for accurate targeting and biopsy procedures. Biopsy target detection relies on MRI images and could potentially benefit from combining the two in a learning framework. Nevertheless, directly processing multi-modal MRI images with biopsy targets in a deep learning-based registration framework is computationally intensive. To address this challenge, we propose a deep learning-based registration framework that processes the target and MRI images in an embedded compressed representation, leveraging the inherent low-dimensional structure of MRI images and their associated tissue types. This strategy reduces computational demands and enables efficient inference on biopsy targets and whole-body MRI images, facilitating real-time target-to-scan registration. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed framework, yielding superior target localization and biopsy target detection accuracy compared to conventional registration methods and a compressed-target-based approach. The implementation of our framework is available online. To further validate our method's performance, we present a comparative analysis with leading deep learning-based registration techniques using public datasets. The code is openly accessible at https://github.com/zhengyuanw/Deep-Compressed-Registration.

We examine the relationship between single-particle entanglement, nonlocal effects, and quantum steering in multipartite systems consisting of two spins and an external spin. By analyzing different types of entanglement, including both genuine and reduced entanglement, we investigate their impact on the nonlocal properties of our system. Our findings indicate that certain types of single-particle entanglement can induce genuine multi-partite correlations in adjacent spins, demonstrating the significance of single-particle entanglement in generating nonlocal effects and quantum steering in multi-partite systems. Furthermore, we show that single-particle entanglement can facilitate the creation of nonlocal effects in quantum metrology with two spins and an external spin, enhancing the precision achieved through quantum interferometry. Our research highlights the value of single-particle entanglement in multi-partite scenarios, showing it as an effective tool for creating nonlocal effects and quantum steering in adjacent spins within these systems. Additionally, we propose the concept of reduced single-particle entanglement as a resource for quantum engineering applications, offering a more manageable alternative to multi-partite entanglement. Our findings also underscore the significance of distinguishing between different types of single-particle entanglement to comprehend their impact on multi-partite phenomena. Lastly, we examine the relationship between single-particle entanglement and the phenomenon of spontaneous synchronization in coupled spin systems, revealing that certain types of single-particle entanglement can contribute to the emergence of spontaneous synchronization. Our research provides an in-depth examination of single-particle entanglement in multi-partite systems, shedding light on its role in the creation of nonlocal effects and quantum steering in these contexts. The integration of cutting-edge technologies from the Internet has transformed the physical world into an "Internet of Things". As vehicles are increasingly equipped with computational capabilities and connectivity, the concept of an "Internet of Vehicles" has emerged. With the growth of Vehicle-2-Vehicle (V2V) and Vehicle-2-Infrastructure (V2I) communications, there are concerns about the security and privacy of these interconnected vehicles. A Blockchain-based approach has gained attention for addressing these concerns through enhanced data privacy and security. This paper provides a comprehensive review of Blockchain applications in V2V and V2I communications, covering the underlying principles of Blockchain and its integration with communication systems. In addition, it discusses various Blockchain-based approaches for improving data privacy and security in V2V and V2I communications, examining their advantages and limitations. Furthermore, it delves into specific use cases such as secure data sharing and payment systems. Finally, it highlights the challenges and open research questions in this field. With its ability to provide secure and efficient data management, the Blockchain-based approach has the potential to play a crucial role in addressing the evolving security and privacy concerns of the Internet of Vehicles.

indicates an enhanced view of the binary system's innermost regions rather than 
excitation due to the outburst's energy release. This research was the driving

To evaluate the accuracy of individual quantum gate operations in a near-term quantum computing system, we suggest using a sequence of randomly selected stabilizer measurements from the toric code - specifically, those associated with the surface code, due to their simplicity and robustness. We demonstrate how to execute this test on a realistic hardware platform using the IBM Quantum simulator, execute the experiment on the ibm-qiskert30 device, and compare the outcomes to simulate perfect execution of the same sequence of operations. We found that average gate failure rates are relatively low, around 0.068, across five runs of 1024 stabilizer measurements each, conducted on the ibm-qiskert30 device. However, we also observed an unexpected disparity in error rates between different types of gates, with some gates exhibiting significantly higher than average error rates exceeding 0.25, despite using the same sequence of gates approximately 350 times each, showing the importance of testing quantum gate performance through multiple experiments with different random stabilizer sequences. Moreover, we show that even with the ibm-qiskert30 device's relatively low average gate failure rate, a relatively small number of 1024-shot experiments are not sufficient to achieve a 0.05 confidence level for a gate failure rate above 0.05, while increasing the number of shots to 5,000 yields a significantly more accurate estimate. Furthermore, we found that some of the large error rates observed for specific gates may be attributed to specific sequence occurrences rather than inherent gate failure rates, and that such large error rates tend to appear more frequently for certain gates. We propose that this method be implemented as part of a larger testing regimen to ensure the reliability of quantum computing hardware. Additionally, we suggest utilizing this test on existing and future quantum computing devices through the QBox API. In multiuser wireless systems, reducing pilot overhead while optimizing data transmission is crucial. This paper reexamines the process of clustering and feedback encoding, offering a flexible and efficient approach that surpasses the capabilities of traditional Lloyd clustering methods. By generating non-uniform clusters based on transmit signal characteristics and feedback variables, this proposed method achieves lower pilot overhead compared to Lloyd clustering. In addition, this proposed approach maintains computational simplicity similar to Lloyd clustering, requiring only minor modifications to existing infrastructure. A simulation environment is established to verify the performance of this proposed method, and results demonstrate significant reductions in pilot overhead – as much as 50% – with minimal impact on spectral efficiency in uplink transmission systems. This proposed method demonstrates particular strength in scenarios with high clustering densities and unbalanced transmit signal characteristics. As an actionable solution, this paper also outlines a practical method for implementing this feedback scheme through cooperative transmission techniques, suggesting a potential solution with coordinated beamforming. Nonetheless, incorporating this method may impose additional signaling and computational complexities at the terminal end. As such, further research is required to fully explore the implications and potential applications of this feedback scheme. We investigate the remnants of binary black holes or neutron stars formed from the merging of Population III binary remnants, specifically looking at a population with a mass of less than 15 solar masses and no direct detection constraints. Our model assumes that these objects are created through the merger of two equal-mass objects made of primordial or very low metal content, and that they form a binary system that separates and merges within a certain cosmological time frame. Using the MESA and PC-DC code to model these objects, we find that they are born in a hot state and go through a series of changes as they cool, with their properties affecting the gravitational waves they produce. Our findings suggest that a significant number of these objects will be detectable by LISA, with a merger rate density that peaks at a redshift of around 7-8 and a rate of approximately 0.02-0.13 per gigaparsec cubed per year inverse, and that they account for a substantial portion of LISA's binary black hole and neutron star detection, particularly at low redshift. However, if we assume a more extensive range of binary systems, including those with mass asymmetry, the proportion of direct detection remnants increases, with a significant overlap in their merger rate density peaks. Our study also highlights the significance of considering the properties of low-metallicity binary systems in the context of LISA observations and the potential for these objects to be identified through their electromagnetic counterparts. By examining the initial conditions of these binary systems, particularly the primary's mass, we can gain insight into the underlying physics of binary evolution and the characteristics of low-metallicity stars, providing a framework for which future observations can be interpreted and potentially lead to a deeper understanding of the fundamental processes of binary evolution and the properties of low-metallicity stars. To test the high-energy burst detection capabilities of the CALIBRA quantum sensor array, we developed a gamma-ray burst (GRB) simulator using an iron calibration source and a lead collimator. The time and energy variability of this simulator were evaluated, with the results showing time jitter similar to observed GRBs and energy dispersion closely aligned with the detector's energy resolution, confirming the effectiveness of our simple simulator for testing the temporal and spectral responsiveness of CALIBRA. Future upgrades plans for the simulator include increasing the energy of the source and developing more sophisticated light curves and spectra. With these enhancements, the simulator will be capable of mimicking a wide range of GRBs, enabling comprehensive testing of CALIBRIA's performance in future space missions. Additionally, the simulator may be adapted for use with other quantum sensor arrays or other types of radiation detectors. Ultimately, this GRB simulator will play a key role in the development of quantum gravitational physics in space.

The Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI) has been proposed as an effective measure to evaluate the level of knowledge represented in a dataset of scientific literature, and recent research has shown its utility in analyzing the knowledge structure in a localized context. This study aims to expand the benefits of KQI by examining the knowledge flow within the scientific literature network. By utilizing the DBSCAN clustering algorithm, we can identify and analyze the knowledge structures at both local and global levels. Our proposed method is demonstrated using a dataset of citation networks in protein folding research, and the results show that the knowledge quality tends to cluster together within the network, with the ability to pinpoint key publications holding significant amounts of high-quality knowledge. Furthermore, the distribution of knowledge quality across the clusters is highly skewed, with a small percentage of valuable knowledge held by a small set of publications. The integration of the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI) and the community structure of the network offers a unique solution for selecting top-k publications that maximize the amount of high-quality knowledge. The advantages of this approach are illustrated by selecting the top 10% of publications, which account for only a tiny fraction (less than 1%) of the total number of publications in the network, yet hold a substantial amount (approximately 10%) of the total knowledge quality. The methodology presented can be applied to any citation network, and the implementation of the proposed method is available online. This research focuses on a multi-node wireless communication system with multiple access points and a destination node, incorporating a new encryption method called a "one-helper" SISO BC with a SISO decryption channel. We've developed an equivalent form of this system and, through a process of standard form transformation, determined the optimal secure data transmission rate and relevant power allocation methods. Additionally, we've established a connection between power allocation and security, as well as provided a framework for implementing this transmission rate in various communication systems. This framework is particularly useful in adapting transmission rates to meet changing system conditions and ensuring the secure and efficient operation of these systems. Moreover, we've investigated the convergence properties of the optimal transmission rate in systems subject to changing conditions and proposed an innovative approach called the "Meta-WGC" for a specific system configuration. Lastly, we've evaluated the performance of these methods through simulations and examined the implications of our research on future secure communication systems. In urban settings, automated vehicles can benefit from connected systems by bypassing the need for sensors and streamlining their navigation through intersections. However, predicting their paths requires more than a simple analysis of traffic signals, as the connected vehicle must also consider the movements of other automated vehicles and the potential for sudden changes in traffic signal phases. In this paper, we address the challenge of generating feasible paths for connected automated vehicles as they approach an intersection, taking into account the possibility of yellow and red light phases and potential cuts caused by these phases. A formal proof is provided for an approach based on predictive models, and this method is applied through computation of reachable sets using decision diagrams. This results in an efficient algorithm for generating a set of possible paths, and this set is take as input for a near-optimal path-finding approach based on partial order. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through simulation on a realistic urban traffic signal system. As the approach scales with increasing computational power, its practical application in real-world scenarios becomes increasingly viable. Furthermore, the method provides a feasible solution for handling the potential cuts caused by red light phases, and it is shown that these phases can be handled with a simpler approach based on zone-based predictions. Although data augmentation has shown significant efficiency in improving NLP models, its full potential remains largely unexplored due to the limited and costly nature of high-quality NLP data. This study investigates the capability of simple data augmentation techniques, including order-independent interpolation, minimum-maximum word replacement, and back-translation, to enhance the performance of NLP models in both low-data and zero-data settings. Our experiments demonstrate that these methods yield substantial improvements across multiple NLP tasks, including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and machine translation. Furthermore, we find that the efficacy of data augmentation is largely task- and model-agnostic, with a robust performance even with increased augmentation factors, and that the incorporation of a label noise augmentation strategy further amplifies the benefits. Additionally, we find that the augmentation models themselves are inefficient NLP models, implying that they possess little useful knowledge beyond the underlying data distribution. As such, we hypothesize that they are ineffective at generating plausible NLP text but rather serve to facilitate the efficient exploration of the data distribution by applying data augmentation. In line with this hypothesis, we demonstrate that the efficacy of data augmentation is significantly tempered when the augmentation models are trained with a task-specific objective, highlighting the critical importance of employing unsupervised methods to develop effective data augmentation strategies. Our research offers a comprehensive exploration of the capabilities of data augmentation in NLP, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms and providing valuable insights for the development of more advanced data augmentation techniques. All code and data employed in this research are openly accessible at https://github.com/zhunghuang/sim-aug.

Variations of the Weak Gravity Conjecture, incorporating self-binding corrections, are proposed for application in anti-de Sitter space. We examine these proposals, considering both scalar and gauge theory implementations, and assess their consistency with existing bounds on the bulk gravitational force relative to other forces. Notably, for a massless scalar in a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, the self-binding energy is negative and equal in magnitude to the mass term, offering a new perspective on the mass term's significance. We also derive an estimated lower bound for the mass of a massless, four-dimensional scalar in anti-de Sitter space, situated at the conformal boundary, of approximately 0.0079 units of the AdS length scale. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the massless scalar's binding energy and the coefficient of its four-dimensional interaction, with the latter being constrained to be greater than the square root of 0.0079. For a gauge theory in the same environment, we are unable to pinpoint a minimum mass, but we can establish an upper limit for the mass in terms of the charge and a constant, and discuss implications for the Swampland program. Lastly, we explore the massless limit in both the strong and weak coupling scenarios, analyzing the conjecture's behavior and suggesting that in the weak coupling regime, the self-binding energy could serve as a suitable proxy for the mass, while in the strong coupling regime, this relationship may not hold. We base these findings on an analysis employing the holographic WGC and consider both scalar field theories and certain classes of gauge theories. We also examine the impact of a non-zero charge on the massless limit in gauge theories, the effectiveness of the holographic WGC in distinguishing between the massless and large mass limits, and the relationship between the massless limit and the de Sitter phase. We conclude by proposing that the massless limit, whether in gauge theories or gravity, may be addressed through the lens of the holographic WGC, and that this problem is relevant to investigating the Swampland's constraints on the mass gap in the absence of a non-trivial vacuum. Finally, we pose several open questions, including the feasibility of extending the holographic WGC to include symmetry-breaking, the applicability of the conjecture to theories lacking a vacuum, and the relationship between the mass gap and the WGC in the presence of a non-trivial vacuum. By leveraging the Gaussian unitary invariance property, we developed a new variational ansatz that combines multiple complex wavefunctions to improve the calculation of excited quantum states. This model-space Hartree-Fock (MSHF) approach applies a constraint to ensure that the total overlap between different trial wavefunctions is maximized, achieving a more thorough exploration of the Hilbert space than single-Riemannian manifold variational algorithms. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of MSHF in simultaneously converging multiple quantum states, surpassing the performance of competing methods such as the full configuration interaction (FCI) and the highly efficient density functional theory. FCI calculations were employed as a gold standard to assess the accuracy of MSHF under various conditions, including different wavefunction dimensions, sampling strategies, and initialization methods. Our findings indicate that, even in challenging scenarios such as the simulation of highly correlated systems and multi-quantum state calculations for large quantum systems, MSHF can achieve precise FCI values with an error margin of less than 10^-5. Furthermore, MSHF exhibits a significant computational efficiency advantage over FCI, with a notable example being the 1.5 orders of magnitude improvement achieved in the ground and excited state energy calculations for the CoH2 molecule using a 20,000-spinor wavefunction. In multi-quantum state calculations, our study shows that MSHF can accurately determine multiple eigenvalues simultaneously, even in situations where the spectra are highly congested. As an added benefit, our methodology can be employed to assess the relevance of different Hamiltonian terms and to identify the primary configurations associated with specific quantum states. Overall, the MSHF framework offers an efficient and robust solution for the simultaneous simulation of multiple quantum states of any type, making it an invaluable tool for a wide range of applications, from chemistry to solid-state physics and quantum physics. Our main goal is to explore these modules' thickness properties, drawing on thickness concepts from the theory of excellent rings. Our primary findings can be applied to rationality questions in the context of excellent rings and might also provide insights into the thickness of modules associated with sheaves on excellent schemes, as discussed in recent literature. If $\mathcal{F}$ is torsion-free and $\mathfrak{p}$ is a non-maximal prime ideal, we find that its associated local cohomology module $\mathcal{H}^i_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mathcal{F})$ has a zero submodule generated by $\mathfrak{p}$-thickened modules, linking the F-rationality of the ring of global sections of $X$ to the zero submodule of $\mathcal{H}^0_{\mathfrak{p}}(\mathcal{F})$. This connection extends the results from literature for coherent sheaves on excellent schemes to coherent sheaves on any Noetherian scheme. Moreover, we establish relationships between the thickness of modules from local cohomology and the function characterizing F-rationality, especially when the scheme is excellent. If $\mathcal{F}$ is a torsion sheaf or $\mathfrak{p}$ is a maximal prime ideal, we still investigate the properties of its associated local cohomology module, which might contribute to the thickness of modules from local cohomology, a topic that requires further exploration. Building on this, we define a probability space to measure the occurrence of Galois groups in a given range, and demonstrate that this allows us to capture the distribution of Galois groups in a meaningful way. Ultimately, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by analyzing the common characteristic polynomials of complex multiplicative systems of polynomials over a finite field. Top quark pair production, a significant background in high-energy particle experiments, also interferes with Higgs boson detection. To mitigate this, researchers are developing new methods to enhance signal sensitivity, particularly when analyzing multi-body final states in Higgs boson decays. This study introduces a statistical reconstruction technique to recover the mass of an undetected bottom quark in Higgs boson decays, even when only observing the energy carried by one of the quark's decay products, namely the photon emitted from a bottom quark decay in the $B\gamma$ system. By utilizing the distribution of this energy, along with the measured energy of the other particle in the system (either a hadronically decaying Higgs boson or an irreducible background), the method effectively separates signal from background, reducing the background by approximately $\frac{1}{5}$ at a $1\sigma$ confidence level without compromising signal efficiency, or sacrificing it by no more than $0.5\sigma$. This technique can be applied to detect Higgs boson production in association with a top quark and a bottom quark pair, significantly reducing the background in a search for a light dark matter particle, and it may be adapted for use in searches for new physics in the $t\bar{t}H$ signal. The methods introduced here can be adapted for other multi-body decays of the Higgs boson, such as the $K_K$ system, and for experiments other than the LHC. For example, with the LHC at its design luminosity, this technique could lead to a discovery of the $B\gamma$ system at a $2\sigma$ confidence level, or a mass sensitivity of at least $m_H \approx 0.15$ GeV. The method introduced here is straightforward to combine with other techniques designed to control the background in Higgs boson searches. The North Polar Stratospheric Vortex of Jupiter has been studied through the analysis of thermal patterns in mid-infrared spectra, obtained from the LRI instrument on board the JIRAM3 spacecraft during the Juno mission. By examining data from 2016 to 2019, a comprehensive understanding of the vortex's behavior was gained, particularly its unusual persistence throughout the summer months at the north pole. Compared to Saturn's polar stratosphere during summer, where the south pole features a persistent hexagonal pattern with temporary vortex openings, the Jovian vortex remains stable, and distinct from the surrounding clouds. Additionally, the Juno data revealed a 160-day oscillation in the vortex's temperature and a westward drift of approximately 344 days, both attributed to interactions with the planet's atmospheric waves. Furthermore, observations from the LRI instrument on board the Galileo spacecraft, obtained in 1995, showed a similar vortex structure and size, indicating the long-term stability of this feature. The ongoing monitoring of the NPSV by the Juno mission provides valuable insights into the evolution of this dynamic and long-lasting polar stratospheric vortex. The unique persistence of the NPSV makes it an ideal subject for studying the interactions between planetary atmospheres and the impacts of changing solar radiation on these regions. The presence of a boundary in a domain forces solutions of the Schrödinger equation in that domain to blow up classically, and this principle has been widely applied across various subdomains within higher-dimensional spaces. However, when dealing with nonlocal energies like the Strauss energy, the situation becomes more complex due to the absence of a clear minimum at the boundary in two-dimensional space. In this study, we address this issue by investigating solutions of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation under the influence of a Dirichlet boundary condition in two-dimensional space, and demonstrate the existence of finite blow-up points within the boundary through an analytical proof, in addition to providing an explicit estimate of the boundary blow-up rate for data with large Strauss energy. This breakthrough is complemented by an accompanying numerical analysis, and the resulting relationship between blow-up points and nonlocal energy dissipation is explored across various domain sizes. This research was initially presented at the 13th AIMS Conference on Dynamical Systems and Applications held in Madrid, Spain.

Our findings show that short-range order develops into a highly correlated, insulating state from a long-range, metal-like situation. Initially, the metal state's spectral weight is dispersed evenly across all frequencies, while the insulating state exhibits concentrated spectral weight at low frequencies. Furthermore, our investigation demonstrates that two distinct types of correlation contribute to the transition's hysteresis effect. Our research also provides a means to directly measure the dynamical correlation function from experimental Hall conductivity measurements. This study explores the notion of a symplectic double vector bundle in relation to symmetric k-fold vector bundles. We establish an appropriate generalization of the Schouten-Nijenhuis bracket for a symplectic double vector bundle. We also examine how this bracket operates on smooth functions a symmetric k-fold vector bundle, establishing a connection to the geometry of symmetric vector bundles. A corresponding Hamiltonian vector field is defined and its connection to the original Schouten-Nijenhuis bracket is revealed. This enables us to extend the notion of a Schouten-Nijenhuis bracket to a broader context, encompassing graded symmetric k-fold vector bundles equipped with a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form. We can then utilize this extension to derive computations for the bracket's expansion on a symmetric double vector bundle, relying on the properties of the underlying symmetric k-fold vector bundles. Finally, we discuss implications of these findings for research in the field.

This shared connection allows us to leverage the in-depth understanding of these classical models to gain insights into the behavior of quantum systems. Conversely, using quantum systems to study classical disordered statistical mechanics models becomes feasible when we recognize that the ground states of these classical models can be employed as states for the quantum systems, essentially transforming the study of these classical models into the study of these quantum systems. By viewing the classical ground states in this manner, we can utilize the principles of quantum field theory to solve long-standing open problems in classical disordered statistical mechanics. As an example, we resolve issues related to the critical behavior of the Ising model on a cubic lattice with randomly placed magnetic interactions, the dimer model on a cubic lattice with randomly placed valence bonds, and the interaction-free replica model on a cubic lattice for any value of the interaction strength other than exactly one. The solution also allows us to determine whether quantum phase transitions occur in these systems and, if so, what the properties of the transition points are. The findings can be verified through numerical methods and experiments with quantum annealing machines. Ultimately, this framework offers a cutting-edge approach that enables the study of classical disordered statistical mechanics by investigating the corresponding quantum systems, potentially offering a powerful tool for solving complex classical problems using quantum computing. This research introduces a novel approximation to the single-phase flow model in the presence of blocking fractures, based on the upscaling approach for periodic Heterogeneous Media. We develop an implicit non-conforming finite-element numerical scheme to solve the resulting PDE model, using approximations of blocking fractures modeled through the Dirac-β function. We leverage the capacity theorem to determine a suitable non-conforming finite-element pair, and prove the convergence of a modified Crouzeix-Raviart element to the original blocking fracture model. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through several numerical experiments. Notably, we compare our results to a recent study by Thornbora and Thompson, showing similar findings as we replicate their results for the same test cases. However, our approach offers a more general framework that can handle various blocking fracture approximations, as evidenced by our novel upscaled model featuring the Dirac-β function, which provides a more realistic blocking fracture representation. Additionally, we showcase the accuracy of our numerical method in tackling this new type of blocking fracture model. Lastly, we examine how our method can capture the effects of blocking fractures on the saturation front.

When in the presence of an external fluid flow, helical swimmers exhibit a unique behavior in which their propulsion direction is reversed due to an interaction with a nearby surface. This phenomenon, which we refer to as the snowman effect, involves the creation of counter-rotating vortices above and below the surface. It is demonstrated that this effect can be utilized to enhance a helical swimmer's locomotion by nearly a factor of two. Furthermore, we show that by incorporating a thin layer of viscous fluid surrounding the swimmer, the performance gains associated with the snowman effect can be realized, even in the absence of external flow. Additionally, we find that this enhancement is predominantly achieved through a gain in the swimmer's circulation, with the surface's impact on reducing vorticity also playing a key role. However, it is also evident that the snowman effect introduces a point of instability at the surface, which, although minimal, has the potential to disrupt the swimmer's movement when paired with other instabilities. To address this issue, we present a simple strategy for mitigating the effects of these counter-rotating vortices through the deliberate generation of additional vortices in the opposite direction, thus regaining the performance gains associated with the snowman effect without incurring the added instability. This achievement is celebrated with our proposed design of a helical swimbler, capable of realizing this level of performance while navigating through a thin layer of fluid surrounding it. This design serves as an answer to the long-standing challenge posed by Purbell in 1950, which questioned whether a helical body could generate net propulsion when moving through a confined, viscous fluid layer in the absence of external flow. This breakthrough, however, comes with the limitation that the swimmer's speed cannot exceed half the rate at which it creates vortices above the surface, due to the formation of an impenetrable barrier around it by its own generated vortex. We examine the impact of droplet size and flight duration on COVID-19 transmission 
in various environmental conditions, using a mathematical model that takes into 
account airflow and gravitational forces. By establishing optimal conditions for 
transmission, we aim to contribute to the development of guidelines for minimizing 
the spread of the disease. For droplets in air, our model shows that larger droplets 
may actually spread further than smaller ones, due to their reduced evaporation 
rate. In contrast, in the presence of gravity and air resistance, smaller droplets 
may travel further than larger ones. We also identify the critical Reynolds number 
at which droplets transition from floating on air currents to being affected by 
turbulence. Our findings highlight the importance of considering the interplay 
between gravity, air resistance, and evaporation in assessing the transmission of 
infectious diseases through respiratory droplets. We suggest that the World Health 
Organization revisit its definition of infectious droplet sizes in light of our 
analysis. Furthermore, we propose potential non-invasive detection methods for 
identifying COVID-19 through analysis of speech and respiration sounds. Finally, we 
examine potential targets for COVID-19 diagnosis through changes in speech and 
respiration patterns. We believe that our study can contribute to a multidisciplinary 
effort to address the global health crisis caused by the ongoing pandemic.

Inverse problems are challenges in both mathematics and computer science, addressing questions about unknown quantities based on incomplete and possibly inaccurate information. Solving such problems requires finding a unique solution given multiple possible answers, which is a complex issue that has proven difficult to tackle using traditional methods such as gradient-based optimization or Bayesian inference. In this paper, we explore a more promising approach using neural networks, which can be designed or trained to solve inverse problems by following data-driven maps from incomplete measurements to desired outputs. We focus specifically on formulating and solving inverse problems within neural networks, discussing both forward-pass-based and backward-pass-based methods. We examine the mathematical properties of these methods and apply them to a range of benchmark problems, including recovering images from blurry observations and estimating densities from random samples. Our results demonstrate that neural networks can efficiently and accurately solve these problems, outperforming competing methods in certain cases. Furthermore, we investigate the challenges of scaling these methods to more complex and higher-dimensional problems. To address these challenges, we outline potential strategies such as designing specialized neural network architectures, leveraging mini-batch inference, and exploring new methods that decouple forward and inverse processes. By developing and analyzing neural network-based solutions to inverse problems, we aim to provide a foundation for future research and a framework that can be applied to a broader range of challenges in both mathematics and computer science. This work is particularly relevant to computer vision, where solving inverse problems is a central goal, and where answering questions about unknown quantities is essential to understanding and interpreting visual data. In this context, we discuss research directions and potential applications, and present a range of benchmark problems that can be addressed using the methods we have developed. Finally, we examine the mathematical properties of neural networks, discussing their consistency and uniqueness in solving inverse problems, and outline potential strategies for bounding their error. To facilitate further research, we have developed a range of tools and techniques, including a neural network library that can be applied to a broad range of challenges in both mathematics and computer science. This library is designed to be highly flexible and customizable, allowing users to easily design and customize neural networks for solving specific problems. We believe that this research has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of and ability to solve inverse problems, and we invite the research community to contribute to and collaborate on this project. Using finite-N matrix theory, we examine the thermodynamic properties of SU(N) and U(N) partition functions in $(3+1)$-dimensional space at finite temperatures. Our analysis focuses particularly on the differences in partition functions for these groups beyond the large-N limit. By applying a systematic method to calculate finite-N trace, we directly determine the partition function for a hot quark-gluon plasma from U(N) representations and identify corresponding SU(N) gauge theory equivalents through an exact bosonization procedure. In this process, SU(N) and U(N) representations become indistinguishable at large N, yet we find distinguishable effects even at N=3. These differences arise due to the distinct contributions of gluons and ghosts in U(N) versus mesons in SU(N). As an example, at temperature twice the deconfinement scale and for N=3, the U(N) partition function exceeds its SU(N) counterpart by 50%. These distinct contributions could be significant for various physical phenomena, such as flavor mixing and the electrical conductivity of the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, since finite-N effects play a crucial role in the transition from SU(N) to U(N) at large N, they may impact our understanding of the deconfinement and chiral phase transitions. Ultimately, taking finite-N and group differences into account will provide a more accurate description of the quark-gluon plasma in relativistic heavy ion collisions. In addition, this framework offers a valuable tool for exploring finite-N group theories in various other contexts, such as the Higgs phase of QCD and the electroweak theory. In such scenarios, even small deviations from large-N behavior can lead to substantial consequences, giving rise to non-trivial phase transitions governed by intricate partition function structures. In conclusion, acknowledging the significance of finite-N group differences is essential for a comprehensive analysis of these complex systems. In the course of our investigation, we also develop a computational method that enables us to directly calculate the finite-N partition function from U(N) representations and, through bosonization, obtain the SU(N) gauge theory equivalent. This approach allows us to explore distinct SU(N) and U(N) behavior in the context of the quark-gluon plasma and set the stage for examining other finite-N group theories in the field. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a deeper understanding of the interplay between confinement, chiral symmetry, and flavor mixing, all of which rely heavily on the intergral N dynamics.

We explore the generalization of the Jordanian twist, a specific deformation of the Uglielini algebra, and demonstrate that it is equivalent to a combination of the simple Jordanian twist and an adjacent cocycle twist. We derive this generalization and its equivalent form using the L-infinity-bialgebra methodology, and examine its properties within the Uglielini algebra framework. Additionally, we identify the particular deformed form of the simple R-matrix. Our investigation indicates that the generalization of the Jordanian twist yields an object that is analytically expressible, in contrast to its counterpart in the U$_{\otimes 3}$ algebra. Furthermore, we establish a connection with the paper by A. A. Bichon, B. J. Davies, and S. Shno, and present an alternative proof of their main theorem. Our study also reveals an intriguing link between the generalization of the Jordanian twist and the Fock-Goncharov quantum YB, paving the way for further exploration of this connection. Lastly, we discuss implications for the representation of quantum YB in the Uglielini algebra. 

Keywords: L-infinity-bialgebras, quantum Yang-Baxter equation, twists, Jordanian twist, Uglielini algebra.

This study introduces a novel approach to name tagging for languages with limited data, utilizing a graph-based neural network model. Unlike high-resource languages like English, where name tagging can be accurately determined with high precision, low-resource languages like Nepali require significant improvement in name tagging quality. Our proposed framework leverages a sequence-to-graph (Seq2Graph) model that incorporates a graph neural network (GNN) to identify named entities from text. This GNN model taps into the semantic properties of named entities, represented as a graph with node and edge attributes, to enhance the naming accuracy. To further boost performance, we employ a multi-task training strategy that combines name tagging with part-of-speech tagging and neural machine translation tasks to exploit the additional information. Our proposed framework achieves exceptional performance on the Nepali named entity recognition task, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art NLP model with a significant 4.13\% improvement in F1-score using only 5000 labeled data and displaying robustness in 10-way random task evaluations. Moreover, our approach demonstrates a notable 11.76% F1-score gain over the conventional sequence-to-sequence model when employing only 1000 labeled data. The success of NLP models heavily relies on robust training using high-quality labeled data.  However, studies have shown that the presence of incorrect labels can significantly impede the training process, especially in tasks like dialogue state tracking.  This paper explores the potential benefits of training models on artificially generated noisy labels, positing that such an approach could facilitate the use of larger datasets.  Initially, we investigate the impact of distinct noise patterns on training and testing models, observing that certain types of noise have a limited effect, while others substantially distort the model's representation.  Furthermore, we find that the influence of noise is magnified when incorporating artificial labels into supervised pretraining.  To mitigate this issue, we propose a method called noise-aware contrastive learning (NAL), drawing upon the principles of contrastive learning to counter the noisy labels' effect.  By reducing the noise's impact, NAL enables models to effectively utilize the benefits of training on noisy data, leading to improved performance when tested with clean data.  Our experiments demonstrate that NAL yields superior performance to baseline approaches across three datasets in the dialogue state tracking task.  Additionally, we showcase the model's ability to balance the trade-off between performance and label noise level, achieving significant gains before degrading in certain scenarios.  To further facilitate further research, we have made the artificial noise data and NAL code publicly available.  Our findings highlight the complex interplay between training models on noisy labels and the model's performance on clean data, underscoring the need for more research into the underlying mechanisms.  In the process, we have established a new research direction centered on the influence of noise in large-scale datasets.  Ultimately, we have achieved a performance improvement of 4.15 F1-score on the Dialog-State Tracking Challenge dataset, representing an advancement of nearly 10% over the current state-of-the-art.  This breakthrough has paved the way for us to invite other researchers to join this new research direction, encouraging further exploration and improvement of models trained with noisy labels.
