In anodized TiO2, both single and double doped states of the interstitial C and N have been previously unexplored. To address this gap, we employed GGA+U and GGA+U with nonradiative surface and interstitial corrections to study C and N doped TiO2, considering both substitutional and interstitial sites. Our findings indicate that when located in interstitial sites, carbon and nitrogen exhibit more negative formation energies compared to their counterparts in substitutional sites. This suggests that TiO2 anodized with C and N, likely in interstitial positions, may hold significant potential as p-type material for solar hydrogen production. Using the GGA+U results, we calculated the defect formation energies at various surface terminations and depths, revealing that the most stable defects reside 2-3 angstroms beneath the surface and that the anatase TiO2 anodized with C and N may serve as a suitable p-type material for photoelectrochemical water splitting, also requiring a significant reduction potential. Nonetheless, when coupled with an Fe-based co-catalyst, even the most stable doped states considered here can induce sufficient currents in water splitting experiments. Consequently, future research should focus on scaling down anodized TiO2 photoanodes with C and N dopants to achieve optimal surface area and efficiently split water. Our study provides a theoretical framework for understanding doped TiO2 photoanodes and suggests that interstitial C and N defects hold key significance in the development of durable and efficient p-type TiO2 photoanodes. This knowledge can be applied to other wide bandgap semiconductors and facilitates a comprehensive examination of photoelectrochemical performance through a combination of experimental and theoretical methods. Ultimately, this study may contribute to the development of cost-effective solar water splitting technologies.

The ATLAS collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has conducted an analysis of top quark flavor-changing neutral current decays using a data sample of 20.3 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data at $\sqrt{s}=8$ and 13 TeV. Semi-elastic top decays, where the neutrino is not recovered, and elastic top decays, are studied to set upper limits on branching ratios for the first time. Semi-elastic decays, resulting in a hadronic system and missing energy, are analyzed to provide upper limits of $0.45\%$ at $95\%$ confidence level (CL), and elastic decays, producing an electron and missing energy, yield upper limits of $0.35\%$ at $95\%$ CL. These limits are obtained using shape techniques for background subtraction and estimation, and are validated through simulated data analyses. Elastic top decays with an electron in the final state are also used to constrain the $t\to c\gamma$ decay branching ratio upper limit to $0.27\%$ at $95\%$ CL. All presented upper limits are more stringent than current theoretical predictions, and this study demonstrates the effectiveness of semi-elastic analysis in providing more stringent limits than elastic analysis for the $t\to u\gamma$ decay branching ratio upper limit, at $0.35\%$ at $95\%$ CL. Upper limits on the product of Wilson coefficients times coupling constants are also presented for the first time. These analyses demonstrate the capability of the ATLAS collaboration to perform precision top quark flavor-changing neutral current physics measurements at the LHC. Further research is being conducted to conduct similar analyses at the High Energy Large Hadron Collider (HE-LHC). The techniques developed in this study can be applied to searches for new physics at the LHC and future colliders. The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on the Athena satellite will significantly enhance our understanding of high-energy phenomena, particularly turbulence within the intra-cluster medium (ICM). The X-IFU's high spatial resolution and spectral analysis capabilities will allow for the precise study of ICM turbulence across various scales. To effectively utilize these capabilities, a thorough characterization of the ICM's velocity and density fields is necessary. We investigate the prospects of using X-ray fluorescence and Bremsstrahlung to diagnose the ICM through observations of compact sources, such as binary black hole mergers. By analyzing the X-ray emission resulting from these events, we demonstrate the potential of X-IFU to accurately measure the orientation of the source, mass of the source, and distance to the source. These measurements could be made even when observing sources with high total luminosity but low surface brightness, such as when approaching the sensitivity limits of the X-IFU. Furthermore, we show that X-IFU can effectively determine the velocity of sources up to several tens of thousands of kilometers per second and locate sources with an accuracy of a few hundred parsecs. These capabilities will allow X-IFU to provide critical information for analyzing gravitational wave signals and studying the ICM's velocity field. The most notable sources of this type include compact binary mergers detected by LIGO/VIRGO and electromagnetic counterparts to soft gamma-ray bursts. The X-IFU can also observe compact sources with known counterparts, such as supernova remnants, supernovae, and X-ray binaries, as well as cosmic-ray accelerators and sources associated with ultra-high energy cosmic rays. The study presents observing scenarios and resulting diagnostics for these sources, considering both X-ray flux and exposure time limits. The analysis indicates that X-IFU can effectively diagnose the ICM through observations of compact sources, providing critical information for analyzing gravitational wave signals and studying the ICM's velocity field, as well as enhancing our understanding of the ICM's turbulence. In this study, we examined the minimum number of edge-colors required to paint graph G, under the constraint that adjacent edges in subgraphs isomorphic to F paint two different colors. We derived general lower bounds for this problem, as well as more specific upper and lower bounds for certain instances, including the cases where F is a path, cycle, tree, or triangle. For example, given any graph G, the smallest number of edge-colors used in a F-induced 2-edge-coloring is at most |E(G)|+∆(G)-1. However, we found that a F-induced 3-edge-coloring may necessitate up to |E(G)|+∆(G) edge-colors in some instances, indicating that this upper bound is not more efficient than the lower bound for some graphs. On the other hand, for F=K1, the problem becomes standard edge-coloring, with an upper bound of ∆(G) and a lower bound of at least 2 for some triangle-free graphs. For F=P2, we found a lower bound of at least |E(G)|+1, and for F=C3, a lower bound of at least |E(G)|+∆(G)-1. Interestingly, this lower bound is achievable for some instances, such as in the case of complete graphs. Furthermore, we proved that for F=T, a lower bound of at least |E(G)|+∆(G)-2 exists, and this lower bound is also efficient for some instances, such as in the case of star graphs. Lastly, upper and lower bounds were established for specific instances, such as in the case of cycle graphs, forest graphs, and graphs composed of multiple connected components. These findings provide new insights into the minimum number of edge-colors required for various types of subgraphs within larger graph structures.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) has piqued astronomers' interest with its unique geometry and velocity patterns. Using high-resolution data from ATLASGAL and the BGLT map, a three-dimensional spatial structure of the CMZ was analyzed through a non-parametric method. By examining the second-order anisotropy parameter Lambda at various scale sizes, a notable change in the density structure of the CMZ was identified. At smaller scales (2.5 pc), the anisotropy increases with a preference for alignment with the great bar, whereas at larger scales (10 pc), this preference disappears. The results also indicate a tendency for the density to decrease with scale size, suggesting a possible hierarchical structure within the CMZ. A bar-like feature, potentially created by the gravitational influence of the bar-shaped bulge, is also suggested by the velocity field along the CMZ's minor axis. The non-axisymmetric density distribution of the CMZ may contribute to a continued retrograde precession of the Sun, potentially leading to a retrograde motion in the inner bar and a possible location of the Sun within this region. The study's findings provide new insights into the CMZ's geometric and kinematic properties, offering a framework for comparing with future observations and simulations. The method employed here can be applied to the analysis of additional molecular zones within the galaxy. The results for the second-order anisotropy parameter Lambda, the bar-like feature, and the potential hierarchical structure of the CMZ raise intriguing questions about the zone's formation and evolution. The study sets the stage for a thorough investigation of the CMZ's kinematic and potential hierarchical structures through N-body simulations. We introduce an innovative method for identifying individuals using a sophisticated computer system that concentrates on the eye region, offering a more human-like approach. Unlike conventional face-recognition techniques, this system excels even when prompted by low-quality images containing only the eyes, without needing the entire face or additional components like pupils or irises. This eye-focused detection system leverages a cutting-edge dual-branch network to accurately pinpoint the exact locations of the eyes and classify individuals. To enhance performance, we developed a pioneering dataset called the Eye-Vessel Dataset, featuring intricate patterns of blood vessels within the eyes: a unique combination of eye-focused detection and vessel segmentation. This dataset serves as a comprehensive platform for eye-focused tasks, surpassing existing eye-detection datasets in both quality and quantity. Comprehensive experiments and rigorous evaluations validate our approach, demonstrating superior performance compared to other eye-detection methods, as well as impressive results for eye-vessel segmentation, a previously unexplored task. This system has significant implications and offers numerous potential applications, including security authentication, access control, and identification in various fields. In order to facilitate research and development in eye-focused tasks, we are releasing the Eye-Vessel Dataset along with the eye-focused segmentation code, paving the way for further exploration in this exciting area. This work has been accepted for presentation at the 13th IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision Workshops, 2019. Using a hybrid classical-quantum model, we examine how accurately qubit and qutrit systems can measure mass by mimicking the properties of the Higgs boson. We investigate the impact of different error channels on this measurement for both two-level and three-level systems. The results show significant differences in the sensitivity of qubit and qutrit systems to errors, with qutrits being more resistant to certain types of errors, potentially making them more suitable for experiments affected by noise. However, under other error conditions, qutrits actually lose precision more quickly than qubits, highlighting the complex nature of these phenomena. Furthermore, we found that qutrits can exhibit greater precision in certain error scenarios, potentially making them more suitable for experiments affected by noise, although this advantage may be short-lived. Ultimately, our analysis indicates that qutrits can provide comparable or better accuracy in mass measurements for both clean and noisy scenarios, with implications for the development of quantum-inspired experiments. These findings also underscore the importance of accounting for the effects of noise in quantum-inspired research, and could inform decisions about the choice of quantum system in such experiments. Moreover, our study paves the way for a more in-depth investigation of $n$-level systems in this context.

To achieve significant scientific outcomes in future Higgs physics or compressed dark matter studies at the LHC, it is crucial to obtain positrons with a polarization level greater than 30%. The LHC's existing design allows for a positron polarization of around 60%, but this level can be achieved more efficiently – with approximately half the desired polarization – by employing a simple technique based on radiative generalization. To provide a comprehensive understanding, we have created a detailed simulation, taking into account various aspects such as initial beam conditions and steering magnet fields. Our simulations, utilizing the design parameters of the LHC's existing particle detectors to model the proposed Higgs factory, yield optimized thin lens solenoid magnets that can achieve a positron polarization of around 95%. This suggests that, with minimal adjustments, the LHC's existing design can already meet the required standards for a 100-250 GeV future Higgs factory. However, as the energy approaches 275 GeV and beyond, with the potential for future upgrades such as CLIC, the required positron polarization may need to increase to over 99%. This study provides a crucial foundation for ongoing R&D efforts in solenoid magnet technology and highlights the necessity for thorough investigation of beam-particle interaction effects as the design parameters of future Higgs factories continue to evolve. This research is also relevant to other proposed future lepton colliders, such as ILC, FCCee, and others.

A temperature sensor based on a thermal electric field in a nanoscale graphene bilayer is presented, utilizing a Hall voltage measurement to determine temperature with high precision. The sensor's temperature measurement accuracy is demonstrated to achieve $\Delta T/\Delta V_{Hall}\approx 1.8\times 10^{-3}$ K/V, surpassing Hall sensors' measurement capabilities. Additionally, the thermal conductivity of the graphene layer is investigated, revealing it to be highly insensitive to the layer's rotation angle and indicative of the intrinsic thermal conductivity of graphene between two dielectric layers. A simple method for measuring absolute temperature with an accuracy of $\pm 10$ K is also proposed, involving a comparison measurement between two points for determining relative temperatures, and has been successfully applied to measure the temperature of air by sandwiching it between two layers of graphene, as well as temperatures within an electrical circuit and across a human body temperature range. The proposed sensor offers a precision temperature measurement capability with an accuracy of $\pm 10$ K in an extremely narrow measurement range. The design is highly versatile, allowing it to be integrated into a wide range of applications, and has potential as a remote temperature sensor utilizing the low energy thermal electric field transmitted through the air. The proposed sensor potentially enables precise temperature measurements in sensitive environments, such as in the near vicinity of a superconductor or quantum device, and could provide efficient temperature distribution monitoring in microelectronic devices, facilitating a faster and more stable cooling process. The design is also suitable for mass production and offers a cost-effective solution for large-scale temperature scanning, with potential applications including the monitoring of temperature in microelectronic devices, food temperature control, and medical temperature management. The design can also be adapted for measuring other physical parameters, such as strain, spin current, and chemical potential, and may provide a new approach to the development of sensors based on graphene multilayers. The design can be applied to a wide range of industries, including the microelectronics, food processing, and medical industries, and may enable the development of new graphene-based sensors, as well as providing a new approach to the measurement of physical parameters in complex systems. The proposed design offers several advantages over traditional sensors, including higher precision, lower cost, and increased scalability, and has the potential to be developed into a commercial temperature scanning technology. In rotating stars, a specific combination of toroidal and poloidal magnetic field configurations can resist change, similar to the equilibrium state achieved in force-free domains. This stabilization phenomenon occurs when the magnetic energy matches a minimum value, indicating the onset of stability. We demonstrate that overconductivity in ohmic dissipation promotes stability in regions where the magnetic field is strongest, and that instability is fueled by ohmic dissipation in these areas. However, if the star rotates rapidly enough, the stabilization effect is diminished due to magnetic field alignment with the direction of rotation, and ultimately gives way to magnetic field growth driven by ohmic dissipation. The influence of this phenomenon is most apparent in the evolution of magnetic fields during main sequence stars with moderate to high internal rotations, and can also impact the generation of magnetic fields in non-rotating stars to some degree. Given the importance of ohmic dissipation in the interior of main sequence stars, this stabilization effect is likely relevant to the development of magnetic fields in stars more massive than the Sun. Given the similarity between ohmic dissipation in stars and resistive magnetic flux tubes on the solar surface, this phenomenon may also be relevant to solar plasmas. The stabilization effect is crucial for magnetic fields in stars with moderate to high internal rotations, and can influence the stability of magnetic fields composed of both toroidal and poloidal components, even if the star ultimately undergoes magnetic field reversal. Given the similarity between ohmic dissipation in stars and resistive magnetic flux tubes on the solar surface, this phenomenon may also be relevant to solar plasmas. The stabilization effect is crucial for magnetic fields in stars with moderate to high internal rotations, and can influence the stability of magnetic fields composed of both toroidal and poloidal components, even if the star ultimately undergoes magnetic field reversal. Given its potential to impact global stability in stars with moderate to high internal rotations, this phenomenon deserves further study through numerical simulations and observations of magnetic fields in these stars. 

This study builds upon previous research addressing the stability of magnetic fields in stars, and addresses criticism aimed at those models. By utilizing a general framework for force-free equilibria and considering ohmic dissipation in ohmic domains, we demonstrate that the key factor influencing stability is the strength of the magnetic field within these domains. The models proposed can be applied to various types of stars, and we examine the implications for A-type stars and solar-type stars throughout their main sequence evolution. The models also shed light on the stability of magnetic fields in lower main sequence stars and giant stars

We employ a straightforward approach to convert Renormalization Group (RG) equations into fluid dynamics equations, applying this to Stochastic RG (SGR) to create a corresponding stochastic fluid dynamics model. By analyzing the RG equations for $\phi^4$ theory and the Hodgkin-Huxley model, as well as the stochastic RG for the Einstein-Hopf system, we successfully derive their fluid dynamics counterparts. Our study reveals that the deterministic fluid dynamics itself cannot generate the level of irreversibility present in RG equations, suggesting it is an inherent property of the RG. Nonetheless, the incompatibility of this irreversibility with the second law of thermodynamics implies that it must manifest as an irreversible heat dissipation in a higher subsystem. We propose that this heat dissipation could be captured by incorporating an irreversible diffusion into the fluid dynamics equations. With this modification, the stochastic fluid dynamics equations become feasible to analyze numerically. Our numerical results for the $\phi^4$ theory show that the introduction of this extra diffusion significantly improves the accuracy of our approximations for RG equations, even when the exact RG equations are highly non-trivial and difficult to solve numerically. By extending this idea, we anticipate it could be applicable to a broad range of RG and stochastic RG scenarios. In particular, we anticipate it could be applicable to various scenarios, including systems with non-perturbative phase transitions, neural networks, and chemical reactions. In these cases, the proposed method may provide a more accurate solution for the RG equations than the conventional decoupling method. Finally, we hope this new approach will contribute to a fresh perspective on irreversibility in physical and biological systems, encouraging further research into its applications and underlying principles. Our code is available online at https://github.com/HiDyNa/FluidDynamicsForSGR.

Music enthusiasts frequently seek out lyrics and audio online, but most users rely on standard web searches, which can be inefficient. To enhance the music-discovery experience, we suggest an innovative approach that leverages a dedicated search engine for music queries. In response to each user input, our proposed system conducts a dual-search across both lyrics and audio, while also providing a unified ranking based on relevance. To test and evaluate this idea, we've created a dataset containing 1.3 million song lyrics from 14 languages and associated audio files. To meet the unique requirements of music searches, we've also designed a ranking model that integrates multiple features, including cross-attention mechanisms and bidirectional GRUs. The performance of our proposed system significantly surpasses existing approaches in both automatic and human evaluations. Notably, our findings reveal that incorporating lyrics and audio information through a joint ranking process leads to a substantial 12% improvement in quality compared to separate searches. Moreover, our model achieves a 26% higher Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) score than the baseline model, indicating enhanced retrieval effectiveness. In human assessments, our proposed system yields a 21% increase in preferred results, demonstrating the significant benefit of our dedicated music search engine. To facilitate further research, we've made the dataset and model publicly available. By providing an effective music search experience, we aim to contribute to the broader music-discovery ecosystem. In addition to our primary contribution, we've also introduced two additional features to enhance music searches: a dedicated interface and a bookmarking system: (1) a dedicated interface enables users to browse search results in a user-friendly environment, complete with audio playback and direct access to lyrics; (2) a bookmarking system enables users to save their preferred search results and related data for later reference: In our experiments, we've integrated our music search engine with Musixmatch and SoundCloud, two prominent music databases, to ensure seamless audio and lyrics access. To ensure the best possible user experience, we've also implemented a dedicated interface and a bookmarking system. Building upon the framework of topological groupoids and stacks, this study introduces the notion of extension for a topological groupoid over a base stack, conceptually equivalent to gerbes over topological stacks. This topological stacky extension, or gerbe, is represented by a pair consisting of a morphism from the groupoid to the base stack, along with an invariant 2-cocycle, defined up to coboundary. Associated with each gerbe is an underlying gerbe of sets, whose path groupoid forms a topological categorical group that serves as the group of units for the gerbe. These gerbes over topological stacks are mapped to the gerbes over simplicial topological stacks via natural transformation, yielding the gerbes associated with simplicial topological stacks as a full sub-2-category of the category of gerbes over simplicial topological stacks. Furthermore, this study introduces the notion of stacky reduction for gerbes over topological stacks, analogous to algebraic geometry's notion of reduction for algebraic stacks. The stacky reduction of a gerbe over a topological stack is defined as the gerbe over the stacky reduction of the underlying stack, resulting in an algebraic gerbe over an algebraic stack that is locally representable by a product of projective spaces over integers. This study also establishes a connection between the fundamental group of topological groups and classifying space of topological groupoids, demonstrating that the fundamental group of the classifying space of a topological groupoid is the fundamental group of the classifying space of the underlying topological group, and that this group determines the classifying space of the topological groupoid itself. This framework is utilized to analyze the topological categorical group of units for gerbes over topological stacks, revealing that it is a topological group characterized by a nonabelian discrete fundamental group, along with an abelian fundamental group of classifying space of its monodromy group, whose underlying set is identified with the underlying set of the gerbe. This study also introduces the Picard stack of line bundles as the gerbe over topological stacks, where line bundles are defined as line bundles equipped with an algebraic action of the multiplicative group of non-zero numbers. This Picard stack of line bundles over topological stacks is achieved by extending the gerbe over topological stacks to line bundles over topological stacks, resulting in a stacky reduction for algebraic gerbes over algebraic stacks that localizes projective spaces over rational numbers.

We performed a statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum sources within the Milky Way's star-forming region, identifying 114 molecular cores and tracking their mass over a period of 5-10 years. Our findings reveal a mass growth distribution governed by a power law with an index of 1.1, indicating that more massive cores form more rapidly. Since even the slowest-accumulating cores eventually surpass 10 times the mass of the Sun, it is likely that all low-mass cores will produce at least one high-mass star. However, about 70 percent of low-mass cores will create multiple such stars and nearly a quarter will produce three or more. These outcomes suggest that the formation of massive stars is a multi-step process, with stars with greater mass forming more quickly. If cores with two distinct temperature zones are more likely to produce massive stars, as implied by the absence of single-zone candidates among our detected sources, then the process's complexity is further underscored. Ultimately, the process's non-linearity is highlighted by the fact that even when we consider the distribution of stars that form within a given core, the relationship between a core's mass and the mass of its stars is not linear. The time it takes for cores to form stars also follows a power-law distribution, with the majority of stars formed within five years, and indicators of core turbulence's impact on star formation are visible in the form of turn-ups in the mass function at specific points, including when a core's mass reaches around 300 solar masses, and when the time to star formation is either extremely short or extremely long. These findings offer a quantitative framework for modeling the formation of massive stars and the processes that create and disrupt molecular cores. Through further study of the relationships we have identified, along with relevant processes such as core disruption and collision-induced star formation, we aim to refine the ability to predict the formation of massive stars and the creation of star clusters, ultimately informing the analysis of observational data on such clusters and enhancing the development of cluster formation models that can be compared to data on a cluster-by-cluster basis. By doing so, we can better understand the relationship between the processes of cluster formation and the processes of galaxy formation and evolution. The research presented here is a starting point for such investigations, and it does so within the context of the largest and most comprehensive molecular core survey conducted to date. Finite Godel algebras are intimately connected with finite forest semantics, which provides a clear picture of Godel algebras through the concept of duals to forest categories. This connection allows us to offer a simplified proof that variety of finite Godel algebras is nonelementary. Furthermore, this relationship enables us to establish a connection between nonelementary classes and forest categories, which is a highly suggestive result in its own right. Along the way, we demonstrate that the class of finite Godel algebras with an additional operation of any finite rank can be reduced to nonelementary via a series of elementary additions, in contrast to the situation for finite Boolean algebras with single additional operation. This conclusion leads us to an unresolved question regarding the nature of finite algebras within the variety of finite Heyting algebras with single additional operation. In our final section, we explore potential applications arising from the nonelementary nature of finite Godel algebras, including potential links to treelike structures and Cayley graphs. Additionally, we identify potential connections to linguistically oriented research within the framework of Context-Free or Tree-Adjoining Grammars. Lastly, we suggest that the relationship between forest categories and nonelementary classes of algebras may facilitate a nonelementary class-based characterization of the category of languages generated through Context-Free grammars. In this context, we introduce the class of algebras that are essentially equivalent to the forest category corresponding to a given Context-Free grammar, only in a highly abstract algebraic sense. We then establish that this class of algebras has a nonelementary property if, and only if, the underlying tree language does as well. This connection between tree languages and nonelementary classes of algebras is the core theme of our research, and we believe it merits exploration within the broader framework of formal language theory. A high-resolution sensor can capture detailed scene information and provide supplementary features related to intensity and wavelength. Introducing the $A^2N^2$ network, a cutting-edge LiDAR classification network that incorporates the context provided by nearby points and tackles the issues of density and resolution. This network increases density-based context to a five-layer spherical context and introduces a density-normalized strategy. It incorporates a resolution-normalized strategy based on the distance between points. The $A^2N^2$ network is evaluated on two dense LiDAR classification datasets and shows superior or on-par performance with state-of-the-art density-based and resolution-based methods. Moreover, the $A^2N^2$ network is capable of handling LiDAR data with extremely high density and resolution, outperforming the existing LiDAR classification density-based methods. Classical differentiation and integration, basic operations in analysis, can unexpectedly disrupt the fundamental properties of zonal functions, which maintain their rotational invariance. We examine how these operations impact the key characteristic of zonal functions - being positive definite. Our study delves into first-order differentiation and second-order integration, and we aim to identify the specific conditions under which these operations preserve the property of being positive definite. We establish the relationship between these conditions and the functional equations that zonal functions satisfy. Furthermore, we provide a condition for first-order differentiation to maintain the positive definite property, and we analyze how this condition is linked to the stability of certain dynamical systems. We also discuss the implications of our findings for harmonic polynomials and show how our results connect to the Rotenberg problem. Additionally, we discuss the case of second-order integration and its relation to the positive definite property. We conclude by examining a notable application to dynamics, specifically the stability of relative equilibria in the presence of a non-conservative force, and we present an associated computational method using zonal functions. This method enables us to determine the stability of relative equilibria on any rotational surface, and we illustrate this by calculating the stability boundary for a rotating elliptical parallel plate in an ideal fluid. The computational approach facilitates rapid assessment of stability for any given surface, and we demonstrate its effectiveness with an analysis of the effect of surface geometry on stability for both elliptical and hyperbolic surfaces. The results demonstrate the significant impact that surface geometry can have on the stability of relative equilibria, and we show that even minor changes in surface geometry can lead to substantial differences in stability, especially for highly symmetrical surfaces. The results also highlight the potential for non-conservative forces to induce stable rotations on certain surfaces, and we identify specific conditions under which surface geometry can lead to stable equilibrium states. The study also reveals that highly symmetrical surfaces are prone to exhibiting non-trivial positive definite functions that can be obtained through first-order differentiation or second-order integration. The research provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the interplay between zonal functions, differential operators, and surface geometry, and it offers a powerful computational tool for analyzing the stability of relative equilibria in rotating surfaces. The results also raise intriguing questions about the potential applications of this framework to other areas of mathematics and physics. The research is further supported by an accompanying computational tool, written in MATLAB, that enables rapid assessment of stability for any given surface and provides a means to explore the results graphically. The connection between ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos remains a topic of interest despite the limited information available. Using data from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the Pierre Auger Observatory from 2004 to 2015, this research analyzes possible links between UHECR events and neutrino events within the same time frame. It identifies 16 neutrino events reported by IceCube that show spatial and temporal correlations with UHECR events from PAO, and vice versa, considering potential observational delays. Among these 16 events, 7 UHECR events show a connection with neutrino events at a 90% confidence level, although none of these events are linked to multiple neutrino events. One open circle in the sky with a radius of 19.5 degrees, defined by avoiding contaminated events, contains potential neutrino sources as seen in data from the Super-Kamiokande and AMANDA observatories. If future UHECR and neutrino data confirm the findings of the present study, it is possible that a significant portion of these extreme events, consisting of about 10%, can be attributed to sources producing both UHECR and neutrino events within this defined circle. However, it is essential to note that the current analysis lacks statistical significance and the findings may be the result of a chance occurrence. Consequently, this research encourages further investigation rather than a definitive conclusion. It is essential that both observatories continue to collect more comprehensive and detailed data to validate or refute the possible connections between these events. In the context of multi-messenger astronomy, discovering a connection between UHECR and neutrino events has significant implications, opening up new avenues for identifying sources of these cosmic phenomena. In addition, studying the UHECR-neutrino connection may provide insight into the maximum energy released by sources and the limitations of general relativity in the most energetic events. In the context of particle physics, studying UHECR and neutrino data together may reveal new aspects of high-energy physics, such as the disappearance of UHECR events or neutrino flavor transformation in sources or during propagation. In the field of astrophysics, studying the UHECR-neutrino connection may lead to a better understanding of the composition of UHECR and its implications for the origins of these cosmic rays. The complex properties of liquid foams are influenced by the interplay between surface tension and the movement of individual fluid particles, which is represented by the Euler-Lagrange equations. We demonstrate that, in the presence of a strong surface force, the Euler-Lagrange equations can be simplified to a continuum model described by the Villermaux-Bouchet equations. By comparing the surface forces experienced by pairs of nearby plateaus in a liquid foam, we determine that the roughness factor affects the apparent surface tension and not the rate at which fluid particles move. Furthermore, we find that the rate at which fluid is trapped is influenced by the roughness factor and the apparent surface tension. We analyze different methods for measuring the roughness factor and its impact on fluid flow within a liquid foam. We also present results from a numerical simulation that show how the roughness factor affects the rate at which fluid is conserved within a liquid foam over time. We discuss the possibility of relating the roughness factor to the average surface area of S_n spheres and propose a simple theoretical model to describe this relationship. We propose that the rate at which fluid is trapped is proportional to the product of the roughness factor, the apparent surface tension, and the rate at which fluid is conserved within a liquid foam. We apply this new understanding to analyze data from previous experiments conducted by Christy and Shafraoui, revealing that the rate at which fluid is trapped does indeed vary significantly with the rate at which fluid is conserved within a liquid foam for S_2 and S_3 plateaus. However, for S_4 and larger, the rate at which fluid is trapped becomes relatively constant and independent of the rate at which fluid is conserved within a liquid foam. We propose that this change in behavior occurs when the diameter of the S_n spheres becomes comparable to or smaller than the average distance between them. We also suggest that the rate at which fluid is trapped becomes relatively constant for S_4 and larger due to the formation of a continuous "skin" layer that limits further fluid trapping within the liquid foam. We support our new understanding with additional results from a numerical simulation, showing that the rate at which fluid is trapped does indeed increase with the strength of surface force and that the roughness factor plays a crucial role in governing this phenomenon. We believe that our new understanding of the roughness factor and its impact on fluid flow within a liquid foam offers a compelling explanation for the diverse range of surface force values reported in previous experiments conducted by Christy and Shafra

The interaction between tension, Marangoni forces, and shear stress is illustrated through a simple quantitative model, showing the presence of two distinct states - a stable nematic brush and a stable spiral - as well as an unstable intermediate state. The model also identifies how increasing the Marangoni force or flow rate can cause a nematic brush to transition to a spiral state. Observations and the model both support the notion that a spiral state can exist with multiple layers of roll convection. The influence of membrane tension on a rotating Hele-Shaw cell's state is further demonstrated through a simple layering diagram. The diagram also highlights the role of surface tension in layering and the possibility of discovering new states of this type. In neural machine translation, attention-based mechanisms have been highly effective.
However, large gaps often exist between reference targets and generated outputs.
To mitigate this, we introduce a look-ahead attention model that allows the model
to consider future targets when producing each output word.
To prevent over-reliance on model internals, we limit the impact of look-ahead
attention on output word probabilities.
Through careful design of attention weights and masking, the model can balance
exploiting target information with avoiding exposure.
Our results show that look-ahead models perform significantly better than baseline
models, especially when targeting longer sentences, and that they perform closest
to lower-target sentences that they can truly see. 

We found that look-ahead models excel at producing future-target words and words
that would otherwise be difficult to predict, and that they produce sentences
that are semantically similar to target sentences.
Our analysis also indicates that look-ahead models reduce the reliance on
syntactic information and that they produce sentences with different structural
propensities.
To facilitate future research, we will make our code, models, and data
available.

The fusion of grid computing and translational research represents a significant approach in the scientific community's current endeavors. This study explores the potential of a translational approach to grid computing development, application, and methodology through case analysis and systematic review. By examining six notable grid computing projects, it identifies key factors that contribute to successful project development and highlights best practices. Furthermore, by drawing on established theories of translational research, it suggests ways to bridge the gap between grid computing development and application. Finally, it presents a framework consisting of four distinct stages to facilitate the translational process of grid computing. This framework is subsequently applied to demonstrate its practical value through the analysis of an actual project. In conclusion, it highlights the importance of considering the social aspects of grid computing projects in the development process and proposes directions for further research. This study is targeted at an audience with an interest in grid computing development and the translational research approach. No prior knowledge of grid computing is necessary to engage with the study's main concepts and contributions. The study's case analysis and case study are rooted in the South African computing community, making it particularly relevant to researchers within this context. The study's framework and proposals for further research, on the other hand, have a broader applicability and can be of interest to a global audience. Recent research in psychology and neuroscience suggests that curiosity and reinforcement learning share similar underlying processes. This work explores the idea that curiosity can be understood as a result of competition between two networks: one that generates curiosity through open exploration, and another that promotes closer examination of items with apparent value. We utilize a neural network model incorporating two competing pathways to model curiosity and reinforcement learning. The network's curiosity component is represented by a freely operating network that generates curiosity signals, while the approach network attempts to minimize the difference between its current state and desired state, driven by external rewards. The two networks compete for control, with the winner determining whether to pursue open exploration or closer examination. We demonstrate that this model captures key phenomena observed in humans under similar conditions. For instance, it exhibits the capacity to balance exploration and exploitation, as well as the ability to learn through trial and error. Additionally, it displays how overestimation in the network's prediction of future rewards can lead to excessive exploration. We also analyze the proposed model from a computational theory perspective, suggesting that the competition between the network's components may be reflective of the interplay between the brain's default mode network and salience network during decision-making. Finally, we discuss potential connections between this model and existing frameworks for understanding curiosity within the scope of psychology and economics. We introduce Graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes, a flexible model that enables
efficient computation in both mini-batch and non-conjugate settings by introducing a new family of kernel and process combinations. Based on the widely-used Mat\'ern kernel, this innovation allows for a variety of kernel and process configurations that can be readily evaluated for efficient computation in complex statistical learning settings. Furthermore, our proposed GP model exhibits excellent performance in various machine learning and signal processing applications, including multi-task learning, meta-learning, and federated learning. We provide a comprehensive framework for computing posterior and predictive distributions, along with a strategic approach to selecting models that balance performance and computational efficiency. Alongside, we develop an efficient PyTorch implementation for our Graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes, leveraging the benefits of the PyTorch library while addressing computational challenges. Through experiments and comparisons with alternative models, our proposed GMPs demonstrate superior performance across multiple datasets and scenarios. Our code is openly available at \url{https://github.com/ghassen-rouhani/Graph_Matern_GPs}.

In monitoring and managing urban road networks, a key challenge lies in maintaining a reliable and comprehensive sensing system, particularly in areas with limited infrastructure. The proliferation of ridesourcing vehicles equips with sensing technology offers an attractive solution to this problem by creating a mobile and dynamic sensing network. This work develops an optimal allocation algorithm, addressing the coverage and reliability issues in this context. It determines the most effective use of ridesourcing vehicles with sensing capabilities to monitor and respond to incidents across the urban road network. This is achieved by solving a Covering Placement Formulation, a computational problem that considers the shortest paths between locations and models the reliability of sensing coverage through minimum weight subgraph selection. This algorithm provides an efficient solution, with the potential for application in real-world scenarios via a metaheuristic approach called the Scatter Search. This research was inspired by the growing number of ridesourcing services in major cities and investigates the potential of these services as a mobile sensing system, exploring issues of coverage, reliability, and management through optimization algorithms. The CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has made the most sensitive dark matter detection to date through the invisible decay of a J/ψ meson. This finding results from J/ψ data at 8 and 13 TeV center-of-mass energies, totaling 19.9 inverse femtobarns of luminosity. J/ψ decays into dark matter and missing energy are modeled by introducing an invariant mass spectrum of dark matter particles, from which lower limits are set on the dark matter nucleon scattering cross section due to the restriction of missing energy in events with low four-momentum transfer. Limits on these interactions, as well as dark matter haloscattering, are presented for various nucleon types and mass ranges of the dark matter particle. For the simplest scenario, where the dark matter particle is a singlet fermion, these limits lower the cross section by a factor of at least twenty compared to previous studies. Similar limits on dark photon decays, where dark photons are absent but the missing energy suggests a dark photon mass less than 100 picoelectronvolts, are also introduced for the first time. These new constraints also apply to the scenario where a dark photon is exchanged in place of dark matter. Dark photon parameters that are within the reach of upcoming experiments with electron beams, such as HIBA and HPS at Jefferson Lab, are excluded for the first time, lowering the necessary luminosity for future experiments by a factor of twenty. Multi-sensor time series data often exhibits complex patterns in its time dependencies. While several methods can handle these complexities, they are typically limited to data from a single sensor. In cases where data is received from multiple sources, such as temperature measurements and financial stock prices, with different sampling frequencies, developing a unified approach to time series analysis is essential. For instance, consider a health monitoring system that uses temperature curves and electrical signal readings to diagnose medical conditions. Another example is the analysis of satellite images and land temperature measurements to study environmental changes. Formulas for operator calculations enable the integration of time series data with different sampling frequencies, allowing the application of Multivariate Fourier Singular Spectrum Analysis (MFSSA) to these integrated datasets. By integrating the application of several operators, the MFSSA technique can be extended to enable the analysis of datasets with different sampling frequencies. A proposed algorithm for the computation of these operators makes the MFSSA method computationally efficient. A study on artificial and real-world data demonstrates the effectiveness and practical applications of the MFSSA method. A remote-sensing image recognition example showcases the technique's capability to extract meaningful information from images, while the analysis of temperature curves in an urban environment highlights the method's ability to account for seasonal fluctuations. Furthermore, financial stock price analysis utilizing the integrated datasets reveals the ability of the MFSSA method to capture complex patterns in financial data. A discussion on the computational implications and potential applications of the MFSSA technique is also presented. A comprehensive evaluation of the MFSSA method's performance in comparison to the Fourier Decomposition and ETS methods is provided, highlighting the benefits of the MFSSA technique in scenarios with significant trends and periodic components. A detailed examination of the remote-sensing image recognition process and the urban temperature curve analysis is also included, along with an in-depth financial stock price analysis. A discussion on the implementation of the MFSSA method, including the algorithm for operator computation, is also presented, along with an evaluation of the method's performance in comparison to the Fourier Decomposition and ETS methods. A comprehensive evaluation of the remote-sensing image recognition process and the urban temperature curve analysis is also included, along with an in-depth financial stock price analysis. A discussion on the implementation of the MFSSA method, including the algorithm for operator computation, is also presented. Recent studies utilizing deep learning for automatic essay scoring have yielded promising results, but research into the underlying properties of these models is still in its infancy. To gain insight into the behavior of these models, this study employs robustness and margin theory to assess their performance on scaled and distorted test essays. The investigation reveals that while deep learning models excel at scoring original essays, they struggle with scoring artificial essays that have been manipulated to appear more difficult. Furthermore, the study finds that these models exhibit two undesirable traits: over-sensitivity to minor changes in essay content and over-stability in response to increased noise. Over-sensitivity leads to inconsistent scoring, while over-stability results in scores that fail to capture the full range of student ability. To mitigate these issues, the study proposes augmenting the training data with artificially distorted essays, which can help reduce over-sensitivity and over-stability in the model. The findings suggest that while deep learning models show promise for automatic essay scoring, they require careful attention to their properties to ensure reliability and fairness. The study's methods and findings are expected to contribute to ongoing research into the validation of machine learning models and their potential to transform high-stakes testing. The study's techniques and results may also inform the development of policies and guidelines for the use of machine learning in high-stakes assessment. Finally, the study's work is seen as a starting point for exploring the relationship between machine learning models and psychometric theories of test score validity. The study's results raise important questions about the role of machine learning in educational assessment and the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complex relationships between models, data, and educational constructs. The study's approach is proposed as a way to move towards a more interdisciplinary study of machine learning in education, one that draws on the theoretical and methodological advances of both machine learning research and educational research. The study suggests that its approach can be applied to other assessment contexts, such as automatic question evaluation and prediction of student performance from freelist responses. The study's results are seen as a call to action for the development of new validation methods that take into account the unique characteristics of machine learning models and their applications in educational assessment. The study's approach is proposed as a way to balance the benefits of machine learning in education with the need to ensure the validity, reliability, and fairness of assessment results. The asymptotic behavior of a random walk under the condition that the increments of the walk have zero mean and are independent and identically distributed has been extensively researched, particularly when the walk is located within a bounded area, often referred to as the "paradoxical" case. Recent studies have extended these findings to cover cases where the walk is not confined to a bounded space, but instead, the sum of the increments is bounded by a fraction of the walk itself. In this paper, we examine the asymptotic behavior of a random walk when the increments have zero mean and are independent and identically distributed, but with no restrictions on the walk's size. We show that by adjusting the walk by a specific factor, it exhibits the same asymptotic behavior as a scaled version of itself, where the scaling factor relies on the second moment of the increments. This finding generalizes a common technique used to tackle the paradoxical case by deriving the desired asymptotic distribution through a combination of the central limit theorem and inverting the cumulative distribution function. In contrast, our approach employs a more direct method that leverages the properties of the walk's increments and their relationship to the walk's asymptotic behavior. We also provide conditions under which the asymptotic distribution is non-degenerate, as well as specific conditions on the increments that guarantee the desired asymptotic distribution is standard normal. Additionally, we establish a lower bound for the asymptotic variance, expressed in terms of the second central moments of the increments, and demonstrate its attainability under certain conditions. This research provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing the asymptotic behavior of a random walk with independent increments, offering a flexible and powerful tool for tackling a broad range of problems and yielding notable results in the paradoxical case. Our findings are accompanied by illustrative examples and counterfactuals that bring the theoretical developments to life. Notably, we showcase the applicability of our methods to settings involving integrable but non-dominable increments, the asymptotic behavior of random walks over finite horizons, and the paradoxical case itself, resulting in novel insights that challenge prevailing intuition. In the process, we establish a general strategy for circumventing the difficulties posed by non-degenerate increments, highlighting the interplay between the walk's asymptotic behavior and the properties of its increments. Our research paves the way for further exploration of the walk's asymptotic behavior over finite horizons, as well as extensions to a broader class of distributions and increment structures. Ultimately, our work lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the walk's asymptotic

A mathematical model is developed to examine the population dynamics of a target insect affected by the fungus Mesonema annulicaudum and entomopathogenic nematodes. The model considers the birth rate and death rate of the host insect in its absence of the pathogen, as well as the impact of the nematodes on birth and death rates of the host. Additionally, the model accounts for the within-host dynamics of the fungus and nematodes. Through mathematical and computational analysis, we identify key conditions that ensure the existence and stability of equilibrium points, including the possibility of half-stable periodic behavior. We also analyze the long-term outcome of increasing the host birth rate and the effect of disease-induced mortality on host population dynamics. Finally, we discuss the implications of our model for the biological control of target insect populations using the entomopathogenic nematodes and fungi.  It is suggested that the model could be expanded to consider multiple host insect species and the impact of environmental factors on host and pathogen populations. The model follows the framework of Pong and Heunert, and the model analysis is conducted with reference to that work. The model is applied to study the dynamics of an specific insect species, the German cockroach, and the cockroach population in general. The model is examined under various conditions and scenarios to explore its outcomes and possibilities for the model's extension. The model-related calculations and results are also supported by graphical representations. The model provides a basis for the investigation of biological control methods and the associated within-host dynamics. The model can be modified to study the effects of environmental factors, the possibility of the fungus being transmitted directly between host insects, and the presence of multiple host insect species. The model can also be compared with experimental data and alternative biological control methods. The model includes two key systems: the host-parasite and the fungus-nematode within-host dynamics. The model accounts for the birth and death rates of the host in the absence of the pathogen, as well as the impact of the nematodes on birth and death rates of the host. The model also considers the within-host dynamics of the fungus and nematodes, and it is suggested that the fungus and nematodes have a direct impact on each other's within-host dynamics. The model follows the framework of Pong and Heunert, and the model analysis is conducted with reference to that work. The model is applied to study the dynamics of an specific insect species, the German cockroach, and the cockroach population in general.

Nucleus detection serves a fundamental purpose in medical image analysis as a base for further identification and analysis. Accurate and efficient detection of nuclei is crucial for both factors. While high accuracy can be achieved with complex models and expansion-based methods, they may lead to prolonged processing times and require significant adjustments for new datasets. In this study, we present a novel, streamlined W-shaped network that simultaneously considers local and global information for nucleus detection. The proposed W-shaped network consists of two primary components: the shape descriptor and the feature extractor. It leverages two unique branches with distinct field-of-views in the encoder, allowing for the extraction of local and global features. These features are combined in the decoder, with an additional shape descriptor branch that helps refine the extracted features and produce the detection results. Notably, the proposed method for automatic nucleus detection achieves a high average precision of 0.83 without the use of pre-trained models and achieves the lowest average precision plus one false positive (P+F) score of 0.15, outperforming existing methods. Furthermore, the introduction of a nucleus dataset, comprising 2000 annotated images, contributes to the advancement of nucleus detection. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/zhengzheng-feng/W-Shaped-Nucleus-Detection. For further research improvements, the challenge is issued at https://competitions.stackmind.ai/competitions/56.

Our research demonstrates that the hamiltonian path index of these constructions can be significantly minimized, and in some cases, this index is as small as the number of hamiltonian paths itself. To achieve this, we present a method for generating all possible hamiltonian paths in a source-out-tree and leverage this by extending our findings to hamiltonian graphs. Unfortunately, the process of cell death from pyroptosis is often hindered by the presence of anti-inflammatory medications, which can result in the persistence of infected cells. To address this issue, we propose a computational model that takes into account the interplay between the host cells, infected cells, pyroptotic cells, as well as the effects of anti-inflammatory medications and vaccine distribution. Through mathematical and computational analyses of the model, we are able to identify the conditions under which the model exhibits fixed points representing various equilibrium states, including stable coexistence between the host and the virus, extinction of the host due to the virus, stable coexistence between the infected and healthy cells, extinction of the infected cells due to healthy cells, as well as the emergence of periodic oscillations in cell populations. Furthermore, we investigate how the model responds to interventions, such as the administration of anti-inflammatory medications and vaccines, and gather insights that could be applied to real-world scenarios. To facilitate numerical computations, we developed a computational tool using a method called Euler's method. To validate the model, we compared its predictions with empirical data, and the results are compatible with available statistical methods. Lastly, we explored the model's sensitivity to various parameters through a technique called sensitivity analysis. To further investigate the model's behavior, we conducted a batch policy search to identify optimal strategies for the administration of anti-inflammatory medications and vaccines within a hypothetical timeframe of 100 days. The results of this optimization process align with our theoretical fixed-point analysis and demonstrate the significance of vaccine distribution in comparison to the administration of anti-inflammatory medications. As the adoption of blockchain technology grows, verifying the correctness of smart contracts before deployment is increasingly vital. programmers and auditors need tools that make verifying contract correctness an efficient, automated process. In our research, we present HELMHOLTZ, a verification tool that can check the correctness of Michelson programs used in the Tezos blockchain. By leveraging the Decidability Theorem for Guarded First-Order Logic with uninterpreted functions, HELMHOLTZ can verify whether Michelson programs satisfy a given specification. To enhance the effectiveness of this verification, we also introduce an innovative approach to simplifying the complex Michelson type system. With this method, we can convert Michelson programs into a more verifiable format while maintaining equivalence. By combining these innovations, we can use Michelson programs with unbounded recursion and mutable data structures for verification. To demonstrate the capabilities of HELMHOLTZ, we applied the tool to a set of real-world Tezos smart contracts. Our results showed that even with the strict type system of Michelson, we can achieve significant reductions in the size of the verification formulas, leading to a notable increase in successful verifications. Overall, our research makes significant progress in the verification of Michelson programs and paves the way for further research in this area. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as a prominent choice for analyzing complex graph-structured data in recent years. Despite their success, there's still a misconception that GCNs are a more advanced, specialized technique, only applicable to unique data configurations. In contrast, we aim to demonstrate the intrinsic connection between GCNs and conventional Neural Networks (CNNs) utilizing a mathematical translation framework. This framework allows us to transform a GCN into an equivalent CNN, and vice versa, based on the underlying graph structure. By establishing this equivalence, we can leverage this knowledge to repurpose existing CNNs, extract meaningful features from data with inherent connections, and devise innovative strategies for designing network architectures. To facilitate this process, we introduce a graphical translation method, providing a clear visual representation of the translation procedure. Furthermore, we explore an energy-based model approach to learn the underlying graph structure automatically from data with inherent connections. This learned representation can be used for unsupervised feature extraction, and we also integrate it into a supervised learning framework by combining it with a classifier. To verify the feasibility of our approach, we conduct a series of experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in extracting meaningful features from data with inherent connections. Formal specification languages for algorithms, particularly in the context of programming courses, have been underutilized despite their potential benefits. Existing research proposes a simple approach to convert logical pseudocodes into checked programming languages, but these proposals are limited to specific pseudocodes and do not address the broader range of pseudocodes used worldwide. In contrast, our study aims to investigate a more comprehensive set of pseudocodes, encompassing both instructional and professional pseudocodes, to establish their foundational commonalities and a standardized framework for verifying the correctness of pseudocodes. To demonstrate the practical applicability of our findings, we developed a prototype language that can compile these pseudocodes into verified programs in Rust, leveraging the DraculaRust compiler framework. By combining formal verification techniques with programming languages, our approach enables the precise checking of algorithms' logical pseudocodes, ensuring the safety and correctness of the resulting programs. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach by verifying the correctness of popular sorting algorithms and a recursive formula for Euler's totient function using our prototype language. To facilitate the adoption of our approach, we are making available both the pseudocodes and the verified programs in our companion repository. Additionally, our approach may be adapted for use in programming courses to educate students about the importance of formal verification in algorithmic reasoning. By integrating our approach into computer science curricula, we believe it has the potential to promote a safer and more reliable programming culture worldwide. Using a diverse range of techniques from combinatorial theory, this study addresses two key problems. First, we determine the boolean rainbow Ramsey numbers for specific subsets in a 3-element lattice for colors 1 through 4. Secondly, we establish an upper and lower bound for the rainbow sum-free partition numbers in a 3-element set for specific subsets. These findings provide answers to previously unanswered questions and raise new questions about the boolean rainbow Ramsey theorem for 4-element sets in a lattice. Additionally, this study introduces new approaches to applying the combinatorial partitioning method, as well as novel applications of the Lovasz Local Lemma and the method of bounded degree. Further, this study highlights the utility of the hypergraph version of the Helly property. Lastly, this study suggests new directions for research on the boolean rainbow Ramsey theorem.

By doing so, the search space is significantly reduced, making it feasible to employ an exhaustive strategy to identify potential evasion paths for robots operating in these environments. However, determining the boundaries of these superstates requires a substantial amount of computational time. In response, we propose a non-uniform partitioning method to break down the grid world into superstates based on a heuristic approach, taking into account the computational costs associated with each subsequent division. As a result, our method yields a more balanced superstate partition, which can be achieved with significantly less computational time, amounting to merely a fraction of the costs associated with the most optimal solution. Furthermore, we investigate the parameters influencing our non-uniform partitioning method, including the number of target robots, obstacles, and whether the primary robot is capable of making movements that overlap with potential evasion paths. Our research demonstrates that the proposed method achieves highly effective partitioning, with a computational time of approximately 1 second for scenarios involving up to 5 robots in a 50x50 grid world, compared to the exhaustive strategy's 30 seconds. Lastly, our method demonstrates the capability to handle scenarios involving multiple targets and obstacles. This study proposes a novel, high-quality image-to-image translation method using adaptive instance normalization layers in cycleGANs. We first analyze the limitations of basic cycleGANs, including the difficulty in obtaining high-quality translation results and the challenge of implementing complex operations. To address these issues, we suggest adapting the use of AdaIN layers within cycleGANs. Specifically, we propose replacing the fully connected layers in basic cycleGANs with AdaIN layers and incorporating source domain feature maps and target domain noise vectors as inputs. This modified approach enables the learning of more realistic and accurate translations. To facilitate training and stabilize the training process, we also introduce a refinement module and utilize a multi-scale guide mechanism. The proposed AdainGAN model exhibits superior performance in generating high-quality images in various datasets, including CeleHA, Portraits, and faces, as demonstrated by evaluation metrics and visual results. The code for this research is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/zh116005/AdainGAN. The paper has been accepted for presentation at the 13th International Conference on Advanced Research on Data and Knowledge Engineering (ICKE 2022).

This paper introduces BasicVSR++, a highly efficient video super-resolution model, 
building upon the foundations laid down by BasicVSR in Video Super-Resolution Benchmark. 
BasicVSR++ achieves a notable enhancement of 0.32 in PSNR average rating across 14 datasets 
following modifications to the input sequence length, from 40 to 3, alongside 
a 1.45 times boost in computational throughput, utilizing a unified transformer encoder. 
We delve into the design choices and the underlying principles governing the 
video super-resolution process. Furthermore, we provide a thorough analysis of 
the posed problems, implicit assumptions, and potential model limitations. 

In particular, we highlight the difficulties in accurately predicting pixel values 
given the assumed stationarity within video sequences and propose a possible fix by 
employing non-stationary transformer encoders. On top of that, we identify the challenge 
of modeling non-stationary noise processes and discuss the implications for video 
restoration tasks. Alongside these concerns, we also examine the issue of implicit 
bias amplification and discuss the requirements for developing more inclusive video 
restoration models, capable of effectively handling diverse video data, including 
those with significant differences in lighting conditions. 

To facilitate further advancement in video super-resolution, we introduce a novel 
benchmark, featuring a dataset with artificially introduced lighting changes, along 
with a customized evaluation metric. On top of that, we introduce a novel strategy 
for reducing bias in video super-resolution, centered around the transfer of 
encoder knowledge, and back-propagated to the decoder as additional input. 

Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance, outperforming the baseline 
model by 0.24 in PSNR, as evaluated on the custom benchmark, and expects this 
advance to stimulate the development of more innovative video super-resolution 
models and techniques.

We tackle the challenge of predicting electroweak vector boson distribution functions (EW-VBFs) at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) by addressing an issue with the current lack of precise data. Our investigation focuses on the behavior of parton distribution functions for W and Z bosons in high-energy collisions and reveals the presence of universal corrections, amounting to approximately 10% of the total, that affect the distribution of these bosons beyond the leading order. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a set of scale variation EW-VBFs, which can serve as an alternative to the traditional Collins-Sotiropoulos function, providing a more direct means of incorporating EW-VBFs into PDFs. When there are multiple tasks in a multi-task reinforcement learning scenario, a single learned dynamics model can be ineffective due to its limited ability to generalize across different policies in separate tasks. In response, we propose utilizing multiple dynamics models, each tailored to a specific task, to enhance generalization. However, training these task-specific models is challenging because we typically don't have access to the ground truth future states needed for supervised learning. To overcome this obstacle, we develop an method to train these models with the help of reward signals. By leveraging a value function in combination with a policy, we can generate a task-specific learning algorithm that efficiently trains models for reward-based dynamics prediction. Our approach was successfully tested on a range-based Walker2d environment and a general MultiWalker environment, resulting in significant performance improvements compared to a single learned dynamics model. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/kuangpunghu/mt-dynamics.

This article examines how the presence of boundaries that compactify a noncompact manifold impacts the behavior of its solutions, addressing a notable omission in standard boundary value problems. We explore the role of compact boundaries in identifying solution classes, the significance of noncompact boundaries in directing solution orientation, and the impact of boundary dimensions in separating solution spaces. Additionally, we discuss the significance of compact boundaries in optimizing control problems and the role of noncompact boundaries in stabilizing unstable solutions. The article ultimately highlights the need for a unified framework that accommodates compact and noncompact boundaries within a single analytical context. We suggest adopting the compact boundary approach as a fundamental model, with the noncompact boundary case being a special instance that requires a separate, more nuanced analysis. We support this perspective through examples and demonstrations of the minimal boundary value problem and the optimal control problem with a noncompact boundary. The article aims to facilitate a deeper understanding of boundary value problems, regardless of boundary compactness, and encourages further research into the theoretical and computational aspects of these problems. In 1936, Max Rosser developed a variant of Kurt Godel's first incompleteness theorem, which effectively demonstrates that within any formal axiomatic system capable of delivering a satisfactory theory of basic arithmetic, there exists a statement formulated within the system itself, which the system neither confirms nor refutes. This statement in question asserts the impossibility of proving a particular false statement from within the axioms of the system. Godel's own contribution to this topic had shown the same capacity for this type of result for any formal axiomatic system capable of delivering a satisfactory theory of basic arithmetic. However, Rosser's variant achieves this outcome with fewer axioms than Godel's version. Furthermore, this variant provides the additional benefit of a meaningful connection to the concept of undecidability, which can be viewed as a central aspect of the broader field of computability theory. In 1970, Paul Cohen exploited a similar approach drawn from Rosser's variant to establish a groundbreaking result in set theory. Cohen's achievement involved the successful construction of a model of less than full strength arithmetic within an axiomatic system that had been shown to be theoretically adequate for delivering a satisfactory theory of basic arithmetic. This model of less than full strength arithmetic effectively incorporated the validity of the original statement of Godel's first incompleteness theorem. Consequently, this achievement of Cohen's effectively confirmed the concept of undecidability within formal axiomatic systems capable of delivering a satisfactory theory of basic arithmetic. In this paper, various aspects and related concepts of Godel's first incompleteness theorem are explored through a review of the key contributions made by both Rosser and Cohen. In addition, the paper will examine the fundamental role played by the concept of undecidability in the broader field of computability theory. The paper will also consider the fundamental relationship that exists between the concept of undecidability and the concept of incompleteness within formal axiomatic systems. In this context, the relationship between the concept of undecidability and the concept of incompleteness is viewed as a central aspect of the broader field of computability theory.
