In this context, the capacity for formal axiomatic systems to deliver a satisfactory theory of basic arithmetic effectively represents a fundamental criterion for the validity of undecidability within these systems. As multi-hop THz communication systems reach higher frequencies, integrating beam training techniques becomes necessary to mitigate severe directional free-space path loss. Conventional beam training methods are often slow due to their sequential nature, but we propose a faster, dynamic beam training approach based on joint optimization. This method leverages the low-latency feedback from the receiver's initial scan to pinpoint the main lobe and estimate the optimal beam, and through numerical and simulated case studies, we demonstrate that dynamic beam training can achieve comparable performance to traditional methods, with latency reduced from milliseconds to microseconds, and with minor throughput degradation. Additionally, we investigate how to further improve the efficiency of dynamic beam training for multi-hop systems by allocating more resources to key nodes, and present a computational model to optimize resource allocation, with results showing significant throughput gains without compromising spectral efficiency. Furthermore, we examine the impact of node mobility and feedback impairments on dynamic beam training, and find that they result in performance degradation, but with room for improvement through advanced receiver design and optimized feedback strategies. With this research, we lay the groundwork for the efficient operation of multi-hop THz communication systems, and identify key areas for further investigation in this field.

By utilizing a sequence of smaller, overlapping sub-networks with increasing sizes and responsibilities, our model can effectively handle the diverse characteristics of speech - from short, monosyllabic sounds to longer phrases and sentences. Annotating large quantities of textual data is often a time-consuming and labor-intensive process, with numerous annotations required for each document to support natural language processing tasks. To accelerate the annotation process, we propose a method that leverages minimal annotations to enable the automatic identification of document sections containing specific task-relevant information. This approach employs a conditional probabilistic model to classify document sections based on labeled subsets of the document, with the model being a probabilistic variation of a novel inter-document section segmentation model. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to the annotation of two key NLP tasks: named entity recognition and sentiment analysis. Results show that our technique achieves significant improvements, with a 6.5% average F1 score boost for inter-document section segmentation and a 4.5% average F1 score boost for full-text annotation, when compared to the current state-of-the-art annotation method, with all annotations available. Moreover, our technique achieves a 11.5% average F1 score boost for full-text annotation when only a limited number of annotations are available, with just 10% of the annotations required for the current state-of-the-art method. To facilitate further research, we have made the dataset and model available publicly. Additionally, we have launched a user-friendly web-based annotation tool that utilizes our technique to enhance the annotation process, with the aim of reducing the cost of large-scale text annotation by at least two-thirds through the effective use of minimal annotations. This research examines the composition of gases in temperate exoplanet atmospheres under various host star metallicity conditions. We analyze six solar-siblings of the Sun in the Kepler field, focusing on planets similar in size and temperature to Earth, and model the atmospheric properties of these planets using the DCache approach in combination with the GASTRO tool. Our model considers the effects of stellar irradiation and the gravitational influence of the host star on the planetary atmosphere. We investigate three primary gas species: CO, CO2, and NH3, and assess their abundance across a range of metallicity levels, from extremely metal-poor to super-solar metallicity, based on the characteristics of the associated star. We also develop a novel approach to estimating the opacity of these gas species in the relevant wavelength ranges. Our analysis reveals that the abundance of the gas species examined increases with increasing metallicity of the host star, and that extremely metal-poor stars like the Provenance system result in significantly reduced abundances of these gases. Conversely, super-solar metallicity stars, such as the TOL 1410-408 system, lead to enhanced abundances of these gases, and we could potentially observe these effects with the James Webb Space Telescope in the near future. We also present a novel method for estimating the gas abundance in a planetary atmosphere based on a linear relationship between the atmospheric metal content and the abundance of the specific gas, and we apply this approach to our analysis. We anticipate that this research will contribute to a deeper understanding of the composition of exoplanet atmospheres and facilitate the analysis of future observations. Additionally, we provide a public database containing the results of our analysis for a total of 1,606 exoplanets, and this database is accessible through the research team's website. In this work, we explore topological Hochschild homology (THH) through the lens of bicategorical shadows, a fundamental concept in the study of categories of algebras and their representations. We initially establish a connection between THH and bicategorical shadows via the functor W_R, which arises from the combination of the THH functor and the suspension spectrum of R(\pi), where R(\pi) represents the category of algebras for a monoidal functor \pi: C \to Set, and C is a small category. In recent years, hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (HGCNs) have gained significant attention due to their ability to represent nodes in a more efficient and accurate manner. However, HGCNs are limited by their requirement of a fixed-point method, which can result in suboptimal solutions. To address this issue, we develop the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which utilizes the power iteration method to achieve optimal node feature representations. By leveraging the Lorentzian distance, LGCN represents nodes using their corresponding positions in hyperbolic space. We demonstrate that the Lorentzian distance is a valid graph distance, thereby ensuring the approximability of substructures within a given error tolerance. Comparative experiments against state-of-the-art HGCNs on six datasets show that LGCN yields comparable or superior performance, while showcasing the network's ability to learn more accurate node classifications using the power iteration method. Additionally, we provide theoretical evidence that the graph distance in Lorentzian space can be efficiently computed with $\Delta^2$ time complexity. The implementation of LGCN is available at https://github.com/zheng062/lacman. To facilitate reproducibility, we have released the code for the experimental setup as well.

We investigate the interplay between atoms and $\mu$-calculus within two-valued arithmetic. The presence of atoms in propositional logic with a countable number of distinct propositional symbols essentially alters the computationally complete $\mu$-calculus, leading to increased expressive power yet also computational limitations in terms of satisfiability, in both the basic $\mu$-calculus and its arithmetic expansion. In contrast, atoms in first-order logic with a countable number of distinct function symbols do not change the computationally complete complexity of the satisfiability problem. However, the addition of uncountably many distinct function symbols does change the complexity of the satisfiability problem for the $\mu$-calculus, causing it to become NP-complete. Additionally, we explore the impact of the number of distinct predicate symbols on the complexity of the satisfiability problem for the $\mu$-calculus within two-valued arithmetic with uncountable first-order logic. The presence of a single unary predicate symbol allows the $\mu$-calculus to express any $\Sigma_1$ formula over two-valued arithmetic. In the field of zero-shot speech translation, our proposed framework addresses the challenge of mapping acoustic signals to written text without pre-existing cross-lingual connections. By connecting the pre-trained models for both speech recognition and text generation, our zero-shot speech translation framework achieves significant improvements in few-shot settings. To further enhance performance, we develop two additional methods that leverage linguistic structure and cross-lingual information. In the multi-speech translation task, our approach demonstrates enhanced performance over the baseline method, leading to improved results in the few-shot setting. The experiments conducted across T2, S2, and M2 settings yield outstanding outcomes, with scores surpassing 19.0 in BLEU in the few-shot scenario and exceeding the baseline by 2.4 BLEU points in the zero-shot setting. Additionally, our method demonstrates reduced vocabulary size while maintaining performance, with a 30% reduction in vocabulary size achieving a 0.6 BLEU point increase. The outstanding outcomes achieved, along with the minimal vocabulary requirement, make our proposed framework an effective solution for zero-shot speech translation. Despite the extensive use of approximate methods for calculating multipoles, these approaches often introduce inaccuracies when dealing with high-energy phenomena. In our research, we present an innovative way to precisely determine generalized spherical multipoles in a quantum system using atomic orbitals. By leveraging the long-wavelength limit of electromagnetic radiation, we simplify the multipoles' calculation and demonstrate its effectiveness with a notable example – the photoionization of a hydrogen-like atom in a strong magnetic field. Our method offers a high degree of precision and is compatible with the extreme conditions covered by current experimental capabilities. In fact, our results reveal significant discrepancies between accurate calculations and previously employed approximate methods, especially for high-l states and large quantum numbers. Notably, our findings agree with recent experimental data and provide a valuable benchmark for developing new theoretical methods. Our results are already available in easy-to-access tables for various multipoles, including electric dipole, quadrupole, magnet dipole, and quadrupole, as well as higher-order multipoles, which can be readily adapted to other atoms and ions within this system. By making these data sets public, we aim to facilitate the comparison with future experimental and theoretical research, opening up new possibilities for the understanding of complex atomic phenomena under intense magnetic fields and high-energy conditions. Using the Langlands program and the Harish-Chandra isomorphism, we establish a connection between shifted Schur polynomials and Schur measures, thereby gaining insight into the corresponding probability process. This relationship enables us to derive the exact expectations and variances for certain statistics within the Schur process. Specifically, we show that the first k moments of the Schur measure correspond to shifted Schur polynomials of degree k. Furthermore, we calculate the expectations and variances for Plancherel measure rank, determinant, characteristic polynomial traces, and the number of distinct eigenvalues. These calculations provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the statistical properties of the Schur process. By leveraging this connection via the Harish-Chandra isomorphism, we also derive results for shifted Schur processes. In addition, we establish a duality within the Schur process, facilitated by a transformation inspired by the inverse of the Harish-Chandra isomorphism. This duality enables us to readily derive statistics for shifted Schur processes from those of the original Schur processes, and vice versa. As a result, we are able to determine the exact expectations and variances for shifted Schur processes with respect to Plancherel measure for various statistics, including rank, determinant, characteristic polynomial traces, and the number of distinct eigenvalues. These calculations equip us with a comprehensive understanding of the statistical properties of shifted Schur processes. Consequently, we are able to derive results for processes obtained through a combination of shifts and truncations. In particular, we are able to determine the exact expectations and variances for the rank, number of distinct eigenvalues, characteristic polynomial traces, and the largest and smallest eigenvalues for several such processes. These results provide a probabilistic analysis of various spectral statistics for certain unitary invariant random matrix ensembles that lie between the Haar measure on U(N) and the Plancherel measure on the unitary group U(N). In addition, we are able to determine the variance for the largest eigenvalue for Haar distributed unitary matrices in N x N matrices, a result that has been previously unknown. We investigate a model that combines dark parity symmetry with a seesaw mechanism for generating neutrino mass. The inclusion of a minimal dark sector, consisting of a dark fermion and a dark scalar, enables us to explore the effects of vacuum stability and dark matter viability within this framework. Employing quantum field thermal corrections, we find that the dark scalar can acquire a positive effective mass at the phase transition in the early universe, thus avoiding the problem of dark scalar overabundance. Furthermore, we find that dark parity symmetry is preserved, and dark neutrinos become quasi-Dirac at the cosmological scale. However, at very high energies, the small mass scales associated with the dark sector may become accessible through high-energy particle experiments. Additionally, we identify potential signatures for the dark scalar and dark neutrinos in oscillation experiments, direct dark matter detection, and future colliders. If the dark scalar's vacuum expectation value is in the range of $10^{16}$ to $10^{18}$ GeV, it may also lead to the generation of the axion's mass, thus explaining the axion's small mass under the Peccei-Quigg-Showler mechanism without needing a natural axion decay constant. Finally, we demonstrate that this framework can accommodate the sum of the dark matter and neutrino energy densities consistent with observational data. Upcoming experiments in neutrino oscillations, direct dark matter detection, and particle colliders may provide significant insights into this model's viability. Furthermore, the model predicts a relationship between the dark neutrino mass parameter and the effective four fermion coupling, which can be verified or disprover through future experiments in particle physics. If the model is validated, it could provide a unifying theory encompassing the physics of dark matter, neutrino, and the phenomenon of fast radio bursts. The model also entails a novel prediction regarding the neutrino mass spectrum, which can be substantiated or refuted through upcoming experiments in neutrino oscillations and particle physics. The incorporation of a minimal dark sector into the conventional seesaw framework, coupled with dark parity symmetry, yields a multifaceted theory that addresses a range of fundamental questions in particle physics and could be substantiated or disprover through forthcoming experiments in neutrino oscillations, direct dark matter detection, particle colliders, and the study of neutrino interactions with the cosmic microwave background. The model's viability would have far-reaching implications for the field of high-energy particle physics. We employ a technique of rotationally invariant unitary transformation to
decompose the Hamiltonian for transition metal oxides, breaking down the
decomposition into individual terms based on spin-orbit coupling strength. This
methodological approach allows us to investigate how interaction effects and
crystal field splitting influence the magnitude of spin-orbit coupling in these
materials. Using a concrete example of a 3D honeycomb lattice with a
$j_l$=1/2 band, we investigate the impact of crystal field splitting on the
electron dispersion and density of states, distinguishing between isotropic and
anisotropic scenarios. Furthermore, we investigate the topological properties of
these materials using the Wilson-Combs Chern number and the overlap charge as
indicators of topological phases, considering both the case when the spin-orbit
coupling is ignored and when it is included explicitly. Our study reveals that
even in the absence of full $SO$ breaking, certain materials may host non-trivial
topological phases, with the conditions required for these phases to emerge. 
This finding challenges a widely-held misconception that only fully $SO$-broken
materials can exhibit non-trivial topology. 
We also demonstrate that interaction effects and crystal field splitting can lead
to the transition between fully $SO$-broken and non-$SO$-breaking phases, with
the electron dispersion and density of states displaying significant anomalies at
these transition points. 
In addition, we investigate the potential for certain materials to host both
fully $SO$-broken and non-$SO$-breaking phases within the same parameter range.
This study sheds light on the complex interplay between interaction effects,
crystal field splitting, and spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides, 
enabling a more nuanced understanding of these materials and their potential
for hosting non-trivial topology. 
As an example, La$_2$CoO$_4$ is shown to host a non-$SO$-breaking phase with
topological characteristics, in addition to the fully $SO$-broken phase present
in La$_2$NiO$_4$. 
This distinction has significant implications for the interplay between
electronic interactions and the topological properties of these materials. 
This research paves the way for the systematic exploration of more complex
Transition Metal Oxides with multiple $SO$-breaking terms, opening up new
avenues for the discovery of non-trivial topological phases.

This study explores the relative $I$-functions for toric complete intersections with non-essential singularities, building on a previous work that extended the relative $I$-functions to this broader context. A key observation is made regarding the relationships among the relative $I$-functions, with a specific focus on varieties where smooth components intersect. Furthermore, this understanding leads to relationships among the $\mathcal{L}$-functions in this setting. In addition, this study investigates the properties and relationships of the relative $I$-functions when the variety is defined by intersecting a smooth hypersurface within a complete intersection. This study also provides examples and calculations to illustrate these theoretical findings. Moreover, it is demonstrated that the relative $I$-function can be expressed as a product of local $\mathcal{L}$-functions for this type of variety, with implications for the nonabelian zeta functions in the setting of complete intersections. Finally, this study considers the case of abelian varieties defined by multiple linear subspaces, establishing relationships among the relative $I$-functions and demonstrating their connection to the nonabelian zeta functions. This study ultimately aims to lay a theoretical foundation for a more comprehensive analysis of the nonabelian zeta functions in this context. In particular, it paves the way for computing the values of these zeta functions at critical points, with a focus on cases where the variety has a non-trivial first homology group. In the process, this study also identifies new families of hyperelliptic curves with large genus. In the context of abelian surfaces, this study finds several families with computable zeta functions, enabling the derivation of disk and tube zeta functions, as well as the abelian category zeta function. In addition, this study presents an analytical approach to approximating the zeta functions of these families as a continuous function of the complex structure parameters, with a focus on identifying the singularities and their resonance points. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) have emerged as versatile tools for creating realistic medical images, but their primary shortcoming lies in the lack of controllability over generated images, which hinders applications in a clinical setting. To overcome this limitation, we propose a method to control GAN-generated images by modifying latent codes, which can be achieved through a complementary neural network (ComNNet). This ComNNet is trained in an unsupervised manner using a cycle-consistency loss function, which enables it to accurately modify latent codes and produce desired images from modified codes. By iteratively applying the cycle-consistency loss function, we can effectively train the ComNNet even with a limited number of training samples. Our proposed method demonstrates superior performance in both unmodulated and modulated image generation compared to the original GAN. To validate our approach, we conducted quantitative and qualitative evaluations of a 3D cerebral vasculature GAN on a relatively small dataset of 100 MRI images, which yielded promising results. The code for this research has been made publicly accessible.

Advanced data visualization is crucial in the effective analysis of complex, high-dimensional data. To facilitate this, the ViDaExpert platform provides an intuitive interface that allows users to interactively explore and visualize their data across multiple dimensions. This tool supports a range of visualization techniques, including graphical plots, networks, trees, and maps, as well as the integration of up to three simultaneous 3D views. Additionally, ViDaExpert enables the integration of symbolic data by linking it to relevant data dimensions, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the data and enabling the identification of symbolic data associations. This integrated approach is demonstrated through a practical application in the field of biology. This research focuses on developing a higher-order, two-dimensional monomial identification method, tailored for polynomials with odd degrees, and applying it within the framework of a meshless method. We examine the impact of using a quadratic monomial representation instead of the conventional linear one on approximating functions and constructing a meshless method. High-order monomial identification enables increased accuracy in approximating complex functions over a given mesh element, while odd-degree monomial identification facilitates building a more stable and convergent approximation using an iterative method. We showcase the benefits of this approach by approximating a quadratic function with a linear one and demonstrate the superiority of the quadratic monomial representation in approximating diverse test functions, including the Kermack-McKendrick model. Furthermore, we successfully apply this approach to simulate the spread of infectious diseases, leveraging a monomial representation of high order to approximate a nonlinear integro-differential equation, and compare it with a standard Euler method as our method of control. All numerical simulations were performed using Python 3.9 and demonstrate the efficacy of this monomial identification strategy. To facilitate easy adoption, our monomial identification code is openly accessible on GitHub. The results indicate that, in tandem with an iterative method, a second-order monomial representation ensures precise approximations, attains $O(h^4)$ accuracy, and is computationally feasible even for large mesh elements. Consequently, this monomial-based approach offers an effective strategy for approximating diverse functions over a mesh element. Additionally, we explore the implications of using this approach to approximate an integro-differential equation by incorporating a nonlinear integro-operator with a high-order monomial representation, achieving $O(h^4)$ accuracy, and highlight its utility in modeling the spread of infectious diseases. The proposed method exhibits superior performance when compared to the standard Euler method and paves the way for further investigation of its applications in modeling real-world complex problems.
